A video purportedly showing Union Home Minister Amit Shah saying in the Lok Sabha that the government is more concerned about elections than the situation in Manipur is going viral on social media (here, here, and here). Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Union Home Minister Amit Shah saying in the Lok Sabha that the government is more concerned about elections than the situation in Manipur.
Fact: The video is from a Lok Sabha discussion on the Delhi Services Bill in August 2023. Amit Shah’s remarks about the government being more concerned about elections than Manipur were made sarcastically while criticising the opposition and accusing it of prioritising its political interests over democracy and the welfare of the nation. He was not expressing his own views or stating the BJP’s position. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to a video uploaded to Sansad TV’s YouTube channel on 03 August 2023. In this video, Amit Shah is seen wearing the same outfit and speaking against the same background as in the viral video. According to the description, Union Home Minister Amit Shah was responding to a discussion on the National Capital Territory of Delhi (Amendment) Bill, 2023, in the Lok Sabha. During the discussion, he also criticised the opposition.
At the 12:26-minute mark in the original video, Amit Shah can be heard making the same remarks as those in the viral clip. However, a careful viewing of the full video shows he wasn’t expressing his own views or explaining the BJP’s position. Instead, he was sarcastically quoting what he alleged to be the opposition’s priorities.
Amit Shah made these remarks to taunt the opposition. At the 12:28-minute mark, he says, “We’re not concerned about Manipur, we’re concerned about elections. We’re not concerned about democracy, we’re concerned about elections. Our party has no principles; we’re in politics solely to win elections.“
Before making these remarks, Shah was seen criticising the opposition over its response to the Manipur situation. In this context, he was accusing the opposition alliance of prioritising its political interests and the survival of its coalition over democracy and the welfare of the nation. Thus, the viral video omits the context in which he made these remarks, making it appear as though he was expressing his own views or stating the BJP’s position.
We also found multiple media reports (here, here) published in 2023, stating that the Delhi Services Bill was passed in the Lok Sabha on 03 August 2023. During the discussion, Home Minister Amit Shah launched a verbal attack on the opposition parties. The reports also stated that the bill was passed by a voice vote after opposition MPs staged a walkout.
To sum up, a video of Amit Shah criticising the opposition over Manipur is shared out of context as his own remarks on the BJP’s priorities.

Here's what you can do if your PC won't read an external hard drive
Bring a dead external drive back to life with these troubleshooting steps, including Disk Utility and swapping cables.
Finding the best portable SSD is almost a must in the modern tech landscape. Although you can get by with internal storage and cloud backup, an external drive makes it far easier to move media and document libraries between machines. It can also be a safeguard against worst-case scenarios by starting to use fail safes such as the 3-2-1 rule, which means keeping three copies of your data stored on two types of media with one copy kept in a safe location at home or away from the workplace.
As with any local storage, though, there's a possibility that a drive will suddenly stop working, or fail to run in the first place. If these things happen, don't panic, at least not yet. There may be troubleshooting steps you can take to get back on track.
A few of these should be relatively intuitive, like testing different hardware combinations. Less so are the ones that involve software, since they involve tools you're probably not using on a regular basis, unless perhaps you're an IT professional. Mercifully, if a software fix is possible, you probably won't have to spend any money.
How to troubleshoot your external hard drive
The first step is to rule out bad hardware that's not your drive. Try plugging it into another port, or swapping in another matching USB or Thunderbolt cable. Thunderbolt cables cover charging, data transfer and video, so it's always good practice to use the right cable and port. Remember also that all external drives require a power supply. Some USB ports on your computer might not have sufficient power, and of course if a drive has a jack for an AC adapter, you're not getting anywhere until that adapter is plugged in. Try plugging a drive into a second computer, if you have one.
Drives can however be detected by Windows or macOS but still fail to load, possibly because they haven't been formatted correctly. In Windows 11, open Device Manager by searching for it in the taskbar, then expand the Disk drives section. If your drive shows up, you may be able to bring it back by right-clicking on it, then selecting Properties > Volumes > Populate.
Next, click on Disk Management and look for the disk number you should've seen a moment ago. If there's no drive letter assigned, you may be able to assign one. But if the drive is missing NTFS formatting, you may have to reformat it if you want it to work with Windows. You'll lose any existing data on the disk, so treat this option as a last resort. Before reformatting, it's wiser to try Windows' CHKDSK utility. Open the Terminal app using taskbar search, then enter chkdsk [drive letter] /r. This will attempt to both fix errors and recover bad sectors.
On Macs, the catch-all software solution is typically Disk Utility. Once you've opened the app, select View > Show All Devices. If you see your drive, click on the indented entry and then select Mount at the top of the app. Should that not work, click First Aid instead. This may let you repair errors without losing data. If not, Disk Utility will let you reformat, once again at the cost of wiping a drive clean.
Other SSD rescue steps you can try
One simpler possibility is that you need to update your hardware drivers. This is dead simple on macOS, since Apple typically bundles these in with the latest OS updates. Just head to Apple menu > System Settings > General > Software Update to check. In Windows 11, swing by Settings > Windows Update to install anything there.
In some cases, though, Windows users may need to return to the right-click Properties menu for a drive in Device Manager. Once you're there, click on the Driver tab, then try updating or uninstalling. If you uninstall without selecting the driver deletion option, restarting your PC should automatically reinstall the correct software, which might repair it.
If you've gotten this far without luck, there may not be much you can do other than cross your fingers that a reboot will solve things or seek out third-party help, such as the drive manufacturer or a repair shop. You might need a recovery firm's help if valuable data is trapped. You can also try your Mac or PC's general OS recovery tools, but these are unlikely to fix anything we haven't already suggested.

The debut novel from iconic British comedian Bob Mortimer is being made into a TV show for Disney+.
The Satsuma Complex comes from Tip Toe producer Quay Street, which also made Disney+’s Stolen Girl.

New Delhi- Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Wednesday lauded the security forces for neutralising Lashkar-e-Taiba’s last known active local terrorist in the Kashmir valley in an operation marked by a “very high level of synergy”.
The security forces shot dead Lateef Bhat, who was wanted for the November 11 attack on a CRPF post, in an encounter in Kulgam district of south Kashmir earlier on Wednesday.
The terrorist had taken shelter inside a mosque in Zangalpora village in the Devsar area and refused to heed repeated appeals by senior officers of the Army and police to surrender, officials said.
“With the coordinated efforts of JKP, Indian Army, CRPF and intelligence agencies, Lashkar’s last known active local terrorist in the valley, Lateef Bhat, was neutralised in an operation in Kulgam in the early morning hours today,” Shah said in a post on X.
“One of his terrorist associates, Umar Nisar, was also neutralised in Kulgam, the day before. The entire operation was marked by a very high level of synergy,” Shah said.
“The nation salutes the brave Jawans of JKP, Army and CRPF and intelligence agencies,” he added.
According to the officials, Bhat and his associate Umar Nisar Dar were involved in the November 11 attack that left three CRPF personnel injured.
While Dar was killed in a gunfight in the Laru bypass area of Kulgam on Monday, Bhat had managed to give the security forces the slip.

Gujarat riots gang-rape survivor 'heartbroken' after bail for two convicts
- Published
The article has details that some readers may find disturbing
A pregnant Muslim woman who was gang-raped and saw 14 family members murdered during the 2002 Gujarat riots has spoken of her "pain, shock and disbelief" after two of her rapists were recently granted bail.
Bilkis Bano said in a statement that she heard about the top court order through press reports and vowed to fight back.
The freed men are from a group of 11 convicts - part of a Hindu mob - serving life terms for the attack on Bano.
All the men were also freed in 2022 after a Gujarat government order. That decision, and the celebrations as they left prison, caused global outrage. In 2024, the Supreme Court overturned the order.
In a short three-page order dated 28 October, the Supreme Court granted bail to Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya and suspended their sentences while their petition challenging a 2017 Bombay High Court order is being heard.
The judges explained that the early release was because the two convicts "have been under incarceration for a period of more than 17 years" and "that one of the appellants has a severe handicap".
On Tuesday, Bano's lawyer Shobha Gupta told the BBC that the news of Joshi and Modhiya's release had left "Bilkis heartbroken".
"She has to restart her battle for justice. She had no information that this case was coming up in the Supreme Court. What is troubling for us is that every time something like this happens, we worry that it could affect her faith in judiciary."
Gupta said it was difficult to understand why the convicts were being released because "it's not a routine criminal case, it's a case that shocks the conscience of the world, of entire humanity".
The attack on Bano and her family was one of the most horrific crimes during the Gujarat riots, which began after 60 Hindu pilgrims were killed in a fire on a passenger train in the town of Godhra.
Hindu mobs attacked Muslim neighbourhoods, blaming them for starting the fire. The riots continued for three days and more than 1,000 people died, most of them Muslims.
When rioters attacked Bano's village and started setting Muslim homes on fire, she and 16 relatives went on the run. She was 19, had a three-year-old daughter and was pregnant with her second child.
They were attacked on the morning of 3 March 2002 by a group of men "with swords and sticks", she'd told me in 2017. Her three-year-old daughter, she said, was snatched from her lap and killed.
Her attackers were her neighbours, men she had seen almost daily while growing up. They tore off her clothes and several of them raped her, ignoring her pleas for mercy.
Her cousin, who had given birth two days earlier, was raped and murdered and her newborn baby was killed too.
Bano survived only because she lost consciousness and her attackers left, believing she was dead. Two boys - seven and four - were the only other survivors of the massacre.
Her fight for justice has been long and nightmarish. The first arrests were made only in 2004 after the Supreme Court called in federal investigators and transferred her case to Mumbai, saying that courts in Gujarat could not deliver justice to her.
In her statement released on Monday night, Bano spoke of "fresh tears of pain, shock and disbelief".
"I still cannot believe that once again, for the second time, an order has been passed by the Supreme Court without calling me up and without hearing me," she said.
"For 24 long years, I have stood up to fight for justice... again and again. Yet today, I find myself losing the very justice I had fought so hard to win.... And I am scared of losing faith in justice, yet again."
Bano vowed to "fight this order... for my children, who do not deserve to live haunted by fears and scars for the rest of their lives".
"I do this for my three-year-old Saleha who deserved to live and whose memory demands justice. I do this for women everywhere. Because no woman, no survivor, no citizen should have to endure this eternal test of belonging and equality, and fight for justice for the rest of her life."
Prime Minister Narendra Modi was Gujarat chief minister at the time of the riots, and was criticised for not doing enough to prevent the carnage. He has always denied wrongdoing and has not apologised for the riots.
In 2013, a Supreme Court panel also said that there was insufficient evidence to prosecute him. But critics have continued to blame him for the riots happening on his watch.

Despite a lucrative ₹50-lakh annual salary, an MBA from IIM Bengaluru, and a thriving career with global automobile giants, 37-year-old Akshita Jain has chosen to walk away from the corporate world to embrace Jain asceticism.
According to an India Today report, Akshita is not embarking on this spiritual journey alone — her 61-year-old mother, Shiromani Bajaj, a retired chief manager at the Indian Oil Corporation (IOCL) — is also joining her.
The Gurugram-based duo is now preparing to leave behind their worldly possessions and family ties to become Jain sadhvis.
Akshita’s professional trajectory was firmly set on a high-achieving corporate track; armed with a management degree from IIM Bengaluru, she built her career working with major automotive brands, including Fiat, Mercedes-Benz, and Volkswagen.
In her most recent role at Volkswagen, she reportedly earned an annual compensation package of ₹50 lakh.
According to the publication, the turning point of her spiritual transition came while she was working on artificial intelligence (AI) initiatives at her company. She grew increasingly concerned about the environmental footprint of building massive data centres—specifically the land excavation required and the resulting harm to microscopic soil organisms.
This realisation, she said, aligned deeply with the core Jain principle of ahimsa (non-violence towards all living beings), ultimately prompting her decision to pursue a life of renunciation.
For her mother, Shiromani, the decision marks the culmination of a lifetime of familial and professional duties. She spent 37 years at IOCL before retiring as a chief manager in October 2025.
Following her husband's passing and after fulfilling her household responsibilities, Shiromani found herself increasingly drawn to Jain spirituality through her close association with Jain sadhvis.
She has reportedly completed several religious observances and rigorous austerities to prepare for this transition.
The mother-daughter duo has been receiving guidance from Jain spiritual teacher Sadhvi Purnapragyashree, India Today reported.
As part of their initiation, a traditional Jain procession—known as a varghoda—was scheduled to take place in Jodhpur, setting the stage for their formal diksha ceremony in Chennai on February 25.
The ceremony marks one of the most significant transitions in Jainism, wherein an individual formally renounces all worldly attachments, relationships, and material wealth to walk the path of an ascetic.

Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all.
The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user’s knowledge.
It’s “worse than a bug”
Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent’s reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.”
The NewCore employees sent the gateway logs to Grok Bot support personnel and asked what was causing the bots to access accounts without prompting or approval. The support team’s reply indicated the behavior was by design and intended to allow the bots to proactively take actions on behalf of users. In other words, the unrequested and unlogged access attempts were a feature designed to make Grok Bot more useful by periodically checking in and finding tasks to perform before a user even asks. The proactive check-in is a feature of Cursor, the AI coding service SpaceXSI recently acquired.

In November, a video circulated online that some social media users claimed authentically showed a pterodactyl flying over Ciudad Juárez, Mexico.
The clip appeared to show a large creature with pointed wings and a long beak flying above a residential neighborhood.
One Instagram account that shared the video wrote (archived):
Some Mexican citizens claim to have captured a pterodactyl flying through the night sky over Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, Mexico. Videos circulating online show a large, dark, winged silhouette that has sparked speculation about the possible sighting of a prehistoric creature. Some have pointed out its unusual shape, while skeptics believe it could be a large bird or digitally altered footage. Pterosaurs have been extinct for approximately 66 million years, but that hasn't stopped the speculation online.
The video also circulated on Facebook and Threads (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us asking about the video.
The video featured in the Instagram post above is fake, meaning it was generated by or edited using artificial intelligence. This was clear because letters on a building shifted and changed at the start of the clip, at times not resembling letters at all. Garbled or gibberish text is a telltale sign that someone used AI to create an image or video.
For example, letters on a building spelling "Jalpan de" are totally illegible shapes at the start of the video but shifted into legible text within a second. This is inconsistent with how printed text behaves in authentic videos.
(@daniela230997, accessed via TikTok)
Aside from the indications of fakery in the video itself, it is simply a fact that pterodactyls have been extinct for more than 60 million years. While researchers have found fossils of pterodactyls and therefore know a lot about what they looked like, no evidence exists that the prehistoric genus somehow survived into the 21st century
The source of the fake clip was unclear. We found versions of the clip claiming it was recorded on both Nov. 14 and 15 (archived, archived).
As we lay out below, people have circulated other videos purporting to show a pterodactyl-like creature in Mexico. Our assessment of the video above as an AI-generated fake is specific to that individual clip.
For example, the Mexican journalist Jaime Maussan, who reports on UFOs, supernatural phenomena and urban myths, shared three clips, starting on Nov. 5, that claimed to show a flying pterodactyl caught on camera near Ciudad Juárez, the same place social media users claimed the fake clip was recorded. It's unclear whether Maussan's reporting may have inspired the creation of the fake clip.
Snopes has previously reported on Maussan's work after he unveiled a mummified body found in Nazca, Peru, in 2015 — purportedly that of an extraterrestrial. That body turned out to be the corpse of a human child. Maussan featured in another Snopes report in 2023, when he appeared before the Mexican Congress claiming to have uncovered two thousand-year-old alien corpses.
Videos on Maussan's YouTube channel posted on or around Nov. 5, 6 and 10, shortly before the fake video circulated, claimed that he had unearthed video proof that bystanders had spotted a pterodactyl in the skies over Ciudad Juárez.
Maussan's researcher interviewed two people who claimed to have recorded videos of the flying reptile. One of them, a man named Miguel Rojas, who reportedly recorded the pterodactyl in the San Antonio neighborhood of Ciudad Juárez in 2024, appeared in Maussan's Nov. 5 video.
Another alleged witness, a boy named Fernando Arteaga who recorded a clip of the alleged pterodactyl on Nov. 7, reportedly told Maussan's researcher the reptile attempted to attack a dog and carry it away but released the animal before flying off. This reported encounter was not part of the video Maussan shared.
Sergio Rodríguez, the head of the Civil Protection in Ciudad Juárez, reportedly told local media that Maussan's videos were "solely for digital entertainment and lack any real basis." He reportedly said that if the videos and the creature seen in them were real, there would be an investigation by Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History, which was not the case.
Snopes contacted Rodríguez to verify the authenticity of the quote reported in local media and Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History for its assessment of the authenticity of Maussan's videos and await replies to our queries.
For further reading, Snopes has previously reported on claims related to dinosaurs and fake videos or images.

First Her Daughter, Now Her Grandson: A Family’s Hospital Nightmare
As the Ebola virus spreads in eastern Congo, health teams struggle to curb fatal delays in seeking medical care and the widespread desire to treat sick relatives at home.
Gorette Mbusi stood on her doorstep and wrestled with a question. Should she let her grandson be taken to the hospital?
Health workers had come to her village, in the eastern part of the Democratic Republic of Congo, to implore her to let them take the young man to a specialized Ebola facility in the nearby town of Nizi. But she was wary. She had already lost two family members, including her daughter, who had been transported to the hospital and then died.
Now, her grandson was sick.
“I don’t know where this sickness is coming from that is killing my family,” she said. “I feel abandoned.”
Ms. Mbusi’s dilemma reflects a central challenge for health workers as they struggle to contain the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record — how to stop people from passing the disease to loved ones at home.
Community transmission happens when family members care for Ebola patients at home and then become ill themselves, spreading the disease and making it more difficult for medical teams to identify and isolate people who have been in contact with those infected. Tracking and tracing the contacts of Ebola patients and educating people about the virus are crucial to ending community transmission.
Health workers must first get more people to seek medical treatment in hospitals sooner and overcome deep suspicions about Ebola in villages like this one, known as Nizi 4.

Palmer Luckey wants to make American industry great again — by taking it out to sea.
In a Tuesday X post, the Anduril cofounder shared his vision for a seastead called "SLAB" off the US coast, upon which critical industries could thrive, unencumbered by local laws.
Luckey said his plan for the seastead was to make it cheaper than land in the US and free of the restrictions that "cripple critical American industries," such as oil refining, chemical engineering, and medical research. He did not specify what laws or regulations he was trying to sidestep.
He added that a facility of this kind would "make America stronger," and act as a "relief valve for ill-considered or outdated rules and regulations."
Selling Oculus to Facebook in 2014 gave me money for helicopter flight lessons and developing a seastead called SLAB with a 1,000 year design life.
The goal was to be cheaper than land and absent state/local laws that cripple critical American industries like metal processing,… pic.twitter.com/aJkd0eOgLF
— Palmer Luckey (@PalmerLuckey) November 18, 2026
Luckey attached what appeared to be an AI-generated image of "SLAB" to the X post, which depicted a massive concrete slab rising above the ocean's waves, with factories and corporate offices built atop it.
He said he was only revealing the plan now because media outlets had gotten wind of the project and started calling it his "new floating AI data center project."
"It is way cooler than that, way older than that, and I hate looking like a hype-chasing consensus loser, so now you have to read this tweet," Luckey wrote.
He said that it would be funded by the money he made from selling Oculus — his virtual reality tech brand — to Facebook in 2014. Facebook bought Oculus for $2 billion. He said that some other unnamed "close friends" injected capital into the project at a $1 billion valuation.
Luckey, the founder of defense tech startup Anduril, has frequently pitched himself as a disruptor of old systems that have caused American industry to wane, and often speaks of aiming to help the US strengthen its dominance in the military and tech sectors.
Anduril specializes in software, drones, scalable weapons, and high-tech combat gear, clinching tens of billions of dollars in contracts across multiple US military branches and allies. It was valued at around $61 billion during a $5 billion funding round in May.
A seastead business would add to Luckey's growing list of projects apart from Anduril. The billionaire has also founded a retro-gaming hardware firm, ModRetro, a digital bank called Erebor, and recently announced a working dog-breeding and cloning firm named Warhound.
Luckey is not the first billionaire who has thought of regulation-free seasteads. In 2008, billionaire venture capitalist Peter Thiel invested $1.7 million in The Seasteading Institute, which aimed to host "startup communities that float on the ocean with any measure of political autonomy," according to the organization's website.
Thiel later resigned from its board around 10 years later, and said that the plan was not feasible.

Srinagar- Jammu and Kashmir is likely to experience an extended dry spell over the next 10 to 15 days, with largely dry weather conditions potentially continuing until December 5, according to a weather update shared by Kashmir Weather on X.
The prolonged absence of precipitation could lead to a gradual decline in water levels in rivers, streams and other water bodies across the Union Territory, the update said.
The Jhelum and several of its tributaries are likely to witness a gradual fall in water levels over the coming days, while smaller streams and water channels with already low discharge could face a more difficult situation.
Some smaller streams may even dry up if the precipitation deficit continues to increase, it said.
The update cautioned that the situation could become more concerning if the dry spell extends beyond the initially anticipated 10 to 15 days.
A prolonged absence of rainfall and snowfall could further reduce river discharge, affect smaller water sources and increase the possibility of drinking water shortages in vulnerable areas, particularly those dependent on springs and smaller streams.
The impact could also be felt in the power sector, as declining river discharge may affect hydropower generation, particularly at projects dependent on adequate natural water inflows.
The weather update suggested that the administration and concerned departments should take precautionary measures in advance, including identifying vulnerable areas, monitoring river and stream discharge and preparing contingency plans to ensure adequate drinking water supplies.
People have also been advised to use water responsibly and avoid unnecessary wastage during the extended dry period.
While the anticipated dry spell may not trigger an immediate water crisis, its continuation into December could aggravate the situation, the update said.
It stressed the need for advance preparedness and responsible water consumption to minimise the impact of any possible shortage.

In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard.
Both movements burst into international public view last month as they became central during election campaigns to the pushback against authoritarianism. What they also offered, however, was a window into a wider phenomenon playing out across the globe, as youth-led movements reshape political landscapes.
“Gen Z is rising,” said Erica Chenoweth, a political scientist at Harvard Kennedy School. “It is abundantly clear that a significant proportion of gen Z is tired of sitting on the sidelines while their political systems fail them.”
Researchers have documented at least 25 protests around the world in which this age group – roughly those between the ages of 14 and 29 – has played a role.
From Bangladesh to Belgium and Italy to India, it seems gen Z, who account for about a third of the world’s population, have found their voice. “Gen Z may be experiencing a global political awakening,” Chenoweth wrote in a recent essay.
Their reasons for taking to the streets have varied widely, from protesting against corruption and an unequal playing field to calling for more investment in education, affordable housing and action on the climate crisis.
Many of the first protests to make waves were in Asia and Africa. In 2024, students in Dhaka, Bangladesh, made global headlines after they pulled off what was described as the world’s first successful gen Z-led revolution.
The protests began over a quota law but swiftly snowballed into a wider show of discontent against the increasingly autocratic rule of the prime minister, Sheikh Hasina. Two months later, Hasina resigned and fled the country by helicopter after being, as the Associated Press reported, “chased out by young protesters”.
Two years later and 4,000 miles away, students were at the helm of another revolution in Serbia, pushing back against a government that had steadily tightened its grip on the media and stuffed institutions with party loyalists.
Late last month, Serbia’s students’ movement was catapulted from the streets to the halls of power as they ousted Aleksandar Vučić in elections, bringing an end to his party’s 14 years in power.
Students and young people have long been at the forefront of the push for change, the analysts Cait Dallaire and Sebastian Dittgen wrote recently, citing the US civil rights movement and the 2011 Arab spring.
“What is unique about the current movement is the infrastructure of mobilisation: TikTok and X amplify and accelerate grievances; Discord servers and group chats enable decentralised planning; virtual private networks and mirrored content help organisers circumvent internet shutdowns,” they said.
It was this potent combination – young people in the streets and social media – that helped drive Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s comeback to win Brazil’s presidential election last month. After a bruising loss in the first round to the rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, there was dismay in the country’s political left.
That was until students from the Fluminense Federal University mobilised in a pro-Lula march, setting off a wave of similar actions across the country. Soon after, the congressman and Lula ally André Janones, 42, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” that attracted millions of people looking to help boost pro-Lula content on social media.
On the night of his victory, Lula recognised their power. “I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” he said.
Some politicians have sought to engage gen Z from the start. In the US, Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for New York mayor combined a canny use of social media with a legion of about 50,000 volunteers that had young people at its heart. The New York Times wrote that “volunteering for Mr Mamdani’s campaign became a salve” for young New Yorkers as the campaign became not just about “mobilising, but socialising”.
It was a nod to the global context in which many gen Zers have come of age; one riven by conflicts such as the Israel-Gaza war, the escalating climate crisis and the rise of nationalism, while the rules that have shaped the international order since the second world war are fraying.
In recent weeks, youth-led protests have begun to sweep Europe, from school students in France demanding better conditions in which to work to those in Spain who pitched tents to rally for affordable housing. In Germany, thousands of people took to the streets to protest against the cost of living and call for more investment in education, health and climate action in a movement organised by a group calling itself Gen Z regelt!, or Gen Z will sort this.
Analysts have been swift to point to the link between the protests. “The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs, told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “In Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”
A similar note of disillusionment threads through India’s Cockroach movement, which began as an online satire and has since swelled into a show of force against the strongman government of Narendra Modi. Fuelled by social media and rooted in democratic ideals, the power of the movement was laid bare this summer after Cockroach-led protests forced the resignation of the country’s education minister.
Equally visible is the pushback by India’s security forces against the movement, detaining thousands, unleashing teargas and beating people with lathis, or wooden clubs. Authorities went to extreme lengths in October to keep them from gathering in central Delhi, barricading roads and shutting down the internet and public transport.
It was a window into another facet that has defined youth-led protests, as research suggests they tend to be met with higher levels of repression, despite the fact that they are no more likely to use violence than others.
In France, lawyers and rights groups say several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons. After the 2024 protests in Bangladesh, UN human rights experts said as many as 1,400 people had been killed, mostly by security forces, while thousands more suffered severe, often life-altering injuries.
In a recent analysis, Civicus, a non-profit that monitors global civic freedoms, said: “Because they question the distribution of economic and political power, gen Z-led protests have invariably been met with state violence,” linking the violence meted out to young protesters with their focus on systems and institutions that have long been generally accepted.
In Morocco, more than 2,000 people were charged and many received harsh prison sentences after a 2025 movement known as Gen Z 212 targeted officials over corruption, neglected public services and the lack of opportunities. Weeks later, in Mexico, youth-led protests over corruption and crime led to clashes with police in which dozens of people were arrested.
The outcomes of both of these movements show the varying success of gen Z protests. But at times, the foundations laid in one protest have given rise to others. In the US, much of today’s youth organising was shaped by the pro-Palestine student movement, in which there were thousands of arrests, expulsions and suspensions. Many schools instated anti-protest policies amid a broader rollback of educational freedom on campus.
Students, however, have continued to push for change. Last month hundreds in North Carolina marched in the heat to the polls after their historically Black university was denied a polling site, while thousands across the country have responded to the Cornell 7 case by skipping class, protesting and launching occupations.
As Chenoweth of the Harvard Kennedy School noted, the wave of recent youth-led protests may mark the beginning of a “profound generational transformation in world affairs” – one that could be capable of countering the global trend of democratic backsliding.
Ultimately, however, as Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris recently told the Associated Press, the explosion of youth movements across Europe hints at a wider truth that has long been overlooked across the globe.
“We all agree on one point,” he said. “That young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”

Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.
Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.
In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.
Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.
The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.
The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.
Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.
The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”
Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.
The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”
Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.
“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.
Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.
Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

(Bloomberg) -- The National Security Agency is suffering an outage of a classified computer network it uses for internal communications and other daily work functions, according to a US official and another person familiar with the matter.
The network, known as NSA Net, has been down since at least early Tuesday morning, said the person, who spoke on the condition that they not be identified because they were not authorized to discuss the matter. Some staff of the electronic spying agency have been unable to access their workplace systems, the person said, and the issue led the NSA to tell some staff to delay their arrival at the agency’s headquarters in Fort Meade, Maryland, the person said.
The US official said the outage occurred during scheduled routine maintenance and that the agency was still able to conduct its mission critical functions. The official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss agency operations, said the NSA systems have multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.
Quick answers to key questions
NSA Net is a classified computer network the National Security Agency uses for internal communications and daily work functions.
A U.S. official said the outage occurred during scheduled routine maintenance. The article does not identify a more specific technical cause.
Some staff could not access workplace systems, and some were told to delay arriving at the NSA headquarters at Fort Meade.
No. A U.S. official said the NSA remained able to conduct its mission-critical functions, supported by multiple layers of system redundancy.
The NSA didn’t immediately respond to emails seeking comment. The outage was earlier reported by CNN.
A series of technology failures have brought down critical systems that disrupted operations around the world in recent weeks.
A technical glitch at JPMorgan Chase & Co. on Monday caused some customers’ transactions to take longer to process. The issue wasn’t related to a cybersecurity event, the bank said, but tied to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems. United Airlines also said on Monday a technology issue impacted its departing flights, and that the problem was traced to equipment problems involving the agency’s aging communications infrastructure.
Microsoft Corp.’s productivity software was hobbled for roughly 24 hours last week after a bug caused a system malfunction during an otherwise routine rerouting of user traffic on Nov. 11. In yet another issue, US air traffic was snarled over the weekend after a problem arose when a government contractor was trying to replace outdated copper wire at a remote location in Arkansas.
US Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told CNBC before the NSA issue was reported that the recent technology failures weren’t the result of a cyberattack.

Gambler who lost over $200K says apps ignored signs of addiction, sent him hockey tickets, bonus cash
Ontario requires gambling companies to monitor, intervene when users show signs of harm
This story is part of a CBC News series examining the public health impacts of online gambling.
When his addiction to online video slot machines spiralled in 2025, Joseph, a legal professional from Vaughan, Ont., says he repeatedly contacted the betting companies in a panic.
He’d been gambling online late at night, depositing tens of thousands a week and chasing his losses — eventually winding up in a $200,000 hole.
These behaviours are key indicators for problem gambling as set out by Ontario’s iGaming standards, which require companies to "intervene and provide supports for all players who may be at risk of experiencing harm."
But CBC News has learned that as Joseph's losses mounted, the companies continued to send him promotional offers, bonuses, free cash and even tickets to NHL hockey games.
"They had a number of warnings that I was a high-risk gambler, and they ignored that," Joseph told CBC News.
CBC News has agreed not to name him as he fears repercussions at work and in future jobs.
His story is one of several cases uncovered by CBC News of high-risk players who say private online gambling sites failed to step in to protect them, including three cases that resulted in fines against PointsBet, Apollo and theScore.
Offers of Leafs tickets, cash
Joseph’s gambling started in 2023 as casual entertainment.
But by 2024, he says it got out of control and he voluntarily registered to "self-exclude" from the Betano betting app in order to block his access.
The company still sent him multiple promotions, which he says caused him to relapse.
Betano sent these gambling messages to a 'self-excluded' player, contrary to Ontario standards. (Submitted by Joseph)
The company apologized in April 2025 and told him the marketing materials were sent inadvertently "due to a technical error," according to an email reviewed by CBC News.
Joseph was also a frequent gambler on the Bally Bet app, which similarly sent out a large number of promotions by email.
As his troubles with gambling escalated, he asked Bally Bet on four different occasions to pause his account, registering each time for a three-month "cooling-off period."
Every time those periods expired, his account was reinstated and he’d get an email telling him he’d have to re-register for "cooling off."
He was automatically signed up to receive the promotional emails again.
His phone would soon light up with repeated offers of bonus cash inviting him to resume betting.
Bally Bet sent repeated bonuses and VIP offers after Joseph's three-month 'cooling-off' period expired. (Submitted by Joseph)
And gamble he did. Between June and October of last year, he made dozens of deposits and racked up tens of thousands of dollars in losses.
In September, Joseph contacted Bally Bet customer support by phone and email to complain about the games’ odds, their upbeat advertising and his own mounting losses, threatening to close his account.
"I shared my frustrations with them. I shared how much I've lost. I said, 'You know, that's it. I'm done with Bally Bet.'"
He argues that given his multiple cooling-off periods, his frequent deposits of thousands of dollars and his clear financial distress, the company should have intervened.
Under Ontario’s iGaming standards, operators are required to screen customers for binge gambling and intervene at signs of financial or emotional distress.
Instead of offering support or closing his account, Bally Bet offered him VIP perks.
"They're like, ‘No, please give us another chance. Actually, we're introducing a VIP program, and you're one of the VIP folks,’" he said.
Bally Bet offered him numerous free tickets and thousands in bonus cash, according to the emails reviewed by CBC.
"I truly appreciate your loyalty and understand your frustration," wrote one Bally Bet representative. "I hope this provides an opportunity to experience the platform differently and enjoy the games with a little extra boost."
"I have some good news. I was able to secure 4 tickets for you and the family to see the Toronto Maple Leafs take on the Boston Bruins for Saturday November 8th!"
Bally Bet sent repeated bonus incentives as Joseph’s losses approached $230,000. (Submitted by Joseph)
"Just added some Bally Bucks to your account. Our secret. Happy Halloween," wrote another agent.
By early November 2025, Joseph’s losses were approaching a quarter of a million dollars.
"You need to hit rock bottom in order for you to realize, right?" he told CBC News.
Joseph emailed Bally Bet and demanded they close his account immediately.
Unsure whether it was closed, in a panic he also signed up to "self-exclude" from the app.
He says he continued to receive bonus offers for two days, and waited four days before the company finally confirmed his account was shut down.
"I was told, via the app, that I had to email them and it could take up to five days for the account closure to take effect," he said. "If someone has that final wake-up call and immediately goes in to want to close the account, it should be instantaneous, not where you're waiting."
Joseph is suing both Bally Bet and Betano, alleging the companies sent him special offers after he showed signs of gambling-related harm and tried to cut ties.
He’s seeking $50,000 in damages from Bally Bet and $25,000 from Betano, alleging their promotional material led him to relapse. His allegations have not been tested in court.
You need to hit rock bottom in order for you to realize, right?Joseph
Bally Bet and Betano declined CBC’s requests for an interview and wouldn’t comment on the lawsuits.
In documents filed in Ontario’s Superior Court of Justice, both companies contend they investigated Joseph's complaints and deny his allegations.
"We remain committed to responsible gaming and the protection of our players and we are continuously working on evolving our approach, tools and practices," a spokesperson for Betano and its parent company, Kaizen Gaming, told CBC News in an email.
Reuben Rothstein, a lawyer for Bally Bet, told CBC News via email that the company remains committed to providing a safe and responsible gambling experience for its users.
"We take our responsibility to our players seriously and work closely with our regulatory partners to ensure responsible gaming principles and safeguards are reflected throughout our products and offerings," Rothstein said.
Ontario fines gambling companies
Joseph also took his complaints to Ontario’s gaming regulator, the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario (AGCO), which investigated. To date, the AGCO has not publicly disclosed its findings.
Ontario has fined three different online betting sites for failing to intervene with problem gamblers.
Apollo Entertainment agreed to pay $65,000 for failing to step in or have proper self-exclusion programs in place in 2023 after a player lost more than $2 million over four months.
PointsBet was fined $150,000 for failing to stop a player who lost more than half a million dollars in less than three months, according to an AGCO news release, even though the gambler was "repeatedly flagged as a potentially high risk by the operator’s systems."
Ontario has fined three different online betting sites for failing to intervene with problem gamblers, including PointsBet, theScore and Apollo Entertainment. (Dave Seglins/CBC)
TheScore agreed to pay a $70,000 penalty last fall after AGCO concluded the company failed to protect a player who lost $230,000 over eight months — nearly $100,000 in the first month of play.
That’s despite "multiple missed opportunities to intervene, including escalating losses, repeated bonus requests, loss-chasing behaviour, expressions of distress to the operator's VIP host," the AGCO said in a release.
The AGCO won’t say whether it was player complaints that sparked those investigations, or whether the regulator can detect companies' failures on its own.
It also won’t explicitly define the threshold at which companies must step in to protect players.
Joseph accepts responsibility for his decision to gamble in the first place, but says gambling operators have responsibilities, too.
"I made the attempts to stop, with the self-exclusions [and] by calling them," he said.
"I feel as though they took advantage."

Is India rethinking its short-term military recruitment scheme?
- Published
For generations of young Indians, joining the armed forces offered something few other jobs did - a steady career, financial security, the promise of a pension after retirement and the pride of serving their country.
In 2022, the government upended that arrangement, announcing a new reform scheme under which young men and women entering the military would serve for just four years. Only a quarter would be allowed to stay on permanently. The rest would return to civilian life with a lump-sum payment, but without the pension and other benefits that had long made military service an attractive career.
Now, as the first batch of recruits prepares to complete its four-year term, the government is offering them a chance to stay longer, in a significant shift in a policy that has been fiercely debated since its introduction.
On 4 November, Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani announced that recruits who failed to secure permanent positions under the Agnipath, or "path of fire", programme would be offered another two years of service at higher pay. They would then get a second opportunity to join the regular forces, provided they met the selection criteria.
Gen Subramani said the decision followed feedback from the forces and insisted that Agnipath would continue.
But the timing is significant. More than 18,300 recruits from the first batch are due to complete their initial tenure by the end of 2026. Officials say the new arrangement will be offered to more than 300,000 Agniveers - as recruits under the scheme are known - currently serving across the army, navy and air force.
Whether future batches will also be covered remains unclear. The BBC has contacted the defence ministry for clarification.
The ministry has defended , externalAgnipath, saying internal assessments found the recruits to be physically fit, motivated and technologically adaptable. It also said the scheme had widened recruitment across districts and made the process more standardised.
But the extension has brought renewed attention to the trade-offs at the heart of the policy - and whether its original ambitions were realistic.
When the government introduced Agnipath, it argued the scheme would reduce the average age of the armed forces, lower long-term salary and pension costs and create a younger, more technologically adaptable fighting force.
But military experts and opposition leaders have questioned whether a four-year contract could replace what had traditionally been a coveted, long-term career in the armed forces.
"Being a soldier in the armed forces was a chance for these young men to make a life for themselves, to get their families out of poor or lower-middle-income conditions," says retired Maj Gen Yash Mor, a vocal critic of the scheme.
These concerns were also amplified by the timing of Agnipath's launch. Recruitment had been suspended for nearly two years during the Covid pandemic, leaving thousands of aspirants waiting for vacancies to reopen.
The changes were greeted by massive protests across the country, with many saying the career path they had spent years preparing for had fundamentally changed.
This sentiment was felt most in states and cities that have traditionally been major recruitment hubs, where military service has been a family tradition for generations.
Kulbeer Singh Chaudhary, who runs a recruitment training institute in Dehradun city, says interest in joining the armed forces fell sharply and he stopped conducting Agniveer training batches.
The latest announcement, he hopes, would reverse that trend.
"The possibility of a longer engagement and eventual absorption into the forces may offer young candidates greater assurance," he says.
The changes also come at a time when the armed forces are facing personnel shortages. In November last year, The Indian Express reported, external that the army alone faced a shortfall of nearly 180,000 soldiers and was considering increasing recruitment.
But the debate over Agnipath goes beyond what happens to recruits after four years. Critics also question whether that is enough time to turn them into experienced soldiers.
Sanjiv Krishan Sood, a former additional director general of the Border Security Force, has argued, external that the shorter training period is particularly problematic for technical roles requiring specialised skills.
Retired Maj Gen Mor says military effectiveness depends on experience and trust built over years.
"It takes eight-to-nine years to turn a raw recruit into a dependable, seasoned soldier - someone capable of handling a tank crew, an artillery gun crew or a small detachment," he says.
"Over those years, a soldier develops the ethos, camaraderie, brotherhood and fighting spirit that bind a unit together. These qualities cannot be built overnight."
Sood says the additional two years could help improve recruits' skills, particularly in handling specialised equipment.
Senior military leaders have also welcomed the extension. Air Vice Marshal Shekhar Yadav told news agency ANI, external it would allow the forces to retain trained personnel for longer.
But the change could create fresh challenges within military units.
Regular soldiers, Agniveers on four-year contracts and those serving an additional two years could find themselves working alongside one another despite differences in pay, promotion prospects and post-service benefits.
Experts warn that these disparities could affect unit cohesion.
There is also the question of whether the changes will undermine one of the government's central objectives: reducing spending. Almost half of India's defence budget, external goes towards salaries and pensions, leaving less money for modernisation and new equipment.
By limiting the number of personnel eligible for long-term benefits, Agnipath was expected to ease that burden. But critics argue that savings should not come at the expense of military effectiveness.
"We are not against making changes, but there are ways and means to go about it," says Mor, adding that the government could instead reduce annual recruitment while retaining soldiers for longer periods.
He also points to India's tense borders with Pakistan and China, where troops remain deployed year-round, placing sustained demands on manpower and operational experience.
Retired Major-General Birender Singh Dhanoa, meanwhile, questions whether shorter service makes financial sense when the military is investing in training to operate increasingly sophisticated equipment.
"The amount of time it takes to train, and the financial outlay for training, is much higher for modern equipment. So shouldn't you get the best bang for your buck?" he asks.
Many retired officers had proposed a different approach when the scheme was announced, he says.
"We suggested that if you want to reduce your financial burden, you increase the terms and conditions of service. Take these guys for eight-or-nine years and retain a larger number after that."
The announcement also comes at a politically sensitive time. Elections are due soon in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand - states that have traditionally supplied large numbers of soldiers and where military recruitment remains an important source of employment.
The opposition Congress party has called the revision a "u-turn", alleging that the government is responding to fears of losing votes.
For young recruits approaching the end of their contracts, the changes offer some reassurance, but few guarantees. Two more years of service could mean more money, greater experience and another chance at a permanent career.
But for many, it also means putting their futures on hold, without knowing whether they will eventually be allowed to stay.

Rosemary Nyirumbe became a nun when she was just in her mid-teens – and she felt her true vocation lay in rehabilitating children who had been through some of the worst trauma imaginable. So that’s what she did. In this episode Mike Wooldridge hears Sr Rosemary’s astonishing story. The feared rebel group, the Lord’s Resistance Army, started to terrorise the north of Uganda in the 1980s. Many children, girls as well as boys, were abducted and forced to become child soldiers. In many cases, the LRA forced them to commit atrocities, leaving them deeply traumatised. Many of the girls also bore the children of rebel leaders. As they started to return home, these children were often rejected by their families and communities, says Sr Rosemary. So she set about giving them a future and a hope: through enabling them to acquire skills like sewing, and by helping them see that God had not rejected them for the atrocities they had been forced to commit. More than once, Sr Rosemary put herself in enormous danger in order to fulfil her mission. But, she says, she also learnt that small acts of kindness can touch the hearts of even battle-hardened rebels.

A 10-year-old with a rare inflammatory blood vessel disease underwent surgery at SIMS Hospital, Chennai, to repair a large aneurysm of the aortic arch, the hospital said on Tuesday (November 17, 2026).
The patient was diagnosed with aortoarteritis, also known as Takayasu arteritis, a condition that causes inflammation and narrowing or enlargement of blood vessels. The aneurysm had enlarged significantly, causing breathing difficulty, palpitations, and difficulty lying down. The risk of rupture made urgent surgery necessary. The patient weighed about 18 kg, adding to the technical challenges of the operation. As the aneurysm was located close to the breastbone, opening the chest through the usual approach carried a risk of injuring the enlarged aorta. The surgical team first connected the patient to a heart-lung machine through blood vessels in the groin.
The patient’s body was cooled to 16°C using a technique known as deep hypothermic circulatory arrest. Blood circulation was then temporarily stopped for about 40 minutes, enabling surgeons to remove the affected section of the aorta and replace it with a Dacron graft. Lowering the body temperature reduces metabolic activity and the organs’ oxygen requirements, helping protect them during the period when blood flow is interrupted.
The patient was subsequently rewarmed, restoring his blood circulation. Post-operative assessments showed no damage to the brain, kidneys, intestines, or spinal cord, the hospital said. The patient has resumed normal activities without breathing difficulty but will require continued medication and monitoring to control the underlying inflammation and prevent further aneurysms.
The surgery was performed by a team led by Bashi V. Velayudhan, director and senior consultant, cardiothoracic surgery, along with Mohammed Idhrees, senior consultant, cardiothoracic surgery, and a team of anaesthesiologists and other specialists.

A new generation of disability rights activists carry on Judy Heumann's legacy
Judy Heumann is known as the mother of the disability rights movement — yet she is lesser known than many of the other civil rights activists of her time. Now, a new film seeks to change that.
Being Heumann, the latest movie from Oscar-winning director Sian Heder, tells the story of the young woman from Brooklyn who led the movement to win the first civil rights protections in the country for people with disabilities.
Before the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) was passed in 1990, there was Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973. It was a single sentence, written into the law, promising people with disabilities the right to fair employment and access to public life without facing discrimination.
But for years, there were no rules or regulations making the federal government actually enforce those protections.
Until the spring of 1977, when a band of activists with disabilities decided to do something about it. Led by Heumann and Kitty Cone, activists took over the former Department of Health, Education and Welfare building in San Francisco for nearly a month — widely considered the longest sit-in of a federal building in U.S. history.
People across disability groups — from wheelchair users to people with intellectual and health-related disabilities — camped out, demanding, and eventually winning the passage of rules that made Section 504 enforceable. The protests paved the way for federally funded institutions like schools, libraries, city buildings and other entities to be made accessible for disabled people.
"Judy always said, 'disability only becomes a tragedy for me when society fails to provide the things we need to lead our lives' — job opportunities or barrier-free buildings, for example," says former NPR correspondent Joe Shapiro, who covered disability and was a friend of Heumann's until she died in 2023.
Regarding disability rights as basic civil rights was a novel concept at the time, but has remained core to the movement today.
Shapiro says Heumann was fueled by the idea of a generation of young disabled people who would come of age under the ADA: "They see the ADA as a floor, not a ceiling, and Judy loved that there's this new generation demanding more."
With the film having opened in theaters this month and now streaming on Apple TV, NPR sat down with some members of the ADA generation to talk about Heumann's legacy, and the threats they see today to the movement she helped launch.
"It is our job to carry on her legacy and keep that fire burning all these decades later," says Kaleigh Brendle, who started a disability rights organization called Judy's League to push back against the Trump administration's efforts to roll back protections attached to Section 504.
Last month, a federal judge dealt a blow to disability rights activists by agreeing to strip out mentions of "integration" of people with disabilities from Section 504 regulations. This erased some of the very language Heumann and her movement had helped win 50 years ago.
As she watched Being Heumann, Brendle says she "felt simultaneously sad that we're here again because I know she would be hurting to see so much of what she fought for at risk. But it also strengthened my resolve."
Brendle, who is blind and has other disabilities, held a watch party of Being Heumann with four other members of Judy's League. They spoke to NPR about their impressions.
These are excerpts from that conversation, edited for length and clarity.
On what stood out most about Being Heumann:
Liam Holland, 25, Philadelphia: The very first line of the movie is Judy chanting "[Sign 504]!" That gave me chills right away, because almost 50 years later, 504 is the exact reason we founded Judy's League. Seeing her lead the chant hit home because we are still fighting those exact same battles today.
Cricket Bidleman, 27, Baltimore: Like Liam said, seeing history come full circle was not particularly encouraging. But we did it once, so we can do it again. We can save 504.
Kaleigh Brendle, 23, Berkeley, Calif.: What I loved seeing over and over on display was just the unshakable resolve that Judy showed, that fire that would not be extinguished … And I think right now we're seeing relentless challenges to our rights from this administration, from every direction. ... It really gave me hope and renewed what I feel we need to be doing right now.
Ellana Crew, 30, Baltimore: I feel I've never seen so many real disabled people on screen in one place ... They are laughing, they are swearing, they're telling dirty jokes … That was one of my favorite things, honestly, it was just like, 'OK, wow, I didn't expect that to be in this movie.' They are not shying away from disabled people as sexual and romantic beings, which is rarely something that society lets us talk about. And ... it's remarkable how many of the sentiments in the movie, based on this time in the 1970s, still feel so relevant today.
On what parts of the disability rights movement back then still feel relevant:
Ellana Crew: A lot of attitudes expressed by non-disabled people [in the film] felt fairly indistinguishable from the attitudes I hear today. Like some of the same sentiments, some of the same opinions of pity, charity-based mindsets of like, "Oh, well we feel bad for you, but we can't do anything about it, it's just too hard." I think people would be amazed how often that still happens today, or maybe they wouldn't.
Cricket Bidleman: It's amazing to see how in some ways we've made so much progress. I mean, now we have computers and technology that work for us, and autonomous vehicles and things like that. But the discrimination hasn't really changed that much.
Kaleigh Brendle: What really moved me was hearing Judy lead the "Sign 504" chant because I, along with several other people in Judy's league ... we were in Austin, Texas on the Capitol steps this July. And all these years later we were having to chant "Hands off 504."
On how the legacy of Judy Heumann and other activists has shaped the disability rights movement today:
Liam Holland: Every week, I roll a mile and back [in my wheelchair] by myself to get chicken for my dinner puree. That trip has a lot of curb cuts. Before 504, sidewalks did not have ramps, which stopped disabled people's access to sidewalks. The [1977] sit-in forced the government to mandate public access. So every curb I go over is directly tied to that fight. ... The people at the deli see me come in every week by myself. They fist-bump me, get my card from my wallet, put it back ... And then I roll home over curb cuts listening to music. So what Judy means to me, quite simply, is independence and normalcy.
Leigh White, 30, Galloway, N.J.: Unfortunately, history rhymes. And we're not right back where we started, but we are in the crucible, if you will, where we're kind of being fired at on all sides. And it's important to remember her grit and her tenacity and her true dedication ... Disabled individuals are the largest minority group in the United States. And it crosses all genders and all races and everything. So by fighting for the rights of people with disabilities, it kind of raises all boats.Kaleigh Brendle: I always say to other people that don't understand the disability experience: If you broke your arm tomorrow, you would expect that the world would accommodate you. You would expect to have the accommodations that you needed as you navigated that temporary disability. Why is it wrong for us to expect what you would expect in that situation?
Cricket Bidleman: We've made so many advancements because of people like Judy and because of … all these activists and advocates who came before us. And although I do have to struggle with people to obtain access to media or textbooks or the standardized testing to get into various education, it's still nothing compared to some of the things we saw in the movie
Leigh White: Us being part of the 'ADA generation,' we're able to reap the benefits. And with hindsight we're really able to appreciate the work that she's done and then kind of carry the torch into the future. So that the struggles we're going through right now, hopefully the next generation of disabled youth don't have to go through the same things.

Rashmi Ramesh, 40, from Mumbai, has been managing Hashimoto’s thyroiditis for nearly two decades. And yet, she continues to experience hair fall and fluctuations in weight. Although she was diagnosed when she was 20, she says symptoms such as puffiness around her eyes and face, lethargy and weight gain had begun when she was about 10.
Staying fit and managing her health require constant attention to sleep, diet and exercise, she says. “It is tough to stay fit. I have to work much harder than someone who doesn’t live with Hashimoto’s.” During pregnancy, she experienced substantial weight gain and water retention, along with puffiness. Managing her condition requires constant vigilance.
