There's a chance your Xbox Series X is plugged into the wrong HDMI port
Make sure you're getting the most out of your Xbox Series X.
This sounds like an idiotic suggestion at first, right? Surely all you need to do is plug the HDMI cable that came with your Series X into your television, and you'll be ready to enjoy the best Xbox games, no? It's not always that simple.
Though your current TV may support HDMI 2.1, the input that ensures the Series X can display its maximum resolution and framerate, that doesn't mean all of your TV's ports are 2.1 compliant. This latest high-def standard really matters, as without it, cutting-edge visual features like Variable Refresh Rate are off the table.
It's important to know the specifics of your current TV. For instance, if it's an aging model that only supports HDMI 2.0, you can stop reading this article now, and content yourself with a top output of 1440p/120 fps or 4K/60 fps from your Series X. However, if you own a semi-modern budget flatscreen, there's a good chance only one or two of its ports will be compatible with HDMI 2.1, enabling 4K/120 fps and framerate-smoothing VRR from the Xbox.
Let's get to know your TV's HDMI sockets a little better, discuss whether you should upgrade the cable that came in the box with your Series X, and go over why HDMI 2.1 is so important for current-gen gaming.
Am I using the wrong HDMI input for my Xbox?
Possibly, but it's entirely dependent on the model of TV you own. If you picked up your screen within the last five years and it wasn't an ultra-budget panel, it probably supports HDMI 2.1. But remember, even with a newish TV, there's no guarantee that all of its ports are HDMI 2.1 compatible.
Most modern high-end sets will have three to four HDMI 2.1 ports total, so if you've bought a premium OLED or MicroLED panel in the last couple of years, it's likely that all of its HDMI inputs will comply. If your set is a good few years old and was one of the first models to support HDMI 2.1 features, there's a decent chance that only one of its ports can take advantage of the Xbox Series X's 4K/120 max output.
To assess your TV's port situation without any awkward bending or flashlight usage, check out your model's online manual. Otherwise, individual inputs tend to be labeled on the backside of the TV itself. My 2023 LG OLED has four HDMI 2.1 ports, so thankfully I never have to worry about connection issues, but it's often the case that certain brands and less-recent models favor HDMI 2.1 in specific slots. Take Sony as an example: Older Bravia displays usually reserve their 2.1 configurations to ports three and four. Again, it entirely depends on your specific model. And when in doubt, reference your TV's online manual.
Should I upgrade the HDMI cable that came boxed with my Xbox Series X?
In the vast majority of circumstances, you should definitely not replace the Ultra High Speed HDMI cable that came in the box with your beloved Microsoft machine. That puppy is fully HDMI 2.1 compliant and it's likely to have a far greater shelf life than any Xbox Series X. For most folks, there really is no reason to upgrade the Series X's standard cable. Of course, there are exceptions.
Depending on the logistics of your gaming setup, you might need a longer HDMI cable than the one Microsoft provides. It's 6 feet long, which will be plenty for most Xbox players. But if for some reason you can't place your Series X as close to the TV as you'd like, investing in a lengthier cable might be worthwhile. Just make sure it's HDMI 2.1 certified and you're good to go.
There's also the case for folks who wall-mount their TVs. I can personally attest that getting the Xbox's HDMI 2.1 cable into one of my LG G3 OLED's outputs was a nightmare, as my screen is flush to the wall. In these instances, it's definitely worth investing in an HDMI cable with an ultra-thin connector. Again, just check that it's HDMI 2.1 compliant.
Please, please never been suckered into buying a "premium" HDMI cable. That word is basically a money-grabbing marketing tool used to lure in impulsive AV enthusiasts. I should know: I still have a painful memory of being sweet-talked into purchasing a $75 HDMI cable back in 2015, right after picking up my first OLED TV. Trust me, the ultra-fast cable that came with your Xbox Series X will do just fine.
Which Xbox Series X games support 120 fps?
There are actually a surprising number of games that can hit 120 fps on the Xbox Series X (and even its smaller sibling, the Series S), as noted by Pure Xbox. The big caveat? Few Xbox games can run at such a high framerate while also outputting at 4K resolution. Last-gen titles that got Series X upgrades like Halo: The Master Chief Collection can output at a full-fat 4K/120, but even popular first-party games like Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, Forza Horizon 6 and Doom the Dark Ages are locked at 60 fps on the console.
Otherwise, the Series X often hits 120 fps with an associated drop in resolution. Pretty much every modern Call of Duty installment supports 120 fps, from Black Ops Cold War right up to this year's Modern Warfare 4. The catch? Dynamic resolution is usually deployed, often dropping in-game clarity to either 1080p or 1400p. If you want faster framerates on Series X, in most cases you're going to have to accept a dip in resolution.
There are drawbacks you should know about before buying an Xbox Series X, but when push comes to shove, its visual output really boils down to having a proper HDMI cable, and the age and manufacturer of the connected display. To get the most out of your Xbox Series X, start by making sure your HDMI 2.1 ports and cables are in order.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says he’s AGI-pilled, at least when it comes to how AI might make startling changes to the structure of the economy and how politics might change because of it. “I am AGI pilled in the sense that at an economy level, what is the political economy’s organization around AGI?” he asked at a roundtable discussion following his Microsoft Ignite keynote at the Chase Center in San Francisco.
Satya Nadella says he’s AGI-pilled now
But he doesn’t think Claude is conscious.
But he doesn’t think Claude is conscious.
But Nadella doesn’t think frontier models like Claude are conscious. “I don’t think so,” he said, adding that he follows Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman’s view that companies should not give rights to models and treat them like they might have a moral status, which companies like Anthropic do as a matter of principle. Suleyman has told me he thinks Anthropic’s team has “wireheaded” themselves, and that this approach is dangerous.
Nadella wasn’t quite as firm about it. “It’s a good debate,” he said. “I’m not sort of dogmatic about it. What I’m saying is the most important social technical issue we have to deal with is how do you ensure that an economy can diffuse this technology broadly?”
I asked Nadella how he was thinking about AI after hearing his response to another reporter’s questions about Anthropic releasing more products in its office suite. Nadella talked at length about the potential collapse of the economy and the end of democracy if one AI model were allowed to achieve monopoly status.
“If the Marxist sort of view is that there’s only one firm, then it’s over, right? For all of us.”
“Most people think about this as a competition between tech firms, which of course it will be,” he said. “But remember, the model has no limits. It’ll be a healthcare company. It can be a financial services company. It can be anything if it wants to be. It can take over the government. Thinking of this as some narrow competition between tech firms, of who is going to get to the next trillion dollars of market cap, is one of the strangest, narrowest ways to think about it.”
Nadella went on to say that the very nature of companies stood to be disrupted in the future. “If intelligence has network effects, what is the future of a firm?” he asked. “If the model sees anything and learns it, and essentially all of human capital collapses into token capital, what is the role of a firm and the human capital in a firm? That’s the debate.”
“I think the political economy is going to get more and more interesting in that context. No one — at least in a democracy — can even win an election if this just goes that way, if there’s only capital and there’s no labor. I mean, I don’t know, that’s not an economy.”
“If the Marxist sort of view is that there’s only one firm, then it’s over, right? For all of us. Not just for me. You are also going to somehow be some affiliate of Anthropic.”
Needless to say, this is not how tech CEOs usually talk about the launch of competing spreadsheet software.
Of course, Nadella was also promoting Microsoft’s various AI tools at Ignite, which promise to let enterprise clients pick the most cost-effective models for various tasks, run their own models, and control their own data in different ways. The idea here is that the market will demand many different kinds of models and sovereign data in order to keep control from centralizing, a theme Nadella kept coming back to as we spoke.
“I think that if you believe that the world, the economy needs more than one firm or two firms, then by definition there need to be as many models as firms of some sort,” he said.

One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built.
A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward.
Finding the centers
The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts.
In a way, that makes this a very conservative estimate, since 272 facilities believed to be large data centers were left out. But if you’re interested in AI data centers, specifically, it’s also true that some of the facilities included may not fall in that category.
That fact also introduces some uncertainty in the actual power usage of these data centers. Relying on other research, they use a range—some conventional data centers run at an average of about 48 percent of capacity, while AI training loads have been running higher, at around 70 percent.
Putting that together, the total power usage for the year by these 403 data centers was estimated at 68 to 99 terawatt-hours. That amounts to 1.5 to 2.2 percent of total US electricity use, on par with the total used by Wisconsin or Indiana.

My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
- Published
When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.
They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there.
"Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.
But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.
This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.
Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.
Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.
After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience.
"As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.
The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.
The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team.
After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve.
Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north.
This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance.
After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.
This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre.
"She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.
Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance.
He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids.
The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment.
"The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea.
In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding.
Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified.
"I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains.
Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok.
The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him.
However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged.
"We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC.
For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region.
He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance.
Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns.
"We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC.
They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola.
Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation.
After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust.
"I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact."
During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real.
But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding.
Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says.
"Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate".
He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion.
But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone.
Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community.
He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly."
He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing.
"The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says.
The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.
Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease.
"Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."

- Contrary to a claim circulating via social media posts, there's no evidence that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries explicitly threatened to withhold committee assignments from House members and members-elect who don't support his bid for speaker when Democrats take control of the legislative body in January.
- This rumor stemmed from Ohio Democratic Rep.-elect Don Leonard's comments about a dinner with senior Democratic representatives who allegedly warned Leonard that his life could become a "living hell" if he didn't support Jeffries. Leonard later told TMZ that potential consequences could include withheld committee assignments, but he framed it as a possibility as to what that "living hell" may entail.
- Snopes will update this report if we receive replies to our queries from either Leonard or Jeffries.
After Democrats won control of Congress in the 2026 midterms, a claim spread online that U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries was threatening to withhold committee assignments for any of his caucus members who didn't support him for speaker of the House.
The rumor circulated on X and Threads, and Snopes readers wrote in to ask us to verify it.
This claim originated from Ohio Democratic Rep.-elect Don Leonard's comments about "friendly advice with very stark consequences" he allegedly received from senior House Democrats in regard to supporting Jeffries' bid for speaker. Social media posts appear to have taken Leonard's comments somewhat out of context. There's no evidence that Jeffries has literally threatened to withhold committee assignments from anyone who does not support him as speaker.
Jeffries and Leonard's offices did not immediately return requests for more information. Here's what we know:
Leonard's allegations
Leonard, an Ohio Democrat who flipped a Republican-held seat, posted a video on Nov. 9 claiming that top House Democrats said his life will become a "living hell" if he doesn't support Jeffries. 
Leonard says in the video that he will not support Jeffries as speaker without the New York Democrat's commitments to two issues: ending U.S. support for Israeli military actions, including the war in Iran, and a constitutional amendment that would reverse Citizens United, a Supreme Court decision that gives free-speech protections to corporate money in politics.
Here's the transcript from that video (emphasis ours):
Tonight, I met with — we'll call 'em senior members of the Democratic House — who told me in no uncertain terms that the decision as to whether or not I support Jeffries, regardless of his willingness to speak with me and meet the interests of my constituents on a couple of key issues: No. 1, getting a constitutional amendment to end Citizens United, and No. 2, ending U.S. support for the war in Iran, and the country, Israel, that led us into it — that that would basically mean both making my life a living hell for the next two years in Washington as well as being sure to lose my election in two years.
You know, we kinda knew this stuff was coming. It's part of the stuff you see in the movies. It's a whole 'nother thing when, you know, it's in person by people who actually care about you and are cheering for you, but expect you to wear the team jersey and, you know, be a good team player. You know, we're searching our hearts tonight as to how we can reach Leader Jeffries and help him be a better speaker. At the end of the day, the big "D" Democratic Party needs some little "d" democracy and I'm just a stubborn SOB, so we'll continue meeting with our fellow members of Congress and members-elect and try and see if we can build support for what we're trying to do here. Please wish me luck. It's getting real, y'all.
On Nov. 11, TMZ posted a video in which a reporter with the tabloid asks Leonard about his comments. In that video, Leonard expands on what "living hell" could mean and says committee assignments could be withheld. However, he also makes it clear that the conversation he was referencing did not directly involve Jeffries, nor was it meant to be threatening.
As such, it's unclear whether anyone actually told Leonard that Jeffries would withhold committee assignments from him or any other Democrat who does not support Jeffries as speaker.
Here's a transcript of the TMZ interview (emphasis ours):
TMZ: You're in a room with top-level Dem officials. They say to you, "Listen, if you don't fall in line, we're going to make your life hell." Walk me through what that experience was like, just on your first couple of days here.
LEONARD: It was so much less cinematic. It was actually a dinner with senior elected officials, and I let them know where my position was on the speaker, and they were offering very friendly advice with very stark consequences. It wasn't in leadership, it wasn't their position to do it. It was just, you know, friendly advice from future colleagues.
TMZ: It doesn't sound that friendly. You literally said — your words — you said it was out of a movie. It sounds like something out of like "The Godfather."
LEONARD: What's out of a movie is the consequences of it, right? And the consequences are very real. Committee assignments will be withheld. You know, The ability to get, you know, legislation on the floor for votes will be difficult. And, you know, the ability to get support for the re-election will be a difficult case to make.
TMZ: Is this not what people criticize Trump for? It sounds very similar.
LEONARD: Yeah, I know, I think, you know, well, welcome to Washington, D.C., right? I mean, it's — I'm not shocked, but I'm —
TMZ: Sounds a little shocking. I think you're a little —
LEONARD: — I'm disappointed.
TMZ: Yeah, well listen. We can say — you already said what you had to say. And it's gone viral. But I think we gotta go the next step further, here, just for Americans. Who were these people who said it to you?
LEONARD: Yeah, no, that's how we build relationships and sustain them going forward. But I appreciate it.
TMZ: You don't want to get in trouble, hey man, I appreciate it.
Axios reportedly asked Leonard about the conversation, per a Nov. 11 story, and he emphasized that it was a "friendly" and "well-intentioned" conversation with senior House Democrats. Here's how he described it to Axios:
"They let me know that while we all agree on a lot of this stuff … the leader is going to pursue his message and agenda as he sees fit, and [said], 'Don't be insane. How could you possibly stand in the way?'"
Leonard also said he met Jeffries for the first time, per Axios, and there's no indication it was a threatening meeting:
The Ohio Democrat said he got a chance to meet Jeffries for the first time on Tuesday and arrange for their staffers to work out a time to sit down and talk.

Magnus Carlsen forfeited his Fast Classic game against Kazakhstan’s Bibisara Assaubayeva at the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot in Budapest on Tuesday after securing the day’s result through blitz and rapid, with the unplayed game having no effect on his classical rating.
Carlsen won the first three blitz games and drew the fourth before winning both rapid encounters to lead 11.5–0.5. With only eight points available from the Fast Classic game, Assaubayeva could no longer overturn the deficit. Her victory by forfeit left Carlsen the day’s winner at 11.5–8.5.
The Norwegian, who was scheduled to play with White, told Norwegian broadcaster TV2 that he saw no reason to contest a game which could no longer change the day’s outcome.
“There will be no classical game as I understood, the match is over. The only consequence of not showing up is that you will lose a totally useless game. I think that if you play a World Championship and it counts for points and such, I can understand,” Carlsen said.
“In the end, if you play games after, it shall not be rated because it’s always been like that. And if they want to do things differently here. This is my decision on this topic.”
ALSO READ: How Laszlo Nagy helped shape Magnus Carlsen, Fabiano Caruana and a generation of Grandmasters
Carlsen had secured only the opening day of the two-day encounter. The pair were competing in the bracket for places 17 to 20, with the second session scheduled for Wednesday. Scores reset each day: a win or a tied session on Wednesday would send Carlsen through to the match for 17th place, while an Assaubayeva victory would force Armageddon.
The knockout format awards one point for a blitz win, four for a rapid victory and eight for a Fast Classic win, with draws worth half those totals.
Under FIDE’s rating regulations, unplayed games, including forfeits, are excluded from rating calculations. The result therefore gave Assaubayeva the tournament points without changing either player’s classical rating.
The decision also removed the risk of Carlsen falling below 2800 in this game. A draw against Assaubayeva would have cost him 3.5 rating points, while a defeat over the board would have cost 8.5. Carlsen, however, framed his refusal as an objection to rating a game after the day’s result had been settled.
Carlsen had lost 21.8 Elo points, nearly 22, over the five-day Fast Classic group stage, finishing without a win after nine draws and one defeat, against Haik Martirosyan. That left him fifth in Group C, with a live classical rating of 2801.2.

'It was really scary': Mother describes sheltering during Russia strikes on Kyiv bridge
- Published
The alarms warning of a ballistic missile threat went off just before 23:30 on Monday in Kyiv. Moments later came the boom of explosions.
Once again, the main bridges over the broad River Dnipro that cuts through the city were the target and this time the Russian missiles hit what they wanted.
Close to one end of the Pivnichnyi (Northern) bridge there is a large crater and in the pouring rain, water now rushes through it to the river below. Chunks of tarmac and metal are scattered around.
At its broadest point, the jagged hole is about eight metres wide.
The crossing is closed to all traffic apart from the occasional fire engine or police car passing at high speed. By contrast, nearby roads are jammed with cars and trucks, forced to take long detours.
Anyone in a hurry to move around this city has to walk, or cycle, across the bridge, picking their way through the wreckage. In the miserable weather, that also means getting very wet.
Masha and her family moved to a flat next to the bridge because they had been living by a power plant that kept getting hit by Russian missiles.
Last night, she was in the kitchen of their new place when the Russians struck the bridge. She thought her windows would be blown out of their frames by the explosions.
"It was really scary. We had no idea they'd hit here so much. It's like we're cursed," Masha told me, describing grabbing her child and running into the corridor for protection.
But somehow, she still managed to sound cheerful.
"It's difficult, but we're used to it. And we try to take the positive from everything. Like: we survived today! So we can be happy about that."
From the damage, it looks like Russia targeted the same spot on the bridge with a volley of three missiles, aiming to keep the road closed for as long as possible.
A major recovery operation is under way, with firefighters and engineers in fluorescent overalls working to evaluate the extent of the damage. But it looks like the disruption will continue for some time.
Further along the Dnipro River, the Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was also hit on Monday night, with four missiles.
The metro line across it was suspended for a while, although by mid-afternoon it had been restored. The mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said road transport in one direction was also being partially restored.
On the Pivnichnyi bridge, a man with a bag of tennis rackets on his back was gazing at the crater in front of him. He was heading home from the courts after he had travelled on foot to the left bank.
"It is upsetting," Anatolii told us. "Then when you read the news of what our side did to the Crimea bridge, you do feel a bit better."
That is because there was a battle of the bridges overnight.
Ukrainian missiles hit the one Russia had built to occupied Crimea, and caused serious damage. That bridge is prized by Russian President Vladimir Putin personally, a symbol of his illegal 2014 takeover.
Ukrainians loathe it for the same reason and now a section has collapsed into the sea, along with its towering arch.
To many here, the timing feels significant: a blow to Putin's image, just as he wants to seem most powerful at this week's summit with the US and China.
But for Kyiv resident Antonina, today is just another challenge to overcome.
The 67-year-old, who we met pulling a shopping trolley through the debris on a bridge in the Ukrainian capital, was heading to see her son on the right bank, but taxi drivers were charging a fortune to go round, so she decided to walk.
"What else could I do?" she shrugged.
"It was a very scary night. It felt like something exploded right over my head. We will get through this, but I just wish the war would end."

Actor Ranveer Singh and boAt cofounder Aman Gupta have teamed up to launch H.I.M (Handsome Indian Man), a men's personal care brand that says its products are formulated for Indian male skin, local climate, and biology. The brand has debuted with eight products across face, body and hair, priced between ₹299 and ₹899. It claims that each product is powered by IN·XT™, a proprietary molecule developed exclusively for H.I.M. The range is available on the brand's website, Amazon and Blinkit. The launch seems to be a part of Gupta's broader plans to build a portfolio of consumer ventures through his venture studio OFF/BEAT, which aims to back new ideas and emerging founders. OFF/BEAT raised ₹100 Cr in a seed funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners in April this year. According to the brand, men account for nearly half of India's population but contribute less than a tenth of the country's beauty and personal care spending. It said products for men have largely been adapted from formulations originally developed for other consumers. H.I.M aims to address this gap with products designed around Indian male skin and local environmental conditions, including heat, humidity, pollution and hard water. It said its formulations draw on research into Indian male skin, including an all-male research panel. Its proprietary molecule is designed to improve the penetration of skincare ingredients. Speaking about the launch, Singh said he realised that existing personal care products were not necessarily formulated for Indian skin, weather and water conditions. He added that he worked with scientists to develop the formulations and tested them from the initial samples through to the final products. Gupta said Indian men are increasingly becoming conscious of skincare, reading product labels and adopting personal care routines. He cited an 850% increase in searches for men's skincare routines over the past five years. H.I.M’s debut range includes a face wash, moisturiser, and sunscreen for face care, an exfoliating body wash, hydrating lotion, and exfoliating soap bar for body care, and a 2-in-1 shampoo and conditioner marketed for hard-water protection and a scalp serum for fuller-looking hair. With the launch, the cofounders are looking to tap into India's growing men's grooming market. Rising disposable incomes, growing awareness of personal wellness and appearance, and the expansion of ecommerce channels are among the key factors driving the market. According to IMARC Group, the country's male grooming products market is estimated to grow from $2.62 Bn in 2026 to $4.46 Bn by 2034.

United Launch Alliance (ULA) confirmed Tuesday morning that its return-to-flight launch of the Vulcan rocket began failing during the initial stages of the mission.
“While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff, the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit,” the company said.
The launch company also confirmed reporting by Ars that the Centaur V upper stage and the solid rocket boosters performed nominally during the flight.
Critically, ULA did not provide any specific information about the “low booster performance.” This matters greatly because the core stage of the Vulcan rocket is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are provided by Blue Origin. That company’s own New Glenn rocket uses a similar but slightly more powerful version of the BE-4 engine. And New Glenn experienced its own catastrophic failure in May during a ground test, a failure that later was attributed to a main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines.
Preliminary data review
Information about the Vulcan failure is being closely held by ULA and Blue Origin, who have only acknowledged that they’re working together to investigate the cause. According to two sources, the investigation is “incredibly complicated” and remains in the early stages.
However, according to preliminary data, two independent sources indicated to Ars that the problem is currently believed to have originated on the launch vehicle side rather than in the engines themselves. The issue may be related to systems that feed methane and liquid oxygen propellant to the engines.
ULA engineers are looking at the possibility that one of the two BE-4 engines started producing lower thrust shortly after liftoff and never ramped back up to full throttle for the remainder of the burn. Video observations from high-zoom tracking cameras appeared to show one engine slightly dimmer than the other after Vulcan jettisoned its solid rocket boosters nearly two minutes into flight. An asymmetric shutdown of the BE-4 engines could also have contributed to the sudden attitude motion indicated by ULA’s telemetry-driven real-time animation near stage separation.

Ghana's new $60m presidential jet sparks public outrage
- Published
Ghana's government has defended its purchase of a new presidential jet amid criticism over its cost, as many citizens continue to struggle with the high cost of living.
The $60m (£46m) French-made Falcon 6X has sparked a political row, with opposition politicians accusing President John Mahama's administration of misplaced priorities.
But the government says the purchase is justified, arguing that Ghana's improving economy makes the aircraft affordable and is needed to replace an ageing presidential jet.
The controversy comes as Mahama's administration seeks to demonstrate an economic recovery after years of financial difficulties that forced Ghana to seek IMF assistance.
- Can Ghana's new president meet the voters' high expectations? 
  - Published7 January 2025
Manufactured by French aerospace company Dassault Aviation, the aircraft was delivered to the Ghana Air Force on Monday at a reported cost of $61m.
Parliament approved its purchase last December as part of a broader programme to modernise Ghana's military aviation fleet, which also includes four helicopters from Airbus.
The jet was welcomed with a water salute on Monday, but its arrival triggered criticism online and among opposition politicians over the cost and timing of the purchase.
While in the opposition, Mahama himself opposed buying a new presidential jet, prompting questions about why his administration has now gone head with the purchase.
Opposition MP Samuel Abu Jinapor questioned the government's priorities, saying the expenditure came at a time when many Ghanaians continue to struggle with the cost of living and youth unemployment remained alarmingly high.
"What was unacceptable in opposition cannot suddenly become acceptable in government merely because the occupants of power have changed," Jinapor added.
He accused the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) of hypocrisy, recalling how its senior figures had strongly opposed proposals for a new presidential aircraft when they were in opposition.
Jinapor also called for greater transparency over the procurement process, how the purchase was financed and the government's justification for the expenditure.
The purchase has also prompted sharp criticism on social media, with some users arguing the money could have been spent on more pressing public needs.
"This money can employ over 100,000 nurses and 200,000 teachers," an X user posted.
But the government has rejected the criticism, saying Ghana's economic circumstances have changed considerably since the NDC opposed a similar purchase.
Peter Lanchene Toobu, chairman of parliament's defence committee, said the party had never opposed acquiring a presidential jet in principle.
Its objection, he said, had been on the timing when Ghana was experiencing severe economic difficulties.
"We agreed in principle that we needed to purchase a new presidential jet," he said.
He argued, however, that Ghana could not justify the expenditure at a time when it was seeking a $3bn bailout from the IMF.
"The strength and macroeconomic stability of this country have enhanced our status in the sense that imports have become cheaper, and this is the right time," he added.
Toobu said the government had purchased the aircraft without borrowing, citing a stronger Ghanaian currency and improved economic conditions.
Government spokesperson Kwakye Ofosu also dismissed suggestions that the purchase was a misplaced priority.
He pointed to falling prices of construction materials and lower borrowing costs as evidence of the country's improved economic situation.
"When I was campaigning in 2024, and I was donating cement, it cost 115 cedis (£7.5) a bag. Today, for 80 cedis, you will get a bag of cement," he told JoyNews.
The controversy has also extended to the aircraft's interior, following claims that it has a dedicated bedroom and bathroom.
But Ofosu dismissed claims that the jet had such luxury facilities, saying the president has no intention of "bathing in the air".
"There certainly is no bathroom. President Mahama has no intention of bathing in the air," Ofosu said.
He explained that the jet has reclining seats that can be converted into sleeping arrangements but denied that it has a dedicated bedroom.
The government says the new jet will replace the 16-year-old Falcon 900EX, which has suffered recurring maintenance problems, including corrosion and leakages in its fuel tank.
The older jet was reportedly grounded in France for several months in 2025 while undergoing repairs.
Officials say the Falcon 6X has a longer flying range, reducing the need for refuelling stops on international trips and improving the reliability of presidential travel.
Professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin, an economist at the University of Ghana said that while the president's safety was paramount, the timing of the purchase was difficult to justify amid severe austerity measures, high unemployment and widespread infrastructure challenges.
"The timing makes it a bit difficult to understand," he told the BBC, adding that the government should provide a cost-benefit analysis explaining why buying the jet was preferable to leasing one and how the decision serves Ghana's interests.

5 old-school charging ports you probably forgot phones had before USB-C
Back when chargers were less standardized, we had some interesting connectors for phone power.
From its reversible design to improved power delivery and high-speed data transfers, USB-C is the connector to beat for smartphones today. A sweeping EU mandate cemented its pole position in the race toward a universal standard. Earlier ports, charming as they were, were often bulkier and not as feature-rich. The lack of a universal connector led to a significant amount of e-waste from switching chargers every time you tried a phone from a new manufacturer.
Despite their limited bandwidth and slower charging speeds, I can't help but look back fondly at these unique connectors from the old days. They came in all shapes and sizes based on what manufacturers thought their customers wanted and what was technically feasible at the time. Before features like Apple's AirDrop, you had to rely on a physical cable to transfer large files, and your collection might have been huge if you jumped between phone manufacturers.
Let's check out some of the old-school, sometimes forgotten or even bizarre, charging ports that made it into yesteryear's phones before the advent of USB-C.
Motorola CE Bus connector
First seen on Motorola phones in 2000, the 17-pin CE Bus connector was gigantic. While it wasn't reversible and had hooks that kept it in place, the connector was notable for managing power, data and audio together. It was used in the Motorola V60, one of the most recognizable models of the clamshell era. The first phone with iTunes support, the Motorola ROKR E1, also launched with the port.
Thinner phones like the Razr V3 switched over to Mini-USB, making the CE Bus connector obsolete. Other companies moving toward Mini-USB also helped lower costs, compared to having tons of proprietary solutions to transfer data or charge devices.
Nokia Pop-Port
Nokia's Pop-Port connector was built with external accessories in mind, from earphones to data transfer cables. Owners of the famed Nokia 7210 from 2002 will remember its 14-pin port supporting camera accessory add-ons and car kits. It wasn't very secure, however, and its plastic clips wore down with time. This made listening to music a chore, especially when you went jogging.
While the Pop-Port could be used for charging, Nokia devices of the time usually relied on a separate 2.0 mm thin-tip barrel connector instead. As Mini-USB ports became common, the Pop-Port slowly faded from existence.
Apple 30-pin connector
Apple's proprietary power connector first showed up in 2003 on the third-gen iPod. This flat and wide port was then used across the first iPhone and iPad models. Speaker systems like Bose's SoundDock and Apple's iPod Hi-Fi also relied on the port. All those pins in the connector helped ensure support for FireWire, Apple's legacy charging standard, in its early appearances.
Apple replaced it with the reversible and smaller 8-pin Lightning connector in 2012, another proprietary option that kept the Apple camp from using chargers compatible with Android devices. These connectors also housed small chips to regulate voltage, which let the company collect licensing fees when third-party manufacturers used it for accessories. In 2018, the iPad Pro made the switch to USB-C and the iPhone 15 lineup followed suit in 2023.
Sony Ericsson FastPort
Built to handle data transfers, charging and audio output, the clunky FastPort showed up in 2005 on the Sony Ericsson K750i. With double-sided plastic hooks that snapped onto matching holes on the device, the flimsy 12-pin connection was reminiscent of a VGI port's screws. If a hook were to break, the plug would no longer snap into place, creating a huge pain.
Despite its flaws, the FastPort's versatility pointed in the direction the mobile industry would take as it hunted for a universal standard. It was replaced by the Micro-USB and 3.5 mm audio jack combo in 2010. A five-year run might not be much in tech time, but its unconventional shape remains iconic to this day.
HTC ExtUSB
The HTC Dream, the first commercially available Android phone, featured the chunky 11-pin ExtUSB port, also known as Extended USB. Recognizable by its slanted corner, it combined the 5-pin Mini-USB port with extra pins that granted it data, power and audio capabilities. Fortunately, that meant regular Mini-USB chargers were compatible with this legacy port.
The connector was exclusive to HTC's early Android devices and Windows Mobile phones before they switched to Micro-USB ports. For a time, phones with this port dropped the 3.5 mm headphone jack long before Apple removed it from the iPhone, forcing users to purchase ExtUSB adapters to connect their headphones.

Andhra Pradesh is set to mark its entry into the high-technology semiconductor manufacturing sector with Advanced System In Package Technologies Private Limited establishing an Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test (OSAT) facility at Tarluvada village in Anandapuram mandal of Visakhapatnam district.
Cleared with a total proposed investment of ₹2,387.81 crore across two phases, the facility is projected to generate direct employment for 1,000 people, beginning with an outlay of ₹542.19 crore and 200 jobs in Phase I, followed by ₹1,845.61 crore and 800 jobs in Phase II.
In the global microelectronics value chain, an OSAT unit performs the crucial back-end stages of chip production. It takes fabricated silicon wafers and carries out precision assembly, protective encapsulation and rigorous electrical testing before the finished integrated circuits are deployed in mobile devices, telecommunications gear, consumer electronics and automotive systems.
Approved by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) under the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) on August 20, 2025, the Tarluvada plant holds strategic significance as the first ISM-sanctioned project to be grounded in Andhra Pradesh.
By building domestic capacity in chip packaging and testing, the project addresses a critical link in India’s semiconductor supply chain while anchoring a high-value electronics ecosystem on the east coast.
To expedite the project, the State government has rolled out an extensive package of fiscal, land and infrastructure support under the Andhra Pradesh Semiconductor and Display Fab Policy (4.0), 2024–29. Following clearance by the State Council of Ministers on February 24, 2026, the Information Technology, Electronics and Communications (IT, E&C) Department issued formal orders on February 27, 2026, treating the venture as a “special case” in view of its status as the State’s maiden ISM project.
Under the order, the Andhra Pradesh Industrial Infrastructure Corporation (APIIC) will allot 30 acres of land at Tarluvada at a nominal rate of ₹1 per acre. The State will also extend special incentives of up to 40% of the project cost on a pari passu basis alongside the Government of India’s 50% grant disbursement.
Additionally, APIIC has been entrusted with developing external infrastructure, including approach roads, power and water supply, funded through the IT, E&C Department, while the Revenue, Energy and Municipal Administration and Urban Development departments, along with the Visakhapatnam District Collector, VMRDA and APEPDCL, have been instructed to work in tandem for early execution.
State IT Secretary Katamneni Bhaskar said regulatory hurdles had been cleared at both the State and Central levels to facilitate rapid execution.
“Work has started on the ground. All statutory clearances have been issued proactively by the State government, and the Government of India has also approved all clearances on its end. The company now has to speed up the works on the ground to complete the project on time,” Mr. Bhaskar told The Hindu.

Nvidia reports bumper results as firm says it's not reinstating Huang
- Published
Nvidia's quarterly sales doubled to top $100bn for the first time as the company insisted it is not reinstating ousted founder Jensen Huang.
In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit, interim chief executive Collette Kress said it is "business as usual" and told investors: "We've got this."
The company's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier, reaching $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping 5% in after-hours trading.
Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following two alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a possible spy for China.
"The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said during a Tuesday call with financial analysts.
The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to October 25, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same time period.
Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise another 13% in the next quarter.
Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worry that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.
"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."
Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout happening throughout the technology industry.
"It is business as usual," she said of what is happening inside of Nvidia now. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."
She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects".
"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."
Despite board chairman Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analyst questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.
Jones said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection.
"With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new CEO will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."

International health officials said Tuesday that measles is no longer considered eliminated in the United States, a finding that was widely expected but that marks an embarrassing and avoidable backslide in the country’s basic public health standing.
The announcement, made after a meeting of a committee of the Pan American Health Organization, a regional World Health Organization body, is a largely symbolic recognition of transmission that’s already occurred. But it could have political ramifications, with resurgent Democrats already attacking the Trump administration — in particular, health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — for not responding forcefully to recent outbreaks and for mixed messaging around the benefits of vaccination.
Health authorities in 2000 determined that the U.S. had eliminated measles, a milestone victory. But the country almost lost the designation after outbreaks in 2019, and has been experiencing far bigger outbreaks in the past two years than in the decades prior.
“Losing measles elimination status is a tragic loss for our country,” Susan Kansagra, chief medical officer for the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials, told reporters Monday. The announcement formalizes what public health departments have been seeing on the ground across the U.S. in recent years, she said. “Measles has taken a hold in our country.”
Officials bestow the measles elimination designation on a country that prevents persistent spread of the virus. Cases can still occur, when people infected outside that country import the virus, and limited transmission can take place from those infected people. But if those chains of spread are not stopped within a year, measles is considered to be endemic again.
“Elimination must be continuously protected,” Jarbas Barbosa, the PAHO director, said at a news briefing.
This year, the U.S. has reported more than 5,000 measles cases for the first time since 1991, a figure that’s widely presumed to be an undercount. Last year’s total of 2,289 cases was at that point also the highest number seen since 1991, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The overwhelming majority of infections — 96% — are in unvaccinated people or people whose vaccination status is not known.
The PAHO commission’s review focused on a period starting in January 2025, and depended on establishing that a series of cases continued for at least 12 months.
“It is unconscionable that we have this amount of measles,” said Noel Brewer, a public health expert at the University of North Carolina, who chairs the group that provides data on the measles landscape in the U.S. to PAHO.
“We need a plan,” Brewer said last week during a briefing for reporters. “We need to have a concrete and integrated measles elimination plan that allows us to either sustain the gains we’ve made in the past or to return to a state where measles is no longer stalking children in their schools, in grocery stores, and in their churches. The United States is no longer a safe place for children with respect to measles. It is not as prevalent as some other diseases. At the same time, it is a fully preventable disease.”
The U.S. has seen 10 measles-associated deaths this year, according to state data, though the CDC’s website currently lists six deaths. Some recent deaths reported by states have yet to be added to the CDC’s count, but federal officials have also squabbled with Pennsylvania over its tally. New York and Wisconsin recently reported their first measles deaths in at least 30 years. Last year, there were three measles deaths.
Experts fear that measles deaths — practically unheard of in the U.S. for over 20 years — could become regular events going forward, even if they are not expected to occur nearly as frequently as in the pre-vaccination era, when some 400 to 500 people died every year from infections.
Doctors are also reporting an increase in complications — both maternal and neonatal — from measles infections in pregnancy.
In a statement Tuesday, CDC Director Erica Schwartz said the U.S. is “focused on stopping outbreaks.”
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” she said. “We know where transmission is occurring and we’ve invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities,” she added, referencing funding the CDC has recently distributed to areas facing outbreaks.
The CDC recommends that children receive two doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine, with the first shot at 12 months and the second at 4 to 6 years. Some doctors offer the first dose to younger babies if they live in an area where the virus is spreading. The CDC’s statement Tuesday said “we will encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection.”
While Kennedy has at times acknowledged that the best way to prevent measles infections and spread is the MMR shot, including in a social media post Tuesday, he also has a long history of attacking vaccines with false arguments. As health secretary, he has downplayed the severity of outbreaks, overstated the risks of the vaccine, and pointed to unproven treatments as possible solutions for infections.
Public health experts have criticized the federal government for not doing more to address measles even as infections mounted and as it became clear in recent months that the country’s elimination status was well on its way to being lost. On Tuesday, Sen. Michael Bennet (D-Colo.) called on Schwartz to resign after the PAHO decision was announced.
“The fact that the flag was raised, and it was not heeded, is to me the most alarming thing,” said Maia Majumder, a computational epidemiologist at Boston Children’s Hospital, who co-authored a Lancet paper in May about the at-risk elimination designation. U.S. health officials are “not interested in doing the things that are necessary to maintain our measles elimination status,” she told STAT.
Kennedy, meanwhile, has argued that other countries have also seen more measles cases.
Canada lost its elimination status last year, and PAHO’s reverification commission also determined this week that measles had returned to endemicity in Mexico and Bolivia. A number of European countries — including the U.K. and Spain — have also lost their designation.
The U.S.’s susceptibility to measles has been building for years. Vaccination rates within certain regions and communities have slipped for any number of reasons: a rise in vaccine skepticism, the spread of misinformation online, failures of public health campaigns, or the perception that measles doesn’t pose a threat. Adults have made up sizable portions of infections in some recent case clusters, a sign that it’s not just a nascent retrenchment of parents not immunizing their children that’s allowing for transmission.
But for a long time, unvaccinated people were generally protected from the highly contagious virus because they were surrounded by so many others who were vaccinated, increasing the chances that any burgeoning outbreaks would be quickly snuffed out. (The CDC defines an outbreak as three or more linked cases.) Now, though, pockets of susceptible people, both adults and children, have grown so large that the virus can circulate among them for extended periods. Plus, more measles spread in other countries increases the likelihood of imported cases.
While vaccine coverage of 95% of people is considered sufficient to keep a lid on measles transmission, the vaccination rates for kindergarteners has dropped below 90% in nearly 20 states. Looking at local levels can reveal alarmingly low vaccination rates within individual counties and school districts.
Brewer noted that the CDC has quietly been supporting states in their outbreak responses, including with the recent funding. But the fact that top U.S. officials, whether Kennedy or Schwartz, aren’t regularly encouraging vaccination, as would’ve happened under previous administrations, including the first Trump presidency, has created a vacuum for rhetoric that undermines vaccination to fill.
“We need leadership to step up,” he said.
Megan Molteni contributed reporting.

AvenuesAI subsidiary Rediff has filed its updated draft IPO papers with the SEBI about two months after the regulator cleared its confidential filing. With the IPO, Rediff, which is one of India's earliest internet portals and digital media companies, intends to raise ₹600 Cr via a fresh issue of shares. The company had confidentially filed its IPO papers in April 2026, with an estimated issue size of ₹600-800 Cr. A large part of the capital raised via the IPO will go towards expanding three businesses — enterprise solutions platform Rediff One; digital payments offering Rediff Pay; video platform Rediff TV. Rediff has earmarked ₹224.8 Cr for capital expenditure across the three businesses — ₹94.5 Cr on Rediff One, ₹64.3 Cr on Rediff Pay and ₹66 Cr on Rediff TV. Another ₹183.34 Cr will be used to fuel marketing and branding while the remaining proceeds will be used for acquisitions and general corporate purposes. Breaking Down Rediff’s Operations For context, Ajit Balakrishnan founded the company in 1996 with a host of digital services like email services, shopping, news, etc, Rediff has evolved significantly into a tech-led business under the AvenuesAI umbrella. Balakrishnan retired in 2024 after Infibeam (now AvenuesAI) acquired a majority stake in the company. Infibeam’s chairman Vishal Mehta took over as Rediff’s MD in October 2024. As of now, the company operates across two broader segments: Consumer Digital Platforms (B2C) and Enterprise Digital Platforms (B2B). Breaking this down further, Rediff operates four primary services in the B2C arena. Its flagship email platform, Rediffmail has 152.46 Mn cumulative registered users as of September 30, 2026. This includes all accounts created since the service was launched in 1998. In digital media, Rediff operates Rediff News and Rediff TV, alongside its homepage. The platforms offer current affairs, business information, editorial and video content. Together, they had 90.83 Mn annual active users (AAUs), with an average visit duration of 321 seconds, as of September 2026. Rediff TV, launched in July 2025, is still in the early stages of its business cycle. The company also operates MoneyWiz, its personal finance information platform, which provides financial news and market data. It had approximately 7.89 Mn AAUs at the end of the September quarter. Its newest consumer offering is Rediff Pay, facilitates bill payments, P2P transfers, merchant payments through QR codes, and mobile and DTH recharges. Having initially been available to a closed user group, Rediff Pay has transitioned to its full-service phase post NPCI's TPAP approval. On the B2B side, Rediff offers its products under the Rediff One brand. The suite includes Rediffmail Enterprise for business email, rCloud for cloud storage, and Rediff Bol for enterprise messaging. It also operates Rediff Commerce, an ecommerce enablement platform acquired through a business transfer agreement from AvenuesAI. The platform helps small and mid-sized businesses build and manage online marketplaces, offering tools for storefront creation, catalogue management, payment integration, inventory, logistics and analytics. It also incorporates AI-assisted features for product categorisation and catalogue optimisation. Rediff plans to expand these offerings using IPO proceeds. Its proposed initiatives include integrating enterprise resource planning (ERP), customer relationship management (CRM) and human resource management system (HRMS) modules into Rediff One, expanding Rediff Pay's payments stack, developing Rediff TV into a broader streaming platform and increasing marketing investments. Rediff's Financial Snapshot Rediff reported a net profit of ₹35.2 Cr in the first quarter of FY27 on a top line of ₹58.4 Cr. For the June 2026 quarter, EBITDA (excluding other income) stood at ₹39.43 Cr, translating into a margin of 67.54%. For the full fiscal year FY26, the company's operating revenue rose 258.7% to ₹133.6 Cr from ₹37.2 Cr in FY25. Its net profit surged almost 9X YoY to ₹55.9 Cr from ₹5.9 Cr in the previous fiscal year. EBITDA, excluding other income, stood at ₹65.24 Cr in FY26, compared with a loss of ₹4.29 Cr in FY25. Its EBITDA margin improved to 48.83% from a negative 11.53% over the same period. The company's net debt stood at ₹261.48 Cr as of March 31, 2026, rising to ₹354.95 Cr by June 30, 2026. Meanwhile, operating cash flow turned positive at ₹160.5 Cr in FY26, compared with an outflow of ₹61.29 Cr in FY25.

A Chandigarh consumer commission has ruled in favour of a man who found a tear underneath the arm of his newly purchased jacket within 46 minutes. The commission directed the retail store to pay ₹31,000 to the customer whom they refused to help. According to a report by Indian Express, the commission ruled that store failed to establish that the damage was caused by the customer's mishandling. It added that the store also didn't conduct an independent inspection or expert opinion in the case. The order was reportedly granted on November 4. The publication added that the commission comprising president Amrinder Singh Sidhu and member Brij Mohan Shama observed that the store could not rely solely on its internal assessment to reject the customer's complaint. Reportedly, the retailer had neither explained the basis of its findings nor submitted technical evidence to prove the customer's misandling of the jacket. The store argued that the customer was given an opportunity to inspect the jacket which costed him ₹10,999 before purchasing it. The commission rejected the claim and pointed out that the tear was located underneath the arm, in a relatively inconspicuous area that would not have been detected during checking. “The principle of ‘Buyer Beware’ don’t apply to Consumers because the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 is a benevolent and welfare Act,” the commission observed, as quoted by the outlet. The customer reportedly purchased three jackets from a store at a Chandigarh mall on December 25, 2025. One of the jackets cost ₹10,999 in which a tear was detected. The jacket is dispute was worn for the first time on January 1, 2026. It is said that within 46 minutes, the customer noticed a small tear in the jacket. The customer reportedly reached out to the store by email on January 10 and sought help with required details and documents the following day. Although the retailer initially said the complaint had been escalated for review on January 12, it later rejected the claim after two days. The store allegedly said that the damage in the said jacket was from the customer's actions rather than a manufacturing defect. The customer claimed that the store neither conducted a physical inspection in his presence nor provided photographs, a technical assessment or any other supporting evidence. After repeated follow-ups and an unanswered legal notice dated January 15, the customer moved the consumer commission, seeking a replacement or refund, along with compensation for harassment and litigation costs. The store, however, maintained that the customer was allowed to inspect and try the jacket at the time of purchase. It added that he had initially approached the store seeking repairs, presenting that the damage occurred from his end. The commission, in the end, held the store guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practice, directing it to refund ₹11,000 towards the jacket. An additional pay of ₹20,000 as compensation for harassment and litigation expenses was also ordered. How the attack on Putin's prized Crimean Bridge unfolded
- Published
Stretching across the Kerch Strait in the Black Sea, the Crimean Bridge was always a symbol: for Russia, a prestige project cementing its claim to sovereign Ukrainian territory, and for Ukraine, a hated piece of infrastructure emblematic of Moscow's occupation of the Crimean Peninsula.
A key section of the double-arched, 12-mile-long bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said that the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".
But eight years after its unveiling, the bridge has now become material proof of Kyiv's ability to pierce through Moscow's military defences to hit even its most treasured and protected structures.
How did the seven-stage operation play out?
The attack on the strategic Crimean Bridge was carried out gradually to cut across several layers of defence, Kyiv confirmed on Tuesday.
For several weeks Ukraine's Security Service and its General Staff gradually destroyed air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets, and other designated targets, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
A significant strike had already been reported on 16 November, when drones hit the bridge at night. Traffic was paused briefly then reinstated, and although the arch over the road section was visibly damaged, the structure remained standing.
But that hit turned out to have been only the penultimate stage of a complex attack.
In the early hours of 17 November, the final strikes dealt a fatal blow to the weakened arch structure.
One verified video - filmed from a camera on board a Ukrainian-made Flamingo missile - shows the weapon approaching the main span of the bridge and heading towards the steel arches, with the footage freezing just before impact.
The Flamingo had potentially been modified to be controlled remotely, which improved its accuracy enough to strike the bridge supports, munitions expert Justin Bronk, from the Royal United Services Institute said.
The missile's "very heavy warhead" made it "more suitable" for attacking the bridge's reinforced concrete spans and supports, Bronk added.
Zelensky later confirmed that several types of missiles and drones had been employed in the attack, which led the massive road arch - weighing thousands of tonnes and measuring about 227m in length - to collapse into the strait.
Daylight images taken from the shores of Crimea to the north show a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was too dragged below into the sea.
This is clearly critical damage to the crossing. Far from just being a decorative feature of the bridge, the arch played a structural role, transferring loads and supporting the span and helping to ensure the stability of the entire structure.
The parallel arch supporting the railway section has remained standing, although it may also have been damaged. All traffic on the bridge was initially suspended, though trains were later allowed to resume running.
But the damage to the bridge's main span is "catastrophic", Colin Capriani, a structural engineer from Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, told BBC Verify. It was "very hard to envisage" how the bridge could be rebuilt given it is clearly well within range of Ukrainian weaponry, Capriani added.
Major attacks in 2022 and 2023 had already caused serious damage to the road spans of the bridge, but the structure survived.
The difference this time is "the most critical and vulnerable part of the bridge has been hit", said David MacKenzie of engineering consultancy COWI, adding that "although the wreckage of the bridge can be cleared fairly quickly, reinstating full road traffic will take over a year".
What effect could the collapse of the bridge have on Crimea?
Moscow uses Crimea as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles. From there it also carries out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplies its troops in southern Ukraine.
The attack comes after a summer of frequent strikes on Crimea, dictated by Ukraine's stated goal of cutting the peninsula off from Russia. At the time, Kyiv vowed to turn the Crimean Peninsula "into an island".
Now - although it is too early to speak of a complete blockade of Crimea – the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis has increased significantly.
There is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions. However, Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar, which has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
Moscow can also still utilise the ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited - and anything on the Black Sea has become vulnerable to attack. Resupplying Crimea by sea is risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge - particularly its enormous arch - may have blocked the shipping channel. This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including the occupied cities of Mariupol and Berdyansk.
Away from the operational value of the damage to the bridge, the symbolic significance remains.
In 2018, Putin triumphantly drove over the bridge representing the unification of Russia and Crimea in a Russian-made truck. That section of the road now lays on the seabed.
Nearly five years since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Putin continues to wreak destruction on Ukraine's civilian population, but his most prized symbols of power are increasingly threatened by Kyiv's reach.

With the Air Quality Index (AQI) crossing 400 at some locations in Delhi, people whose work keeps them outdoors for long hours say they are experiencing breathing difficulties, persistent cough, headaches and burning eyes, often without adequate protection against pollution.
For traffic police personnel, domestic workers, roadside vendors, mechanics and gig workers, staying indoors is rarely an option.
Yogendra Kumar, a traffic inspector posted in outer north Delhi, said pollution-related health risks for traffic personnel persists throughout the year but increases significantly when air quality deteriorates.
“The impact on health is inevitable in the outskirts, as road dust also contributes to pollution alongside emissions. We have no safeguards apart from masks. Prolonged exposure causes breathing problems and a persistent cough,” he said.
Reena Chaudhary, a domestic worker in Palam Colony, said she began experiencing breathing difficulties on the night before Deepavali, with her symptoms worsening on the festival day.
“I leave home around 7 a.m. and return by 9 p.m. I began having headaches and burning eyes the day before Deepavali, particularly while passing through smoke-filled lanes between houses at night. On Deepavali, my condition worsened. I felt dizzy throughout the day, had a persistent cough and just wanted to lie down. But who would work if I did?” she said.
Ms. Chaudhary said she had to walk through smoke on Deepavali night with her dupatta wrapped around her face. Since then, she has been taking her daughter along in case she falls ill and is unable to work.
Ravi, a 21-year-old gig worker who attends college during the day, said he works through the night, picking up rides across the city to support his family.
“Even at night, I can see that the air is dense and heavy. At times, I have to stop near a green area, such as Vande Mataram Marg, just to be able to breathe,” he said.
Mukesh Yadav, an e-rickshaw driver in Palam, said road dust remains a problem throughout the year, apart from smoke from firecrackers and vehicular emissions.
“The area remains dusty even on normal days. Since Deepavali, I have been tying a towel around my face,” he said.
Mr. Yadav works eight to 10 hours a day, making several trips between Palam metro station and Kailashpuri, a one-kilometre stretch that witnesses heavy traffic.
“The only time I am not outdoors is when I am charging my e-rickshaw. I thought my cough was due to the cold, but everyone seems to be coughing, even the passengers. It could be due to pollution,” he said.
‘Pollution higher this year’
An analysis by the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) found that Delhi’s average PM2.5 concentration in the week preceding Deepavali reached 236 micrograms per cubic metre, the highest in three years. This was 97% higher than the 120 micrograms per cubic metre recorded in 2025 and 32% above the 179 micrograms per cubic metre recorded in 2024.
The study also found that time-bound restrictions on vehicles had failed to ease traffic congestion, with nitrogen dioxide, a marker of vehicular pollution, accumulating during the evening and remaining elevated until midnight, even after traffic had eased.
“Deepavali pollution is an annual tipping point, but elevated particulate levels before the festival this year show that baseline pollution is higher than in previous years,” said Anumita Roychowdhury, executive director (research and advocacy) at the CSE.
She said cleaner air ahead of winter and measures to contain episodic pollution spikes from farm fires and firecrackers could have prevented such severe pollution during seasonal weather changes.
