Federal officials on Thursday announced new funding to explore the medical potential of ibogaine, a controversial psychedelic drug championed by veterans, conservative lawmakers and podcasters aligned with President Donald Trump.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said his department is awarding up to $4.9 million to prepare for the first U.S. studies of ibogaine for post-traumatic stress disorder, a hard-to-treat condition linked to higher suicide and substance abuse rates among veterans.
The money will not go directly to patient research, Kennedy said, but to lay the groundwork needed to manufacture, dose and design studies of the drug.
Ibogaine is made from a shrub native to West Africa. It can cause intense hallucinations, nausea, vomiting, tremors and sometimes deadly irregular heart rhythms. Ibogaine is currently illegal, in the same ultra-restrictive class as LSD, ecstasy and most other psychedelic drugs.
Veterans organisations and psychedelic advocates contend that ibogaine has great promise for intractable conditions such as PTSD, severe depression and opioid addiction. U.S. research on the drug has essentially been frozen for decades due to ibogaine's restricted status.
Kennedy said the government will receive data and treatment guidance from Beond Inc., a Texas-based company that has treated more than 3,000 patients with ibogaine in Mexico, where the drug is not illegal.
“That is going to allow us to dramatically accelerate the clinical trial process,” Kennedy said. “We’re going to have, I think, a record drug approval process.”
Additional funding awards may explore ibogaine's use for addiction, he said.
Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins, who joined Kennedy for the announcement, said the collaborative effort would focus first on safety and “best-in-class research.”
“For veterans living with PTSD, we owe them both urgency and the best science we can produce,” Collins said.
Kennedy and Collins have previously voiced support for the potential of psychedelics, citing the experiences of veterans who have traveled abroad for therapy with ibogaine and other mind-altering substances.
Thursday's announcement was previewed in April, when Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to speed up review and research of psychedelics that could help with mental health conditions.
Three applications for psychedelics are pending review at the Food and Drug Administration. They include the first potential medicines made from psilocybin, the active ingredient in magic mushrooms, and MDMA, also called ecstasy. Decisions on those drugs could come within weeks or months.
Because of its safety risks, ibogaine research has moved more slowly.
The little data currently available mostly comes from patients who have traveled to Mexico or other countries where ibogaine is not heavily regulated. Ibogaine clinics typically charge $10,000 to $20,000 for one course of treatment, which often involves monitoring of a patient's heart readings while emergency medical workers are on standby.
Trump's order on psychedelics came after podcaster Joe Rogan said he texted Trump about ibogaine, which he repeatedly has discussed on his show. According to Rogan, the president quickly responded: “Sounds great. Do you want FDA approval? Let’s do it.”

Wales vs Portugal; UEFA Nations League Group A4
Wales vs Portugal. UEFA Nations League Group A4.
Cardiff City Stadium.
Wales 2-3 Portugal: Craig Bellamy's side lose final Nations League Group A4 match as Pedro Neto sent off
Match report as Wales lose final Nations League Group A4 game to 10-man Portugal in a 3-2 home defeat; Man Utd's Bruno Fernandes hit opener; Chelsea's Pedro Neto scored Portugal's second but was sent off in second half for two bookings in two minutes; Portugal finish top with Wales bottom
Tuesday 17 November 2026 22:11, UK
Wales ended their Nations League group campaign with a 3-2 defeat against 10-man Portugal in Cardiff after Chelsea's Pedro Neto was sent off.
Although there was little riding on the contest, with Wales guaranteed a League A relegation/promotion play-off in March and Portugal having qualified for the quarter-finals, the two sides produced an entertaining spectacle.
Portugal skipper Bruno Fernandes blasted the opener after 11 minutes, but that was immediately wiped out by David Brooks' ninth goal for Wales.
Sorba Thomas broke free to put Wales ahead before the break, but again there was a quickfire response as Neto pounced to restore parity.
Substitute Carlos Forbs stroked Portugal ahead in the final quarter, and the visitors had to negotiate the final 16 minutes a player short after Neto was sent off after receiving two yellow cards in the space of two minutes.
Wales finish bottom of League A4 with one win and five defeats, and end a disappointing 2026 with a solitary victory, three draws and six losses from 10 games.
Portugal, meanwhile, finish the campaign as group winners as they earned their first win since Cristiano Ronaldo's international retirement.
How Wales lost five-goal thriller...
Craig Bellamy's side had lost 1-0 in Lisbon in September in a game that was to prove Ronaldo's last for Portugal.
Ronaldo's subsequent retirement from international football probably had an impact on the attendance at Cardiff City Stadium, with some seats unfilled, despite the game being officially declared a sell-out.
There would be no clean sheet for Danny Ward on his 50th appearance as Joao Neves robbed Josh Sheehan and Fernandes lashed home from the edge of the box.
Wales responded immediately with Rubin Colwill twice involved, first setting up Harry Wilson for a shot Diogo Costa blocked with his legs and then Brooks, who swept home his ninth international goal, and second in two games.
Wales hit the front five minutes before the break after Brooks worked a one-two with Wilson before releasing Thomas, who advanced from his own half to slot past Costa.
The lead lasted three minutes as Neto lost Jay DaSilva from Trincao's cross to finish at the far post.
A breathless first half was not finished as Wilson hit the roof of the net from halfway with Costa retreating frantically, and the Leeds midfielder then forced a sprawling save from the Portugal goalkeeper.
Portugal regained the lead 20 minutes from time when Club Brugge winger Forbs - wearing Portugal's new-styled number seven shirt in the post-Ronaldo era - collected Ben Cabango's poor header and stepped inside Ben Davies to find the bottom corner.
Neto clattered into Brennan Johnson just one minute and 59 seconds after being booked, but Portugal held on for a fifth Nations League win to seal top spot.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.
Good morning and happy Tuesday! Today’s newsletter includes good news for international students, bad news for the makers of signs proclaiming “zero tolerance” for violence in hospitals, and mixed news for children with rare brain disorders. Read on!
NIH’s infectious disease unit has a new head
No branch of the NIH has faced more scrutiny than the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. For nearly four decades, the institute was run by Anthony Fauci; it’s since become a major focus of Republicans looking to re-litigate the Covid pandemic.
The institute has been without a permanent director since Jeanne Marrazzo was forced out in 2025 for objecting to grant terminations. Now officials have announced that acting director John Powers III will take the lead role.
Powers is a physician-scientist who’s worked at NIAID in several clinical research positions. He has run the institute in an acting capacity since June. Earlier this year, he co-authored a paper with NIH director Jay Bhattacharya that argued NIAID should move away from its focus on HIV and pandemic preparedness, instead prioritizing broader categories of infectious disease and immunology.
Read more from STAT’s Anil Oza, including Powers’ response to questions about health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s position on vaccines.
RFK Jr. favors faith-based addiction treatment. That has experts worried
One of the key tenets of Alcoholics Anonymous is surrender to a higher power. There, and in other organizations, faith-based addiction recovery can serve an important role in supporting people trying to stay sober.
But experts warn the Trump administration’s full-throated embrace of these programs will result in federal grants to centers that don’t always provide evidence-based treatment. As STAT’s Theresa Gaffney explains, some faith-based addiction centers don’t allow participants to use drugs like methadone, which is approved by the Food and Drug Administration for opioid use disorder.
Kennedy also has expressed support for unconventional (and scientifically dubious) approaches to treatment, including “wellness farms,” where people reside in nature and engage in manual labor. Read more about the tricky balance experts hope Kennedy can strike.
20.8%
That’s the share of women who provided care to a friend or family member with a health problem in the past 30 days, according to a new analysis of 2025 data from the National Center for Health Statistics. Women were about 32% more likely than men to have provided care, offering a real world data point to back up the viral Saturday Night Live sketch about the gendered dynamics of caregiving (which makes it sound much less funny than it is! Give a watch here).
Scientists probe why a 3-year-old died after a novel gene therapy
Last year, researchers thought they’d had a breakthrough — they finally engineered a virus to ferry gene therapy to the brain. Experts were hopeful this innovation could cure Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and slew of rare diseases.
Then the first person to undergo treatment with this new technique — a 3 year old — died of brain swelling 65 hours later, sending fear and uncertainty through the industry. Nearly a year later, researchers have unveiled how the process can be shored up for the future, with ideas for new tests and trials to ensure safety. Read more here.
Judge strikes down Trump administration time cap on international students
A proposal by the Trump administration to cap the amount of time foreign students and scholars can spend in the country has been struck down in court. In a decision Monday, a federal judge said the rule was “arbitrary” and “capricious,” writing that the government did not sufficiently consider the ramifications of the new policy.
In his story on the ruling, Anil Oza breaks down why this matters: “International researchers make up nearly a quarter of life science Ph.D. graduates and around 60% of postdoctoral researchers. About 40% of American Nobel laureates in the sciences are immigrants.” Read more.
Why hospitals should reconsider ‘zero tolerance’ notices
Violence against doctors and nurses has jumped in recent years, due to an ugly swirl of understaffing, overcrowding, and pandemic-era stress that hasn’t quite faded. In response, many hospitals have started to hang signs declaring “zero tolerance” for violence or other bad behavior from patients.
The problem, according to three professors, is that these signs don’t actually help protect workers. Instead, they signal to families that care is something that can be withheld. The signs often include long lists about things that patients shouldn’t do, without a similar standards for nurses and doctors.
“The content of the signs sends clear messages to patients and families about their tenuous status and value in the institution,” they write. Read more.

The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned.
On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, announced he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis.
Mark Brantley, the premier of Nevis, which has autonomous self-governance in some aspects, said he understood that the “country was given very little choice”, but did not “support the winding down of the program”.
The 42-year-old CBI programme, which St Kitts and Nevis pioneered, allows wealthy foreigners to obtain citizenship and ultimately a passport by investing in infrastructure and other development projects. It has brought billions of dollars into the country and in some years accounted for the largest share of government revenue.
In June, the European Commission wrote to the five Caribbean nations that currently operate CBI programmes: St Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and St Lucia. It warned that countries may lose visa-free access to its 29-country Schengen area if they did not phase out CBI.
In Friday’s statement, Drew blamed concerns over the programme on mismanagement by previous administrations, including years of underselling to undercut other countries, a controversial prison project, weak escrow protections and investment sums not being properly paid into the citizenship unit.
He said his government had led major reforms to the Caribbean’s programmes with international partners, including the US treasury, but argued that continuing the programme risked visa-free travel to parts of Europe and access to international banking. That could disrupt services allowing visitors to use overseas cards and families abroad to send money home.
Brantley, however, argued it was unfair for the EU to force St Kitts and Nevis to make a move without offering assistance to navigate the transition to other industries.
“I have not yet seen from the EU any corresponding suggestions of assistance. And we have to realise that these citizenship-by-investment programs, not only in St Kitts and Nevis, but … smaller countries of the Caribbean, have contributed significantly to our gross domestic product and also to ensuring that our people … can get adequate access to water and to education, to healthcare and the like,” he said.
Brantley described the 1 June 2028 deadline the EU gave the country to phase out the lucrative programme as “frankly ludicrous”.
In his statement, Drew said the CBI programme “did a lot of good, but it also created a danger”.
“When one source pays for half or more of everything, you are at its mercy. If it stops, everything stops. That is putting all of your eggs in one basket,” he added.
The prime minister said the government aimed to diversify its economy by strengthening tourism, yachting, and digital and creative industries, among others. He added that the sale of clean, geothermal energy is “at the heart of it” with drilling and exploration already planned.
“I will not pretend that the road is easy. Less CBI money means we must spend wisely and plan carefully. We will. Our plan is to make this change by growing our economy. Raising taxes is not part of that plan,” Drew said.
Antigua and Barbuda has also expressed willingness to end the programme, though it is trying to negotiate a longer transition period. The five Caribbean governments have taken differing positions on the EU demand. According to local media, Grenada has indicated it wants its programme to continue until 2032, while Dominica and St Lucia have responded to Brussels without publicly committing to ending their programmes.
Jermine Abel in Basseterre contributed reporting

The integrity of South Korea’s career-defining university entrance exam has been thrown into doubt after the top scorer in a recent professional exam admitted using a concealed camera and AI to cheat.
On Thursday, more than half a million people, mostly school students, are due to sit the exam, known as the suneung, at 1,312 centres across the country. The exam runs for a gruelling eight hours over a single day and determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.
The country goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended.
The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre. Extra trains run from 6am, police drive latecomers to their exam halls, and tourist attractions open late to ease traffic. Offices are asked to open at 10am.
But in recent days, exam organisers have faced a renewed threat to the validity of the entire exercise, after the top scorer in this year’s tax accountancy exam- who got just one question wrong out of 160– admitted on Sunday he had cheated by using AI.
Prime minister Han Seong-sook told a cabinet meeting in Seoul on Tuesday that AI-assisted cheating was a “social evil” that the government would “root out”.
“We will block outright the carrying of smart devices during the exam,” she said. The education ministry and other agencies should approach it “as if staking their jobs on it”, she added.
Han said smart devices must be turned off and handed in, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.
The government will also send emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sound at full volume and cannot be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.
More invigilators will be deployed, and the government said it was preparing to switch off school wifi inside exam centres and public wifi nearby, and that personal hotspots, which cannot be blocked, would be traced through connection records.
The weekend’s cheating revelation captured national headlines in South Korea, stoking concern about the security of the suneung.
In a video posted to his lawyer’s YouTube channel, the exam cheat said he had photographed the questions with a concealed microcamera, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone. “I cheated in the tax accountant exam,” he said. “My top placing is not the result of legitimate effort.”
His lawyer handed police a camera, a laptop and a phone. No charges have been brought, and the prime minister has ordered procedures to begin that would void his result and bar him for five years.
The education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, told parliament on Monday that while authorities could screen out the smart glasses already on sale at Thursday’s exam, newer variants could not be dealt with perfectly.
Choi has ruled out postponing the exam, which has been delayed several times before, including in 2017, after an earthquake struck the south-eastern city of Pohang, and in 2020 due to the Covid pandemic.
Smart glasses have been banned in exams since the end of June. In October, several candidates were caught with them while sitting university-run admissions exams. At the suneung, wearing a pair counts as using one even when switched off.
The education ministry looked at using radio-frequency equipment to detect the glasses in exam halls, but concluded conditions varied too much between venues for deployment this year. Checks will instead rely on visual inspection, with at least one dedicated official placed in each exam centre.
Teachers’ unions have criticised the government response as belated. A survey last month of 2,716 secondary school teachers by the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union showed that 82.3% said they could not tell whether a candidate was wearing smart glasses under the current procedure, with only 3.5% saying they could.
To avoid facing scrutiny on exam day, some candidates are reportedly switching to contact lenses. An optician in Suwon, south of Seoul, said students who had never worn contacts were coming in to ask how to put them in.
Han said on X on Monday that the checks would be handled carefully “so that candidates acting in good faith do not suffer unnecessary anxiety or inconvenience”.
In his video confession, the accountancy test cheat addressed suneung candidates directly. “The suneung is coming up soon,” he said.
“To anyone thinking of cheating as I did: I am going to tell the investigators everything, so please don’t think, ‘I won’t get caught.’”

Old Park Star, Sober Glory and Baron Noir clash at Ffos Las
Having been declared to clash at Cheltenham over the weekend, Old Park Star and Sober Glory both swerved commitments at Prestbury Park in favour of more suitable conditions in South Wales on Wednesday, and we are treated to a fascinating contest with Baron Noir also thrown into the mix.
Tuesday 17 November 2026 17:32, UK
Cheltenham's loss is Ffos Las' gain on Wednesday as old rivals Old Park Star, Sober Glory and Baron Noir are set to face-off on chase debut and At The Races' Declan Rix previewed the contest.
You always need a bit of luck in this game, no matter what your role or ability. While the elements have unfortunately conspired against those at Exeter so far this season, Ffos Las is the beneficiary of what they are calling The Welsh Arkle on Wednesday, live on Sky Sports Racing.
The race got a huge boost with the somewhat surprise addition of 2026 Supreme Novices' Hurdle winner Old Park Star, a high-profile non-runner on Cheltenham's Saturday card due to the ground being deemed too quick. His inclusion means we have a huge early season clash with an old foe in Sober Glory, last season's unlucky Supreme runner-up.
The inclusion of Old Park Star is no doubt bad luck for those connected to Sober Glory et al; after all, the Henderson-trained horse was meant to run last Saturday, but it's a huge stroke of luck for Ffos Las and indeed, Sky Sports Racing. Exciting early season clashes like this are incredibly rare for novice chasers in Britain - and in general given the monster that the Cheltenham Festival has morphed into - so it's understandable there is a bit of a buzz around the industry ahead of the five-runner Golwg Gwendraeth Beginners' Chase, due off at 13:18pm.
Ground and weather
As of 8.37am on Tuesday, on the back of 16mm since 6pm on Monday, the ground is officially Good (good to soft in places), but with significant rain due. According to the BHA site, tomorrow's forecast reads as, 'blustery with persistent rain, heavy at times throughout the day'. Hopefully it leads to beautiful soft ground which the horses will get through nicely.
The big guns
As the official ratings and betting suggests, Old Park Star (155; 4/6) and Sober Glory (153; 15/8) are the standouts and are set to renew their rivalry having served up a fantastic Cheltenham Festival curtain raiser in March, along with Mydaddypaddy back in third. At the line, the winning margins were 1½ lengths and a nose, with the also reopposing Baron Noir (146; 10/1), Wednesday's third favourite, a further 6 lengths back in fourth.
Wednesday's prices and a glance at the formbook in black and white could lead you down the garden path of just siding the unbeaten hurdler Old Park Star, but replaying the final flight of their Supreme clash is wise, given it had such a significant impact on the race.
Heading to the last in the Supreme, Sober Glory looked to have everything in trouble with a good 1½+ lengths lead before he put in an extra stride, hit the hurdle and landed steeply, losing critical momentum. It was a huge shame for his connections because up to that point he had jumped so well and looked the best horse in the race going to the last.
That mistake cost him dearly, along with many punters having been a huge gamble from 16/1 in the morning to an SP of 9/2. The Philip Hobbs & Johnson White yard clearly felt like they had their charge in great order, produced him beautifully on the day only for that famous last flight on the Old Course at Prestbury Park to scupper a dream start to the 2026 Festival.
His disappointing run 31 days later at Aintree is easily excused on the back of a long season after a huge Cheltenham run and now with his attentions turned to chasing, this former Irish point-to-point winner for Cormac Doyle rates an exciting prospect for the upcoming campaign for owners Brocade Racing.
Standing in his way again is fellow six-year-old Old Park Star, who, to be fair, didn't exactly ping the final flight in the Supreme himself, also putting in an extra stride which led to the son of Well Chosen landing awkwardly but crucially, not losing as much momentum as Sober Glory.
That saw him stay unbeaten in four hurdle starts, after wins at Kempton, Cheltenham and Haydock, showing good versatility in terms of the tracks he could handle along with also displaying tactical adaptability. Having jumped right in places on debut, his hurdling got better and slicker as the campaign progressed and he looked a straight-forward character throughout.
Having been put away after Cheltenham, Old Park Star's attentions now to turn chasing, a game he possesses the physical scope and athleticism for, although unlike Sober Glory he has no point-to-point background. While not ideal, it's possibly a good sign that Nicky Henderson was willing to pitch him into Grade 2 company at Cheltenham on chasing debut before the ground ruled him out.
A horse said to be big and weak last season, there could be much more to come from Old Park Star, his trainer's comments of 'he's still a shell of a horse' last year continually playing on my mind. If he was able to achieve what he did last season when weak, you cannot but be excited about him after another summer on his back.
Chasing to put manners on Baron Noir?
Baron Noir is certainly no no-hoper against Old Park Star and Sober Glory, with 7½ lengths and 6 lengths, respectively, to find with the leading pair, especially if he has settled down for a summer's break and/or fences curb his keen-going ways.
It's in his breeding to be highly-strung, being by Vadamos out of a Dylan Thomas mare, but he's a horse with plenty of ability and it was a clear sign of the belief his trainer Alan King had in him to run in a Supreme when only rated 130.
While essentially well-held at the line, the six-year-old shaped better than the distance beaten, not getting up the hill as well as his Wednesday rivals. With that in mind, the much flatter nature of Ffos Las should suit.
He too has no point-to-point background, but with the King yard ticking along nicely, he is certainly worth a market check.
Skelton pair make up the field
It's not often you would get prices of 33/1 about a Grade 2-winning novice hurdler from the Skelton yard who looks all-over a chaser on novice chase debut, but that's the task facing Carlenrig. His odds are not just about the horses he is taking on, but also the trip, mind.
A winner of the Grade 2 Bristol Novices' Hurdle at Cheltenham last December, he showed a good attitude to win over that 3m trip. On the back of that given his unexposed nature, he looked a big player in the River Don Novices' Hurdle at Doncaster 42 days later - despite carrying a penalty - but having been a stinking drifter (4/1 out to 14/1), fell two out when his race looked to be run.
The former winning Irish pointer picked up a small injury that day and hasn't been seen in 298 days so this looks like a starting point to get his campaign up and running.
Stablemate Bobby's Nelson has his first run for the Skeltons and should be more at home over this 2m trip. He also looks a chaser physically and his three-quarter of a length defeat to Baron Noir last December at Uttoxeter doesn't half look bad now; indeed, you could argue he is overpriced at 80/1 on that effort, but is probably best watched.
A bet?
In truth, this looks a race to watch for the future, but if forced to have a bet, at the prices, it would certainly be SOBER GLORY. I don't think it's far fetched to say he looked the best horse in the Supreme before his final flight mistake, and with his point-to-point background, might have a jumping experience edge over Old Park Star. That said, the Hobbs and White yard are only operating at a 5% strike-rate currently, for all they've had plenty of others run well. Either way, I am very much looking forward to seeing how all these horses take to fences.

The Tamil Nadu Medical Officers Association (TNMOA) has urged the Chief Minister, Health Minister and Managing Director of Tamil Nadu Medical Services (TNMSC) to cancel the corporation’s recent tenders to carry out repair works at warehouses of Tamil Nadu State Marketing Corporation (TASMAC) and to direct that the works be undertaken through the Public Works Department or another agency.
When TNMSC was earlier made to procure gold coins (for ‘Thaimaaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam’), it drew strong criticism. Now, using TNMSC to take up repair works at TASMAC warehouses is strongly condemnable, TNMOA said in a statement.
Earlier, The Hindu had reported that TNMSC has invited tenders for special repairs at TASMAC warehouses in three locations.
Core function of TNMSC
TNMSC was established to procure quality medical equipment and medicines at affordable cost for the Health department, it said. The association said that already, several irregularities were reported in TNMSC’s core function of procuring medicines. There were repeated instances of TNMSC issuing ‘No Objection Certificates’ instead of procuring essential medicines and asking college deans and joint directors to purchase them using funds under the Chief Minister’s Comprehensive Health Insurance Scheme (CMCHIS).
The association expressed concern that instead of addressing the shortcomings and strengthening TNMSC, a model agency in the country, the State government is taking steps that undermine the institution.

The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.
The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.
The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.
Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.
The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.
Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.
In confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.
If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).
According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.
In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.
“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik said. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”
Under the plan, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.
The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.
The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.
One of the EU conditions for Egypt to gain the first €1bn loan was to increase the number of Takaful and Karama beneficiary households by 100,000 to 4.7 million.
In a leaked report to lawmakers in the EU council of ministers and the European parliament, the commission described that requirement as “broadly fulfilled”.
The data in that report, however, reveals a net fall of 62,281 households during this period, owing to what the EU officials describe as “a multi-annual recertification process”. Some beneficiaries were added to the list but a larger number were removed because they were deemed ineligible.
In order to achieve a later instalment of €1.5bn, Egypt was required to “further expand” the programmes, adding 60,000 households to the Takaful and Karama beneficiaries list. A second leaked report to EU lawmakers shows that the commission concluded the target was “fulfilled” because 442,118 families were added to the list.
On this occasion, the commission did not report on numbers removed. Figures from Egypt’s ministry of social solidarity, however, show a net reduction of 23,453 beneficiaries to the programmes in the 11 months until June 2026, the period leading up to the release of that payment. The EU announced the release of the €1.5bn payment in July 2026.
The data has since been deleted from the Egyptian ministry website but the Guardian has seen screenshots and archived webpages.
During a period from 2024 to 26 when the EU required Egypt to add 160,000 households to the rolls of the Karama and Takaful programmes, there was a net decline of 85,734 households.
Timothy Kaldas, the deputy director of the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, said the commission had generally “done a poor job of leveraging the funds of European taxpayers to support genuine stabilisation” on the other side of the Mediterranean. “The strategic interest of Europe is seeing a more economically stable Egypt with a population that is less precarious,” he said.
Sandra Gómez López, a Spanish socialist MEP who recently visited Cairo to assess human rights in Egypt, said the data presented by the Guardian raised important questions. “The commission must explain transparently why it considers these commitments to have been fulfilled and demonstrate that European funding is genuinely contributing to improving social protection for the Egyptian population,” she said.
She stressed that the EU should not withdraw support, “but neither can we allow the country’s strategic importance to lead us to lower our standards when it comes to human rights”.
For critics, the questions about the EU’s willingness to hold Egypt accountable on very precise socioeconomic targets do not bode well for the broader but less defined goals for democracy and human rights.
Strik said: “The fact that Egypt and the commission even seem to ignore the crystal-clear socioeconomic conditions doesn’t increase my expectation that they adhere to the vague precondition on democracy and the rule of law.”
Claudio Francavilla, an associate EU director at Human Rights Watch, said: “Without benchmarks, the EU has turned a human rights conditionality into a blank cheque for Egypt’s authoritarianism.”
In a statement to the Guardian, the European Commission said the policy target on Takaful and Karama referred to new beneficiary families “and not to its net increase”. The spokesperson said there was “no contradiction” between this statement and that in a confidential document that said Egypt was required to “further expand cash transfer programmes”.
Asked about the release of the remaining €1.5bn in promised loans, the commission said it “will be made once all conditions have been met”, referring to 24 economic policy conditions, keeping an IMF programme on track and “taking concrete and credible steps towards respecting effective democratic mechanisms, including a multiparty parliamentary system, and the rule of law, and guaranteeing respect for human rights”.
It added: “Compliance with the conditionality is examined thoroughly” by EU officials and diplomats based on “information provided by the Egyptian authorities and other relevant sources”.
Egypt’s mission to the EU in Brussels did not respond to a request for comment.

NEW DELHI: India and Sweden are looking to move industrial decarbonization from commitments to execution, with the third phase of their Leadership Group for Industry Transition (LeadIT) initiative focusing on scaling low-carbon projects, mobilising private capital and accelerating emissions cuts in hard-to-abate sectors such as steel, cement and transport. LeadIT 3.0, covering 2027-30, was announced by Union environment minister Bhupender Yadav at an industry leaders' roundtable on the sidelines of the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, on Tuesday, according to a government statement. The roundtable was co-chaired by Yadav and Sweden's state secretary for Climate and Enterprise Helena Dyrssen. The new phase will shift the initiative's focus from establishing partnerships to scaling industrial projects, mobilizing capital and delivering tangible results. Its three priorities are technology development and diffusion through industrial projects; capital mobilization and de-risking to connect projects with finance; and capacity building and policy support, including carbon markets and workforce transition. Quick answers to key questions LeadIT 3.0 is the 2027–30 phase of the India-Sweden Leadership Group for Industry Transition initiative. It aims to turn industrial decarbonisation commitments into projects and measurable emissions cuts. Its priorities are developing and sharing technology through industrial projects, mobilising and de-risking capital, and providing capacity-building and policy support. The policy work includes carbon markets and workforce transition. The initiative focuses on hard-to-abate sectors such as steel, cement and transport. Earlier projects explored hydrogen-based ironmaking, industrial heat electrification, carbon capture and utilisation, and lower-carbon cement production. The new phase shifts the focus from establishing partnerships to scaling projects, mobilising finance and delivering results. The second phase facilitated 11 pre-pilot projects in steel and cement. India says the transition should create opportunities for workers and communities, particularly in developing economies, rather than focus only on emissions cuts. It also needs to progress alongside priorities such as poverty alleviation, energy access, jobs and infrastructure. “Geopolitical conflicts, volatile energy markets and competing development priorities make international cooperation even more important, particularly in hard-to-abate industrial sectors,” Yadav said, adding that India's priorities of poverty alleviation, energy access, job creation and infrastructure development must progress alongside its transition to a low-carbon economy. The launch comes as governments and industries face mounting pressure to cut emissions from energy-intensive sectors, where decarbonization often requires substantial capital investment, technological innovation and changes in production processes. India and Sweden launched LeadIT in 2019. Its second phase facilitated 11 pre-pilot projects in steel and cement under the India-Sweden Industry Transition Partnership. These cover hydrogen-based ironmaking, electrification of industrial heat, carbon capture and utilisation, clinker substitution, industrial circularity and the use of artificial intelligence to reduce cement demand. LeadIT has also supported South Africa's investment plan under the Climate Investment Funds and Ethiopia's engagement on low-carbon cement, Yadav said. The initiative's membership has since expanded to 20 countries and 33 companies, with Brazil joining as its latest country member, strengthening participation from the Global South. Yadav called on countries and companies to move beyond feasibility studies towards pilot projects, demonstrations and replication, arguing that industrial transition commitments must translate into measurable outcomes. Highlighting India's climate progress, the minister said the country had reduced its emissions intensity by 37.38% between 2005 and 2022 and achieved 50% of its installed electricity capacity from non-fossil fuel sources, five years ahead of its target. India's additional forest carbon sink has reached around 2.44 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, he added. Yadav said the industrial transition must create opportunities for workers and communities, particularly in developing economies, rather than focus solely on reducing emissions. The launch at COP31, which the Turkish presidency has described as the 'COP of Implementation', is intended to strengthen international cooperation and accelerate the shift from industrial transition commitments to on-ground projects. Angry crowds rally against Slovakia's pro-Russian leader on Velvet Revolution anniversary
Crowds have gathered in Slovakia to protest the government of pro-Russian Prime Minister Robert Fico on the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended communist rule in Czechoslovakia
BRATISLAVA, Slovakia -- People in Slovakia took to the streets Tuesday to rally against the government of pro-Russian Prime Minister Robert Fico on the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution that brought an end to decades of communist rule in Czechoslovakia.
Opposition parties organized the protests in dozens of communities across the country, where Fico remains as Europe’s most pro-Russian leader since Hungary’s Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April.
“We’ve had enough of Fico,” chanted people in Bratislava, where organizers estimated 25,000 gathered in the downtown SNP square. One banner had a message for the prime minister: “Go to hell.”
The capital's rally united the liberal groups Progressive Slovakia and the Democrats with pro-business Freedom and Solidarity, the conservative Christian Democrats and an alliance of ethnic Hungarians. Together they hope to defeat Fico and his coalition government in next year’s parliamentary election.
“Just as in 1989, what unites us must be stronger than what divides us,” said Michal Šimečka, leader of the major opposition Progressive Slovakia party. “We’ll win only if we stick together.”
The government angered opponents by sending Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár to Russia for talks about renewing economic cooperation and other ties between the two countries for the first time since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Fico agreed on the plan during one of his trips to Moscow to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin, and held a Cabinet meeting to discuss a report about Blanár’s visit just hours before the rally on Tuesday.
“Shame, shame,” the crowd chanted in condemnation.
Fico has long been a divisive figure in Slovakia, and thousands have repeatedly rallied to protest his policies. Czechoslovakia split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia in 1993.
His views on Russia’s war on Ukraine and other issues sharply differ from the European mainstream. Fico ended Slovakia’s military aid for Ukraine, opposes EU sanctions on Russia, wants to block Ukraine from joining NATO and rejected EU loan guarantees for Ukraine.

On Monday, the Department of Health and Human Services issued a long-awaited update to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act privacy rule. Originally proposed in January 2021, HHS’ Office for Civil Rights finalized several updates to the rule intended to make it easier to share health information — to coordinate patients’ care between health providers, but also to make it easier for patients to access and share their own data.
The HIPAA privacy rule update puts a particular focus on measures to support patients’ access to their own records. “It’s fair to say that two-thirds of the content of the rule is about this problem, the problem of individual access,” said Lucia Savage, former chief privacy officer at HHS’s Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT.
The final rule reduces the maximum time for covered entities to respond to patient requests from 30 to 15 days. It prevents them from imposing unreasonable measures for individuals requesting records to prove their identity. And it establishes standards for accessing those records through a newly defined category of tools called “personal health applications,” which can include wellness apps and tools linked to fitness trackers. Some of those products have been headlined by other federal agencies during the Trump administration, including the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.

Khalistani supporter who glorified Punjab blast arrested after US deportation
Surinder Singh alias Thikriwal, a supporter of the banned Khalistan Zindabad Force (KZF), was arrested by the NIA at Delhi airport following his deportation from the US.
The National Investigation Agency (NIA) on Thursday arrested Surinder Singh alias Thikriwal, a supporter of the banned Khalistan Zindabad Force (KZF), at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International (IGI) Airport following his deportation from the United States in connection with the April 27 blast on a railway line in Punjab.
According to the NIA, Singh was detained by US authorities and deported to India in coordination with the US government. He was arrested immediately after arriving at the IGI Airport.
The case relates to a blast on the railway line of the Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation of India Ltd (DFCCIL) at kilometre marker 1174-5, between Shambhu and Rajpura railway stations, on April 27. The blast was allegedly carried out by KZF operatives to advance the organisation's terror activities, disrupt communal harmony and destabilise law and order in Punjab.
During the investigation, the NIA found that Singh had allegedly posted a video on his Facebook account after the blast, glorifying and supporting the incident. In the video, he also extended support to those accused of being part of the criminal conspiracy, including Jagroop Singh, who died while carrying out the blast.
The agency said Surinder Singh had referred to the banned Khalistan Zindabad Force as a "Qaumi Organisation" in the video. He also described Ranjeet Singh alias Neeta, a Designated Individual Terrorist (DIT), as "the general of the Qaum".
The NIA had issued a Look Out Circular (LOC) against Singh during the investigation to prevent him from evading the probe. Multiple criminal cases are also registered against him in different districts of Punjab.
With Singh's arrest, the number of accused arrested in the Shambhu-Rajpura railway blast case has risen to eight, the agency said.
The NIA is continuing its investigation into the wider conspiracy behind the blast. The agency is also focusing on dismantling the alleged nexus between terrorists and their associates based abroad and disrupting their funding networks and infrastructure.
The anti-terror agency added further investigation into the matter is progressing.

FA wants to host Nations League finals in England
- Published
England could host the Nations League finals this season after Football Association officials registered their interest.
The semi-final and finals of the competition, due to take place in June, are held in one country.
As well as England, it is understood that Spain and France have also contacted Uefa to register their interest in hosting the final four games, including the bronze medal match, which will run between 9-13 June.
The FA, it is understood, is still discussing potential venues with some doubt over whether Wembley would be available. The only publicly announced Wembley events in June are two concerts by singer Sam Fender, although these are for after the Nations League.
Since the tournament began in 2019, England have never held the finals, with Portugal, Italy, Netherlands and Germany the hosts to date.
Generally, only nations who reach the last four of the Nations League are considered to host the latter stages.
Thomas Tuchel's team will be seeded in Friday's draw for the quarter-finals following their euphoric 3-2 victory over Spain in Madrid, which secured top place in the group.
They could face Belgium, Netherlands, Denmark or Norway in March in the next round before June's finals.
If the FA's bid is successful, it will provide the governing body with an opportunity to host a mini-tournament before Euro 2028, which will be held in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

As Kolkata choked on toxic air following Diwali and Kali Puja celebrations, West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari accused those raising concerns over firecracker pollution of being communists opposed to Hindu traditions. His remarks were consistent with the concerted push by a section of the Right wing to portray criticism of firecrackers as an attack on Hindu religious practices. However, among those complaining about noise levels and pollution in Kolkata were members of Adhikari’s own party and cabinet.
The Bengal CM made the remarks while addressing the media during a visit to the coastal town of Digha on Monday, where he had gone to attend an administrative meeting and visit the Kali Puja organised by the Shyama Prasad Mukherjee Traders Association.
Speaking to reporters, Adhikari said, “There has been an awakening of Sanatan in this state, and some people have a problem with that. The people making these allegations (about firecrackers) had turned Hindu religious festivals into cultural fests… These people do not apply ‘tika’ or religious markings on their foreheads, they do not wear ‘dors’ or religious threads on their wrists, nor do they wear tulsi beads around their necks.”
Adhikari further said, “The communists are raising this issue of firecrackers. We have controlled it in accordance with the Supreme Court’s directives. Firecrackers were burst in some places even after 10 pm, and the police took necessary action. We have stopped DJs, and we do not want environmental pollution. But people will have fun during Diwali. They will celebrate with lights and burst firecrackers. Where is the problem with that?”
While acknowledging that firecrackers had been burst beyond the time limit prescribed by the Supreme Court, Adhikari sought to deflect criticism by pointing to action taken by the administration.
“Those complaining that sound crackers were burst for a few hours longer than the time stipulated by the Supreme Court should know that the Pollution Control Board and the police are taking action against such violations. I would request those complaining about firecrackers to also congratulate the state government for stopping DJs. I will not say that DJ incidents did not happen in remote corners, but I did not hear them blaring, at least near the roads,” he said.
Firecrackers can Cure Diseases, Says Bengal Minister, then Apologises
According to the Supreme Court’s directives, only green firecrackers were allowed to be burst between 8 pm and 10 pm on Diwali. However, statements by ministers, the West Bengal Police’s deletion of a post urging responsible Diwali celebrations, and the general perception that a BJP government would not impose restrictions on Hindu festivals had collectively sent out a clear message: When it came to celebrating a majoritarian festival, the rules could be bent, if not ignored altogether.
BJP leader and Tollygunge MLA Papia Adhikary said on Monday, “Our honourable chief minister has said that people will definitely burst firecrackers. How can we celebrate Kali Puja without firecrackers? But we will burst them in accordance with the instructions of the local police station. Also, many diseases can be prevented simply by lighting firecrackers.”
Although Adhikary later apologised and backtracked on her statement, claiming that the media had misinterpreted her remarks, the message had already got across.
A section of social media users also began targeting dissenting voices who tried to reason with their fellow citizens. A user named Partha Pratim Kundu, who describes himself as a wildlife photographer, asked in a post how elderlies, children and birds and animals survived in earlier times when there was no curb on firecrackers.
Another Facebook user, Chayan Mukherjee, who hailed the chief minister’s indulgence on firecrackers, claimed in a post that “most of the Indian environmentalists and human rights activists, as well as professors at various institutions, receive funding from outside to oppose the country’s development.”
Domkal’s CPI(M) MLA Mostafijur Rahaman Rana had urged people to celebrate Diwali as a festival of lights, without noise and loud firecrackers. BJP MLA Tarunjyoti Tiwari gave the issue a communal twist by asking whether the legislator would also call for a ‘bloodless Eid’.
State BJP leader Keya Ghosh also criticised Mostafijur Rahaman for advocating a noise-free and smoke-free Diwali.
The lone CPIM MLA of West Bengal had wished smokeless, soundless Diwali.

The political messaging was accompanied by widespread violations on the ground. A large section of the public openly flouted firecracker regulations. Almost all media outlets reported that loud firecrackers were burst throughout the night severely inconveniencing elderlies, children and also pets, birds and stray animals.
Kolkata’s AQI reached 623 around 11 pm on Sunday night, reported The telegraph. At 12.51 am on Monday, IQAir classified the city’s air quality as hazardous, recording an AQI of 532, with PM2.5 at 342 and PM10 at 405. Both particulate matter concentrations were several times higher than the WHO’s recommended limits.
Left with no other option, residents in several localities took matters into their own hands, protesting against the rampant bursting of firecrackers and intervening to stop it. Facebook user Anitesh Chakraborty narrated his experience in a post.
Chakraborty went up to a neighbouring apartment’s rooftop around 1.45 am to ask people bursting firecrackers to stop. While some residents supported his objection, others on nearby rooftops mocked him with gestures and taunts. Nevertheless, the intervention succeeded in stopping the firecrackers. He observed that the rooftops of apartment buildings had become spaces where people felt free to flout restrictions, and argued people to raise their voices against such violations.
According to a report by the Times of India, by 1 am, the West Bengal Pollution Control Board had received 84 noise-related complaints, while Kolkata Police had recorded 434 complaints.
Police rounded up 371 people for bursting illegal firecrackers, arresting 205 of them. Another 387 people were arrested for disorderly conduct. Several commentators pointed out that the most effective way to curb the use of illegal firecrackers was to stop their manufacture and sale. This year, only 238.6 kg of such products were seized, compared to 853 kg last year.
Kolkata’s high-rise buildings were particular hotspots for violations of firecracker and noise restrictions. Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari himself acknowledged that the rules could not be enforced in every high-rise apartment building, as the state did not have enough police personnel.
Even hospitals located in silence zones were not spared. According to a report by The Telegraph, areas near hospitals such as B C Roy, R G Kar, M R Bangur and Sishumangal also faced onslaught of loud firecrackers.
To Celebrate Responsibly or Not? Bengal Police in a Fix
Signs of this situation had emerged earlier, when the West Bengal Police deleted a firecracker awareness post within hours of publishing it, as previously reported by Alt News.
Published on the morning of November 5 with the caption, “Please celebrate responsibly. It’s our Diwali too!”, the AI-generated poster featured two stray cats and a dog shivering due to the loud noise of firecrackers. However, it was deleted within three hours.
The post’s comment section was flooded with threatening messages directed at police and familiar Right-wing arguments, including questions about whether the police would also call for a ‘bloodless Eid’ and why the police and administration interfered only in Hindu festivals.
Similarly, Delhi Police, too, deleted a firecracker awareness post, while the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) removed a video featuring actor Dia Mirza advocating for a pollution-free Diwali from its social media accounts. Both decisions followed social media outrage from BJP-RSS supporters who claimed that the posts hurt Hindu religious sentiments.
A similar message by AISA leader Neha Bora also faced backlash from the far-right social media ecosystem.
It is that time of the year where our conversations will be accompanied by sore throats and respiratory problems.
But who is responsible for this?
Clean air and a pollution free city is a right and must be demanded from the government. https://t.co/SZHAC7l1fl
— Neha (@neha_aisa) November 4, 2026
BJP MLAs Complain about Noise Levels
Although a section of the Right wing encouraged unrestrained celebrations during Diwali and Kali Puja in the name of upholding Hindu traditions, some voices within the BJP struck a different note.
BJP leader and Sonarpur Dakshin MLA Roopa Ganguly tagged Kolkata Police in a post on Facebook stating she was unable to sleep because of the noise of firecrackers. However, the post is no longer available now.
State urban development minister Agnimitra Paul was seen roaming around the city in a police vehicle, attempting to curb the firecracker menace.
Paul said, “Please think about other people. Consider the condition of the elderly and the sick. The firecrackers are bursting so loudly that my heart is trembling.”
However, these interventions came too little, too late. The ruling dispensation had, through its rhetoric and its reluctance to enforce restrictions, effectively given people a free hand to flout the law, with the environment and public health bearing the consequences.

Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
And now Kimi, who turned 20 only in August, has dominated F1 in only his second season, and become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he entered, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He took the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli took six poles and six wins in the first 11 races, establishing a 50-point lead in the championship.
Mercedes lost their dominant form in the second half of the season in the face of challenges from first McLaren and then Red Bull.
But Antonelli remained a consistent threat at the front, and he killed off his Monza ghosts in the Italian Grand Prix with a stunning victory after an engine penalty led to him starting 19th on the grid.
He put in a drive of clinical excellence and, with help from a safety car, chased down and caught Russell in the final laps to take a win that will go down in folklore.
The extent of his turnaround in form has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says.
"We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said 'Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1'," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

Rooney says he considered taking his own life at Man Utd
- Published
Warning: This article contains references to suicide
Wayne Rooney says he was "contemplating suicide" during his playing days at Manchester United and was "speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up".
The former England captain joined United from Everton in 2004 and went on to become the club's record goalscorer, with 253 goals in 559 appearances.
But Rooney, speaking with Gabby Logan on the Life at the Midpoint podcast, external, detailed his struggles off the pitch when eldest son Kai, who is now 17, was a baby.
"When I was drinking, I would lock myself in my house for two days and just drink," said Rooney, when asked about the lowest point in his life.
"This is probably in my best part of my career playing wise."
The 41-year-old went on to explain how he "struggled to deal with it all" and, after opening up to his wife Coleen and his mother, knew he "needed help to get through it".
"I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with," he added.
"I didn't want Kai seeing me like that, so that's why I'd hide away as well.
"I got to a place where you're contemplating suicide. I just didn't want to be around anyone. I didn't want to see people in the streets. I didn't want to go into shops.
"I was always comfortable on a football pitch, but everything else, [I] really struggled with it."
Rooney, who scored 53 goals in 120 England appearances, was recently named pundit of the year at the Broadcast Sport Awards and is currently appearing on reality TV show I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.
He helped United win five Premier League titles, the Champions League, Europa League, FA Cup and three EFL Cups before leaving them to return to the Toffees in 2017.
But the former forward said he learned to mask his feelings during his lowest moments.
"You don't want to show any weakness, so you try to mask it," Rooney added.
"Even though I knew the position I was in, it was difficult to actually admit that I was in that position because I felt like you feel less of a man, if you like, for doing that.
"I was speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up with me because when I look back I was probably at the height of my career, I've just had a young son, I've just been married.
"It should be the happiest point in my life and it wasn't.
"It was probably the lowest point because of the selfish acts I was taking.
"Coleen helped me massively. She could have walked away, it was that bad, but she stuck by me and helped me get through it."

The Mundka monitoring station of the Delhi Pollution Control Board recorded a PM2.5 concentration of 3,744 µg/m³ at 2 am on the Diwali night, which is 60 times the standard measure. Yes, you read it right. 60 times. Reports emerged the next day that 93 of the top 100 cities with worst AQI were from India following Diwali celebrations on November 8. AIIMS pulmonologist Vijay Hadda told ANI on November 9, “I am honestly surprised that we are still alive. I do not think this kind of air is suitable for human survival.”
In any country with a functional government, this would warrant the environment minister to at least make a statement, even if not take direct accountability. Not in India.
Union minister of environment, forest and climate change, Bhupender Yadav, has remained conspicuously silent on the country’s deteriorating air quality before or after Diwali.
From the days preceding Diwali to four days after the festival when this article is being written, Yadav neither issued a single public appeal urging citizens to responsibly engage in celebrations, nor used his social media handles to spread awareness about the environmental consequences of bursting firecrackers or to address the mounting pollution crisis affecting major parts of the country.
Did Bhupender Yadav go Missing from Public Platforms?
Far from it. Yadav remained active on social media throughout this period. Between November 1 and November 12, he made 29 posts on his X account. Not one of them addressed the worsening air pollution, deteriorating air quality across Indian cities, or the need for public awareness and precautionary measures.
The days before Diwali are also crucial because pollution levels skyrocketing on the day of the festival and immediately after has become an annual phenomenon. It is reasonable to expect the minister holding the environment and climate change portfolio to make a public appeal ahead of Diwali, more so because firecracker pollution has been a matter of contention and has reached the Supreme Court in recent years.
Clearly, the Alwar MP thinks otherwise.
Modi Reigns Supreme on Yadav’s X Timeline

These included amplification of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Diwali greetings to citizens, Modi’s Diwali celebrations and interactions with jawans at the CoBRA (Commando Battalion for Resolute Action) Operations Base in Karanpur, in Chhattisgarh’s Bastar district, as well as Yadav’s own festive greetings.
