Iran launches a third round of strikes on Bahrain, host of U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet
CAIRO — Iran fired drones on Tuesday at a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain in the third Iranian attack in recent days on American military targets in the Persian Gulf island kingdom, and the U.S. retaliated by firing at Iranian targets along an important shipping route.
The attacks and counterattacks interrupted a roughly two-month lull in fighting, as Iran's targeting of Bahrain brought condemnations from the region. Analysts said stalled peace negotiations and Tehran's growing economic pressures were raising the risk of a substantial escalation.
Bahrain said that its air defense systems had successfully intercepted the "treacherous Iranian aerial attacks." The U.S. military likewise said the attack inflicted no damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel.
Hours later, a U.S. fighter jet carried out a strike on a missile launch site in the Strait of Hormuz belonging to Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard, a U.S. official said.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to detail sensitive military operations, said "precision munitions" were used in the strike on Qeshm Island and that the U.S. was responding to "aggression" toward U.S. personnel.
A local official, Ahmad Nafisi, said the strike caused no damage to residential or commercial areas or infrastructure.
The U.S. military has periodically carried out what appear to be limited strikes on Qeshm Island and other Iranian targets this month. Iran's attack Tuesday was its third on American military targets in Bahrain in five days.
Iran may be shifting its strategy amid economic pain
Iran has been suffering under a naval blockade that the U.S. has enforced on it for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for the world's energy supplies where Iran and its proxies have disrupted shipping since the war began Feb. 28.
U.S. President Donald Trump has been circumspect on his next steps for the Iran war, now in its eighth month despite an initial promise it would last only a matter of weeks. He has said new strikes are highly unlikely, but he has also sent a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East — and told Vice President JD Vance that talks aren't needed at this time.
Oil tankers moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection have helped return oil shipments from the Gulf to roughly prewar levels. The blockade, meanwhile, is damaging Iran's economy by curbing the flow of Iranian crude to the global market.
Iran's attacks could signal a shift in its strategy after months during which it waited for an attack and then retaliated to target the operational capability of bases, Tehran-based security analyst Mostafa Najafi told The Associated Press.
Bahrain hosts the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet, which has already sustained damage in previous attacks by Iran since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.
Iranian leaders will now be weighing whether "breaking the blockade through escalation is less costly than accepting its continuation," Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote in an analysis posted to X.
"In other words, the risk of renewed war no longer depends solely on whether Trump decides to attack Iran again," he said. "It also depends on whether Tehran concludes that the costs of continued restraint have become greater than the risks of escalation."
U.S. expands its Middle East naval presence
With the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group in the region, the combined U.S. naval assets in the Persian Gulf, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Mediterranean now exceed the force deployed when the U.S. and Israel launched the war.
The presence provides greater offensive firepower and missile interception capacity, according to a new analysis by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.
The Roosevelt joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller U.S. Navy ships, which are in the region to maintain the blockade of Iranian shipping. U.S. Central Command wouldn't comment on whether it plans to keep all three carrier strike groups in the region.
Iran says it's responding to U.S. attacks
Iran's attack on Bahrain on Tuesday came after it targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in the country on Friday, and on Sunday fired at a radar system at an American helicopter base there. Despite claims of success, there appeared to be little or no damage done.
The attacks followed U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers and ongoing drone surveillance operations, and Iran said it was retaliating.
"Continued aggression against the country's airspace, as well as the use of regional military bases and facilities for hostile acts against Iran, will not go unanswered," Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement.
Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates each condemned Iran's attack on Bahrain, calling it a violation of Bahrain's sovereignty and a threat to its security and stability.
Negotiations to end the war have stagnated, despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar.
In a statement, Qatar said Iran's "continued attacks" on Bahrain "undermine diplomatic efforts" and Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari, speaking at a news briefing in Doha, warned that any escalation in fighting posed an "extremely grave danger" to the prospects of reaching an agreement.
Iran may be losing patience as conflict drags on
The attacks are a sign that Tehran is growing impatient as its economic woes mount, said Sascha Bruchmann, a Bahrain-based defense analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
"Shooting at ships causes fear, but is not effective enough to change the strategic equation," Bruchmann told the AP. "Tehran knows it needs to do something, but I wouldn't overestimate what we saw against Bahrain this week. This is not it — yet."
Iranian officials have termed the current situation "no war, no peace" and vowed to end it.
Tehran has said that it's open to a negotiated deal, but also signaled a readiness to escalate the conflict in the face of tightening sanctions and the blockade that are throttling Iran's economy.
Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran's influential parliamentary chief, posted on social media on Monday that leaders view U.S. economic pressure as an effort to create a domestic "security crisis."
Iran has continued to attack ships seeking to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which leads from the Persian Gulf toward the open seas. In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthi rebels now have solidified their control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another critical shipping route.

Bengal Christian group advises churches, schools to remain vigilant to prevent attacks
Bangiya Christiya Pariseba (BCP) said ringing the bell three times at an unusual hour will serve as a distress signal
An umbrella group of West Bengal’s Christian organisations has asked churches and schools to remain vigilant during the Christmas festivities amid reports safety concerns. “Instruct church staff and members that if any suspicious or unfamiliar group enters the church or pastorate compound, anyone present should immediately ring the church bell three times,” said Bangiya Christiya Pariseba (BCP) in an advisory.
It added that congregants and neighbours should be informed in advance that ringing the bell three times at an unusual hour will serve as an emergency distress signal, prompting them to gather at the church immediately and stand peacefully in solidarity beside the pastor. “Ensure that anyone on the premises promptly alerts the local police station without delay at the first sign of intrusion or threat.”
The advisory urged churches to install CCTV cameras covering critical vantage points facing the main entrance gate and the outer compound. It added that one camera should cover the main church interior area.
BCP spokesperson Herod Mullick said head pastors, parish priests, and church secretaries have been advised to inform the police and the administration in writing in advance regarding Christmas programmes, Sunday services, and special gatherings, and to retain a stamped copy of the receipt.
Mullick said that there have been nearly 50 attacks against Christians since May and blamed Hindu organisations. He added that cases have been registered in only about one-third of the incidents. “In many cases, the victims could not even go to the police station to lodge the complaints, fearing more attacks.”
Police maintained that action was taken whenever they received complaints. “Police have taken action whenever any complaints were registered. In most cases, the investigation revealed that clashes were not related to any religious activities. A few people were arrested, and police pickets were set up to ease tensions,” said a police officer.

Bengal Christian Council president Reverend Paritosh Canning cited considerable anxiety and apprehension among the community and sought chief minister Suvendu Adhikari’s intervention.
BJP spokesperson Debjit Sarkar said Bhattacharya’s comments were against a particular school. “Even they know which school committed this act. The party is not against the Christian community. We are just following the Constitution and the existing anti-conversion laws.”

Quick Answer
If your Android phone’s battery drains too quickly, try enabling auto-brightness, using dark mode, limiting background apps, reducing screen timeout, and turning off unused features. These 15 practical tips can improve battery life and help maintain battery health.
I cannot function without my phone. It makes my experience better during my walks, jogs, and all other activities throughout the day. Unfortunately, I have to charge my phone multiple times a day or keep a power bank as a backup, just in case. The ease created by my Android phone is instantly undone by the quickly draining battery. Along with the phone, I should carry a cable, an adapter, and a power bank.
In that frustration, I started looking into why my Android phone battery was draining fast. I checked the battery usage data, identified what was causing the drain, and fixed those issues. Now, my battery lasts longer. These are the tips that helped me improve the battery life on my Android phone.
Table of Contents
Android Phone Battery Draining Fast? Try These 10 Tips
I used these tips to improve my Android phone’s battery life on a single charge. You can use the tips that work for you without sacrificing the functionality you need.
Enable Auto Brightness
Brightness affects how visible the display is, irrespective of the light in our surroundings. When we keep the brightness too high, it affects our eyes in the dark. In addition to that, the battery drains too quickly when powering the high brightness for your phone’s display.
If we keep the brightness low, it affects the visibility of our phone’s display during daytime when we are out in the open under the sun. To not affect the visibility and save the battery from draining quickly, we can enable Auto Brightness on our phone.
The auto-brightness feature on our phones adjusts the brightness of our display based on the light in our surroundings. For example, when you are outside where there is abundant sunlight, the auto-brightness feature increases the brightness to make visibility better for you. Similarly, it decreases the brightness when you are in a dark or dimmed environment.
To enable auto-brightness on your phone, open the Settings app and go to Display or Display & brightness settings. The jargon for options varies by manufacturer.
Find Brightness options and toggle the button beside Auto brightness to enable it. You will see the brightness of your screen increase or decrease as per your environment in real time.
Enable Dark Mode
Android phones with OLED or AMOLED displays consume more power for display. If it is set to light mode, a major chunk of battery life goes to power. Setting the screen to dark mode makes it easier on the battery. The battery does not need to power the entire display by switching off the black pixels.
You can enable dark mode in the display settings of your phone. Open the Settings app and find the display settings. Set the display mode to Dark mode.
Dark mode, at first, may look odd. Once you get accustomed to it, there is no going back.
Disable Always-On Display
Always-On Display consumes a significant amount of power from the battery. The display always shows time or notifications even when you are not using the phone actively.
You must disable the Always-On Display feature if you do not have any use for it. Open the Settings app on your Android phone and search for Always-On Display. It will show the option. Tap on it. Toggle the button beside Always-On Display to turn it off.
It may not reduce battery drain noticeably, but small things like these can help optimize battery life.
Set Screen Refresh Rate to Auto
The screen refresh rate feature on Android gives us a smoother display experience. Manufacturers flaunt the screen refresh rate while launching and advertising new smartphones. The higher the refresh rate of a screen is, the more battery it consumes. If you are not a gamer or do not use your phone for experiences that demand a higher refresh rate, you may set the Screen refresh rate to Auto.
Open the Settings app on your phone, search for refresh rate, and open the refresh rate options. Then, set the refresh rate to Auto or Auto-select. Instead of using a higher refresh rate that consumes more battery, your phone now optimizes the screen refresh rate based on the app or activity for a smoother experience. You may also set it to Standard or anything that offers a 60 Hz refresh rate to extend battery life.
If you are a gamer, Auto refresh rate would be the best option.
Decrease Screen Off Time
Screen off time is something we mostly overlook when looking to optimize battery on our phones. If the screen off time is set to a longer time, it consumes battery and aids in draining faster. Small things like these add up and drain the battery.
Open the Settings app on your phone and search for screen off. You can find the Screen off feature in Display settings. Tap on the Screen off or Auto Screen off options (based on your manufacturer) and select a shorter time.
Now, when you do not use the phone, the screen will be turned off as per the time you have selected. The shorter the time, the more you optimize the battery.
Disable Unnecessary Sounds and Vibrations
Sound and vibration for ringtones and notifications are okay. But touch vibrations, keyboard sounds, dial pad tones, lock sounds, and other such sounds or vibrations when we do something on our phone are not necessary. They stress the battery and make it drain faster.
Disabling those unnecessary sounds and vibrations enhances the battery life and saves you from charging the phone frequently.
Open the Settings app on your phone and go to Sound & vibration settings. Go to More sounds (on OxygenOS) or similar settings where you can enable or disable additional sounds, based on your manufacturer.
Then, disable the sounds that you feel are unnecessary by toggling the buttons beside them.
This can optimize battery life, and you can notice the difference within a few hours. Additionally, you can tweak the vibration intensity to optimize your battery further regarding sound and vibration settings.
Check for Apps That Use a Lot of Battery
Android provides detailed battery data where we can see which app is consuming more battery, how long each charge lasts, etc. Using the battery data, we can optimize the apps that consume a lot of battery or install alternatives that consume less battery.
We can access the battery data through the Battery settings. Open Settings and go to Battery settings on your device. Scroll down to the Battery usage by app section in the Battery settings and see which app is using more battery. Tap on the app that is consuming a lot of battery.
It opens the detailed view of battery consumption in the last 24 hours. You can also see options to control battery consumption for the particular app by restricting background activity, etc. Select Restrict background activity if you want to optimize battery and extend its life.
If you want the app to run in the background, you can set it to Smart mode if your manufacturer provides such an option. Repeat the process until you restrict all the power-hungry apps on your device. This significantly improves the life of your battery in each charge.
Turn On the Option to Enter Power Saving Mode Automatically
In the Battery settings, you will find Power saving settings or options. Go to Power saving settings and toggle the button beside Automatically enter Power saving mode. Then, set the battery percentage that should trigger the power saving mode on your device.
Your device will enter Power saving mode when it triggers the battery percentage you set, and it will last longer.
Disable WiFi, Mobile Data, Location, and Bluetooth When Not in Use
You might have noticed your phone battery drains quicker than normal when you pair Bluetooth devices or use location actively. It is better to turn them off when you do not use them.
Keeping WiFi, mobile data, location, and Bluetooth on, even without any usage, consumes a good amount of battery. When you are not actively using any of them, turning them off saves you some battery.
Turn Off Additional Features
There are many features that we rarely use, but consume a good amount of battery. They are live wallpapers, widgets that we do not use, opening web pages and leaving them running in the background, manufacturer apps that run automatically, etc.
Disabling or turning them off saves us a lot of battery. In addition to them, when we install a new app, it asks for notification permissions, location permissions, etc. Disabling notifications for unimportant apps also saves our battery from draining quickly.
These tips, when used together, will optimize your Android device’s battery and extend its life in each charge cycle. Even after doing all this, the battery may drain quickly due to deteriorated battery health. Let’s see how to check and optimize battery health on Android.
How to Optimize Battery Health on Android
The battery on our Android phone degrades with use, and the health drops from 100% to lower levels. The lower the health of your battery, the less power it stores. The capacity keeps on degrading. This is not limited to iPhones. Android phones also started showing battery health. It depends on your manufacturer.
To check the battery health on your Android, you can use third-party apps like Battery Guru or AccuBattery. You may use the app of your choice too, if your manufacturer does not provide an option to look at your battery’s health.
To expand the life and usability of our Android phone, we need to preserve the health of the battery. If not, we may have to replace the battery or the phone altogether. You can preserve the battery health on Android by following these simple tips.
Set a Custom Charging Limit
Android phones let us set a custom charging limit to preserve battery health and protect it from fast degradation of capacity. Manufacturers recommend setting the charging limit to 80- 90% and not beyond that. Charging our phone up to 100% every time is actually not recommended by manufacturers.
We always need to make sure our phone battery never falls below 10% or charges beyond 90%. You can set a custom charging limit in the Battery settings of your phone.
Open the Settings app on your phone and search for Battery health. Open the Battery health options. Toggle the button beside Custom charging limit. Then, set the limit as per the recommendations of the manufacturer.
These options may vary based on your phone manufacturer. The options remain the same, but the wording may change. Follow accordingly to set a custom charging limit.
After setting the custom charging limit, your phone will never charge beyond that percentage. If your manufacturer offers Smart Charging, Adaptive Charging, or Smart Charge options, you may even enable them to let them implement charging patterns based on your charging habits.
Use Chargers or Cables From Device Manufacturers
Charging phones with the available charger is bad for our device’s battery. We must get an adapter and cable made by the manufacturer to save the battery. If they are not available, we must ensure we get charging accessories that are compatible with our device from trusted brands.
Before getting a new charger for your phone, look at the specifications of your device and get the adapter and cable that support the power specified for your device.
Never Let Your Phone Overheat
Batteries degrade faster when they overheat or are exposed to heat. Do not expose your phone to direct sunlight or hot areas. Do not use your phone for heavy activities like gaming while it is charging.
Use Recommended Battery Settings
Phone manufacturers recommend certain settings to preserve battery health and extend its life. They can be found under the options provided in the Battery settings or the Battery optimization app provided by the manufacturer.
Follow those recommendations strictly to save your battery from degradation and faster draining.
Install Updates Regularly
It is not a wise choice to ignore installing pending updates. Android phones get monthly security updates and software updates regularly. We need to make sure they are installed automatically.
Fix a Fast-Draining Battery on Android
If you notice the battery of your Android phone is draining fast, you need to make sure there are no apps running in the background. Limit app activity in the background, update apps, turn off features that you do not use, install updates, and fix all the issues that are contributing to fast battery drain.

Hajra Begum rolls a potato in her hands, checking its skin for cuts, soft spots and signs of rot. After a day harvesting in her family’s field in Chorwan, a remote mountain village in Gurez, Indian-administered Kashmir, she is sorting the crop for winter storage. Some of the potatoes will feed her family through the cold months; others will be saved for planting in spring.
“It should be perfect for planting,” she says. “If you keep a bad potato, you will waste the whole next year.”
Begum, 40, is preparing to lower the potatoes into a khraw, a traditional underground storage pit lined with straw and sealed against the cold. For generations, khraws have kept potatoes, turnips and cabbages through Himalayan winters, when heavy snowfall cuts villages off from the Kashmir valley and temperatures fall below -20C (-4F) – cold enough to crack pipes and freeze diesel.
But the practice is slowly dying out. As roads have improved and young people have left for work and education, fewer families maintain the pits. Their decline threatens not only a traditional way of storing food but also the local potato varieties themselves and the knowledge of which ones store well, resist rot and produce reliable harvests.
“When I was young, almost every family had three or four pits,” Begum says. “Now, down in the main valley, they have abandoned the practice altogether. Only a handful of families still use them. The rest buy from the market or subsidised ones from the government.”
Begum learned from her mother how to tell potatoes that store well from those that rot or sprout too quickly. She is passing this on to her daughter, but is unsure whether the skill will survive into another generation.
Gurez is a high-altitude Himalayan valley perched near the Line of Control, the heavily militarised boundary separating Indian- and Pakistani-administered Kashmir. About 80 miles (125km) from Srinagar, the valley remains cut off each winter when snow closes Razdan pass, its main road link, which sits at roughly 3,600 metres.
It is home to the Dard-Shin people, an Indigenous community who speak Shina and have a culture that is distinct from Kashmiri, with community links across the border in Gilgit-Baltistan, administered by Pakistan.
Potatoes account for about 45% of Gurez’s cultivated area, according to a 2019 study by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research’s National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources (ICAR-NBPGR), a government body that studies and conserves India’s crop diversity. Yet the genetic diversity of the valley’s potatoes has not been systematically documented.
Dr Sheikh M Sultan, a senior scientist based at ICAR-NBPGR’s Srinagar station, surveyed the valley and later struggled to find some of the varieties he had once encountered. “When I first visited, I saw many varieties,” he says. “Later, I could hardly locate even one sample of some. The loss of genetic diversity is tremendous.”
Sultan says migration, improved roads and changing lifestyles have contributed to the decline. As traditional farming disappears, so does knowledge about selecting, cultivating and preserving local varieties.
“When people stop producing their own seeds and start relying entirely on commercial varieties, the loss can be irreparable,” he says.
He warns that research institutions often prioritise introduced varieties over indigenous crops whose characteristics remain poorly understood. “Our indigenous varieties may possess valuable characteristics, including tolerance to cold and resistance to certain pests and diseases,” he says.
“These are resources we should be studying and improving, rather than neglecting.”
Climate breakdown is adding to the pressures on farmers across the Himalayas. People in Gurez report drier springs, reduced snowfall and water shortages, which they say have affected potato production.
Abdul Jabbar Mapnoo, 70, a farmer in Chorwan, remembers winters when deep snow covered the valley. “Every house used to have two or three khraw, each holding about five quintals – 500kg – of potatoes,” he says. “The springs are drying up, and there is less snow in winter. Potato production has fallen. I remember winters when six feet of snow would cover the valley in January or February.”
As farming becomes more difficult and markets easier to access, households have less incentive to grow their own potatoes. Varieties adapted to local conditions over generations could disappear from cultivation before researchers establish what makes them distinctive.
Dr Parveen Kumar, a scientist at the Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology of Kashmir, says locally adapted varieties should not be overlooked. “Climate change is a reality, and farmers need to be aware of adaptation strategies,” he says.
Pressure on farmland poses another risk. In Gurez, where cultivable land is scarce, the Kishanganga hydroelectric project has affected land in the valley through acquisition and submergence. Among the areas affected is Badwan, a village known for its potatoes.
One potential route for preserving the varieties could be through using geographical indications – a designation granted by the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization, and is similar to the French appellation d’origine contrôlée. It can be used on goods that have a specific origin and possess qualities or a reputation linked to this – which can help increase the market value and give them greater recognition. This, and the globally important agricultural heritage systems programme have helped areas such as the saffron-growing landscape of Pampore in Kashmir.
However, recognition alone will not preserve the varieties. They must be identified and documented before they disappear from cultivation, along with farmers’ knowledge of how to select, store and replant them.
In Chorwan, Begum unloads the last sack of potatoes into the pit and covers it, ready for another winter. Some will feed her family; the rest will be replanted in spring. Knowing which potatoes to eat and which to save as seed relies on knowledge passed down through generations.
If these varieties are not documented while they are still being cultivated, Kashmir may lose a living agricultural treasure trove before scientists can fully understand what it contains.

Sandpapergate: Usman Khawaja and David Warner question Cricket Australia’s new forum following explosive fallout
Cricket Australia: "After careful consideration, the CA Board has decided to establish a forum that will allow players and staff involved in the events of South Africa in 2018 to share their experiences and perspectives"; forum set up following explosive claims in Usman Khawaja's book
Wednesday 18 November 2026 08:21, UK
Usman Khawaja and David Warner have questioned Cricket Australia's decision to set up an independent forum to explore the 'Sandpapergate' scandal.
Debate about the ball tampering drama of 2018 has been raging Down Under since the publication of explosive claims in Khawaja's autobiography.
Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft suffered lengthy bans eight years ago after a short investigation found them to be solely guilty, but Khawaja has alleged the entire squad and staff were aware of the plot.
Warner and reserve seamer Chadd Sayers have backed his account, while current Australia captain Pat Cummins has issued a comprehensive denial.
But Cricket Australia (CA) has already ruled out the prospect of any new punishments and has instead invited all parties to share their recollections - without fear of reprisals.
Warner: There should be an open inquiry
The reaction of two of the main protagonists to the announcement was not entirely positive, with both Warner and Khawaja expressing reservations about whose version of events would emerge.
"I appreciate where their heart is, and I'll support the board in this. I just wanted to take accountability, and I've done it for the three guys who I think were unfairly treated," Khawaja told Fox Sports.
"I could go in there and say something, but then the board can decide that they're not going to release that, and I just feel like then we just go in a circle again."
Warner, sat with Khawaja on a punditry panel for Wednesday's ODI between Australia and England, echoed his former opening partner's comments.
"I would have liked an open, independent inquiry, and the people that were there at the time actually can come forward and speak, because we have no idea about what's happened behind closed doors," he said.
"Look, we put our hands up. We accepted what Cricket Australia handed down to us. It's not about penalties. It's just about coming up with transparency and accountability."
Darren Lehmann, Australia's head coach in 2018, was more positive.
"I actually like it, I do," he said.
"I think we've done the best of a terrible situation. For me, it's the light at the end of the tunnel."
CA chief explains new sandpapergate forum
CA chief executive Todd Greenberg and interim chair David Boon appeared at a hastily convened press conference in Hobart to announce a move they hope will take the heat out of the controversy.
"After careful consideration, the CA Board has decided to establish a forum that will allow players and staff involved in the events of South Africa in 2018 to share their experiences and perspectives," said Boon.
"We believe this is in the best interests of the game. For almost a decade, the fallout from those events has remained part of the conversation around Australian cricket.
"It has been a difficult chapter for many people and, increasingly, the ongoing debate has become a distraction from the game. We believe it is time for a circuit breaker.
"This forum is not about relitigating the past. It is about creating an opportunity for those who wish to be heard to tell their stories in a respectful environment, and for our sport to listen.
"Australian cricket is at its strongest when it is united. We owe it to everyone who loves the game to make every reasonable effort to move forward together, with understanding, respect and perspective."
Healy: Rehashing Sandpapergate a massive stain on cricket
Also on Wednesday, Australian Test great Ian Healy questioned why Khawaja had reignited the debate with the release of his book eight years after the fact.
Healy claimed Australian cricketers on the sandpaper tour will now be remembered as "liars forever" following the claims.
"Hopefully we got close to the truth in the investigation; those who didn't get an interview and didn't go forward, they're guilty whistleblowers now," Healy said on SEN radio.
"They didn't come forward when it was saveable, now there's a massive stain on cricket and they'll be known as liars forever.
"There is no reason this should have been rehashed. This was not Uzzy's story to tell, he wasn't involved and didn't do anything. Why write about that? He should have done it the day after the occurrence. It's Davey's book to write."

Rights beyond the pad: making menstrual health services work in every school
The Supreme Court has recognised menstrual health as a constitutional right and laid down obligations for schools and governments. The real challenge now is making these services function reliably, every month, in every school
Recognising menstrual health as a right requires more than distributing sanitary napkins. It requires safe products, clean and private toilets, water, covered bins, regular waste disposal as well as accurate information and access to health services. File photograph used for representational purposes only
The Supreme Court’s January 2026 judgment in Dr. Jaya Thakur v. Government of India recognised menstrual health as part of the right to life under Article 21 and directed States and Union Territories to provide free sanitary napkins, functional gender-segregated toilets, usable water and safe menstrual waste disposal facilities in every government and private school.
The success of this judgment, however, will not be measured in courtrooms. It will be measured in whether a girl can access a sanitary napkin, use a clean toilet with running water and dispose of menstrual waste safely.

A Russian military transport plane has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, the country's defence ministry said, according to state-run media.
The An-12 aircraft went down during a "scheduled flight" in an "uninhabited area" in the Kemerovo region, the ministry said in a statement.

Leaked Files Show Deutsche Bank Protected Russian Profits Despite Warnings
“As you know we have a large Russian Oligarchs client population,” an analyst wrote as the bank braced for sanctions against wealthy clients.
When Russian missiles began pummeling Ukraine in February 2022, executives at one of the world’s largest banks sensed trouble headed their way.
Within hours of an invasion that set off a war that is now in its fifth year, Western governments issued new financial sanctions intended to further isolate Russia from the world economy.
At Deutsche Bank, a longtime bank of Russian industry titans and oligarchs, officials scrambled to get ahead of the damage. “Russian Sanctions Urgent Request” read the subject line of an email sent by one of Deutsche’s anti-financial crime specialists to her colleagues.
“As you know we have a large Russian Oligarchs client population” and other clients with investments in Russian companies, she wrote. She asked which of those clients “we potentially could unwind and which not.” Should the bank advise them, she wondered, to withdraw their money “while they still can?”
This email exchange was the beginning of a frenzied reckoning within the scandal-plagued bank over its long resistance to breaking with Russia’s most important business titans under Vladimir V. Putin, the Russian president. The bank’s clients included the Russian billionaires Oleg V. Deripaska and Viktor F. Vekselberg. Time and again over many years, records show, Deutsche Bank’s risk managers warned that such relationships were perilous.
But profits associated with maintaining its Russian clients won out every time.
Russia’s war in Ukraine swept up Deutsche Bank in a larger shift. For decades, German politicians and business leaders believed that working with Russia and deepening economic ties between the two countries would discourage Russian aggression. That strategy collapsed after the invasion.

Wall Street prepares for Anthropic IPO frenzy, despite broader AI stock slump
NEW YORK, Nov 18 : Wall Street, expecting that wealthy investors and retail buyers will battle for shares of Anthropic, is rolling out products tied to the stock, hosting client events and giving away merchandise ahead of the AI company's potentially record launch.
Despite the steep losses among the hyperscalers and other stocks linked to the AI trade in recent weeks, there is building anticipation from these investors for the Anthropic initial public offering, which is expected on Thursday.
The IPO is expected to value the company, which created the Claude chatbot, at up to $1.4 trillion. But it has a hard act to follow after the SpaceX launch, earlier this year, created a frenzy of excitement and events.
"Judging by the number of people interacting with us and asking us about this, and filling out forms, this could be even bigger than SpaceX," said Will Rhind, founder of GraniteShares, who plans to launch a 2x bull Anthropic exchange-traded fund along with a 2x bear product next week.
A successful IPO could boost confidence in other AI-related stocks, including many of the largest technology companies that have powered the stock market rally to a series of record highs, even as shares have recently swung sharply amid questions over the industry's ability to generate measurable profits.
According to industry estimates based on regulatory filings, the market was preparing in coming days for at least 11 leveraged single-stock ETFs from seven issuers, with retail investors accounting for much of the interest.
One advertisement, on the StockTwits investing social media website, read: "Artificial intelligence meets human conviction with the 2X Long Anthropic Daily ETF from Tradr. Coming soon!"
"It’s going to hinge on the bull/bear case for AI," said Rhind. "The believers are not going to be put off by this volatility in the broader AI trade."
Vanda Research, which tracks retail trading activity, said it expects Anthropic itself to attract about $250 million in net retail buying, based on its analysis of activity on listing days and the volume of the company's pre-IPO perpetual futures traded on Hyperliquid.
Such a level would double the record $118 million of retail buying for the SpaceX IPO.
Karl Cheong, head of ETFs at Ninepoint Partners in Toronto, points to the selloff in bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies as a sign that retail investors want to raise cash to buy Anthropic. "This will be the first frontier model that retail investors can access easily on a public market," he said.
Ninepoint plans to launch an ETF for Canadian investors that would combine leveraged exposure to Anthropic, with a covered call strategy generating income.
WEALTH CLIENTS, LIVESTREAMS, MERCH
Banks have also planned select events.
Goldman Sachs organized a launch event on Tuesday for its wealth clients that was attended by the bank's president, John Waldron, as well as Anthropic Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao and its co-founder and president, Daniela Amodei, according to a person familiar with the matter.
JPMorgan plans to livestream the IPO for clients and has prepared merchandise such as t-shirts and laptop covers, according to another person familiar with the matter. Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei and his team were at the bank's offices all day on Friday meeting investors, the person said.
Anthropic declined to comment on the two events.
Still, not everyone is jumping on the bandwagon.
London-based Ben Preston, responsible for the Orbis Global Equity Strategy, a long-only stock-picking fund which also has a retail investor base, said the fund will not be buying Anthropic at the IPO.
“If it comes in at an IPO value of whatever it is – one and a half trillion dollars – that is a very expensive valuation to pay for a company which is unproven," said Preston.
Although StockTwits users give the anticipated IPO an "extremely bullish" score of 85 out of 100, based on a poll on its site, 67 per cent of the more than 18,000 members who responded said they did not plan to buy Anthropic during the initial offering. Only 20 per cent said they will buy, while another 13 per cent said they would wait to see the price.
Some on social media were skeptical about the potential price of the listing. Others said it has been tougher for ordinary investors to get their hands on pre-IPO shares of Anthropic than for SpaceX shares before the latter's IPO in June.
SpaceX has since had a mixed record, with shares priced at $135 in the IPO, jumping to $150 then briefly as high as $225, before dropping as low as $104. They now trade around $142.
Still, "as it has gotten closer to (Anthropic's) launch date, I've seen the excitement and the clamor to get a piece of whatever is allocated to retail grow and grow," said Mitchell Caplan, chairman and CEO of Willow Wealth and former CEO of E-Trade Financial.
OVERSEAS INTEREST
Interest has also been building abroad, with many British platforms inviting retail investors to send orders for shares.
“Historically, retail investors have been on the sidelines when it comes to public listings," said Jordan Sinclair, president of Robinhood UK.
Yet Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, a British investment platform serving high-net-worth investors, said the IPO highlights the divide between connected buyers who can get in pre-IPO and retail investors who end up pleading with their brokers for part of an allocation.
"It's a bit like arriving at a glamorous launch party – institutional backers on the VIP guest list gain early entry, enjoying the vintage champagne and finest canapés behind closed doors," Streeter said in an email.
"By the time the doors finally open to the general public, the risk is that the best of the festivities are well underway and latecomers are left paying a steep entry fee to pick over the flat prosecco and leftover crisps."

On the operational front, the payments bank said that monthly transacting users (for savings bank account) grew 21.1% YoY to 3.1 Cr during the quarter under review, while customer balances grew 10% YoY to nearly ₹4,385 Cr. Formula 1's one-race wonders
- Published
You've been handed the chance of a lifetime.
A chance to sit in the cockpit, on the grid, at motorsport's top table: Formula 1. The very pinnacle of everything you've strived for in your whole life.
What would you do?
"I sang the Grand Prix theme tune while I was sat on the grid. I thought I was watching it on telly," says Tiff Needell - one of 166 lucky or unlucky drivers, depending on your standing in motorsport, who graced an F1 race only once.
There are many reasons why a driver may only get one chance to race elite sport's fastest and most sophisticated machines, and, although F1's super subs were more of a feature in the 1960s and 1970s, the helmet-for-hire phenomenon is alive and driving in ultra-professional, modern F1.
Just ask Japan's Ryo Hirakawa, who only last month achieved his "dream", external when he got behind the wheel of a Haas at the Mexican Grand Prix following Esteban Ocon's controversial departure from the team.
"I just need to taste this moment. I'm really happy," Hirakawa said after scoring a point - admittedly, following a few demotions for others. "Just enjoy this moment and see what we can do."
Within a week there was nothing the Toyota factory driver could do as Haas' 2027 driver Rafael Camara was drafted in for the American team early, for the rest of 2026.
Hirakawa is a reserve driver for Haas as a result of the team's association with Toyota - the Japanese being in the right place at the right time.
The percentage of F1 test and reserve drivers who make it to the grid is typically low, and those who do tend to be drafted in for one shot at very unlikely glory.
The days of the aristocrat who fancies a pootle around the track are gone, and years of preparation are required even to be standing in the pit garage.
Injuries, sponsorship fails and outright cheating are just some of the reasons why it does not work out for some hopefuls.
Needell, known better for his time behind the wheel on Top Gear and other auto TV shows, got his big break at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. But his journey to the paddock was initiated a few years earlier - in the media.
"I won a car in a magazine competition," he says. "I was the kid on the terraces, on the fences - and made it on to the grid. We had no money at all in our family, so I was a working civil engineer five days a week and a mechanic in my garage five nights a week. At the weekend I was the van driver, the mechanic and the racing driver.
"I bumbled my way up to the top of the national scene and then got offered a professional drive in Formula 3. And after two years of that I moved up into the [long since defunct] Formula 1 British championship.
"I was out at the Nurburgring trying to get an F1 drive when I got the call. I was hanging around the paddock trying to chat up an F2 team, trying to say I had a sponsor, which of course I didn't.
"Ensign called me and said: 'This weekend would you like to drive?' I rushed home from the Nurburgring in my orange Ford Capri, had half a day's test at Donington and on to qualifying for the Belgian GP at Zolder.
"I got my chance because Clay Regazzoni crashed and hurt his back at Long Beach.
"A lot of that in the olden days was due to injuries - chances would come up when someone had crashed and got injured. It was dangerous back then."
Needell was in, but this was old-school F1 where you had to pre-qualify to show you were fast enough to qualify for the Grand Prix itself.
"There was something like 30 drivers trying to pre-qualify, and somehow I made it to the back of the grid - 23rd in the Ensign. It was so much cheaper then - aluminium chassis and a Cosworth DFV engine and away you go."
While the back of the grid beckoned, a 29-year-old Needell was in very good company in the form of double world champion Emerson Fittipaldi, who was having a bad weekend in his Skol Fittipaldi car.
"I found myself on the back row of the grid, sitting by one of my big heroes. It was all a bit of a dream," says Needell.
In contrast to today's VIP treatment, Needell's parents and his girlfriend (now wife) drove to Belgium in the family car and watched from the crowd as he lined up on the grid.
"When the mechanics started the engine and left me sitting there - me and Emerson - I actually started humming the theme tune [to Fleetwood Mac's The Chain]," Needell says.
"For 12 laps I battled with Emerson for the honour of being last place at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. Then the engine broke."
A failed attempt to qualify for Monaco a week later put the brakes on his F1 dream and eventually resulted in Needell pursuing a career as a Le Mans racer and TV presenter.
Often the reason F1 careers could be so fleeting would be of a driver's own making.
Hans Heyer did not qualify for his one and only race - the 1977 German Grand Prix at Hockenheim - but he thought he would contest it anyway, starting from the pit lane for the ATS team in a car that was never supposed to be there.
The German may have achieved his dream at his home race, but it came with disqualification after he had already retired with gearbox failure on lap nine.
And what of Marco Apicella? It has taken 73 years, since Alberto Ascari triumphed, for Italy to celebrate one of its own F1 world champions in Kimi Antonelli as he secured the 2026 title in Mexico last month.
For a country and a Ferrari team so important to the sport, that is a long time to wait - and Apicella was a good example of why it may have taken a while.
Rushed in at the last minute after only two hours of testing to replace a disgruntled, if experienced, Thierry Boutsen in the underwhelming 1993 Jordan, Apicella lasted approximately 800 metres of his home race after a multi-car collision during the first lap of the Italian Grand Prix at Monza.
That was the end of Apicella's F1 career and he would end up embarking on five unsuccessful attempts to win Le Mans.
1 of 5
So what's the best any of the one-hit wonders have done in their first and only grand prix?
There have been a smattering of points finishes over the years, and Dorino Serafini's shared second place on the podium with legend Ascari at Monza in the final race of F1's maiden season is difficult to top for an F1 one-shot.
But Germany's Markus Winkelhock is surely up there as one of sport's super-sub icons of the modern era.
A last-minute replacement in the newly acquired, yet painfully slow, Spyker team's car at the 2007 European Grand Prix at the Nurburgring, the touring car driver took up the F1 super sub's favoured qualifying position on the grid: last place.
F1 ran in Winkelhock's family - father Manfred contested 56 grands prix in the eighties before his death from a crash during a sportscar race in 1985.
But Markus went one better than his uncle Jo, who never contested an F1 race despite trying to qualify seven times.
But, by his own admission, Winkelhock was a long way from ready. "I had one day testing in Silverstone and one day in Paul Ricard," Winkelhock told Motorsport magazine., external
"The first couple of laps it felt like a PlayStation - so unreal, everything was so fast. You're accelerating till you reach the braking point.
"But after all the [practice] sessions I could feel my neck already.
"I told my mechanics to put some beddings on the side of the headrest, in case the neck is completely done, to lean on with the helmet."
Then came some early rain from the Eifel mountains and an inspired decision from the pitwall of a team with very little to lose.
Winkelhock was on exactly the right tyres, at exactly the right time, as the rain came down, and Lewis Hamilton and Jenson Button slid helplessly into the gravel trap along with several others.
Winkelhock's orange Spyker simply danced through the rivers of rainwater flowing across the tarmac, sitting 33 seconds ahead of the field - a country mile for F1.
He said: "I didn't know it was for the lead. I was just driving. At the point they told me, 'You're P1'. I really didn't understand anything that was going on because this race was really crazy."
But when the rain stopped, so did Winklehock - first swallowed up by the faster cars on a drying track, and then by a hydraulic issue on lap 15, having led for six laps.
Make no mistake, a lost F1 career is very often a driver's glittering career in the making in sportscars at Le Mans, or on the ovals of American Indycar.
But even back in the day when other sporting codes, such as rallying's frighteningly fast Group B, were at the height of their popularity, F1 was the pinnacle for most.
"Being a grand prix driver was where you wanted to go," concludes Needell. "But I always had my eye sideways for any other drives.
"Single-seaters are the best cars to drive and they are made and designed to race. And the ultimate is the grand prix car. Everything else is second best.
"I was so proud I got there on no sponsorship and no money. I suppose I was a bit annoyed I couldn't stay for longer.
"But as I always say, 'unluckier than a few, but luckier than millions'."

David Beckham sues after his fragrance is sold in gas stations and discount stores
David Beckham’s company is suing beauty group Coty for at least $41 million, alleging that sales of his perfumes in discount stores breached their licensing agreement and damaged his luxury brand
LONDON -- A dispute over the sale of David Beckham perfumes has struck a sour note with the soccer star turned style icon.
Beckham’s commercial company is suing a beauty firm after his “luxury” fragrances were allegedly found for sale in discount stores and a gas station bargain bin.
DB Ventures has filed a claim in the New York Supreme Court against German beauty group Coty, which makes and distributes a range of Beckham-branded fragrances and toiletries. They include the Classic and Instinct lines and the eaux de toilette Intimately and Exquisite Leather.
The claim argues that Beckham’s “world-renowned global brand is synonymous with excellence and refinement,” and “David Beckham products are a symbol of everyday luxury.”
“Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station,” the legal document says. “How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”
Lawyers for DB Ventures allege that Beckham-branded products “ended up in the bargain bin inside a gas station” and at British budget retailer Poundland, “allowing the product to be sold for dollar store prices and associating the David Beckham brand with cheap, discount products.”
DB Ventures is seeking at least $41 million in damages for breach of its licensing agreement.
Coty has asked a judge to dismiss the lawsuit, which was filed in April. The company argues that New York courts have no jurisdiction in the case, and says DB Ventures is using the claim to “manufacture its early exit” from its licensing deal and hand over the Beckham contracts to another firm, Interparfums.
Coty and DB Ventures did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Tuesday.
Beckham, the former soccer star for Manchester United and Real Madrid and captain of the England men’s national team, parlayed success on the pitch into a lucrative business career that includes co-ownership of soccer team Inter Miami. He was knighted last year by King Charles III, becoming Sir David.
He also has had a very public persona as a fashion model, “Bend it Like Beckham” movie muse and is husband to Spice Girl-turned-fashion designer Victoria “Posh Spice” Beckham. The couple have four children.
The Sunday Times Rich list earlier this year estimated the Beckhams' wealth at almost 1.2 billion pounds ($1.58 billion).

Mario Balotelli heard it all.
Perhaps better known for off-field antics than his undeniable - yet arguably wasted - talent with the ball at his feet, the Italian has always attracted headlines.
Fifteen years have passed since his famous 'Why always me?' Manchester derby T-shirt celebration, which came just days after a firework was set off in his own bathroom, causing a house fire.

Mancini to Mourinho - cracks begin to show
Typical of his unconventional footballing life, Balotelli's career did not begin in an elite club's academy.
Instead, by his mid-teens he was turning out for Italian third-tier side Lumezzane, close to the family home in Concesio.
A trial at Barcelona did not lead to a long-term stay, and instead he was picked up by Inter Milan in 2006.
It was at Inter that Balotelli first came across his great mentor - Roberto Mancini.
The relationship between the two has been likened to that of a father and son. Under the Italian coach's tutelage, Balotelli flourished.
Aged 17, Balotelli helped Inter win the 2007-08 Serie A title and reach the Coppa Italia final, memorably scoring twice against Juventus to send his side into the semi-finals.
Life changed for Balotelli with the arrival of Jose Mourinho in the weeks after that campaign ended.
There would be disagreements, disciplinary action and accusations that Balotelli's attitude was not up to scratch. Mourinho said Balotelli was "unmanageable" and described one performance as "close to a zero rating".
The relationship with Mourinho was fractious - a rare occasion when the Special One was confounded by a player.
Balotelli still won three Serie A titles and one Champions League with Inter, but his reputation as a supposed loose cannon was already beginning to overshadow his feats as a player.
Hitting the headlines in England
Logic dictated that Balotelli's next step should be to reunite with mentor Mancini. That happened in August 2010 when the 20-year-old joined Manchester City.
Mancini set out to show that the unpredictable ways of Balotelli could be harnessed for the team's good, aiming to get more out of him than Mourinho could.
A hardline stance on discipline often appeared to soften when Mancini dealt with Balotelli, who by spring 2011 had garnered a reputation in England as a fantastic footballer who could not stay away from controversy.
Having already been sent off twice for City and been involved in a car crash - not in his famous camouflage Bentley but an Audi R8 - the striker threw a dart at a youth-team player, an act that showed a level of immaturity.
After helping City to win the FA Cup in 2011, ending their 35-year major trophy drought, Balotelli came under scrutiny after attempting a backheel trick shot when through on goal during a pre-season friendly against LA Galaxy.
Mancini swiftly hooked him, later questioning his mentality by saying: "If you are serious, you can play 90 minutes. If not, you can come and sit by me on the bench."
Sometimes the audacity paid off - like the famous shoulder goal and subsequent nonchalant celebration against Norwich.
On other occasions, not so much.
In October 2011, emergency services attended his Cheshire home to deal with a firework lit in his bathroom. Balotelli said a friend had been responsible.
BBC Sport reported at the time that four firefighters used two hose reel water jets to douse the flames, with a large fan deployed to clear smoke.
Days later he was in the spotlight for the right reasons as he scored City's opener in a 6-1 win over Manchester United, celebrating with the 'Why always me?' T-shirt.
There were other stories - that he had given a homeless person £1,000, that he had turned up to a young boy's school to confront the headmaster about the child being bullied, that he drove around Manchester handing out presents while dressed as Santa.
True? Perhaps only Balotelli knows and he has often denied such rumours. But such was his reputation at the time that the stories became plausible.
A chant City fans coined made reference to his ironic allergy to grass - which kept him out of a Europa League match in 2011 - and driving around Moss Side with "a wallet full of cash".
Was the 'nonsense' worth it?
On the pitch, Balotelli was sent off against Arsenal in April 2012 in what, at the time, seemed like a season-defining moment that could end Manchester City's title bid.
But one month later he assisted Sergio Aguero's last-gasp goal against Queens Park Rangers that gave City a first Premier League title. It was his only Premier League assist that season.
Micah Richards, who was a team-mate and friend to Balotelli at City, said: "He was crazy in a good way. He was brilliant to have around the squad - a cult hero not just for the nonsense he did off the field but on it as well.
"The best thing about him is he's a lovely guy - he's not arrogant or how the papers try to perceive him, he's just a bit mad."
But did the moments of brilliance make the "nonsense" worth it?
Despite once insisting his patience with Balotelli was "limitless", Mancini ultimately had a rethink.
The final straw came in January 2013 when the pair had an argument at the training ground. Balotelli left for AC Milan later that month.
Mancini said: "He is not a bad guy, and a fantastic player, but I'm very sorry for him as he continues to lose his talent and his quality. I don't have any words for his behaviour.
"I hope for him he can understand he is in a bad way for his future."
Affection remained on both sides, but the relationship had become too fraught.
"Once upon a time, Mario did genuinely believe he was one of the best players in the world," said Nedum Onuoha, another former City team-mate.
"There are lots of stories about him from his time at City, but the one I remember is at our old training ground in Carrington when someone was talking about Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, and Mario said he was as good as them - and he was deadly serious.
"It obviously hasn't worked out that way, but he still has done so much more with his career than most players could even dream of."

Highs and lows with the Azzurri
Balotelli never threatened to have an international career to rival Ronaldo or Messi.
But there were still moments that linger in the memory.
He became the first black player to feature for Italy at a major tournament when he starred at Euro 2012.
And, more than that, he hit three goals to finish as the tournament's joint top scorer - with five others - as Italy lost to Spain in the final.
An abiding image is that of a shirtless Balotelli flexing his muscles after scoring the goal that sent the Azzurri to the final, with a 2-1 win against Germany.
Yet that tournament proved to be the peak of Balotelli's international career.
Italy's national team took a downward turn, and so too did his club career. By 2015, Balotelli had more or less became an Azzurri afterthought.
While Balotelli enjoyed some big moments in an Italy shirt, he did not always feel the love reciprocated from his country of birth.
Before Euro 2012 he threatened to leave the pitch if he was subjected to racist abuse and spoke openly about the vitriol he suffered while playing for Inter.
In fact, racist abuse has followed Balotelli throughout his career and he has commendably refused to tolerate it.
Born Mario Barwuah in Palermo to Ghanaian parents, Balotelli was placed into foster care aged three.
Initially, he stayed with his foster parents - Silvia and Francesco Balotelli - in Brescia during the week, then returned to his biological parents at weekends. He was eventually fostered on a full-time basis and took on the Balotelli surname.
Balotelli identifies with both parts of his heritage - Ghana and Italy - and he struggled to reconcile his love for a nation with the people who aimed verbal abuse his way.
The good times were all too brief: 36 caps and 14 goals has been his tally since 2018. He wanted more and has often made it known.
Onuoha said: "Playing for his country was always so important to him and that's another really positive thing about him, that he had that drive and ambition."
From freefall to fulfilment
Mancini told AC Milan that Balotelli could become one of the world's best while in Serie A.
A glut of goals followed the striker's return to the San Siro in January 2013, before a surprising move back to the Premier League followed 18 months later.
Liverpool had been impressed, but Balotelli's spell on Merseyside would prove forgettable for all. One goal in 16 Premier League games under Brendan Rogers was not what was expected from the £16m buy.
The failed transfer sparked a loan move back to Milan, where injuries hampered his progress. When it was time for Balotelli to return to Merseyside, Jurgen Klopp had arrived and said the striker would not be part of his Liverpool plans.
Balotelli later called the move to Anfield "the worst mistake of my life".
Was it that Liverpool move that sent Balotelli's career spiralling into freefall?
Spells in Nice, Marseille, Brescia and Monza followed - each to varying degrees of success but never with a feeling of stability.
Then came Turkish club Adana Demirspor, Swiss outfit Sion and Italian side Genoa. He spent no more than one season at a time with any of these clubs, although he did return to Demirspor for a second stint.
And so to the present day, with Balotelli aged 36 and plying his trade in the UAE.
It is easy to wonder what might have been had Balotelli stayed in Manchester, had he managed to settle enough to entirely fulfil his potential.
But, after so much media attention and a career that has spanned more continents and leagues than most, it is perhaps also understandable that Balotelli has settled on fulfilment through simply playing the game he loves with his brother.
"Playing with a family member like he is will give him that happiness," said Onuoha.
"And yes, it is not Serie A, La Liga or the Premier League, but Mario is on a field sharing it with his brother - for him that will mean everything.
"At this point there aren't many people that would hold much against him. I think when he was younger, some people would.
"But now I think it is more a case of almost allowing him this happiness, and enjoying seeing him finish off the last days of his career in a place that makes him happy.
"So many people end their careers on a sour note, but for him he is going to be ending it doing exactly what he wants to do."
