Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.
For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.
Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.
US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.
The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.
For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.
Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.
Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.
Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger.
Democrats, who will control Congress come January, have made their position clear. Last Wednesday top Democrat Ted Lieu told Politico the Trump administration had been "1,000%" too deferential to Nvidia, putting national security at risk, while fellow Democrat Zoe Lofgren suggested Congress would now be more likely to restrict sales of AI chips to China.
The BBC has approached the White House for comment.
Beijing's foreign ministry had described the spy claims as a "smear against China".
"The US should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives to find pretexts for imposing technological blockades," spokesperson Mao Ning said last week.
The ministry also seemed keen to keep the meeting on track, saying the two countries had kept "close communication regarding interactions between the two heads of state".
Another 'spy balloon' incident?
For the last year, Trump and Xi have been seeking to stabilise relations after a damaging tariff war that almost brought trade between the two countries to a standstill.
The Trump administration's decision to permit sales of advanced Nvidia H200 chips to China in late 2025 was seen as evidence that both sides were searching for areas of co-operation, even while competition intensified.
It was a rare move given Washington had spent years trying to limit China's access to the most advanced chips.
Many in the US have long viewed these chips as a national security issue, arguing they could strengthen China's military and surveillance capabilities. Jensen Huang, who rejects that claim, advocated lifting bans on the export of high-performing chips to China. Beijing argues the restrictions are an attempt to contain its rise.
Now that opening may be under threat.
History has taught Beijing and Washington that spy scandals rarely remain confined to the intelligence world.
Analysts in China already see echoes of an incident in 2023 when a suspected surveillance balloon drifted through the skies over the US before an American fighter jet shot it down. Beijing insisted it was a civilian meteorological airship that had strayed off course.
But a planned trip by then US Secretary of State Antony Blinken was cancelled and communication between the two governments deteriorated sharply.
The incident showed how quickly a security dispute could overwhelm diplomatic efforts and push relations into a deep freeze.
"The mere passage of a balloon sent American public opinion and politicians into a state of high alert, as if a "Chinese threat" were looming directly overhead," said the state media outlet, the Global Times this week as it made a direct comparison with the Nvidia scandal.
"No-one on the US side has ever apologised or taken responsibility for the genuine damage this caused to US-China relations," it added.
The state-run outlet also questioned why the Nvidia story had emerged so soon after "the hard-won detente" between Beijing and Washington, following a meeting between the two countries' leaders in September.
"Is someone behind the scenes pushing an agenda and stirring up confrontation?" it asked.
Trump-Xi summit unlikely to collapse
Both Trump and Xi have significant incentives to keep talking.
China's economy remains under pressure and is increasingly reliant on exports. Xi needs trade to keep flowing and this meeting is a key stepping stone to replacing the current trade truce that is due to expire in January.
Meanwhile Trump has repeatedly touted his close relationship with Xi and argued that maintaining dialogue is essential to managing competition between the two powers.
The US president is in his last two years and faces an uphill struggle to pass domestic legislation after the midterms. To counter this, he could be looking for some foreign policy wins.
He may also hope for Xi's help to end the war in the Middle East.
Neither side will want to be discussing intelligence concerns and technology controls instead of trade, investment and economic co-operation.
The summit is also being carefully choreographed by Beijing to show off its technological prowess in Shenzhen - a deeply symbolic choice of city.
It's home to some of the country's biggest tech companies and has become a showcase for Beijing's ambitions in AI and advanced manufacturing.
Also, given Washington's tighter restrictions on advanced chips, Beijing has options for retaliation.
One of its most powerful tools is its dominance of key rare earth minerals. China processes much of the world's supply for materials that are used in everything from electric vehicles and smartphones to military equipment.
Analysts have long warned that technological restrictions can trigger a cycle of retaliation in which each side reaches for its strongest economic leverage.
That would shift the current trend of US-China relations from engagement back towards mutual suspicion.

A video showing Akhilesh Yadav speaking to the media is being shared (here, here, here) with the claim that he was drunk while addressing reporters. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video shows Akhilesh Yadav in an intoxicated state while addressing the media.
Fact: The viral video is altered. The original video shows him speaking normally, and the audio has been altered to make his speech sound unclear. When the original video is heard at 0.75x speed, the audio matches the viral video. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to the same video, uploaded on 19 August 2026, on the official Facebook account of the Samajwadi Party. In this video, Akhilesh Yadav speaks in his normal tone. From the 50-second mark, he makes the same remarks heard in the viral video, but without the slurred tone.
Further, when we listened to the original video at 0.75x speed, we found that the audio matched the viral video. You can watch and listen to our edited video below.
We also found videos of the same interaction uploaded on 19 August 2026 by news agencies Bharat Samachar, IANS, and PTI. The microphones of these news agencies are also visible in the viral video. These videos show Akhilesh Yadav speaking to reporters after attending a Bhagwat Katha in Lucknow. He is seen speaking normally, without the slurred tone heard in the viral clip.
To sum up, this video claiming to show Akhilesh Yadav addressing the media in an intoxicated state is doctored.

Ukraine strikes major Russian bridge with drones and missiles as aerial attacks escalate
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian drones and missiles struck the vital Kerch Bridge linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday, calling it an "unprecedented" operation as Russia reported that its forces downed a record number of Ukrainian drones for the second straight day.
Zelenskyy portrayed the bridge operation as a masterstroke following a weekslong effort by Ukrainian forces to gradually wear down Russian air defenses before bombarding the prized target with a barrage of missiles and drones overnight.
Zelenskyy didn't detail the damage, but the Ukrainian General Staff said that an arch and a span of the bridge's road section collapsed, severing the road link, while the railway line was still standing but with a damaged arch.
Russia's Investigative Committee, the nation's top criminal investigation agency, said the bridge was attacked by drones and sustained damage but didn't elaborate.
The Kerch Bridge is a crucial link in moving military and civilian supplies from Russia to Crimea and for supporting troops on the front line. The construction of the bridge, a potent symbol of Russia's illegal annexation of the peninsula in 2014, was inflammatory to Ukrainians.
"The symbol of the occupation has cracked," the Ukrainian General Staff said in a statement.
Moscow's forces, meanwhile, fired ballistic missiles and drones at Kyiv, hitting two of the Ukrainian capital's main bridges and killing at least two people.
A recent escalation in aerial attacks came as Russia and Ukraine await a date for the next round of U.S.-mediated talks aimed at ending the war that began with Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor on Feb. 24, 2022.
U.S. President Donald Trump says he plans to talk about the war in Ukraine during his highly anticipated meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China this week.
Missiles delivered the final blow in the 7-stage operation
The Kerch Bridge attack was the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes over seven stages of the operation, Zelenskyy said on social media.
Ukrainian forces knocked out defense systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment and other designated targets before launching Monday night's final attack, he said.
Domestically developed long-range drones struck the bridge's road section during the night while Ukraine's Neptune missiles and other drones aimed at the rail section, he said. Precision-guided Flamingo missiles delivered the final blow, he said.
Zelenskyy and the Ukrainian military published videos showing what they said were the attacks and subsequent damage to the bridge, with part of the deck in the water and a fallen arch. The Associated Press wasn't able to verify the images.
The Russian-installed governor of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said traffic across the bridge was halted but rail traffic was restored by Tuesday afternoon. He didn't mention any damage.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that "there is no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than it was before."
Zelenskyy noted that Russia has battered Ukrainian infrastructure, especially the power grid, every day. There were significant power outages Tuesday in three Ukrainian regions, he said.
"We have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation — and every proposal has been met with loud rejection," he said.
U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, meeting at NATO headquarters in Brussels with Ukraine's Western backers, said the Kerch Bridge strike was "another example of Ukrainian ingenuity and Ukraine's absolute determination to defend itself against Russian aggression."
The United Kingdom announced £240 million ($317 million) in air defense support for Ukraine this winter, including more than 1,000 short-range missiles and more than a dozen radars.
Russian air defenses downed 1,441 drones during a second straight night of major Ukrainian attacks, Russia's Defense Ministry said Tuesday.
That was a day after Russia said that it downed 1,336 Ukrainian drones in the highest number of interceptions it had reported so far during the war.
Ukraine also attacks industrial areas deep inside Russia
Elsewhere, authorities in Bashkortostan, a Russian region in the southern Ural Mountains, said that defenses repelled a "massive" drone attack on industrial zones in the cities of Ufa and Salavat. All plants there worked as usual, officials said.
However, independent news outlet Astra reported a huge fire at the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refining and petrochemical complex in Bashkortostan, nearly 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) east of the Ukrainian border. The major petrochemical complex has been attacked a number of times before.
In Moscow, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that around 800 drones flew toward the Moscow region overnight. Most were downed far away, and 321 were shot down as they approached the Russian capital.
Russia hits bridges in Ukraine's capital
Seven Russian ballistic missiles hit two of Kyiv's main bridges during the night, Zelenskyy said. Both were closed to traffic.
The Pivnichnyi and Pivdennyi bridges are key commuter routes across the Dnipro River connecting Kyiv's two banks. The left bank is largely residential with numerous apartment buildings and shopping malls. The old town and many government offices are on the right bank.
On Tuesday morning, long lines of traffic formed on a third bridge linking the two sides of the city.
Russian attacks damaged other infrastructure and started fires in four districts of the Ukrainian capital, officials said, as Moscow continued its campaign to make life difficult for Ukrainian civilians.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Tuesday that its forces overnight hit Ukraine's military industrial facilities, energy, transport and port infrastructure, as well as vessels used for Ukrainian armed forces.
Russian forces launched a combined attack on industrial facilities in three districts of the southern Ukraine region of Zaporizhzhia, killing two people and wounding 18 others and leaving a large number of consumers in the region without power, local authorities said.
The possibility of more talks
Meanwhile, the negotiating teams of Ukraine, the United States, and European partners held a working video call Monday in which they discussed the results of recent talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, and the agenda for the next stage of negotiations, said Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service.
"We aligned our positions and our next joint steps," Umerov said on Telegram following the conversation.
Representatives of France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy, Poland, NATO and the European Commission joined the conversation.
The United States was represented by envoys Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner, and Alexus Grynkewich, the commander of U.S. forces in Europe, Umerov said.

(Bloomberg) -- The Trump administration paused further installation of equipment linked to last week’s nationwide flight stoppage and may seek additional help improving its systems after the disruptive incident.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Tuesday said his department is considering bringing in an outside party to help monitor the telecommunications network used by air traffic controllers, after an equipment failure grounded flights for more than four hours Friday and caused days of travel disruptions.
The government has traced the failure back to a malfunctioning router installed at a Federal Aviation Administration facility in Arkansas. The work was carried out by contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc., part of maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire to fiber. The FAA separately said it had paused installations of those devices as it investigates the root cause of the mishap.
Quick answers to key questions
A malfunctioning router at an FAA facility in Arkansas caused the failure. The outage grounded flights for more than four hours and led to travel disruptions over several days.
The FAA paused installations while it investigates the root cause of the router failure and examines whether the equipment can be installed safely.
L3Harris Technologies carried out the work as part of a project to replace old copper telecommunications lines with fiber.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said replacing the contractor would be difficult because it has a “vendor-lock” and owns and monitors the telecommunications network. He said the department expects L3Harris to improve its performance.
The Transportation Department is considering bringing in an outside party to help monitor the telecommunications network used by air traffic controllers. No decision or details about that help were provided.
“It took longer than I would have liked to identify that router with L3Harris,” Duffy told reporters on Capitol Hill Tuesday. “We have to have them perform better, and then we’re going to look at bringing some outside help in.”
Duffy’s comments mark the first time Duffy has suggested the US might seek to enlist an additional firm following the episode. Duffy has been critical of L3Harris in the wake of the outage, saying that officials were examining whether “incompetence” was a factor.
A representative for L3Harris did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Asked Tuesday whether L3Harris would be fired, Duffy said the company has a “vendor-lock” with the government because it essentially owns and monitors the telecommunications network, making it difficult to replace. L3Harris’s predecessor, Harris Corp., was first awarded the FAA contract in 2002.
“I’m going to have to work with them,” Duffy said, adding that department expects the company to improve its performance.
Duffy’s comments came after Democrats on a key Senate committee called for an immediate pause on the deployment of new routers earlier Tuesday until the FAA demonstrates the work can be done safely.

A lawyer for the Saudi national accused of bugging OpenAI's San Francisco office is making another attempt to get him released from jail, saying that Justice Department prosecutors haven't dug up any evidence that would support espionage charges.
"Government counsel acknowledged that if there were supporting evidence, new charges would have been brought when Mr. Alfozan was indicted," David Rizk, the attorney for Abdulrahman Alfozan, said in a court filing ahead of his client's Tuesday court appearance.
"Instead, Mr. Alfozan was indicted solely on the Wiretap Act count that was the subject of the Complaint."
Federal prosecutors in San Francisco arrested Alfozan in October, accusing him of planting a listening device in a conference room at OpenAI's office, where he worked as an engineer. The criminal complaint accused him of interception of oral communications.
Prosecutors brought a grand jury indictment against Alfozan later in October, but didn't include more severe charges, such as espionage or theft of trade secrets.
Rizk said prosecutors said in two meetings this month that no evidence emerged to bring additional charges against him.
Rizk asked US District Judge Vince Chhabria, who is overseeing the case, to order the Justice Department to hand over additional information that would enable the defense lawyer to formally request Alfozan's release from jail.
A spokesperson for the US Attorney's office in San Francisco didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Alfozan has pleaded not guilty to the charges against him. A federal judge ordered him to remain in jail while awaiting trial, ruling there was a high risk he would flee if released because the Saudi government offered to pay his bond and because his wife and son had already flown to Saudi Arabia.
Photos included in the criminal complaint show images of a USB device plugged into the back of a conference room TV and wrapped in toilet paper. The complaint also included what prosecutors said was a photo of Alfozan checking on the device a week after another OpenAI employee found it hidden there.
According to Rizk, the discovery material produced by the federal government so far doesn't indicate that prosecutors took any steps to investigate ties between Alfozan and the government of Saudi Arabia.
Rizk also said Alfozan voluntarily offered to unlock his cellphone, which was seized by the Justice Department, after prosecutors said they lost access to it earlier this month because of a power failure at an FBI facility.
In addition to seeking Alfozan's release from jail, Rizk asked the judge to modify a previous order restricting his use of AI while he prepares to defend himself in court.
"The U.S. Attorney's Office should not be in the business of policing defense counsel's discovery practices," Rizk wrote.

Home services platform Urban Company has opened its QIP, setting a floor price of ₹161.03 per share. The company is issuing equity shares to institutional investors after securing shareholder approval to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr. Urban Company may offer a discount of up to 5% on the floor price. The company’s board approved the fundraise on October 16. Shareholders cleared it through a special resolution by postal ballot, with 99.3% of votes cast in favour. The company’s fundraise committee approved the launch and the preliminary placement document yesterday. Urban Company has set out ₹1,475 Cr in proposed allocations across five uses in its preliminary placement document. It plans to deploy ₹600 Cr to grow InstaHelp, ₹540 Cr for marketing, ₹200 Cr for technology development and cloud infrastructure, ₹85 Cr for office rent, and ₹50 Cr for research and development for its Native products. Urban Company expects to deploy ₹150 Cr for InstaHelp in FY27, ₹300 Cr in FY28, and ₹150 Cr in FY29. InstaHelp competes with Snabbit and Pronto in the instant domestic help market. Urban Company said InstaHelp completed 6.2 Mn orders in Q2 FY27. Snabbit founder Aayush Agarwal said his startup fulfilled 6.45 Mn orders in the same quarter. When it announced the fundraise plan last month, Urban Company said fresh capital would give it room to invest across its businesses, strengthen InstaHelp’s market position, and pursue acquisitions. The company is also expanding into residential air conditioners under Native, which currently sells water purifiers and smart locks. Urban Company has cited its experience servicing millions of residential ACs annually as the driver for this business vertical. InstaHelp Weighs On Earnings On the financial front, Urban Company reported a net loss of ₹182.5 Cr, more than tripling from ₹59.3 Cr in the year-ago period. Operating revenue grew 41.4% YoY to ₹537.3 Cr from ₹380 Cr, while total expenses surged 61.5% to ₹745.7 Cr. The widening losses were largely driven by investments in InstaHelp, on which the company spent ₹174 Cr during the quarter. Its adjusted EBITDA loss stood at ₹144 Cr, but excluding InstaHelp, the company reported an adjusted EBITDA profit of ₹30 Cr. Notably, its management has maintained that it can achieve its profitability targets without the fundraise and rejected the suggestion that the fundraise is necessary to offset InstaHelp’s impact on its financials. In the past, Urban Company has indicated that the vertical is likely to remain a low-margin business compared with its core operations, adding that it does not expect to make money from the vertical over the next five years. It expects InstaHelp to break even by FY31.

Telangana IT and Industries Minister D. Sridhar Babu has urged Mumbai’s business and industrial community to make the most of the growth opportunities Telangana offers across sectors such as manufacturing, technology development and innovation.
Manufacture, scale and grow in Telangana while continuing to retain their corporate headquarters in Mumbai, the Minister said, seeking to project the State as a complementary investment destination for businesses and an ideal location for existing investors to expand manufacturing and operational capacities.
Economic partnership rather than competition
Mr. Sridhar Babu, who was speaking at the roadshow in Mumbai for Invest Telangana Global Summit 2026 on Wednesday (November 18, 2026), urged the business community to make Telangana their preferred destination. The State was keen to build stronger economic partnerships with Mumbai’s business community rather than compete with the city for existing investments. “A century ago, the people of Telangana came to Mumbai to help build its future. Today, Telangana invites Mumbai to come and build ours,” he said, recalling the longstanding historical and economic ties between Telangana and Mumbai.
Outlining the growing opportunities across technology, global capability centres (GCCs), data centres, pharmaceuticals, textiles and apparel as well as media and entertainment that the State offered, the Minister called upon Mumbai-based industrialists and entrepreneurs to leverage Telangana’s industrial infrastructure, skilled workforce, business ecosystem and investor-friendly policies to expand their operations. He also highlighted the State’s commitment to facilitate investments through its time-bound approvals mechanism under TG-iPASS.
The Invest Telangana Global Summit is scheduled to be held from December 7-9 at the Bharat Future City, near Hyderabad. The Minister highlighted the State’s commitment to facilitating investments through its time-bound approvals mechanism under TG-iPASS.
A dedicated officer for every company from Mumbai
Mr. Sridhar Babu said every company coming from Mumbai would be assigned a dedicated officer to provide end-to-end assistance throughout its investment journey — from the initial visit to Telangana to the commencement of commercial operations and generation of its first revenue.
A number of roadshows are being organised for the Invest Telangana Global Summit, by the State government, in major cities. On Tuesday, the Minister had addressed the event in Ahmedabad.

Palestinian woman, 72, shot dead by Israeli settlers in West Bank, health ministry says
- Published
A Palestinian woman in her 70s has been shot dead, and several other people wounded, in a village in the occupied West Bank where Israeli settlers recently moved in, the Palestinian health ministry says.
There are conflicting accounts of what happened. Local Palestinians said there was an attack by settlers in part of al-Duyuk al-Tahta, near Jericho, which is meant to be under the full control of the Palestinian Authority.
According to the Israeli army, there was a Palestinian car-ramming attack on an Israeli vehicle. It said rocks were then thrown at the Israelis, who opened fire in response. It did not mention the fatal shooting of a woman.
There have been high tensions in the area since a group of settlers recently set up a new outpost.
They moved into eight houses in the village on 4 November after buying them, they have said, in a secretive operation. The properties are in an area where Israel retains full security control.
All settlements are illegal under international law.
- UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements 
  - Published6 hours ago
Local Palestinians said that the events in al-Duyuk al-Tahta on Monday night began with harassment by Israeli settlers. Palestinian children threw stones, they said, and the settlers opened fire, killing Fadda al-Fahidat, who was 72, outside her home.
Fadda's daughter-in-law, Nema al-Fahidat, told the BBC that she died from a single bullet wound to the head. "It destroyed her brain," she said.
According to the Palestinian accounts, Fadda's son, Arafat, rushed to the scene in his car after hearing the news and collided with an empty Israeli settler car parked outside his family home, injuring settlers who were standing nearby. The settlers then fired more shots, they said, injuring several Palestinians, including Arafat.
"My husband, when he saw his mother, was not paying attention. He crashed into the vehicle. The vehicle was empty," Nema said.
"My husband got out of his car and tried to reach his mother and the injured young men. Then he was shot."
She added: "We tried to gather the injured people and move them away from the settler. We brought them here. But he kept firing, firing, firing. Even after we had brought the wounded young men here and moved them away from him, he continued shooting."
Nema said young Palestinians threw stones at the settlers after seeing what happened, but asked: "What can stones do against bullets?"
The statement from the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that "terrorists accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it", and then "exited their vehicle with weapons and attacked and harmed the occupants of the Israeli vehicle".
Afterwards, it said, "rocks were hurled at the Israelis, who responded by firing in order to remove the threat."
Later, an Israeli military source said Fadda was shot by an Israeli civilian and that there was no evidence that she had been involved in the confrontation near her home.
Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Israel's police force said it had opened an investigation, and that officers and forensic technicians had been collecting evidence and interviewing witnesses.
The Israeli human rights group B'Tselem says there has been a prolonged campaign of settler attacks, intimidation and land seizures in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, with Israeli troops now stationed nearby to secure the new settlement.
Residents and activists say armed settlers walk and drive quad bikes around the neighbourhood as they threaten Palestinian residents.
A BBC team saw settlers at the end of the street where Fadda was shot on Tuesday, as well as Israeli flags flying from four of the houses that they had moved into earlier this month.
In a separate incident on Monday evening, eight Palestinians were injured when they were hit by a vehicle driven by an Israeli settler on a main road in Tuqu, south of Bethlehem, according to Palestinian officials and the Palestinian Red Crescent.
The IDF said the incident was a traffic accident. But the Palestinian foreign ministry called it a "terrorist attack", saying the driver hit a group of Palestinians who had gathered near the scene of an earlier traffic accident.
Also on Monday, the Civil Administration - the body that implements Israeli government policy in the West Bank - announced the allocation of more than 28 sq km (6,945 acres) of land in the northern Jordan Valley to nine settlers for grazing, according to the Israeli anti-settlement watchdog Peace Now.
It said handing over vast tracts of land to settlers for grazing outposts constituted "direct support for the systematic expulsion of Palestinians from their lands and the rampant criminal violence in the West Bank".
The UK government announced on Tuesday that it was imposing sanctions on eight companies building Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
It is the first sanctions package since Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's pledge in September to respond to the accelerating rate of settlement expansion in the West Bank, which he said risked rendering a two-state solution unviable.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called the sanctions a "hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies".

You might be excused for forgetting about the existence of 3 Body Problem, Netflix’s heady sci-fi series adapted from the award-winning novel The Three-Body Problem by Liu Cixin, the first book in his Remembrance of Earth’s Past trilogy. After all, it debuted in March 2024. But it was an exceptionally well-done, thematically rich series, and we’re finally getting the second of a planned three seasons in January. Netflix just dropped the first teaser.
(Spoilers for S1 below.)
Created by David Benioff, D.B. Weiss (Game of Thrones), and Alexander Woo (True Blood), the first season followed two primary timelines. In the earlier one, a young Chinese astrophysicist, Ye Wenjie (Rosalind Chao), witnessed her father being beaten to death by Red Guards during the Cultural Revolution. Ye figured out a means of sending an interstellar message to possible extraterrestrial civilizations, receiving a response from a planet called Trisolaris.
The planet had three suns, which wreaked havoc on Trisolaris via unpredictable “chaotic periods”—hence the novel’s title, which refers to a classic problem in celestial mechanics. Despite being warned that the aliens intended to invade and conquer Earth, Ye responded to the message and invited them to do so, bitter and disillusioned by the state of the world. She eventually became an established professor (Zine Tseng played the older version).
In the present day, the consequences of Ye’s fateful decision began to play out, beginning with a series of mysterious suicides by scientists, many of whom had possessed a highly advanced VR gaming headset. Among the dead: a particle physicist named Vera Ye (daughter of Ye Wenjie). Five of her former students (known as the Oxford Five) joined forces to figure out what was going on, eventually finding themselves caught in a global fight to save Earth from the invading Trisolarians (or San-Ti). Another human cult faction was just as intent on enabling the San-Ti invasion, believing they would be spared as a reward, while Ye Wenjie still believed the entire human race deserved to be annihilated.

AT&T on Friday accused Comcast of false advertising in a lawsuit challenging the marketing claim that Comcast’s cable broadband service and Wi-Fi is “fiber-powered.”
“This case challenges Comcast’s false advertising campaign for its residential Internet service, marketed under the Xfinity brand to consumers nationwide,” AT&T’s lawsuit said. “At the center of that campaign is Comcast’s claim that Xfinity Internet and its associated Wi-Fi service are ‘Fiber-Powered.’”
While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. This results in upload speeds being far slower than download speeds.
In contrast, fiber-to-the-home service can provide symmetrical upload and download speeds. Comcast has deployed fiber-to-the-home in only small portions of its cable territory while advertising its service as fiber-powered in the majority of areas where cable makes the final connection.
AT&T’s lawsuit said that in describing its cable broadband as fiber-powered, Comcast “conveys to reasonable consumers the misleading impression that Xfinity Internet is a fiber-to-the-home service comparable to AT&T Fiber. In fact, the vast majority of Xfinity Internet runs over a hybrid fiber-coaxial (‘HFC’) network, where the critical ‘last mile’ connection to the customer’s home uses copper coaxial cable, not fiber.”
AT&T has its own history of ads that mislead customers about the nature of its network. It used to advertise 4G LTE service as “5GE” or “5G Evolution,” and displayed a 5GE network icon on 4G phones. AT&T claimed that its 5G Evolution ads “served to educate customers about the billions of dollars AT&T has invested to give customers an outstanding experience,” but the BBB National Programs’ National Advertising Division found the term was likely to mislead consumers into thinking they had 5G connections.
AT&T: Fiber-powered is “literally false”
AT&T’s lawsuit said that Comcast’s fiber-powered claim “is literally false” because the cable firm’s HFC “architecture is fundamentally different from true fiber-to-the-home services like AT&T Fiber, which deliver fiber optic cables directly to the customer’s premises.”

- In November, after a string of major outages occurred at government and commercial networks including the nationwide air traffic system, social media posts claimed the conservative Heritage Foundation's blueprint for reshaping the federal government, Project 2025, called for "dismantling" or "destroying" the Federal Aviation Administration.
- There are elements of truth to the claim depending on how it's worded. Project 2025 did propose restructuring the agency (or "dismantling the FAA as we know it," as some phrased it) and moving toward a privatized air traffic system.
- It's inaccurate to say Project 2025 called for the FAA to be "destroyed," much less that its recommendations regarding the agency played some role in the Nov. 13 ground stop that shut down air traffic nationwide.
- According to the FAA, a technical problem caused by data flooding the agency's telecommunications infrastructure network and disrupting aircraft communications and radar feeds led to the ground stop.
As officials in the U.S. traded blame for the nationwide flight grounding that took place Nov. 13 — with President Donald Trump's administration pushing Congress for $50 billion to address an aging air traffic control system — a rumor circulated that the Republican-driven Project 2025 called for the dismantling of the Federal Aviation Administration.
Project 2025, a nearly 1,000-page document intended to reshape federal government policies, was created by The Heritage Foundation, a conservative nonprofit organization, and has been directly mirrored in some of the policies Trump has enacted during his second term in office.
According to the FAA, the Nov. 13 ground stop was caused by data flooding the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure network, which disrupted the system and made aircraft communications and radar feeds unstable.
"I can't apologize for what was passed off to us, and I can't blame Republicans or Democrats because it's all of them," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on NBC News on Nov. 15.
With an aging communication system and public demand to know what was going to be done to fix it, questions about Project 2025's vision for the future of the FAA gained momentum on social media.
"Pages 632–635 of the Heritage Foundation's Mandate for Leadership call for dismantling the FAA as we know it — starting with splitting the Air Traffic Organization out of the FAA and the Department of Transportation entirely, moving toward a privatized air traffic system funded by user fees," one Facebook post read (archived). "Remember, destroying the FAA is part of Project 2025," the post's image read.
We looked into the claim by parsing Project 2025's section addressing its vision for the future of the FAA. We found that while it did not call for the wholesale "dismantling of the FAA," it did call for drastic changes that would separate the agency from government bodies that imposed regulations the authors deemed limiting to modernization, as well as for the privatization of several aspects of the agency.
So, the claim that Project 2025 called for the "dismantling of the FAA, as we know it" leans heavily on the latter half of the statement. The claim that "destroying the FAA is part of Project 2025" is based on opinion, not factual evidence.
Below is the relevant section of the full Project 2025 text (pages 632-634) detailing the project's proposed changes to the FAA:
As illustrated above, Project 2025 did call for a drastic overhaul of the FAA's structure, including separating the FAA from the Department of Transportation or, at a minimum, separating the Air Traffic Organization from the FAA on the grounds it would result in an overall reduction in oversight and the "constraints imposed" by the annual congressional appropriations process:
The FAA's overly bureaucratic, legalistic, byzantine, and more recently hyperpoliticized way of processing regulations, adopting innovation, publishing rules, and procuring new technologies has been eclipsed by foreign CAAs and ANSPs that are eagerly certifying drones and creating environments in which new technologies and new entrants, such as air taxis, can thrive.
The project called for the FAA to operate more like a business than a government entity, with a shift from funding provided by aviation user taxes to fees for air traffic services paid directly to the Air Traffic Organization, allowing the ATO to issue long-term revenue bonds for major projects.
In sum, there's no truth to claims that Project 2025 proposed "destroying" the FAA. Rather, it outlined several changes that would reorganize its operations and separate it from historic governmental structures and processes.

Five European Countries Plan to Deport Migrants to Rwanda
Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Greece and Denmark are seeking to establish a hub for rejected asylum seekers. Here’s what to know about their effort.
Five European countries announced a plan on Monday that would send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda, an experiment that comes as governments across the continent toughen their stances on migration.
The joint push from Germany, Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands and Greece was pitched as a way to handle migrants who had no right to stay in Europe but who, for one reason or another, could not or would not return to their home countries.
The project, which is not yet finalized, shows how European leaders’ stance on migration has hardened since the arrivals of 2015-16, when countries like Germany admitted more than a million asylum seekers. With far-right groups like the Alternative for Germany rising in popularity, centrist leaders have gradually taken a less welcoming stance.
“For me, today marks a crucial step toward a new migration system,” Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister of Denmark, said at a news conference on Monday.
The pilot project is expected to start on a small scale, with perhaps 100 or 200 deportees. Critics are already worried both about the idea of sending people to a nation to which they have no connection, and about the risk that human rights will not be sufficiently protected in Rwanda.
Why Rwanda?
The country has a history of courting migration-related deals.
Britain developed a plan to send asylum seekers there in 2022, though judges in London ultimately ruled the effort unlawful and it was later abandoned. The United States has recently deported people to Rwanda.

Trump lands in China with key meetings with Xi and Putin on the agenda
SHENZHEN, China — President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the U.S. status as the world's leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public.
The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the United States worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.
"It's fine," Trump pronounced on Tuesday from the Philippine capital of Manila, suggesting it was all just a consequence of being a nation that is "big and powerful."
But then the outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase and the National Security Agency's communications network began to overshadow Trump's visit. They raised the specter that artificial intelligence can disrupt daily life, as new cyber vulnerabilities identified require software to be constantly upgraded to fix flaws or other security holes, known as patching, which is supposed to improve how the technology runs.
So at the start of the second day of Trump's trip, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stepped in to reassure Americans on Trump's behalf. He told reporters there was "zero" evidence that the outages are connected or tied to rival nations, cyber hackers or criminals.
"Sometimes when you are going in to fix your system because you've identified a vulnerability, it creates a short-term disruption," said Rubio, who is also Trump's national security adviser.
Trump is trying to project strength in Asia, but the outages challenge that image
Xi paid Trump a special honor by greeting him on the tarmac after Air Force One arrived in Shenzhen, China, reciprocating a gesture made by the U.S. president during Xi's state visit to Washington in September.
The two leaders greeted each other at the foot of the airplane's stairs in a handshake that became a hug as group of dancers waved flowers and flags. When Putin arrived earlier on Wednesday, Xi did not greet him at the airport despite their longstanding friendship.
Trump has signaled that he wants to take an improvised approach during his time in Shenzhen, the skyscraper-filled tech hub that is hosting world leaders for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. It's a bet that his unscripted brand of diplomacy based on personal relationships can create some kind of legacy to reshape world affairs during his final two years in the White House.
On Thursday, at a first-ever trilateral, Trump said he plans to talk with Xi and Putin about limiting nuclear weapons and bringing an end to the war in Ukraine, which began in 2022 with Russia's invasion. Analysts are not expecting substantive breakthroughs, despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting.
Before the trip, Trump's aides had told reporters that the war in Ukraine would not be on the agenda. But Trump said on Tuesday that the deaths of tens of thousands of Russian troops every month had created an opening to resolve the conflict.
"I think it's very close to getting it done," Trump said. "We're going to have a good meeting on that."
Trump also teased the possibility of a private meeting with Putin and a separate sit-down with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Rubio clarified on Wednesday that Trump was "serious" about meeting with Kim as a way of resolving tensions with North Korea. But he suggested no meeting was currently scheduled between Trump and Kim for Thursday.
Trump has a reunion with old friend Imelda Marcos
Before he landed in Shenzhen, Trump had lunch in Manila with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the Malacañang Presidential Palace.
Marcos noted that he had sent fried chicken from the Philippine chain Jollibee to the U.S. delegation for a late-night snack Tuesday and complimented Trump for "working very hard."
Trump praised the U.S. bond with the Philippines and the interior decoration of the presidential palace.
"Our people share common history, common values, common interests, common architectural tastes," Trump said. "I love what you've done here."
He said after their meeting that the two nations had reached a trade deal on Wednesday, though he had also said last year that an agreement had been reached. The U.S. trade deficit in goods with the Philippines has risen under Trump, climbing from $4.9 billion in 2024 to $12.8 billion during the first 9 months of this year, according to the Census Bureau.
There were no details about the new agreement, although the White House said it will involve Manila buying more energy and farm products.
Trump also had a short reunion with Imelda Marcos, the former first lady and mother of the Philippines' current president.
Famed for her lavish shoe collection, Imelda Marcos knew Trump decades ago through the New York City party scene. During the 1986 "People Power" uprising, her husband, Ferdinand Marcos, was ousted as the Philippines' strongman leader.
Trump called her "always the most beautiful" and the 97-year-old matriarch appeared to hand him a gift, according to a video posted by the White House.
What's on the agenda for Trump's meetings with Xi and Putin
The prospect of Trump meeting with two of America's largest geopolitical rivals has been a source of unease as the U.S. president has been less welcoming of historic allies such as Canada and NATO partners in Europe.
His tariffs that were intended to curb China's trade surplus have done little to stop the progress of the world's dominant manufacturer, which for the second straight year will have exported $1 trillion more in goods than what it imported.
Even without the digital outages in the U.S., questions about how to handle AI loom over the summit.
The technology is viewed as key to unlocking faster economic growth, but its rapid development has meant it poses national security risks and could evolve in ways that put AI beyond human control.
Trump's close tech industry ally Jensen Huang was recently removed as the CEO of Nvidia after he admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an agent of the Chinese government. Beijing has denied that she was a spy, yet the affair raised concerns about how China has been able to access Nvidia computer chips to develop its own AI models that are competing with the U.S.
When asked this week why the U.S. had not been more aggressive in cutting off China's access to advanced computer chips, Trump said there were differences of opinion inside his administration and that "We have a very good relationship with China, and you don't want to insult them."
Trump has said he does not plan to bring up Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as its own. Taiwan is the leading manufacturer of advanced computer chips, including those designed by U.S. companies.
Still, Trump expects that Xi will push him on Taiwan's sovereignty.
"I'm sure he'll raise it," Trump said. "I won't have to raise it."

Bancroft sandpaper claims heap pressure on Cummins
- Published
Cameron Bancroft has claimed the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot in explosive revelations that will heap pressure on current captain Pat Cummins.
In a detailed testimony, published by the West Australian, batter Bancroft - the player caught with the sandpaper during the Test match against South Africa - has given arguably the most complete account of the events in Cape Town eight years ago.
For the past two weeks, Australian cricket has been embroiled in a debate over the ball-tampering saga following the publication of Usman Khawaja's autobiography.
Khawaja wrote that the whole Australia team knew of the plot, claims supported by David Warner and Chadd Sayers. Cummins described Khawaja's account as "wrong" and "nonsense".
On the day Cricket Australia announced a forum into the sandpaper episode, Bancroft published his account, explaining he was motivated by the news conference given by Cummins.
"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference," said Bancroft.
"It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.
"What I saw, experienced and lived with - not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa - is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time."
Opener Bancroft was given a nine-month ban for his part in the plot.
Steve Smith was stripped of the Australia captaincy and given a year-long ban, the same suspension given to vice-captain Warner. No other players or coaches were punished.
In his more than 4,000-word piece, Bancroft has claimed:
- Sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa – the match before Bancroft was caught
- Bancroft had conversations with the Australia seamers – Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether the ball was "swinging enough"
- Before the third day of the second Test, the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaper
- When Bancroft was caught during the third Test, then Australia coach Darren Lehmann told 12th man Peter Handscomb to "get the sandpaper off Bangers now"
- Bancroft found the publication of a joint-statement by the Australia bowlers in 2021 "deeply painful".

Big tech giant Google has begun rolling out its new agentic AI assistant Tasks, formerly Gemini Sparks, to users in India. In a blogpost, Josh Woodward, the vice-president of Google Labs and the Gemini app, said that the new feature will enable users to assign tasks to the AI assistant, including making calls, booking appointments, comparing products and completing purchases. The service comes bundled for free with Google’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. “Starting now, this update is rolling out free of charge for hundreds of millions of people across the US, Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India, using our new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model,” said Woodward. It is pertinent to note that Tasks was reportedly initially launched to select testers back in May as Gemini Spark, an agentic AI helper. It was subsequently expanded to the US-based subscribers of the Google AI Ultra tier. Google is now rolling out this feature for free in six markets. Unlike Gemini’s Chat that only generates responses to a user’s queries, Tasks goes one step further and enables the chatbot to perform basic functions. With the rollout, Google could be looking to expand the role of AI assistants beyond answering questions to embedding them in daily life. In his blog post, Woodward noted that Gemini can draw on information already available within Google services, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, files and payment cards, to carry out tasks on a user’s behalf. With Tasks, he also said that Gemini can call businesses, wait through hold periods, identify available appointment slots and add bookings to a user’s calendar. Under the hood, Gemini uses the agent payments protocol (AP2) to enable Tasks to make purchases online. Going forward, the big tech giant said that it plans to integrate the universal commerce protocol (UCP) into Gemini to further streamline the checkout experience. Google also said that it is working with American Express, Mastercard and Visa to enable tokenised card transactions via Tasks. However, the big tech juggernaut did not specify whether partnerships extend to India too. That said, India’s inclusion in the initial rollout gives Google a large market to test consumer adoption of the personal AI assistant feature. To further scale the rollout, Google has also invited app developers to join its Connected Apps Platform, which could pave the way for Indian consumer, fintech, travel tech and foodtech brands to build task-based third-party integrations with the assistant. These features could make Gemini Tasks a channel for online shopping, bill payments and routine purchases. However, adoption will depend on the availability of supported merchants, payment methods and third-party apps in the country. There appears to be no clarity on this front. The launch is part of a broader wave of big tech giants rolling out personal AI assistants to capture the masses. In September, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg showcased the company’s new offering called Muse, which allows an AI agent to send emails, fill forms, make plans and even make purchases autonomously. Prior to this, OpenAI also introduced Dots that can draft board meeting decks, conduct background research, and handle multi-step project management. xAI has also been developing Grok Bot, which sees cleaning up sales records and processing invoices as potential uses for agents. Microsoft is also pursuing agents, built on OpenClaw, which can function as digital teammates. Back home, Emergent, better known for its vibe-coding platform, launched Wingman, an autonomous agent that handles routine actions and seeks approval before taking bigger steps.

Tokyo protests after two suspected Russian aircraft violate Japanese airspace
Japan said it has protested to Moscow after two suspected Russian warplanes temporarily entered Japanese airspace off the country’s southwestern coast on Tuesday as tensions escalate between the two sides
TOKYO -- Japan said it strongly protested to Moscow on Tuesday after two suspected Russian aircraft entered its airspace off its southwestern coast, the latest incident fueling escalating tensions between the neighbors.
Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi told reporters the suspected Russian aircraft early Tuesday violated Japanese airspace for about five minutes near Fukuoka, long enough for the Air Self-Defense Force to scramble fighter jets and send warnings.
Japan's government has lodged "an extremely stern protest" and “strongly” demanded preventive measures be taken, Koizumi said. He did not specify the types of aircraft involved.
“The violation of the Japanese airspace by the Russian aircraft is not only a serious violation of our country's sovereignty, but also a threat to our safety,” Koizumi said. “It is absolutely unacceptable.”
The Russian aircraft flew across the Tsushima Strait, then headed south and flew above the waters between Taiwan and Japan's westernmost island of Yonaguni, Koizumi said.
Separately, South Korea’s military said several Russian military aircraft temporarily entered the country’s air defense identification zone over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan on Monday, though they did not violate South Korean airspace.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said the military had detected the aircraft before they entered the zone and scrambled fighter jets. The South’s military did not disclose the number of Russian aircraft it detected or what types of planes they were.
Koizumi did not comment on why the violations took place but said Japan continues to closely monitor Russian military activity “with strong interest."
Japan has raised growing concern over growing joint military activity between Russia and China around the Japanese coasts.
The airspace violation was the latest sign of deteriorating relations between the two countries. Tensions have risen since Russian President Vladimir Putin visited Iturup in August, one of four Russian-controlled islands off Japan’s northern coast that Tokyo also claims.
Tensions escalated in mid-October after the arrest of a Japanese journalist in Russia on suspicion of spying. Despite repeated protests and demands for his immediate release, the journalist, who works for the Hokkaido newspaper, remains in custody.
Earlier this month, Russia placed several subsidiaries of Japan Tobacco Inc. under the temporary management of a Russian company following a presidential order issued by Putin. Japan protested and demanded the measure be withdrawn.
The Soviet Union seized the Kuril Islands from Japan in the final days of World War II. The territorial dispute has prevented the two countries from signing a peace treaty formally ending hostilities.

The Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodríguez, who gained prominence for publishing allegations against suspected drug traffickers and politicians, was shot dead on Monday, authorities said.
The first known killing of a journalist in Costa Rica in 25 years, Rodriguez’s death comes as the country grapples with a surge in drug violence driven by international trafficking groups, despite long being regarded as one of Central America’s most peaceful and stable democracies.
Rodriguez, 51, was attacked at about 3.20pm local time amid heavy traffic on a main highway on the outskirts of the capital San José, the Red Cross reported.
President Laura Fernández condemned the attack in a video message.
“I am filled with indignation and outrage over the cowardly murder of communicator Camilo Rodríguez. Regardless of the content of his communications, what happened today in our country is a stain on freedom of expression,” Fernández said.
The attorney general, Carlo Díaz, told the local news outlet Extra Noticias that investigators found multiple bullet impacts and a crime scene resembling a contract killing, probably linked to the allegations Rodríguez had published. He gave no further evidence and did not name suspects.
“We know he was a communicator who publicly identified people for alleged links to drug trafficking,” Díaz said, adding that Rodríguez had previously reported threats but had declined protection.
“Silencing someone who reports on drug trafficking or corruption, in this case a communicator, is a signal we cannot tolerate in a democratic society.“
Díaz pledged efforts to hold those responsible for the murder accountable.
The last such attack on a media worker happened in July 2001 when the radio producer Parmenio Medina was gunned down on a Santo Domingo highway, in roughly the same area as Rodríguez’s attack took place.
Costa Rica’s homicide rate doubled between 2013 and 2023 and has only eased slightly since then.

Australian cricket's sandpapergate is back - and it cuts deep in a 'nation of good sports'
- Published
As Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins spent more than an hour being grilled by reporters over one of sport's biggest cheating scandals, the tension in the hall was occasionally pierced by muffled cheers.
Outside, a crucial match in the top tier of domestic cricket was getting under way. Cummins was clear he'd rather we all be talking about that.
But inside the nets at Cricket Central in Sydney, he faced more than a dozen TV cameras and a gaggle of journalists several times as large. His goal: to put rumours of his involvement in "sandpapergate" to rest.
"I don't want to talk about this again after today," he said. "Even if it takes all day... I'll stay here until we have no more questions."
A book by his friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja has renewed scrutiny on a 2018 plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town.
Three players admitted they were involved at the time and were handed lengthy bans, but in a memoir released last week, Khawaja said the entire Australian team knew about the sandpaper scheme.
His claims have plunged the Australian cricket world into chaos, thrown speculation over key figures from that Test - including star bowler Cummins who has since risen to hold what many joke is Australia's most important job - and reopened wounds for fans.
Josh, 28, told the BBC he thought everyone had moved on: "It's just a bit crazy that it's all blown up again... I think it is a bit ridiculous, after eight years."
"I'm a bit bored of it," one woman watching the New South Wales vs South Australia Sheffield Shield match said.
Among fans, there's frustration that Khawaja has chosen to come forward now, almost a decade on and at the start of an exciting summer, and year, of cricket. Though there's an argument there'd never be a good time for Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, to make these allegations.
There's worry about the impact on the men's team's performance this summer, after a lacklustre showing in South Africa last month - its first Test matches there since the 2018 incident.
There's a sense of injustice that Australia can't escape the scandal, given - according to many players themselves - how common boundary-bending on ball tampering apparently was in that era.
"It's a bit of a stitch up," 21-year-old James said.
"Every country has done it... if it wasn't us, it was probably going to be someone else."
Khawaja's memoir is also causing rancour among current and former players and coaches.
David Warner, who received the most severe punishment of the Cape Town trio, said Khawaja was telling the truth and that Cummins' press conference denying the claims "threw him under the bus".
Steve Smith, the captain at the time who was also suspended, has been travelling overseas and is yet to say anything publicly about the claims in the book. Cameron Bancroft is also staying silent for now despite previously suggesting the bowlers knew.
But half of Australia's living cricket royalty and a slew of former coaches - some of whom have been accused of wrongdoing too - have thrown in their two cents.
And Cricket Australia is under pressure from some to reopen its investigation into sandpapergate - something chief executive Todd Greenberg has already ruled out.
Prof David Rowe of the University of Western Sydney told the BBC the saga was still so painful for many players and fans as the country sees itself as "a nation of good sports".
"The idea of being a good sport is two things. One is being good at sport, so you actually win. But the other side is that you do it honourably and fairly," he said.
"Many Australians would see themselves as above all that. That is: cheating is what other teams get up to... not the nation of good sports."
He said the revelation was a "nasty shock" which brought the country "collective shame" which lingers today.
He says he doubts that the cricket scene would be able to move on without a fresh response from the governing body, Cricket Australia.
"One of the best ways to fuel conspiracy theories and keep sandpapergate going is to essentially say 'there's no more to see here' - especially when that comes from the authorities," Rowe said.
Asked about a fresh investigation, Cummins said it was a matter for Cricket Australia.
Over the marathon press conference - which one reporter suggested was the longest in Australian sporting history - Cummins was cautious, pausing often to consider his responses and to make sure they answered the questions being asked of him.
But he was also frank - using strong words to reject Khawaja's claims and admitting he was frustrated a friend had put him in this position. "Friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations... That's something I've been grappling with the last couple of days."
As the reporters ran out of steam, Cummins said it was "annoying" that sandpapergate scandal was still a distraction for Australian cricket. He gestured outside to the Sheffield Shield match and mentioning Friday's one-day international against England in Perth, from which he and other key players are being rested.
"It's been eight years... Hopefully today we put a line through it and we're done and we can all move on to much more fun topics, like actual cricket."
Few people think he'll get his wish.
"It's going to be hard to move on, given that there's two sides of the story and it doesn't look like either side is going to back down," James said.
"I don't know what the outcome will be."

Exposure to extreme heat during pregnancy can lead to severe outcomes, including preterm birth, stillbirth and congenital abnormalities in newborns, prompting experts at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) to highlight maternal health risks and call for targeted adaptation strategies.
The issue comes into focus as countries at COP31 prepare to discuss progress towards the Global Goal on Adaptation, a framework to help nations develop key adaptation measures, including those needed to address the health impacts of climate change.
However, translating growing recognition of climate-related health risks into action remains a challenge, particularly in the absence of adequate financial support.
According to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), only about one per cent of formal climate finance under its financial mechanism is currently directed towards health.
The broader issue of adaptation finance for developing nations is also expected to feature prominently in discussions in the coming days.
Speaking to PTI on the sidelines of COP31, Alan Dangour, Director of Climate and Health at the Wellcome Trust, said the foundation is seeking to highlight the evidence of heat-related impacts on pregnant women through three key areas -- elevating the issues as a risk for women, developing guidelines and preparing health systems.
“We have three key points: recognising that pregnant women are a particularly vulnerable group when it comes to climate-driven extreme heat, developing guidelines to help nurses, midwives and doctors respond to the challenges pregnant women face during heatwaves, and prepare health systems for a new world shaped by climate change, and identify the most vulnerable people so they are protected,” Dangour said.
He said pregnant women were not always recognised as a particularly vulnerable group and stressed that health systems must specifically account for their needs and risks during heatwaves.
“At the moment they are not recognised as such, and they need to be included in clinical guidelines. When it comes to data, we are keen that countries record the impacts of climate change on pregnant women and then work out how their guidelines and processes can protect them,” he said.
“That evidence is important because we can see what works and what doesn’t in different parts of the world, and share that knowledge,” he said.
Former World Health Organisation (WHO) chief scientist Soumya Swaminathan stressed the importance of highlighting the issue at COP31, saying the health impacts of climate change were already being felt and required immediate action.
“It is good that for the last three COPs or so we have had a day focused on health and climate, because everyone is increasingly recognising that the health impacts of climate change are already happening and need immediate action. They are also hitting certain vulnerable groups disproportionately, and pregnant women are one of them,” Swaminathan told PTI.
Citing studies showing that exposure to extreme heat can affect pregnant women's health, pregnancy outcomes and the health of newborns, she said the WHO had recently released a document identifying pregnant women as a high-risk group and recommending measures countries should take to protect them.
She also stressed the need to integrate climate and health data, saying policymakers must urgently begin linking exposure to extreme heat and air pollutants with their effects on human health.
“When heat and air pollution occur together in the same place, the impacts are three times as high as from either risk factor alone. India has many places with both heat and bad air pollution, so we must start looking at these data and correlating exposure to climatic and weather variables, such as heat and pollutants, with health outcomes,” the former WHO chief scientist told PTI.
Swaminathan said there was an urgent need for a research programme to address the issue, adding that sufficient evidence was already available to warrant action. She also called for the government's and states' Maternal and Child Health Programme to factor in heat exposure and take proactive and preventive measures to minimise its impact on pregnant women.
Youssef Nassef, Director of the Adaptation Programme at UN Climate Change, said the first 1,000 days, from conception until a child turns two, were considered the most critical period, as climate-related harm could begin even before birth.
“A lot of what we're talking about in terms of climate impacts generally, but heat in particular, has a severe impact on maternal health, on newborn babies. Unfortunately, in climate finance, about 1 per cent of formal climate finance under the financial mechanism goes to health. There is an incongruence between the needs, the demand and the supply,” he said.
Bhavreen Kandhari, an environmentalist and the co-founder of the ‘Warrior Moms’ movement, underscored that heatwaves have had a significant impact on pregnant women, particularly those living in more vulnerable areas or working in more vulnerable occupations, such as daily-wage workers, construction workers and farmers.
“Daily-wage workers, for instance, have to earn a living. They have to continue working because they simply cannot afford to stop. There is no looking back for them. Vulnerable mothers and other at-risk groups are not thinking about the future, but simply trying to survive this particular season, or, at most, looking ahead to the next one,” she said.

Oregon is the latest state to sue OpenAI over child safety
The state’s lawsuit calls on the company to address child safety issues and pay at least $2 billion in damages.
Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield has filed a lawsuit accusing OpenAI of endangering the state's children, misleading the public about the safety of its product and violating the state's Unlawful Trade Practices Act. The lawsuit is the latest in a string of legal actions taken by state AGs, many of which have taken issue with the design of ChatGPT, how OpenAI advertises its services and, in the case of California's recent lawsuit, the company's role in the Hugging Face incident.
The Oregon lawsuit claims that OpenAI's push to grow its user base led it to make ChatGPT respond to prompts in a way that's overly affirming and "calculated to tell users exactly what they want to hear," something the state claims is particularly dangerous when children discuss sensitive topics. The lawsuit also alleges that despite recognizing the risks posed to children, OpenAI pursued them directly with an experience called ChatGPT for Teens. Child safety groups have raised concerns about the teen accounts, saying the safeguards are, in some cases, very easy to work around.
Those issues, along with OpenAI's imperfect approach to automatic age prediction, are evidence, according to the state, that the company is profiting off of Oregon residents and creating a public nuisance that threatens their safety. In response, Oregon is asking the court for an injunction that would force OpenAI to stop "misrepresenting the safety and age-appropriateness of ChatGPT and ChatGPT for Teens" and adequately disclose the harms its products pose to children. The state is also seeking at least $2 billion in damages and civil penalties.
"OpenAI knows that ChatGPT is harming children, and has failed to meaningfully fix their dangerous platform," Rayfield said in a statement. "On top of that, they've misled the public about the safety of their products, putting profits ahead of children's safety. Their platform is encouraging kids to commit suicide — we cannot let this be an acceptable business model."
Engadget has asked OpenAI to comment on the lawsuit and Oregon's claims. We'll update this article if we hear back.
Besides trying to create versions of ChatGPT that are safer for kids, OpenAI has also rolled out parental controls and other child safety features to try to give parents more insight and control over what their kids use the chatbot for. None of these changes have been enough to dissuade states from pursuing lawsuits, and given the settlements Meta has recently reached over its child safety issues, AGs likely feel emboldened to pressure OpenAI into concessions.

Security forces on Wednesday (November 18, 2026) killed LeT terrorist Lateef Bhat, who was hiding inside a mosque in south Kashmir’s Kulgam.
A team of security forces, who were tracking on-the-run Bhat, came under fire from inside a mosque around 3 a.m. in Kulgam’s Zangalpora. “We had a long conversation with him on the phone. We asked him to surrender but he refused. We exercised maximum restraint given he was hiding inside a mosque,” said Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Anayat Ali Choudhary.
“It’s a big success, given the fact he joined (the terror outfit) in November last year. He was radicalised and would take guidelines from across to hit peace, tourism and economy here (Kashmir),” said SSP Choudhary.
Senior officials said Bhat, 22, was later killed in the joint operation of the Army and the J&K Police.
Bhat attacked CRPF personnel in Kulgam’s Akhran area on November 11, which left three jawans injured. In the past eight days, security forces continued multiple anti-terror operations in the district and killed Bhat’s accomplice Umar Nisar Dar, a baker by profession, two days ago in Kulgam’s Laroo Bypass area.
According to the police, both Bhat and Dar were behind the November 11 attack in Kulgam. Bhat was also behind the twin attacks in Anantnag and Kulgam, which left one policeman and two non-local labourers from Chhattisgarh dead in July this year. The J&K Police had announced a cash reward of ₹15 lakh on him.
Bhat was a resident of Khrewan Chader in Kulgam’s Ashmuji and would work as a carpenter.
Meanwhile, an Army spokesman said security forces displayed exemplary restraint during the conduct of operations “ensuring the sanctity of the religious place and neutralised the terrorist with precision by forcing him to move out of the mosque premises”. “The operation is in progress,” said the Army.
Nation salutes brave jawans, says Amit Shah
Union Home Minister Amit Shah said “With the coordinated efforts of JKP, Indian Army, CRPF and intelligence agencies, Lashkar’s last known active local terrorist in the valley, Lateef Bhat, was neutralised in an operation in Kulgam in the early morning hours today. One of his terrorist associates, Umar Nisar, was also neutralised in Kulgam, the day before. The entire operation was marked by a very high level of synergy.”
He added “The nation salutes the brave Jawans of JKP, Army and CRPF and intelligence agencies.”

Gilead Sciences said on Monday it had signed royalty-free deals with three generic drugmakers to make its experimental Ebola prevention drug available in 127 mainly low- and lower-middle-income countries if it succeeds in trials and wins regulatory approvals.
The deals with Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories, Eva Pharma and Ferozsons Laboratories cover obeldesivir, and include all African countries reporting cases in the current Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak. Obeldesivir has shown activity against several Ebola-related viruses in preclinical studies but is not approved for any use in any country.
A late-stage trial is testing the drug in people at high risk after exposure. The deals are intended to line up manufacturing and supply before trial results and regulatory filings.
Gilead is also expanding remdesivir licences to cover Ebola-related diseases if trial results are positive and regulators approve the drug. The company has donated more than 38,000 remdesivir vials to the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda and Kenya, including more than 2,000 recently sent to Kenya for investigational treatment and post-exposure prevention.
Remdesivir is not approved to treat or prevent Ebola Bundibugyo disease, and its clinical effectiveness has not been established.
