Quick Answer
LastWave, Musify, Convx, Spotube, and SimpMusic are free open-source clients for YouTube Music and Spotify. They unlock premium perks without subscription fees or ad tracking, offering background playback, offline downloads, time-synced lyrics, lossless audio, and customized interfaces without locked controls.
Subscription prices are going through the roof. And when you stack multiple subscriptions together, it can put a big hole in your pocket. For listening to music, we usually depend on Spotify and YouTube Music. They are the default music streaming sources for millions across the globe. Though there are alternatives from which you can hear high-quality audio, they just can’t match the ease of popular apps. But you are bombarded with ads, and several features are locked behind a paywall unless you pay.
Thankfully, you don’t have to search the internet for free options. Developers around the world have built free apps that give you many of those perks. Below are five of the best, what each does well, and what to watch out for before installing.
Table of Contents
Why are open-source music apps worth a look?
To be clear, most of these apps are clients. This means that they don’t store any music themselves. They plug into a service like YouTube Music and show it in a cleaner, ad-free interface with extra features on top, which you’d usually get after paying for a premium subscription. For me, Spotify has been the go-to music streaming app, but slowly the app has become quite greedy.
After a few times, the next and previous song buttons get locked, and it asks you to pay to unlock them. I mean, what is wrong with companies today? Thankfully, I have now ditched Spotify and have picked one of the below open-source music options.
That has three practical effects:
- No ads and no subscription fees. Everything below is free.
- Most of these apps have no ad trackers or tracking SDKs.
- New features are constantly added, and some of them aren’t even available in paid apps.
The catch is that these apps rely on unofficial methods to fetch music, so they can break when YouTube or Spotify changes something. Treat them as great free alternatives, but not as rock-solid replacements. Let us take a look at the free alternatives.
Best free open-source music apps
LastWave
If you care about how your music sounds, LastWave is the one to install first. It’s a free YouTube Music client for Android, Windows, macOS, and Linux. Most of us would care about the free music that we get with LastWave, but you will soon appreciate the quality of music that it offers. And since it is a YouTube Music client, you are getting access to almost every song that is available on YouTube.
The headline feature is lossless FLAC audio, up to 24-bit/192 kHz. When you press play, the song starts playing right away on the fastest available stream, and while you listen, the app fetches the lossless version in the background and switches over once it’s ready. On compatible phones and headphones, LastWave also plays the Dolby Atmos version of a song automatically. For those who own a USB DAC or a pair of IEMs, there’s a bit-perfect mode that sends raw, unprocessed audio straight to your device.
The app is packed with features that normally sit behind a subscription. The lyrics are synced word-by-word and pulled from sources like Apple Music, Musixmatch, and LRCLIB. There’s a 10-band equalizer with presets for thousands of headphone models, and smart playlists that build mixes from your listening history. Plus, you have the option to import playlists from Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube Music in seconds, and even sync your Spotify liked songs.
Musify
Not everyone wants a hundred settings and toggles. Some people just want to listen to their favorite music without having to deal with ads and a hundred pop-ups about purchasing the subscription between two songs. Musify is for people who just want to open an app, search for a song, and press play. It’s a lightweight Android app built around Material You, which means its colors automatically match your phone’s theme and wallpaper.
Using it is fairly easy. You search for songs, albums, artists, or playlists and start streaming over Wi-Fi or mobile data. If you want to save data or listen on a flight, you can download tracks and play them offline. It lets you create your own playlists, rename and reorder them, or import existing ones from online sources. The player shows lyrics so you can follow along. You can also control the quality of the audio.
There are no annoying banner ads, no audio ads, no sign-up, and no tracking inside the app, and the interface is translated into dozens of languages by the community. I found this to be a great choice for older phones, or for a parent or sibling who finds complicated apps annoying.
Convx
While most open source music apps work well, there are only a few that also feel nice to use. Convx comes in the second category. If you like iOS’s “Liquid Glass” design, then you would love Convx. It brings iPhone’s Liquid Glass design to Android, with frosted, see-through menus, floating controls, and album-inspired colors that change with whatever you are playing.
Under the pretty surface, Convx is a complete music player. You can browse and stream music, save songs for offline listening, build queues and playlists, set a sleep timer, change playback speed, and tweak the sound to your taste with an equalizer. What makes it stand out among the heavy hitters is its DJ-style playback. You also get automix, crossfade, and smooth transitions between one song and the next. Lyrics are synced word by word and come from several providers, plus it gets animated artwork.
Convx can play local files and even songs stored on a home server or NAS through SMB and WebDAV. You can choose the option to import your Spotify playlists, show what you’re playing on Discord, scrobble to Last.fm, recognize songs playing around you, and use Listen Together to sync playback with friends.
Spotube
Spotube is the veteran here, with over 46,000 stars on GitHub, and it works differently from the rest. Instead of being locked to one service like Spotify or YouTube, it runs on plugins. You choose your own music sources, metadata, and playlists through plugins made by the community, or if you’re good with it, you can write one yourself.
The biggest advantage is that it works everywhere. Spotube runs natively on Android, Windows, macOS, and Linux. This means you can use the same app on your phone and your laptop. It’s small, fast, and light on data. You can import and sync playlists from popular music services or manage them locally. It gives time-synced lyrics from public lyric databases no matter which source you use. Offline downloads are supported, with proper metadata and ID.
Privacy is one of the biggest highlights of Spotube. It collects no telemetry and no user data. Installing it is also easy, because you can download it through winget, Scoop, Chocolatey, Homebrew, Flatpak, and F-Droid.
SimpMusic
SimpMusic is that one app that does everything. It’s a free YouTube Music client for Android and desktop that borrows many of Spotify’s best ideas. You can play music from YouTube Music or regular YouTube without ads, and it gets you background playback. You can browse the home feed, charts, podcasts and moods, search everything on YouTube, cache songs for offline playback and use Android Auto.
SimpMusic Wrapped gives you a year-in-music recap just like Spotify’s. Then there is monthly recap playlists and listening charts that stay on your device. There are three Now Playing styles, including one that looks like Apple Music, and the lyrics are synced in 12 languages. You can even share lyrics as an image.
You can switch to 1080p video with subtitles, skip sponsor segments with SponsorBlock, see dislike counts with Return YouTube Dislike, and use a 10-band equalizer with AutoEq headphone profiles.
Which one should you pick?
If you care most about sound quality, I would suggest LastWave. If you want something simple, pick Musify. If design matters to you, try Convx. If you want plugins and an app that runs on every device you own, choose Spotube. If you want the most features in one place, install SimpMusic. The best part is that all five are free and can be installed side by side, so you can try a few and keep your favorite. You will get access to unlimited songs from the best sources in good quality. Let us know which one you chose, and comment below if you have a different app that you use for listening to music.

Shiv Sena tears pages from Sonia Gandhi's book over Savarkar remarks, demands ban
Shiv Sena protested Sonia Gandhi's memoir, accusing it of insulting Savarkar and Marathi pride, tearing pages and demanding the publisher withdraw the book until corrections are made.
The Eknath Shinde-led Shiv Sena on Wednesday launched a protest against Sonia Gandhi's memoir, tearing pages from the book over remarks on Hindutva ideologue VD Savarkar and demanding its withdrawal from circulation in Maharashtra. Accusing the Congress leader of insulting Savarkar and undermining Marathi pride, the party sought the removal of two contentious passages from the memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love.
The party also demanded that circulation of the book be stopped in Maharashtra until the publisher makes the necessary corrections. Shiv Sena leaders Sanjay Nirupam, Shaina NC, Anand Dubey and others participated in the protest.
The controversy centres on remarks about Savarkar, who was from Maharashtra and the RSS in two passages cited by the protesters, appearing on pages 201 and 443 of the book.
On page 201, while mentioning Indira Gandhi's antipathy to the politics of the RSS, Sonia Gandhi wrote that while Congress freedom fighters were facing assaults and imprisonment under British rule, senior RSS ideologues such as Savarkar were writing mercy petitions to the colonial authorities.
"While Congress freedom fighters were enduring assaults and imprisonment at the hands of the British rulers, senior ideologues of the RSS like Vinayak Damodar Savarkar were writing mercy petitions to their colonial masters and their members were colluding with the British authorities as informers," the passage reads.
Another passage, on page 443, describes Savarkar as the founder of the ideology of Hindutva and says his vision viewed India primarily as a nation where Hindus were supreme. It further links this outlook to the RSS, the BJP and their affiliates, collectively referred to as the Sangh Parivar.
"That ideology dismisses the delineation of the country and the rights of its citizens set down in the Constitution as ideas opposed to the ethos of Hindu civilisation, ideas they dismiss as being derived from Western countries with fundamentally alien values," the book said.
Reacting to the passages, Shiv Sena leader Sanjay Nirupam launched a sharp attack on Sonia Gandhi, describing the book as "Belonging: A Journey of Hate" rather than Belonging: A Journey of Love.
"Sonia Gandhi harbours deep hatred towards the freedom fighters and revolutionaries of this country. She also has hatred towards the country and its Hindus," Nirupam said.
He accused the Congress leader of insulting Savarkar through her remarks and said the party had gathered to protest against the alleged disrespect.
"As a mark of protest, we tore out the page of the book that contains the insulting remarks about Savarkar," he said. "The Shiv Sena in Maharashtra will not tolerate any insult to Savarkar".
Nirupam outlined three demands on behalf of the party. First, HarperCollins should withdraw the book and remove all pages containing what the party considers derogatory remarks about Savarkar. Second, circulation of the book in Maharashtra should be stopped until the necessary corrections are made. Third, the party would take its protest to various online platforms.
Shiv Sena national secretary and spokesperson Shaina NC also launched a scathing attack on Sonia Gandhi, accusing her of attempting to undermine Savarkar's legacy.
"Sonia Gandhi humiliates Savarkar. She calls him a Hindutva exclusionary. But Balasaheb Thackeray always said that Savarkar is the soul of Hindutva," she said.
Drawing a comparison between Sonia Gandhi's citizenship and Savarkar's imprisonment, Shaina questioned her authority to comment on the freedom fighter's contribution.
"Sonia ji, it took you 15-plus years to even initiate the process of Indian citizenship. Savarkar gave 50-plus years of his life, not just in jail, but also for the cause of Bharat. Who are you to judge?" she said.
She added that while writing a book was welcome, attempts to rewrite history would not be tolerated. Shaina also demanded that HarperCollins eliminate pages 201 and 443, reiterating that Savarkar had spent 11 years in the Cellular Jail for India's freedom.
BJP MLA in Maharashta, Ram Ladam, also criticised Sonia Gandhi's remarks, questioning whether the book was an autobiography or an account of personal anguish.
"Mr Gandhi, is this Sonia Gandhi's autobiography or an account of her personal anguish? There is some controversy on every page," he said.
Ladam referred to Savarkar's imprisonment in the Cellular Jail in the Andaman Islands and his sacrifices for India's freedom. He said Savarkar had endured imprisonment and continued to live a life akin to that of a prisoner for another four to five years after his release.
The NDA leaders also invoked a 2004 incident, when Shiv Sena founder Balasaheb Thackeray slapped an effigy of Congress leader Mani Shankar Aiyar with a slipper during a protest at Mumbai's Shivaji Park over alleged disrespect towards freedom fighter Veer Savarkar.
However, while tearing pages from the memoir, Shaina NC ripped a photograph of Bal Thackeray, which showed the Shiv Sena founder hitting an effigy of Aiyar with slippers.
SHIV SENA TARGETS UDDHAV THACKERAY
The protest also turned into an attack on Shiv Sena (UBT) chief Uddhav Thackeray, with the Shinde-led faction questioning his decision to accept a copy of Sonia Gandhi's book. Sanjay Nirupam said Uddhav Thackeray had accepted the book despite the alleged insult to Savarkar and Marathi pride.
"When action was proposed against Union Minister Mani Shankar Aiyar, Balasaheb Thackeray had launched a protest against him. Will Uddhav Thackeray now launch a similar protest against Sonia Gandhi?" he asked.

October has rolled around, and that means only one thing: Spooky season is here! And what better way to celebrate Halloween than with some of the finest fright fests of the last 50 years?
We’re bringing you a more retro-tinged selection of the best films on streaming this month, but the mix of crowd-pleasers and cult classics offers something for horror fans of all tastes. For instance, David Cronenberg’s grotesque revamp of The Fly, buzzing onto Hulu, and Ken Russell’s Altered States materializing on The Criterion Channel, both bring uniquely visceral takes on body horror to your screens, while sleeper hit Under the Skin on Netflix offers slow-burn sci-fi scares, and Midsommar on Prime Video takes to the hills for a sun-drenched approach to folk horror.
If you fancy something a bit newer, fear not. Well, fear lots actually—Zach Cregger’s shockingly original horror debut Barbarian smashes its way onto Hulu, while Netflix brings the final chapter in the sumptuously scary Mononoke trilogy, an anime extravaganza that looks like nothing else. Plus, there’s even one post-credits stinger of an entry that’s too scary to mention here …
Here are WIRED’s picks of the best movies to watch right now.
Barbarian
When Tess (Georgina Campbell) finds her Airbnb in a sketchy neighborhood double booked with Keith (Bill Skarsgård), you’ll probably think you know where Barbarian is headed. You don't—and you should brace yourself for everything that follows. Written and directed by Zach Cregger (in a seismic departure from his early comedy background), Barbarian constantly flips the script, regularly subverting viewer expectations of horror movie clichés at every turn.
Smartly written, brilliantly shot, and psychologically disturbing on multiple levels, Barbarian is a genuinely terrifying entry in the modern horror canon. If you’ve discovered Cregger’s work from the Academy Award–winning Weapons or his recent horror-comedy reboot of Resident Evil, this is where he first made his mark on the silver screen.
Under the Skin
Under the Skin almost defies explanation. Scarlett Johansson plays an alien in human form, roaming Glasgow and the Scottish Highlands, luring isolated and lonely men to their doom, drowning them in an inexplicable oily abyss that seems to exist in a null space. All the while, she’s observed by a motorcyclist, trailing her from victim to victim.
No names are given, no purpose explained (not even to the cast; director Jonathan Glazer shot many of the alien’s initial encounters with humans using hidden cameras, only explaining and asking for their involvement afterward), but it’s far better to watch this blind and make your own mind up. Be warned, though—Johansson’s performance is truly unearthly, and in conjunction with Glazer’s bizarre imagery and a soundscape that maddeningly claws at your nerves, this is a deeply unsettling slice of sci-fi.
Midsommar
This acclaimed indie horror movie stars Florence Pugh as Dani, an American student struggling to deal with a family tragedy, who joins her boyfriend Christian (Jack Reynor) and his friends on a trip to Sweden. The vacation sounds like the perfect escape—nine days of communing with nature at a festival held only once every 90 years; a true once-in-a-lifetime experience. The problem? The festival is a front for a pagan cult, and things get rapidly, wildly out of hand.
Midsommar is a deeply effective and distressing folk horror film, with none other than Jordan Peele, director of the smash hit Get Out, declaring it has "the most atrociously disturbing imagery I've ever seen on film." Perfect date night material for Halloween season, then.
Train to Busan
South Korean cinema seems to love combining the end of the world and trains. Bong Joon Ho’s Snowpiercer got things on track in 2013, but director Yeon Sang-ho really left the station with this 2016 zombie horror masterpiece.
Seok-woo (Gong Yoo) starts his journey on the express train from Seoul to Busan just wanting to drop daughter Su-an off with her mother. Unfortunately, the last passenger to board might be a teensy bit infected with the zombie plague that’s kicking off outside, turning the ride into the express train to hell. The tight confines allow for some incredibly inventive action choreography, while genre fans are treated to a revolting twist on the undead themselves, a misshapen, juddering, ravenous horde that moves like a liquid mass of corpses.
Like all the best zombie films, though, it’s the social commentary that really elevates Train to Busan, with its exploration of class and status standing alongside Romero’s work at his peak. A decade on from release, this is still one of the freshest takes on zombies you’re likely to find—look up animated prequel Seoul Station and stand-alone sequel Peninsula if it leaves you wanting another bite.
Altered States
A bit of a deep cut, but director Ken Russell’s 1980 outing will really mess with your head. No, really—this tale of psychological horror and transformational terror is loosely based on real-world tests of the effects of psychoactive drugs and sensory deprivation on the human brain. The film sees researcher Eddie Jessup (William Hurt) subjecting himself to highly questionable experiments with hallucinogenics and isolation in an effort to tap into other states of being. Unfortunately, he’s wildly successful, not only opening his mind to genetic memories and shared consciousnesses, but seeing his physical body horrifyingly warp and devolve beyond recognition with each trip.
And what a trip—Russell masterfully creates a sense of psychedelic overload with a pioneering use of bizarre imagery and sound, the film shifting with each of Jessup’s transformations until you feel you’ve taken mind-altering substances yourself. An uncomfortably weird experience, Altered States will stay on your mind long after the credits roll.
Colossal
Anne Hathaway is literally a monster—at least she is in this darkly comedic crossover between kaiju flick and character study. After her life in New York falls apart, Gloria (Hathaway) moves back home to New Hampshire. At the same time, a giant monster starts rampaging across Seoul, destroying buildings and causing mass panic. Yet these two incompatible events aren't unrelated, as Gloria starts to realize that she can somehow control the beast from half a world away—but her heavy drinking and constant bad decisions may get in the way of saving the world. Director Nacho Vigalondo lovingly pastiches the likes of Godzilla, Gamera, and King Kong in this quirky film festival favorite.
Mononoke The Movie III: The Curse of the Serpent
A nameless Medicine Seller (Hiroshi Kamiya in Japanese, Crispin Freeman in English) traveling Edo period Japan may seem a humble figure, but his strange tinctures and concoctions make him one of the few capable of tackling mononoke—powerful spirits corrupting places and people alike. This trilogy-capping third movie takes the enigmatic traveler back to the cursed Imperial Palace visited in predecessors Phantom in the Rain and Ashes of Rage, seeking to uncover once and for all why it seems to attract so many dangerous monsters.
A master class in tension and otherworldly horror, Mononoke maintains its stunning visual approach of kaleidoscopic watercolors swirling on parchment, making for one of the most sumptuous and visually striking pieces of animation you’ll ever see. It’s worth noting that there is some real-world controversy over a returning voice actor embroiled in a scandal in Japan, so this might be a rare case where the English dub is the better option.
The Fly
Despite being a remake, David Cronenberg’s quintessential slice of 1980s body horror has almost completely supplanted the 1958 original in the public consciousness (although the original stars Vincent Price and is definitely still worth checking out on Prime Video).
This wholesale reimagining twists expectations away from mad science clichés—it almost feels like a superhero origin movie to start, with scientist Seth Brundle (Jeff Goldblum) accidentally splicing his genes with a fly during a teleportation experiment, and emerging with enhanced physical prowess in every respect. But with great power comes great personality shifts, wiry black hairs growing along his back, and the need to vomit acid onto his food before eating. And, as animal instincts take over, the self-proclaimed “Brundlefly” starts looking at science reporter Ronnie Quaife (Geena Davis) very differently.
The groundbreaking effects work that marked Brundle’s slow metamorphosis into a repulsive hybrid monster won the film the Oscar for Best Makeup, but its ability to pack in some genuine emotion alongside the scares make it easy to see why this is the de facto iteration of The Fly.
The Social Network
Oh, you think this isn’t horror? Ask yourself: What could possibly be scarier than the deleterious impact social media has had on the human condition? Director David Fincher and writer Aaron Sorkin’s biopic telling of the rise, and rise, and rise of Facebook, is the kind of film you watch through your fingers, too.
There’s an almost predatory hunger in Jesse Eisenberg’s Mark Zuckerberg, as he goes from a Harvard student whose hotness-ranking website was popular enough to crash the college’s whole network to a Silicon Valley darling attracting unheard-of sums of investment and power. Like most “based on a true story” horror films, it’s not entirely historically accurate and, true to genre norms, there’s a not-as-good sequel, with Sorkin returning to write and direct the newly released The Social Reckoning, but if you’ve been paying attention to reality the past few decades, this will definitely chill you to the bone.

Mozambique opposition leader faces trial over deadly 2024 election unrest
- Published
Tensions are running high in Mozambique's capital, Maputo, with a heavy police deployment as a prominent opposition leader goes on trial over deadly protests that followed the country's disputed 2024 elections.
Venâncio Mondlane faces several charges, including incitement to terrorism and civil disobedience, over protests that left hundreds of people dead. He denies any wrongdoing.
Security has been tightened around the Supreme Court, where Mondlane is due to appear on Tuesday, with authorities fearing a fresh wave of demonstrations by his supporters.
Police have appealed to citizens to follow the proceedings calmly and avoid actions that could threaten public order.
The trial is widely seen as a major test of Mozambique's political stability, nearly two years after disputed elections triggered some of the country's deadliest political unrest in decades.
"The trial is a real test for Mozambique. It is is an important opportunity to demonstrate that the rule of law applies equally to everyone," said Luis Nhachote, a political analyst.
Mondlane, who challenged the presidential election results that declared Daniel Chapo of the ruling Frelimo party the winner, accused the authorities of widespread electoral fraud and called for nationwide protests and work stoppages.
- Children shot dead after joining pot-banging protests in Mozambique 
  - Published23 November 2024
The demonstrations continued for months, with rights groups accusing security forces of using excessive force against protesters.
Amnesty International, citing local civil society organisations, said more than 300 people were killed during the unrest, which was one of the country's worst post-election crises since independence.
Mozambican police put the death toll at 96, including 17 police officers.
European Union election observers also reported irregularities in the October 2024 vote, raising questions about the credibility of the results.
Prosecutors accuse Mondlane of encouraging demonstrations that disrupted public services, damaged property and threatened public security.
The charges include publicly glorifying criminal acts, incitement to collective disobedience, public instigation to commit crimes and offences linked to terrorism.
He could face up to 24 years in prison if convicted of the most serious charge.
Mondlane has rejected the accusations, insisting that his calls for demonstrations were aimed at demanding electoral transparency rather than encouraging violence.
His party, the National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (Anamola), has described the prosecution as politically motivated.
The Supreme Court has denied allegations of political interference in the proceedings.
A heavy deployment of police has been seen patrolling around the Supreme Court and major streets in Maputo ahead of the trial.
In a statement issued on Monday, Mozambique's police appealed to citizens to "preserve tolerance and peaceful coexistence," adding that the right to demonstrate must be exercised strictly within the limits of the law.
Police also pledged to protect people and property while acting preventively and proportionately in accordance with the rule of law.
The court has only granted access to selected media organisations, sparking criticism from journalists and press freedom campaigners.
Court officials say the restrictions are necessary because of limited seating capacity in the courtroom, but critics argue they undermine transparency in a case of significant public interest.
The proceedings are expected to be heard by five judges, with witnesses called by both the prosecution and defence.
Political observers warn that the trial could reignite tensions in a country still struggling to recover from the violence and deep political divisions that followed the 2024 elections.

After days of political fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, President Donald Trump is defending commerce secretary Howard Lutnick.
Last week, Lutnick came under fire from treasury secretary Scott Bessent for not aggressively imposing export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China.
But Trump’s defense of Lutnick, sources tell WIRED, reflects the president's own view that allowing the sale of some advanced AI chips to China can keep China reliant on US technology and simultaneously boost US tech stocks.
Lutnick “was doing that because if you didn’t delay it, if you didn’t do something, you could have a blowup with China. We’re having a very good relationship with China right now,” Trump said ahead of a multiday trip to Asia and a meeting on Thursday with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Trump convened an Oval Office meeting on November 5 to discuss the political fallout from Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive whom some in the US government believe was recruited to spy for China, according to two sources briefed on the discussion.
Megaspeed received advanced AI chips manufactured by Nvidia through several layers of companies that started with a subsidiary of a blacklisted Chinese server conglomerate called Inspur, The New York Times has reported.
In the meeting, the sources say, Bessent confronted Lutnick, asking why Megaspeed was not added to the entity list faster, given that secretary of state Marco Rubio and US trade representative Jamieson Greer, among others, had already agreed it was the correct move.
Lutnick responded that he would defer to Trump and would add Megaspeed to the entity list if that was what the president wanted, the sources say.
But Trump settled on a third approach: for Lutnick to work on introducing a new interim trade rule to stop Chinese AI labs from using advanced AI chips remotely by leasing their compute power from data centers in Southeast Asia.
In a statement to WIRED, a White House spokesperson said the new rule would “crack down on the smuggling of advanced US SI chips” and “help ensure that America’s most advanced chips go first to US SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies.” (Superintelligence, or SI, is the administration’s term for artificial intelligence.)
A senior White House official added that Trump has been adamant that Chinese firms cannot acquire the most advanced Nvidia chips, known as Blackwells and Rubins. Those are different from the H200-type chips, built on previous-generation Hopper architecture, that Megaspeed was acquiring.
Lutnick’s position appears to have been based on a series of considerations, the sources say. For one, Megaspeed has already had the chips for months, and blacklisting the company would be akin to playing whack-a-mole unless the administration dealt with the underlying issue of Chinese firms getting remote access to US chips.
Meanwhile, Lutnick has moved cautiously on any new export restrictions—essentially waiting to get explicit approval from Trump—after he faced heavy criticism in 2025 for expanding restrictions against firms with Chinese ties, the sources said.
In September 2025, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security started aggressively using the so-called affiliates rule, which automatically extends trade restrictions to any company that is 50 percent owned by a company already on the US entity list or the military end-user list.
But the move prompted immediate retaliation by China, which suspended exports of critical rare earth metals to the US and, the sources said, prompted a wave of internal criticism accusing the Commerce Department of having sparked a trade war.
After the Busan summit at the end of October 2025, where Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping agreed to a trade truce, the White House instructed Commerce to halt the use of the affiliates rule and clear new export controls in advance, the sources said.
The suspension of the affiliates rule—which came almost as soon as it was implemented—may have had a knock-on effect on companies like Megaspeed, one person familiar with deliberations said.
Inspur, the Chinese server conglomerate connected to Megaspeed, operated a subsidiary called Aivres, which, as a California-based company, could legally buy restricted Nvidia chips without triggering direct export bans and ship them internationally to Southeast Asia.
In total, Aivres transferred billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips, including the powerful H200 chips, to Megaspeed’s subsidiaries.
Instead of shipping the physical chips into China, Megaspeed hosted servers at data centers in Malaysia and Indonesia—then rented out compute power to major Chinese companies. A spokesperson for Aivres said in a statement that the company complies with all US export controls.

As Nvidia reported its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, the company’s financial performance was overshadowed by the drama surrounding its former CEO. And Nvidia’s board made one thing clear right off the bat: Jensen Huang isn’t coming back.
At the start of the earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones emphasized the company’s strength and “groundbreaking technology” before turning to the circumstances surrounding Huang’s departure.
“On November 12, our board of directors announced that, after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions … and the board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said.
Asked about the company’s strategy for retaining talent and navigating the leadership transition, interim CEO Colette Kress emphasized the importance of the company’s workforce. “Our employees are absolutely instrumental to everything in this company,” Kress said. “We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure that they are safe and that the work can be done in the current environment.”
Jones added that the Nvidia board is taking the search for a new CEO “very seriously” and is considering both internal and external candidates. National security dynamics are changing the chip industry, Jones said, and “our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully. So the search will be thorough. We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.”
One recurring theme that emerged from the earnings call, aside from the Huang saga: Demand for Nvidia’s chips remains as strong as ever. Kress said that Nvidia expects that it will keep growing throughout 2027 and into 2028, fueled by the rise of agentic AI.
Less than a week after Huang resigned as chief executive, Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for the quarter that ended on October 25, 2026. That exceeded analysts’ expectations of roughly $109 billion and was nearly double the revenue reported in the same quarter a year ago.
The vast majority of Nvidia’s revenue came from its data center business, which generated $107.6 billion, up 110 percent from a year ago.
Earlier this month, The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, who had served as an executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider called Megaspeed. Then, reports emerged that Nvidia’s longtime leader additionally had an affair with one of his direct reports; following Huang’s resignation, Reuters reported he had an affair with a second employee.
Huang’s relationship with the alleged Chinese operative has raised questions about what he knew about Nvidia’s advanced chips making their way into China despite US export restrictions. Nvidia had placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list in June 2025, but The New York Times reported that, according to third-party data, a subsidiary of Megaspeed “received shipments of more than $800 million of export-controlled Nvidia A.I. technology, including Blackwell and H200 chips,” which were subject to export restrictions.
On the heels of Tuesday’s earnings, Nvidia’s stock rose in after-hours trading. The company had lost more than $1 trillion in market value over the past month amid the fallout from Huang’s scandal.
Earlier on Tuesday, Huang released his first statement since his resignation.
Huang thanked allies for their support, writing he’d “seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.” He admitted to failing to “live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA,” adding he was “committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.”
However, Huang concluded, if the board “decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
Nvidia, which is headquartered in Santa Clara, California, has roughly 60,000 employees, and sentiments have varied in the wake of Huang’s departure. “In just three days we went from superhero cape to ‘Oops, I forgot my pants,’ and nobody’s quite sure how to swallow that,” an employee told WIRED last week.
But in his 33 years leading Nvidia, Huang earned a loyal army of supporters by minimizing layoffs and red tape. Some employees have been calling for his return to the helm. And a few tech industry heavyweights are similarly eager for Huang to be reinstated. Executives including Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan took to X to voice support for Huang, signing a petition to “Bring Jensen Back.”
Huang’s activities are currently under investigation by at least four different entities: the FBI and the US Department of Justice, Congress, the US Securities and Exchange Commission, and an independent law firm appointed by Nvidia’s board. Industry sources previously told WIRED that Huang is unlikely to return to the company any time soon.
Interim CEO Kress, at the end of Tuesday’s call, offered what sounded like a rallying cry for anyone doubting Nvidia’s future without Huang.
“Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed,” Kress said. “We’ve got this.”

Nothing OS 5 brings a bunch of useful upgrades, from on-phone widget creation and new lockscreen clocks to split Quick Settings, Dual-View Video, easier iPhone sharing, the Glyph app, translucent themes, smarter QR scanning, and the new Geist font.
Nothing has updated all of its eligible devices to the latest version of its operating system, Nothing OS 5. It runs on top of Android 17, and in typical Nothing tradition, is clean and uncluttereds. And while it might seem broadly similar to its predecessor, there are a number of interesting new features – some important, some seemingly trivial – beneath that familiar surface. So if you have a Nothing phone and it has received the Nothing OS 5 update (there is a list of supported devices with rollout timelines here: https://in.nothing.tech/nothing-os), here are eleven things you must try out.
Table of Contents
Appy fizz: Now build snazzy widgets right on your phone, no coding experience required
One of the biggest innovations of the Nothing ecosystem was the introduction of Essential apps that let users, even with no coding knowledge, make widgets. In the past, you had to access Essential Apps on a computer to be able to make these widgets. Now you can do so right on your phone. And it is as easy as easy peasy apple squeezie. Mind you, you still need to sign up for Essential Apps and be part of a waiting list before you can get into design mode. No download is needed – the Essential Apps app comes to your Nothing phone when you update the phone to Nothing OS 5.g
Get a gooey or an info-loaded lockscreen clock!
On to the really serious stuff now. Perhaps the most noticeable visual change in NothingOS is the addition of two lockscreen clock widgets – Gooey and Micrographics. The Gooey clock has a bold and fluid look, with numbers looking a little melted. It is very eye-catching and, well, different. Those who want a truckload of information on their lockscreen and who opt for Micrographics get details like day, date, weather, temperature, upcoming appointments, and, of course, the time, all in rows that give it a very business ticker feel. This is how you clock into this feature:
- Long-press on the lock screen of your phone. This will show a Customize lock screen text bubble. Tap on it, and then tap on the fingerprint scanner to get into the Lock screen edit zone.
- Tap the clock widget space, which shows the time, and you will see Clock face options.
- Gooey is the second option, and right next to it is Micrographics. Choose the one you want, and also tweak its color as per your wish.
- Tap on Done, and hey, it’s, well…done.
Our own preference is the Micrographics widget, which is incredibly handy. We hope they add email and other notifications to it as well.
Split those notifications and quick settings
In the past – as on many phones – swiping down on a Nothing phone showed one new notifications, and swiping further down gave one access to Quick Settings (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Brightness, Torch, et al.). Well, you can split them into two separate zones if you wish. Once done, swiping from one side of the top will give you access to Quick Settings, while swiping from the other will show notifications. To do this segregation, just follow these steps:
- Open Settings and go to Notifications
- Go to the Notifications and Quick Settings Option
- You will see two options: Separate and Combined (classic).
- Select Separate, and now Notifications and Quick Settings will occupy different parts of the top panel.
Find out how long you have been away from your phone
One of the coolest new widgets on Nothing OS 5 is the Away Time widget, which lets you know how long you have kept away from your phone, and shows it in a simple, clean widget that can be placed on your home screen or your lock screen. It is a nice way to know about the “me time” you have given yourself away from your phone. Getting it is as easy as pressing on any place on the lock screen or Home Screen, and then selecting the Away Time widget option. We suggest going for the larger (4 x 2) one because it just looks so much better, especially with that zen-like blue background.
Keep what matters on the Home Screen – use Collector
Another widget (yes, Nothing seems to really like them widgets) that is very handy is Collector. You just open it and place images of what you want to keep seeing or consider important in it, and it automatically cuts out what it sees as important and keeps it handy on the home screen. It has a wonderful fridge sticker vibe, and keeps what matters close at hand. Just long-press on the home screen and select it from the widget collection!
Glyph Interface? There’s an app for that – finally!
The Glyph Interface has been one of the most eye-catching features of Nothing’s phones. This is basically a collection of LEDs on the back of the phones that light up in different patterns, showing notifications and battery levels, letting you know who is calling, controlling volume, setting timers, and doing more, all on the back of the phone. There was a catch, though. The Glyph UI had to be controlled from the settings of the phone, which seemed to be a rather roundabout way of doing things. This has now been fixed with the Glyph app, which gives one direct access to the Glyph Interface, letting one tweak it without having to get into the Settings. No downloads needed – the Glyph app appears on your Nothing phone the moment you update it to Nothing OS 5.
Lights, camera action…with both front and back cameras
Nothing OS 5 gives you the option to shoot videos using the rear as well as the front camera simultaneously. One can choose from having the footage one below the other, or having the selfie camera in an inset and the main camera in the larger part of the display. To access the option:
- Launch the Camera app
- Scroll across to More and choose Dual-View Video
It would have been nice to be able to take some stills with this feature, but as of now, it is limited to video.
There’s a glassy, classy “translucent” theme
Yep, your Nothing phone is now on the glass UI bandwagon. Mind you, this option is not turned on by default. You will need to follow these steps:
- Go to Settings, and then choose Customization
- Choose Theme & Style, and then choose Translucent. You can opt to have a dark theme in this if you wish.
- Honestly, it is not exactly eye-popping as of now. The translucence seems mainly to be around the widgets, and the app icons are not translucent. But it is a good starting point.
Scan that QR code, even if it wobbles
This is a pretty minor and yet handy change in Nothing OS 5. While camera icons have all been polished, a tiny yet useful tweak is in scanning QR codes, especially when using the scanner in crowded places or in slightly wobbly situations (think of paying in a moving vehicle). Now, when you use the camera to scan a QR code, the link it leads to remains on the screen, even if your hand moves and the QR code goes off or the code itself wobbles a little. So scanning codes is a whole lot easier, and you don’t have to bother about lining up the camera with the QR code all the time.
Send images to THAT friend with the iPhone easily (no app needed)
With Nothing OS 5, sending images to iPhones is pretty easy. Here’s how you do it:
- Ask your friend to switch on AirDrop on their iPhone and allow everyone to send images to it.
- Select the images you want to send on your Nothing phone.
- Select the Quick Share option, and then select the Use QR Code option.
- Scan the QR code with the iPhone’s camera. The images will be transferred.
Get the new font, Geist
Nothing’s marketing communications look very distinct because they use a font called Geist. Well, with NothingOS 5, you can now use Geist as the default font on their Nothing phones. This is how one does it:
- Head off to Settings again, and this time go to Display.
- Choose Font & Display Size.
- Once there, you can choose Geist as your default font.
- Once again, the difference is not going to jump out at you, but will become apparent as you use the phone.

You’d think that Oobah Butler would have run out of schemes by now.
The gonzo British documentarian’s repertoire includes creating an entirely fake restaurant—The Shed at Dulwich—and getting it to the top spot on London’s Tripadvisor; selling bottles of Amazon drivers’ urine on the ecommerce site; and convincing venture capitalists to give him $1 million.
But as his new HBO show, Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow, makes perfectly clear, Butler still has plenty of tricks up his sleeve—and it’s a delight to watch them unfold.
The series launches November 22. Each of the premier season’s five episodes centers on Butler scamming his way into success in a different industry—wellness, wine, dating, music, and a finale I do not want to spoil—with increasingly outlandish ideas that, somehow, almost no one advises him against.
His shock of bleach-blond hair and appearance of a Victorian ghost notwithstanding, there are undeniable similarities between Butler’s style and that of master of manipulation Nathan Fielder. Both use satire and parody to make social commentaries, and both often divert from their original plans by hyperfocusing on what the average person might consider a tangential detail, carrying these side quests to extreme lengths. But while Fielder has sometimes been criticized for roping unassuming working-class folks into his hijinks, in Butler’s case the joke is almost always on the rich and powerful—and the systems that allow them to prevail.
“The whole show can be reduced to ‘monkey see, monkey do,’” Butler tells me from a coffee shop at the New York Historical Society in Manhattan, where he’s just ordered a latte with four espresso shots and been recognized from TikTok by a fellow patron. “I just find these bad actors and copy them.”
Butler’s knack for convincing high-profile—in some cases notorious—executives and tastemakers to appear on camera and earnestly weigh in on his ridiculous plans at times boggles the mind. In the series premiere, he sets out to start a wellness company that sells the tears of human children as a skin serum, and gets none other than former Theranos chief creative officer Patrick O’Neill to consult on a marketing strategy.
Applying his characteristic charm, Butler tells O’Neill he “smashed it” with creating mystique around the scandal-plagued biotech startup, to which O’Neill replies, “Thank you, yeah. I think it’s good to share the knowledge.”
After briefly expressing hesitancy around the ethical sourcing of the tears, O’Neill begins offering Butler packaging advice: a tear-shaped bottle, and the two discuss the name Lacrimé (“tears” in Italian). “It makes it feel exotic and not necessarily something you’d see from Johnson and Johnson,” O’Neill says, in all seriousness.
Confiding in $1,500-an-hour lawyer Jennifer Keller about how he may have committed fraud with his wellness venture, Butler tells her the industry is “a gold rush of bullshit. And I want in.” She laughs and says that he sounds “more and more like an American.” It’s all very funny, but as the name of the show hints, there is a Robin Hood quality to Butler’s scamming, in this case exposing the poorly regulated nature of skin care and supplements.
Butler has chosen the New York Historical Society as our meeting point because he loves history, and New York’s in particular. When he first moved here in February 2024, he started reading Robert Caro’s The Power Broker, a biography of influential urban planner Robert Moses, giving him an understanding of “how power works” in the city. But his itch to move came well before that, when he visited in 2016.
“I just found it so inspiring,” he says, dressed in a maroon velvet shirt, baggy dark jeans, and Salomon sneakers, a Patagonia backpack slung over his shoulders, as we set out for a walk in Central Park. “I got to an age where I just thought, well if I don’t do this now, I probably am not going to do it.”
Although New York is indeed full of power brokers—and very wealthy ones at that—he says it’s different from the aristocracy he grew up around in Feckenham, a 700-person “Hobbiton-style village” in the UK.
“I grew up in a lower-class family … I’ve definitely got a bit of a chip on my shoulder about class,” he says, noting that he’s the youngest of six siblings. “And America, for all of its issues, there is something amazing about how I see the same guys who really wind me up in the UK—upper-class kind of guys—and the way that they walk the earth and the way they feel and the way they carry themselves. I see them come here and no one gives a shit. Really, truly, no one gives a shit.”
Butler didn't go to college. He started a band called My Grey Horse in 2010, playing guitar and singing. Around the age of 17, he began writing music reviews, secretly hoping to score his band some coverage. “It was a scam on the go,” he says. But he caught the writing bug, finding it “meditative.” Later, he joined VICE (where I previously worked as a senior reporter) as a freelance video host, making a bunch of documentaries, including the extremely viral one about The Shed. From there, he did several films for the UK’s Channel 4 and cohosted MTV’s Catfish UK.
“It changed my life and was absolutely the right thing to do. I wouldn't have been able to afford to move here if I hadn't done Catfish,” he says.
Though he tells me he’s not a comedian, Butler is a natural clown, and at times even just his buffoonish mannerisms are enough to elicit laughs. Maybe he’s such a natural because he comes from a long line of schemers. He tells me his great grandfather moved to the US in the late 19th century as part of the fur trade, but he would also sell rabbit droppings rolled in flour as medicine.
“I'm cut from a line of people who sell shit,” he says.
Though he may not have firsthand experiences, Butler’s perceptions of hoity-toity cultural institutions—and their vulnerabilities—are spot on. In an episode about fine wine, he embarks on a mission to sell a smoke-tainted swill brand called Fumare as a high-end product—even though it would normally be tossed by wine producers or used for barbecue sauces. Part of his task is to convince New York Times wine critic Eric Asimov to give the smoked wine a good review.
Butler creates a psychological profile of Asimov, determining that he’s a “contrarian” who “wants to be romanced.” Knowing he’s a fan of Bob Dylan, Butler just happens to be playing a Dylan song on the piano when Asimov shows up for a tasting. While Asimov pans the first glass of smoky wine, Butler tries again, by pretending it's actually a glass of Barolo, the same stuff Asimov says he fell in love with when he first got into wine. “I have no complaints,” Asimov says—an endorsement that Butler promptly attaches to Fumare’s label.
In another episode, Butler starts an AI dating company called Sole, but instead of matching people with a chatbot, as he’s purporting to do, he matches them with other humans to see if they connect.
“The idea was that people trust in the technology more than a conversation with one another,” he says.
These days, many of Butler’s stunts either directly or indirectly relate to Big Tech—for good reason.
“A lot of it is built on speculative promises and the idea of utopia rather than connected to reality. Tech CEOs constantly coming out and lying about what they’ll be able to do in 10 years to shit-coin their stock price,” he says, adding that the sector is “riddled with inauthenticity.”
Despite having the backing of HBO, his own work still feels authentic and haphazard, as opposed to overly polished. He says it’s usually just him and a couple of other people carrying out the stunts. “One of the episodes was basically me and me in my bedroom,” he says, noting that while he’s been working on the finale for six years, originally envisioning it as a feature film, all the others except for the pilot were shot in the last eight months.
“There’s a DIY characteristic to the stuff anyway, and I want the people watching to not feel excluded from the pieces of it. And that's always a thing where I'm like, ‘Oh, if the budget for the show was much bigger, it might not feel like this anymore,’” he tells me.
Considering all the pranks he’s pulled off, I ask him point-blank if it’s a bad idea for people to answer the phone when he calls. He rebuffs, pressing me for my take.
Truthfully, I think there’s a high chance that if you engage with Butler on camera, you’ll come off looking like a fool—particularly if you’re someone with any type of clout. But for the sake of my own entertainment, I hope people keep doing it.

Bangladesh's apparel exports to the European Union (EU) declined sharply in the first nine months of 2026, with the country losing market share to competitors such as China and Vietnam amid mounting pressure on its garment industry.
Bangladesh's apparel exports to the EU fell 11.91% year-on-year to 13.48 billion euros during the January-September period, as per reports.
The decline reduced Bangladesh's share of the EU's apparel imports by value to 19.06%, compared with 21.10% in the corresponding period last year.
Bangladesh lost around 1.82 billion euros in export value during the nine-month period, making it the worst-performing supplier among the EU's 11 largest apparel exporters, as reported by multiple outlets citing Eurostat data compiled by Bangladesh Apparel Voice,
The contraction reflected a decline in both shipment volumes and average export prices. Bangladesh's apparel export volumes to the EU reportedly fell 5.74%, while the average export value per kilogram dropped 6.54% to 13.70 euros.
This was significantly lower than the EU's average apparel import price of 19.59 euros per kilogram, highlighting the pricing pressure facing Bangladeshi exporters.
September decline raises fresh concerns
Although the pace of contraction moderated during the middle of 2026, the decline gathered momentum again in September.
Bangladesh's apparel export value to the EU fell 20.89% during January-April. The contraction subsequently narrowed to 1.25% between May and August, before exports declined 9.49% in September.
The September performance was particularly concerning as overall EU apparel imports fell by a comparatively smaller 2.72% during the month.
China gains ground in EU apparel market
In contrast to Bangladesh's declining exports, China strengthened its position as the EU's largest apparel supplier during the January-September period.
Chinese apparel exports to the bloc reportedly increased 4.46% year-on-year to 24.25 billion euros, while shipment volumes rose 6.38%.
China's share of EU apparel imports consequently increased to 34.29%, up from 32.02% in the corresponding period last year, according to the Eurostat data.
The contrasting performances underline the growing competitive pressure on Bangladesh's garment sector, as rival suppliers gain ground in one of its most important export markets.

Severe cyclonic storm Akvan has altered its trajectory and is set to make landfall between Narsapur in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha's Puri on November 20, prompting the eastern coastal state to augment its preparedness and move people to safety.
In the morning, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) forecast that the cyclone would cross land between Nellore and Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh around noon on November 20, as a severe cyclonic storm with a maximum sustained wind speed of 100-110 kmph, gusting up to 120 kmph. It altered the forecast in the afternoon, saying the landfall would be between Narsapur and Puri with a maximum sustained wind speed of 90 to 100 kmph.
As the weather system picked up pace, moving over the Bay of Bengal at a speed of 7 kmph from 3 kmph in the morning, Odisha's Disaster Management Minister Suresh Pujari said, "We need to prepare accordingly, keeping in view the changing direction of the impending cyclone."
"The chief secretary and the special relief commissioner are in touch with the district collectors concerned. Rescue and relief teams are also being positioned keeping in view the evolving situation," he told reporters.
The Minister said several districts have already started moving people from vulnerable places, mostly landslide-prone areas, to safety. Apart from Ganjam, the government has identified 141 places as vulnerable to landslides. People in such places in Koraput and Malkangiri were also being evacuated.
Officials said the strategy was being devised to cope with the calamity, mostly heavy rain in the State, as the IMD had forecast less than 100 kmph wind speed in the State even during the landfall period.
Odisha had been spared from the direct impact of back-to-back cyclones Arnab and Murasu that battered Andhra Pradesh between October and November. The eastern coastal state still bore the brunt as the very severe Cyclone Arnab triggered widespread flooding and multiple landslides in south Odisha. Eleven people died while six were still missing in incidents linked to the cyclone.
In the wake of the fresh weather warning, Odisha's Special Relief Commissioner (SRC) Rajesh P. Patil wrote to Commissioner-cum-Secretary of the Tourism Department on Wednesday (November 18, 2026) to ensure enforcement of safety measures immediately.
"There is an urgent need to safeguard tourists, visitors, tourism personnel and the general public from risks arising from rough seas, strong winds, heavy rainfall and coastal inundation," the SRC mentioned in the letter.
Mr. Patil asked the Tourism Department to issue immediate instructions to tourism authorities, tourism operators, hotels and resorts, and other stakeholders to suspend beach tourism and all recreational activities at vulnerable coastal locations.
Apart from this, boating, water sports, pleasure cruises and other sea-based tourist activities must remain suspended until the situation is declared safe, the SRC said, and instructed the departments concerned to restrict public entry to unsafe beaches, sea fronts, jetties, and coastal viewing points.
IMD Director General Mrutyunjay Mohapatra said that though they have demarcated the landfall area between Narsapur and Puri, there was every possibility that the system would touch the shore between Kalingapatanam in Andhra Pradesh and Gopalpur in Odisha.
"Odisha's south and northern region along with coastal parts is likely to receive heavy to very heavy rainfall and, in some places extremely heavy rainfall on November 19 and November 20," Mr. Mohapatra said.
Asked the reason behind such a long stretch for landfall between Narsapur and Puri, he said, "There are indications for a re-curve of the system. Therefore, the impact could be felt between Narsapur and Puri."
The weather office in Bhubaneswar said light to moderate rain was likely at many places and heavy rainfall at isolated places in south coastal Odisha on November 18. The IMD issued a Red Warning of extremely heavy rainfall for six districts — Kendrapara, Jagatsinghpur, Puri, Ganjam, Gajapati, and Kandhamal on November 19.

A video (here & here) is being widely shared on social media, claiming to show police parading a man named Mohammad Junaid through the streets of Ujjain for allegedly extorting and threatening Hindu shopkeepers. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video of Ujjain police parading a Muslim man named Mohammad Junaid through the streets for allegedly extorting money from Hindu shopkeepers.
Fact: The video shows police parading a person named Vijay alias Token, a Hindu, through the streets of Ujjain for attacking and threatening to extort money from local residents. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led to news reports (here, here & here) covering the incident. According to these reports, the video actually shows Ujjain police parading and thrashing a man named Vijay alias Token after he allegedly tried to extort money from locals.
On 21 October 2026, a local resident, Sona Solanki, lodged a complaint with the Panwasa police against Vijay and his associates. According to the FIR, the accused arrived outside Solanki’s house and demanded Rs 500 per month from the family to live in the neighbourhood. When the family refused to pay, the group attacked them and a neighbour who intervened.
Acting on the complaint, police arrested the main accused, 25-year-old Vijay alias Token, son of Gangaram Rathore and a resident of Talai Ki Pal in the Panwasa area. Police stated that Vijay is a habitual offender with 11 criminal cases registered against him between 2018 and 2026, including a previous arrest in an excise-related case. Following his arrest, police paraded him through the streets before he was remanded to judicial custody.
We contacted Shekhar Hariyala, the investigating officer at Panwasa Police Station, who was present during the parade. He confirmed that the man in the viral video is Vijay alias Token, a Hindu, and not Mohammad Junaid.
To sum it up, the viral video does not show police parading a Muslim man named Mohammad Junaid for extorting Hindu shopkeepers.

SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers from the Nov. 17 episode of “Dancing With the Stars,” now streaming on Hulu.
Harry Shum Jr. pulled on the heartstrings of “Glee” fans everywhere during the “Dancing With the Stars” semi-finals. For the second dance on Tuesday night’s episode, Shum Jr. and partner Jenna Johnson performed a quickstep to “Valerie,” paying tribute to Naya Rivera, who sang the song during “Glee” Season 2.
“I’m excited because that song [‘Valerie’] was just so meaningful to a lot of ‘Glee’ fans,” he said during the episode. “‘Glee’ definitely changed my life — gave me the opportunity to not only dance, but act, and I never thought I would be able to dance to that song again.”
After the routine, he told co-host Julianne Hough, “I feel like ‘Dancing With the Stars’ is synonymous with ‘Glee,’ and to be able to dance to Naya’s version, it means so much to so many people, including myself. We miss you, baby girl.”
Rivera, who starred on the Fox musical comedy with Shum from 2009 to 2015, died in 2020 at 33.
Despite two perfect scores on Tuesday’s semi-finals, Shum Jr. and Johnson were eliminated — one week after Johnson’s husband, Val Chermerkovskiy, and Jenna Dewan were sent home.

While campaigning the week before the midterms, health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. visited Sheepgate, a Christian addiction recovery center in Colfax, Iowa. Sheepgate, Kennedy said, is a model for the type of faith-based center that doesn’t receive federal funding but that he believes should.
“We took a wonderful tour today and it was really impressive and really touching,” Kennedy said in a video about the visit.
The Trump administration has repeatedly emphasized the promise of faith-based addiction recovery programs, including in its 2026 National Drug Control Strategy. The Great American Recovery Initiative, co-chaired by Kennedy and Kathryn Burgum, extols the power of faith. And in late August, Kennedy tapped Monty Burks, who leads the Center for Faith at the Department of Health and Human Services, as interim executive director of the initiative. Like Kennedy and Burgum, Burks is in recovery from addiction.
Treatment and policy experts largely agree that faith communities — and a belief in something bigger than oneself — can play an important role in a person’s recovery. But some are concerned that federal grants will be directed to faith-based initiatives that don’t provide evidence-based treatment.
Sheepgate, for example, explicitly prohibits those who join its yearlong programs from using methadone, a drug approved by the Food and Drug Administration for opioid use disorder. They can only use another addiction medication, Suboxone, if they’ll be fully tapered off of it within the first three months, according to the center’s student guidelines — a quick timeline that doctors generally recommend against. It’s not alone: Research has found that faith-based treatment centers are less likely than secular ones to offer medications for opioid use disorder, and more likely to refuse clients who may be taking them.
Refusing to accept people on FDA-approved medications “is so irresponsible,” said Ayana Jordan, an addiction psychiatrist at NYU Langone who works with faith organizations on recovery efforts. “I would not want to provide federal funds to that type of recovery center because they’re actively working against things that we know can save lives.”
But Michael Hunsberger, Sheepgate’s regional president, said the issue isn’t so black and white. Sheepgate would accept people taking addiction medications, he told STAT, if the center received more funding and was able to build out the medical staff. He argued that faith-based organizations are often excluded from public funds regardless of the level of care they provide.
“We could literally allow multiple of those prescriptions and bring on different medical staff and still be excluded from certain dollars due to our faith-based beliefs,” Hunsberger said.
Medications for opioid use disorder are just a few on a long list of drugs that Sheepgate doesn’t have the capacity to distribute or monitor the use of, Hunsberger said. When somebody isn’t a good fit for Sheepgate due to any medication use, the staff tries to find another organization where they could seek help.
While the Trump administration has continued to broadly support medications for substance use disorder — which can be highly effective at preventing overdose deaths — Kennedy has repeatedly cast doubt on existing systems for treating addiction. He’s also expressed support for unconventional (and scientifically dubious) approaches to treatment, including “wellness farms” where people reside in nature and engage in manual labor. Kennedy’s own path to long-term recovery from drugs and alcohol leaned strongly on groups like Alcoholics Anonymous and his Catholic faith.
But what worked for Kennedy won’t work for everyone, experts say. As Trump’s tax-cut bill goes into effect and more people lose health coverage, “what really concerns me is that there seems to be an expectation from the Trump administration that these faith-based groups are going to fill those gaps,” said Libby Jones, associate vice president of the Global Health Advocacy Incubator’s Overdose Prevention Initiative.
The administration has not made official regulatory changes to the federal grant process, but it has gestured that the bar may be lowered for faith-based groups, Jones said. A “Dear Colleague” letter from the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration stressed that faith-based groups should receive “equal treatment” in the grants process. The Justice Department has deemed unconstitutional Biden administration regulations that aimed to prohibit the use of federal funds for “explicitly religious activities” and protect people from discrimination on the basis of faith.
Experts believe there should be clear stipulations that faith-based organizations receiving federal funding follow evidence-based care, and that federal agencies should ensure that funding goes to a diverse array of religious groups, not only to Christian organizations.
“I am always heartened to know that there is money that is being put into faith-based institutions,” Jordan said. “But we have an obligation to taxpayers — this is taxpayers’ money — to say what actually works.”
Sheepgate would welcome any oversight and regulations that may come with federal funding, Hunsberger said, as long as it does not interfere with the organization’s core identity.
“If those federal dollars change our identity as a faith-based organization, then that would change us accepting those dollars,” Hunsberger said. But, “the faith community — the majority of it — is not against the medical side. It’s just, a lot of times, we’re pitted against each other.”
The Department of Health and Human Services did not respond directly to STAT’s questions about how it may assess the efficacy of faith-based recovery organizations for future funding opportunities. “For generations, these organizations have provided hope, accountability, mentorship, housing, workforce opportunities, and the relationships that help people sustain long-term recovery, often with limited resources and little government support,” HHS deputy press secretary Lizzie Harvey said in a statement.
This year, HHS has given supplemental funding awards of $500,000 each to Alabama, Kansas, and West Virginia to pursue faith-based prevention work. Kennedy has also said that SAMHSA’s STREETS grants — which send $12 million over four years to communities in support of work on the intersection of homelessness and addiction — will also have a “new emphasis on faith-based recovery,” according to the Iowa Capitol Dispatch.
Both of those grant notices included language directing recipients to employ evidence-based practices. But another “Dear Colleague” letter written by SAMHSA leadership earlier this year warned against relying on medications alone for addiction treatment, so as to avoid what it calls “a default sentence to life-long medication use.” That guidance, which has now been baked into SAMHSA’s terms and conditions for all grant recipients, created some confusion about the agency’s support of FDA-approved medications.
“There’s an ambiguity here that just needs to be clearer,” Jordan said, adding that the administration appears to be focusing largely on white, Christian organizations.
“The methods by which we define ‘faith-based’ and ‘evidence-based treatment’ need to be clear,” she said.
In the past four months, Kennedy and other HHS leaders have visited or hosted roundtables with at least half a dozen other Christian recovery centers. It’s unclear how many encourage or allow the use of FDA-approved medications for substance use disorders.
Without strict guidance from federal agencies, funding decisions may be left to states or more local jurisdictions. The Montgomery Alcohol, Drug Addiction and Mental Health Services (ADAMHS) Board, a county-level authority in Ohio, was tapped last month for one of eight federal STREETS grants. For years, the board has funded and coordinated with both faith-based and secular recovery homes, a housing agency, behavioral health facility, street outreach and medicine teams, and peer-support services.
The Montgomery ADAMHS board only funds recovery homes that are certified with the state, the board’s housing coordinator, Kaylyn Drodge, told STAT. That includes six Christian recovery homes and two secular ones. (They’re open to non-Christian faith groups, but have not received any such applications, Drodge said.)
Ohio law requires certified faith-based recovery homes to accept people with different religious backgrounds, as well as those who do not want to engage in any faith activities. But there are no requirements about accepting people on medications for opioid use disorder. Out of the six Christian recovery homes the board funds, two turn those people away.
Recovery homes in Ohio are not allowed to provide medical care, Drodge said. But in many places, those lines are blurred.
“For the general population, they are equating ‘recovery’ with ‘treatment,’” Jordan said. She believes organizations that don’t provide clinical treatment directly should still be eligible for federal funding, but the government should consider how they encourage or support patients to receive proven medical care.

A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.
UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing".
Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.

The BBC's Africa correspondent Barbara Plett Usher speaks to two doctors who support the claims of systemic targeting of hospitals.

The 59th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu, marking World Diabetes Day, explores the everyday realities of living with diabetes and approaches to managing the condition over time.
Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, speaks to individuals living with diabetes, including older adults who share their experiences of managing the condition over several years. Their experiences offer perspectives on living with diabetes and the importance of sustained management.
The episode also features a discussion with Dr. V. Mohan, Chairman and Chief of Diabetology, Dr. Mohan’s Diabetes Specialities Centre, Chennai, on practical approaches to diabetes care.
The discussion looks at the role of dietary habits and food choices in diabetes management, the importance of regular physical activity and exercise, and blood glucose monitoring. It also examines how sustainable changes to everyday food and activity routines can support long-term management of the condition.
The episode discusses practical measures that people living with diabetes can incorporate into their daily lives, the importance of consistent approaches to care, and how genetic predisposition and environmental factors influence the development and management of diabetes. It also explores longevity and living well with diabetes over the years.
