An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country.
Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said a 28-year-old player named as Greene Da’monte Khiree from the state of Georgia was arrested at Lagos’s main airport last Wednesday after he arrived on a flight from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.
The NDLEA said the player told them he had come to Nigeria to “build networks” for his basketball career. The agency said evidence on his phone suggested he had “knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity”. The NDLEA said it detained the player when he attempted to leave the airport with his hand luggage after abandoning two checked-in bags. The agency said those two bags were found to contain 32 parcels of marijuana, and a tracking device.
Nigeria has strict drug laws, and trafficking carries a sentence of life in prison.
A basketball player by the name of Damonte Greene is listed on the roster of the Pattani Raptors in the Thai Premier Men’s League. Greene, a Georgia native, played college basketball for Reinhardt University and South Georgia Technical College. He played semi-professional basketball in the US before representing a number of teams in Thailand.
WNBA star Brittney Griner and former Utah State player Jarred Shaw were imprisoned in Russia and Indonesia respectively for marijuana offenses. Griner was released in December 2022, while Shaw remains in prison.

Real Madrid's Vinícius Jr sends surprise message to boy who lost his legs in Sudan's war
- Published
In a dark room in Cairo, a 13-year-old boy looks up at a television screen, barely blinking.
The screen flickers and Real Madrid's superstar winger Vinícius Júnior appears addressing the young boy directly, in Arabic: "Zaher, mahaba" - Hello Zaher.
Zaher barely moves, his eyes wide, locked on his favourite footballer.
We first met Zaher a year ago in the ruins of Sudan's capital, Khartoum. He was a small quiet child, scarred by war - one of millions of children whose lives have been upended since the country's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) started fighting in 2023.
More than 17 million children are now in need of humanitarian assistance in Sudan, according to the UN children's charity, Unicef. It says it has been able to verify that at least 4,300 have been killed or maimed, although it believes the true figure is far higher.
Zaher had lost both his legs in a drone strike. With little access to specialist treatment, he dreamed of the day he might walk and play football again.
More than a year later, as we walk into an apartment in the Egyptian capital, Zaher greets us with an enormous hug. His mother, Habibah, embraces us too.
The boy we remember as shy and withdrawn is almost unrecognisable. He is confident, cheeky and full of smiles. And he is standing tall on two new prosthetic legs.
For almost a year, Cairo has been his home. Here, he has undergone surgery and months of rehabilitation, and is now able to walk and kick a ball again.
When we met in 2025, he had told us his favourite footballer was Vinícius Júnior. We were able to pass this on to the Real Madrid star, who said he wanted to send a personal video message of support. Reunited in Cairo, we gather round to watch it together.
"I was made aware of your story. I know how difficult the last few months must have been for you," the Brazilian footballer begins.
Vinícius has become a leading voice challenging racism in football and supporting black people, and a smile spreads across Zaher's face as the player tells him: "You are a hard-working black man. I really hope you will make good use of your new prosthetic legs, that you return to playing football and that you find happiness. You deserve it."
Then comes an invitation: "I would like to invite you to attend a Madrid match. We can spend the day together."
Overwhelmed, Zaher gets up and leaves the room. A few moments later, he returns wearing his new Vinícius Jr football shirt. He hopes that one day he will be able to get a visa and accept the offer.
"Tell Vinícius, I love him," he says. "His message has really uplifted me." His mother Habibah says she feels "like the whole world is cheering Zaher on, wanting him to succeed".
Zaher lost his legs in 2024, when he and his mother had been trapped in Khartoum. Much of the city had become a battleground as it was torn apart by fighting between Sudan's army and the RSF.
Food and basic supplies were running short and the family did not have enough money to flee. To survive, they sold lentils on the streets.
Then one morning, as Zaher and his mother worked side by side, a drone struck.
"I looked at him and he was bleeding. There was blood everywhere," Habibah explained last year.
She was devastated. "He would wake up and ask: 'Why did you let them cut off my legs?' I couldn't answer."
Back then, Zaher was wheeling himself through the rubble of his neighbourhood in a wheelchair, past burnt-out cars, abandoned tanks and shattered homes.
Before the war, Zaher had loved football. After the drone strike, he could only play on his knees, a painful process that put him at risk of serious infection.
"I wish I could have prosthetic legs so I can play football with my friends like I used to," he said at the time.
There seemed little prospect of that happening, but his story resonated far beyond Sudan, prompting an outpouring of support from people around the world.
Among them was Dena Latif, a UK-based lawyer of Sudanese origin. After seeing the BBC report, she helped spearhead an online campaign raising £45,000 ($60,000) for his medical care.
Unable to get the treatment he needed in Sudan, Zaher had to leave the country, which was far from straightforward. He and his mother had no passports and their birth certificates had been destroyed during the war.
After months of planning, he and his mother were able to fly to Cairo where an apartment had been prepared for them, with food in the fridge and medical appointments arranged.
For the first time in years, their immediate concern was no longer simply how to survive.

  - Published16 October 2025
- A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan 
  - Published13 November 2025
Zaher underwent further surgery, followed by months of physiotherapy and training to learn to use his prosthetic legs. He also received psychological support to help him process the trauma he had been through.
"He was shy, a little bit depressed, sad," says Dr Bintelmuna Eltayeb , one of the doctors involved in his care. "To get a smile out of him was almost impossible, but now you can see he's laughing. He has great confidence in himself."
His transformation has been as much psychological as physical, say those close to him, and Dena says Zaher now approaches life with a determination that has surprised them.
As we spend time with Zaher, he laughs and jokes, making up for some of the childhood that war has taken from him.
He is eager to try new things, from horse riding to cycling, and wants to become an airline pilot. He hasn't had a game of football yet but is looking forward to playing with his friends back home.
For Habibah, watching her son regain his confidence has brought enormous relief. But she worries about his future, his education and how he will be received in Sudan, a country still locked in civil war.
The state of emergency has been lifted in their home city, Khartoum, with the Sudanese army back in control there. But throughout the capital, buildings have been left destroyed - burned, blackened and looted.
Concerns over security remain and 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of food insecurity, according to a recent statement released by the US and 30 other Western states. The group also warned of "potential famine".
"I hope that Zaher's story doesn't end with him," says Dena. She hopes his recovery will attract more attention and funds for the thousands of other Sudanese children who have suffered life-altering injuries.
Zaher and his mother are now back in Khartoum. They hope that as the city is more stable at the moment, he will be able to get his prosthetic legs checked and adjusted there as he grows.
Despite the safety they found in Cairo, they missed their home, family and friends. And while Zaher has been given a chance to reclaim his childhood, millions of other Sudanese children are still waiting for theirs.

Pope forgives person who nailed him in the eye with a rosary in Peru
Pope Leo XIV has forgiven the person who threw a rosary at him before his final Mass in Peru and nailed him in the eye
ABOARD THE PAPAL PLANE -- Pope Leo XIV has forgiven the person who threw a rosary at him before his final Mass in Peru and nailed him in the eye, saying it was merely a sign of the person’s profound faith.
Leo got hit during a popemobile ride Monday through the estimated 1.5 million people who had flooded a Lima air base for the service. Leo grimaced and touched his eye but proceeded as if nothing had happened.
During an in-flight press conference en route home, a Peruvian reporter apologized for the incident. Leo, who lived in Peru for two decades and has Peruvian citizenship, brushed it off as merely someone trying to get close to the pope.
And he also joked about it.
“The nice thing about Peruvians, including the person who with a lot of faith simply wanted to offer me a rosary, are things you carry in your heart – or maybe in your eye – but that mark the life of someone,” he said.
“It tells you that here truly there is enthusiasm. Here there is profound faith. Here there is a desire to receive the blessing of the Lord,” he said.
People often toss rosaries, stuffed animals, sports jerseys and other items toward the pope when he is in the popemobile and he has often wowed crowds with his quick reflexes and ability to catch them. His bodyguards, however, say these tossed items are some of their biggest security concerns when he’s out in public.

Intel is being sued by shareholders, who are accusing the chipmaker of misleading them about the impact of the PC sales slump that contributed to a drop of 28.6 percent in the price of Intel’s stock on October 30.
The lawsuit (PDF), filed on Friday in the San Jose, California, federal court, is seeking class-action certification and lists the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System and “all others similarly situated” as plaintiffs. In addition to Intel, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and Intel’s EVP and CFO David Zinsner are listed as defendants.
The plaintiffs claim that Intel made “materially false and misleading statements and omissions” between July 23 and October 29. They are seeking unspecified compensatory damages, plus legal and other associated fees, for shareholders during that period.
In the complaint, the shareholders argue that Intel misled them by failing to disclose: the full impact that the PC market sales slump would have on Intel’s third quarter and beyond; the impact of increasing PC component prices on PC sales for Intel’s OEM and distribution partners; that Intel was dealing with substrate supply constraints that would limit its ability to meet data center CPU demand; and “that any positive impacts to Intel’s business and financial results resulting from data center construction and other aspects of the AI boom were more than offset” by the PC sales slump.

Instagram is filled with people posting deepfaked content — including, as of late, from one of Meta’s most prominent executives.
Not even Sam Altman is safe from AI deepfakes on Instagram
Meta’s chief AI officer posted an AI video of a top competitor. It’s allowed under Meta’s AI policy.
Earlier in November, Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, shared a short clip to promote Muse, the company’s consumer AI agent. In the AI-generated clip, Wang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Jolly, the anthropomorphic mascot of Muse, are on a four-way video call. When Altman joins the call he’s dressed like Jolly, wearing a furry hooded suit and face paint to look like the cutesy character. The clip is captioned “When the homies meet about openai product strategy,” a reference to the AI agent race and the recent popularity of Muse.
Just a few years ago, AI content portraying real people led to strong public statements rebuking the use of the technology to imitate humans. In some cases legal action was threatened. Now, AI content has become part of the texture of a new reality, especially on social media. Leading up to the midterm elections, for example, political groups ran millions of dollars’ worth of AI-generated ads attacking opponents.
Wang has been doing a lot of what some have described as “anti-PR” to promote Muse, tweeting hundreds of times and referring to more traditional marketers as “corposlops.” Still, a major tech executive posting an AI video of a competitor is notable, especially on a platform that’s been criticized recently over AI-generated content. After an AI-generated image of actress Mia Goth gained traction in October, the Pearl star’s representative told The Verge it was “incomprehensible” that Instagram allowed the image to spread instead of focusing on the “protection and integrity of a public figure’s likeness.” Other celebrities, including Scarlett Johansson, are regularly the subject of sexualized AI imagery; Meta has removed some accounts in the past that it found to be posing as someone else and using their likeness.
Meta requires AI-generated videos depicting people to be labeled as AI, like Wang’s post is. Static images, however, have no such requirement, meaning the AI image of Goth had no disclosure. To make matters worse, the image was shared by a fan account with a blue verification badge given by Instagram.
Reached for comment, Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton noted that Wang’s post is labeled as AI content. Clayton also pointed out that Altman has made his likeness available for AI content generation, as when OpenAI launched its Sora app (and it was quickly flooded with fake Altman videos). OpenAI didn’t respond to requests for comment.

New Delhi: From ‘maida-free bread’ and ‘100% whole wheat’ to ‘no added sugar’ and ‘pimple-free’, product labels are full of promises. But can companies back them up? The government now wants to put such claims to the test, in a move that could force consumer goods makers to rethink what they print on their packaging.
The consumer affairs ministry is working on a plan to scrutinize trademarks and front-of-pack claims across food, cosmetics and other consumer products and non-compliance could invite serious action, including delisting of such products, said three people in the know.
Manufacturers could be asked to substantiate their claims with credible evidence or face action, including recommendations to delist products found to carry misleading or unsupported claims, they said, adding that the current laws give enough teeth.
“The Department of Consumer Affairs is examining front-of-pack trademarks because these labels influence purchasing decisions, with consumers often relying on claims made by companies on product packaging. If consumers pay a premium based on specific product claims, companies must substantiate them with credible evidence,” said the first of the two people cited above.
Plan of action
To be sure, the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has found instances where such claims were not supported by the products’ actual composition or performance.
“The department is writing to DPIIT (Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade) to explore a mechanism for scrutinizing such trademarks and ensuring that claims are backed by evidence and do not mislead consumers,” the second person said.
“The department will also hold consultations with stakeholders and ask companies to rectify their product labels. Where products are found to be inconsistent with the claims made on their packaging, it will recommend delisting them and take other necessary action,” said the third person.
The CCPA has adequate powers to initiate investigations and impose penalties if companies are found guilty in an inquiry, as has been done in previous cases. A case in point is its action in June against Storia Foods and Mrs. Bectors Food Specialities over misleading front-of-pack claims on tender coconut water and whole-wheat bread, respectively. The authority imposed a penalty of ₹1 lakh on each company over misleading claims.
Section 9(2)(a) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, bars registration of marks that are deceptive or likely to cause confusion, while Section 57 provides for cancellation or rectification of registered trademarks on specified grounds.
Regulatory flak
The plan comes amid growing regulatory action against companies over product descriptions, labelling and advertising claims. It could widen the compliance burden for manufacturers, who may have to strengthen scientific testing, documentation and legal reviews before introducing or retaining claims on packaging.
The issue has already led to disputes between food companies and regulators. Manufacturers including ITC, Dabur India and AWL Agri Business have approached courts challenging action by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) over claims on their products.
In August, ITC challenged FSSAI notices directing it to remove ‘100% Atta’, ‘100% Madhya Pradesh Wheat’ and ‘0% Maida’ claims from packaging and advertisements for Aashirvaad MP Chakki Atta. The company argued that the regulator's notices were procedurally flawed and had relied on unsubstantiated assumptions. The Delhi High Court granted interim protection against cancellation of its food business licence while the matter was being heard.
Dabur also approached the same court after FSSAI restricted its claims such as ‘100% Pure’, ‘100% Natural’ and ‘100% Organic’ on several food products, including honey, ghee, coconut oil and coconut water. The court granted interim relief, and said the company should have been given an opportunity to respond before the directive. Dabur argued that complying with the order could require it to withdraw or repackage products worth more than ₹150 crore.
AWL Agri Business, which sells edible oils under the Fortune brand, challenged FSSAI notices over claims including ‘100% Veg’ and ‘Cholesterol Free – For Healthy Lifestyle’ on its Fortune Soya Health refined soybean oil. The Delhi High Court sought responses from the Centre and FSSAI. These cases are pending and do not amount to final judicial findings that the companies' claims were misleading.
Need for scrutiny
In Storia's case, the CCPA had found that its ‘100% Tender Coconut Water’ product was made by reconstituting coconut water concentrate with water, while the qualification appeared in the ingredients panel rather than prominently alongside the main claim. In Mrs. Bectors' case, the authority examined claims including ‘100% Atta Bread’ and ‘100% Whole Wheat Bread’. The CCPA said the expression ‘100%’ is an absolute numerical claim and must accurately reflect a product's composition.
Queries on the scrutiny plan sent to the consumer affairs department and top FMCG firms such as Procter & Gamble, Godrej, Emami, HUL, Britannia, Marico, Tata Consumer, PepsiCo and Dabur on 13 November remained unanswered.
“Any gap between the claims on the packaging and the product’s actual composition or performance can mislead consumers, particularly when they pay a premium based on those claims. Stronger scrutiny is, therefore, necessary to ensure transparency and accountability,” said Ashim Sanyal, managing trustee, Consumer VOICE, a consumer rights non-profit.
Legal experts said the scrutiny layer is likely to increase companies’ compliance obligations and they may need to ensure all claims on packaging is backed by scientific evidence and can withstand regulatory examination.
“Companies will need to ensure that claims on product packaging are accurate and supported by verifiable evidence. Any inconsistency between the claims and a product’s actual composition or performance could invite regulatory action under consumer protection laws,” said Vijay Kumar, partner at law firm Fox Mandal.

Sanjay Leela Bhansali's Bhansali Productions is gearing up for an exciting 2027. The year will begin with the release of Love & War, one of the most awaited films of Indian cinema, starring Ranbir Kapoor, Alia Bhatt and Vicky Kaushal. Ashish Pandey is a senior industry professional with more than two decades of experience in the entertainment business. The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.
The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.
The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. Some animal rights activists have compared authorities’ baboon management to apartheid.
During Friday’s relocation, outraged protesters tried to stop vehicles taking the baboons away. One person sprayed a fire extinguisher, according to the Daily Maverick, a local news outlet.
After the confrontation, the local Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals branch urged those opposed to the baboons’ capture not to try to stop the vehicles. “Capture and transport are already stressful for the baboons,” it said in a statement. “Delaying their arrival prolongs their time in crates and risks adding to that stress – this is not fair on the baboons.”
It said it remained opposed to the baboon’s relocation, adding: “Our presence did not imply support … our inspectors are present because the animals need someone looking out for them.”
On Sunday, dozens of people sat outside the wildlife centre in a silent protest, some tying flowers to the fence. Baboons from a different troop also gathered at the boundary, calling to the newly captive animals, the Daily Maverick reported.
“We stand together for the Seaforth and Waterfall troops, for their freedom, their dignity and their right to live as wild animals,” Mandy Neal, the administrator of the Save Kogelfontein Baboons Facebook group, posted on Monday, calling for weekly Sunday silent protests. “ Our message is simple: CAPTIVITY IS NOT CONSERVATION.”
The City of Cape Town said in a statement on Sunday that the relocation had been successful, with the baboons being monitored 24/7 after being checked by vets and the females receiving contraceptive implants.
It said: “The Waterfall troop has been relocated due to the severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment, the limited available natural low-lying habitat, the increasing risk to the baboons’ welfare, and public safety concerns … [and] as a very last resort after other interventions were evaluated and deemed ineffective, and as an alternative to culling.”
Prof Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town, said the baboon management plan had undergone two years of public consultations. “It has thus been disappointing watching members of the public and select NGOs, many which did not engage in the stakeholder process, now compromising the safety and welfare of the baboons and people through violent actions directed at staff and baboons in transit.”

Finnish satellite developer ICEYE announced Tuesday that it is seeking to buy Italian rocket-maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion in a transaction aimed at creating Europe’s first true vertically integrated end-to-end space company.
The announcement came as an all-cash voluntary tender offer from an Italian subsidiary of ICEYE to Avio’s shareholders, led by the Italian defense conglomerate Leonardo. Avio said its board of directors “has taken note of the notice” from ICEYE and is considering the purchase offer.
Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. The Vega C has flown successfully seven times in eight attempts since 2022. It is a follow-on to an earlier version of the Vega rocket that amassed a 20-for-22 record since debuting in 2012.
ICEYE is, by far, the most successful space startup in Europe, where access to private capital, regulatory barriers, and fragmented markets often hinder startup growth, according to a recent report from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. ICEYE’s valuation stands at more than $12 billion after the company’s most recent fundraising round in June.
In pursuit of sovereignty
In a statement, ICEYE said it wants to join forces with Avio to meet Europe’s need for “sovereign space and defense capabilities.” ICEYE manufactures and operates its own satellites for radar surveillance and sells data to commercial customers and national governments, including Ukraine, which uses ICEYE imagery for targeting and tracking Russian troop movements.
“Governments need control of their critical space infrastructure, and Europe needs it most,” said Rafal Modrzewski, CEO and co-founder of ICEYE. “Avio has built the launch and propulsion capability Europe relies on. With ICEYE’s long-term capital behind it, we can integrate the supply chain, grow output and strengthen the European programs that already depend on it. Together we can build, launch and operate sovereign space systems end-to-end, made in Europe for governments across the world.”

Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese have heralded plans for new joint Quad military exercises designed to push back on China’s expansionist ambitions, with the US president promising the grouping with India and Japan will guarantee “peace through strength”.
Albanese met Trump, India’s Nahrendra Modi and Japan’s Sanae Takaichi in Manila late on Tuesday in talks about enhanced cooperation on AI, critical minerals, infrastructure and maritime security.
“These nations represent some of the most important partnerships in the entire world,” the US president said.
“They’re among the most successful nations in the world, and in certain ways among the most powerful nations of the world. Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific.”
Trump said: “As we continue to protect peace through strength, we are also working together to advance super intelligence, SI, the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the industrial revolution.”
The Australian prime minister praised Trump and said a new Quad business forum to be held in 2027 would build economic growth across the region.
Leaders in the group – established as China seeks to build its military might and exert influence across the region – say they will cooperate to maintain peace and stability with Beijing.
“When we work together for our common view in the Indo-Pacific of peace, security, stability, and prosperity, then the world will be a safer and more secure place, and the Quad has a critical role in achieving that,” Albanese told the summit.
The plan for new military exercises involving maritime patrol aircraft is likely to prompt strong criticism from China.
Albanese said Australia would deploy its P8-A Poseidon and P3-C Orion maritime patrol aircraft as part of the operation in early 2027.
Asked what he would tell Chinese leader Xi Jinping later this week about the plan, Albanese said military exercises were common.
“We want peace and security in the region. That’s the objective here. It’s not about any one country. It’s about our own sovereignty, but also about peace and security in the region,” he said
The Quad leaders want the group to present a multilateral coalition of resistance against Beijing, seeking to undermine its dominance, including in the South and East China seas.
Takaichi said the Quad would help shape the future of the region.
“We would like to realise a free and open Indo Pacific by strengthening resilience of countries in the region and promote their freedom to decide for themselves across a wide range of areas including maritime security, economic security, energy and critical and emerging technologies.”
Before the meeting, as the four leaders posed for a group photo, Trump praised Modi and Takaichi as “tough”, before gesturing to Albanese and saying: “We’re OK too.” Albanese laughed at the remark.
The first meeting of the Quad leaders since 2024 came as Albanese and Trump both prepare for setpiece engagement with China’s president later this week. Albanese will visit Xi in Shenzhen on Friday, a day after three-way talks between Trump, Xi and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Trump said he wanted talks with the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, but conceded he was not the host of the China summit and it was up to Xi to issue an invitation. The US president said he could have a one-on-one meeting with Putin “if it’s available”.
Quad military exercises would build on progress from the recently completed Malabar joint exercise near Japan, where sailors completed anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare drills.
Trump also talked up the Aukus nuclear deal with Australia. “We make the greatest submarines anywhere in the world, and we’re working with Australia and others on that,” he said.
Trump said the US was poised to catch up to China on rare earth production within 10 months, backed up by speedy progress from Australia, Japan and India.
He was accompanied by cabinet members Marco Rubio, Scott Bessent, Howard Lutnick and Jamieson Greer, as well as his new chief of staff, Stephen Miller.
Privately, officials believed the meeting alone showed the group was progressing. Australian officials welcomed the engagement of Trump in regional affairs as he enters the final two years of his presidency.
Trump took credit for reinvigorating the grouping, and said he placed a premium on relations with Albanese, Modi and Takaichi.
“When they have difficulty, when they want to tell me something, my phone is always open, and the Oval Office is always open to you, and you know that,” he said.
Albanese said before the meeting he would push Trump on ending the war in Iran, a conflict which has produced an unprecedented global energy shock and badly distorted conditions in the Australian economy.
It was Albanese’s first meeting with Takaichi since a weeks-long saga about comments he made on a podcast about her gift of melons presented to him during a visit to Australia in July.
Earlier, Albanese took part in the East Asia Summit where he called for regional partners to work together to boost AI protections. Trump, who calls the technology “superintelligence”, said it represented “the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution”.

ANTALYA, Turkey—After their big gains in the 2026 midterm elections, a delegation of Democratic US House members appeared at the United Nations COP31 climate change conference Monday, pledging to rejoin the international fight against global warming.
Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, said it is a “pivotal time” for US climate and energy policy.
“The wrecking ball of Donald Trump and this out-of-touch administration, and the temporarily empty chair of the United States at this COP31, does not represent what the Americans want or need,” Huffman said.
President Donald Trump has pulled the United States out of the Paris climate agreement twice and is trying to quit the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The current administration has also tried to cut all funding for climate programs.
Since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, the United States has had no formal government presence at the UN talks, but was informally represented by America Is All In, a coalition including local governments, businesses, faith groups, Native American tribes, and universities.
Huffman said the midterm election shows that Americans have rejected the current administration’s efforts to “turn the United States into something like a petro-dictatorship.” The results could pave the way for the country to reestablish a formal presence at the annual talks.
Given legal uncertainties about Trump’s efforts to completely withdraw the US from the UN’s climate framework, the extent of US participation in the talks is unclear. But Huffman said that, in the past, US congressional delegations have attended the annual Conference of the Parties, as the meeting is formally known, under both Democratic and Republican majorities.
“The next time we’re here, we will be an official congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives,” Huffman said in an interview with Inside Climate News.

California sued OpenAI yesterday, alleging it has tried to evade responsibility for the Hugging Face attack and about 80 other incidents in which the company lost control of its AI. The lawsuit was filed under the state’s public nuisance and unfair competition laws.
The July 2026 hack of Hugging Face and other attacks carried out by OpenAI’s autonomous agents “may just be the tip of the iceberg,” said a lawsuit filed in a state court by California Attorney General Rob Bonta. “OpenAI recently admitted to the Attorney General’s Office that it has lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing.”
OpenAI had publicly reported only 27 such incidents, showing that “OpenAI’s public reports do not represent the full scope of loss-of-control incidents involving OpenAI’s models that have impacted third parties,” the lawsuit said. OpenAI “knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in a press release.
OpenAI models are “able to find novel vulnerabilities in computer networks, quickly break down defenses, and autonomously carry out cyberattacks,” Bonta’s lawsuit said. OpenAI puts safeguards in its publicly released models to prevent this behavior, “but deliberately omits or removes these protections while experimenting with and training its models,” the lawsuit said.
In the attack on Hugging Face, OpenAI agents “employed complicated hacking methodologies and involved coordinated actions by hundreds of individual autonomous AI agents that should have been contained in OpenAI’s research environment,” the lawsuit said.
Known attacks “include unauthorized access of and cyberattacks on databases containing code that powers countless applications; informational websites that are trusted and valuable resources for the public; and foreign government databases storing sensitive health information,” the lawsuit said. “Swarms of OpenAI’s experimental AI agents have even compromised OpenAI’s own internal infrastructure, in an attack that managed to obtain administrator-level access to critical OpenAI systems.”

Jeff Bezos has some advice for Nvidia's board as it searches for a permanent successor to Jensen Huang:
The Amazon founder told Semafor's Liz Hoffman during the Silicon Valley & The World conference that Nvidia would be wise to look inside the company.
"If you don't bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider," Bezos said. "NVIDIA is too complicated.
"I think outside CEOs in complex companies have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding," Bezos added. "And so I would always think that's a last resort."
Bezos, who stepped down as Amazon's CEO in 2021 after nearly three decades leading the company, said Nvidia's situation was different from Amazon's carefully orchestrated leadership transition, adding that his departure was the result of a "multi-year planned transition."
Bezos's advice comes as Nvidia faces the challenge of replacing a founder whose leadership helped turn it into a central player in the AI boom.
Huang, who resigned last Thursday amid reports of extramarital affairs and questions about a possible foreign intelligence effort, broke his silence Tuesday, saying he would be "honored" to return if the board determined it was in Nvidia's best interest. The board has said it does not intend to reinstate him.
Nvidia Executive Vice President and CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent replacement. The board is also investigating whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
Huang's potential return has drawn support from employees and industry figures. An online petition calling for his reinstatement has garnered more than 190,000 signatures.
When asked whether Bezos thinks Huang should be brought back, he declined to weigh in, saying he didn't know enough about what had happened behind closed doors.
"Jensen is a remarkable guy who founded and built a remarkable company with a lot of hard work and foresight," Bezos said, "And he deserves admiration and respect no matter what, and that will never go away."

Secretary of State Marco Rubio says some intelligence sources are ‘liars and criminals’ and explains why software disasters are ‘actually a positive development’

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has tried to calm American nerves over an alleged Iranian plot to target Washington, D.C., with a “dirty bomb” and the recent spate of tech outages.
The secretary was delivering a press conference in Manila Tuesday – where he is part of President Donald Trump’s entourage that will meet with Chinese Premier Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin Thursday – when he was asked about possible threats against the U.S. from outside actors.
Addressing the alleged Iranian plot, which was first reported by CNN, citing seven anonymous U.S. intelligence sources, Rubio was dismissive.
“Let me tell you guys something,” he told the assembled press corps. “Some of your intelligence sources are liars. Others are liars and criminals.
“They’re liars because they’re making up [stuff]. They’re arguing they have access to something they don’t and because they have an email address in the government, they somehow have credibility with you.
“So number one, you have a bunch of liars out there that pitch stuff to people. I’m not talking about that reporting specifically, just in general.
“As far that specific report is concerned, the United States is always on the lookout for anyone who tries to do harm to our country and to our people. And we have threat streams every day, and the majority of them are not credible.”
A reporter pressed him on whether or not he was “concerned about an imminent attack on Washington.”
“I am not, but again, we’re concerned everyday about anything that threatens our country,” the secretary answered.
“And sadly, unfortunately, if they’re good at what they’re doing, you oftentimes won’t see it. The intelligence may not gather it, you know, if they’re good at their job or what they’re trying to get done.
“But I feel a lot of confidence in our intelligence services. I have a lot of confidence in our systems on being able to identify these things ahead of time. I don’t think there’s any imminent threat.”
Turning to last week’s tech outages –which hit Microsoft, air traffic control systems and banks over successive days – Rubio said the three disasters did not appear to be connected.
“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation-state, with a malign actor of any kind,” he said.
“We fully acknowledge that this is unsettling to see these reports day after day of some technical failures,” the secretary continued. “We get it. In our own lives, we see it the same way.
“We take these things very seriously. Obviously, we’re always vigilant. We’re always on the lookout for anything that poses a threat to the American people, to the American economy, or to national security. We are always hyper-vigilant about that, and we’re also on the lookout for it.”
Asked if AI might have played a part in the outages, as Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has suggested, Rubio said all of the companies impacted have “full-scale cybersecurity” teams in place devoted to defending them against attacks.
“In terms of the role that AI might have played in it, I don’t want to speculate on it, because again, every one of these instances is distinct and unique, and I would refer you to the companies,” he said, going to to suggest the outages were “actually a positive development” because they demonstrated businesses’ willingness to come forward and report problems, rather than attempt to conceal them to safeguard their reputations.
“I think we’ve now reached a different era, which is companies – which is a good thing – are now immediately sharing vulnerabilities because they don’t want to be accused of covering up something,” the secretary said.
Trump himself addressed the dirty bomb report in the Philippines Tuesday, saying that, if it proved accurate, Iran “will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before. I hope it’s not [true]. But we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy.”
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis meanwhile told The Independent the executive remains “vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland.”
Iran Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei in turn addressed CNN’s report in a post on X, dismissing it as “baseless” and a “fabricated media narrative.”

The Telangana State Women’s Commission (TGSCW) has initiated an inquiry into an alleged illegal oocyte donation racket in Hyderabad, issuing notices to eight Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) centres and egg banks over suspected irregularities in their donor records and procurement practices.
The Commission examined representatives of the eight institutions on Friday, November 13, after directing their managements to appear before it. However, TGSCW Chairperson Nerella Sharada expressed dissatisfaction after some centres sent staff members and other representatives instead of senior management, despite being specifically instructed to attend in person. The inquiry was subsequently adjourned after the institutions assured the Commission that their management would appear at the next hearing.
During Friday’s proceedings, the Commission scrutinised reports, records and details of egg donors submitted by the ART centres and egg banks. “Several irregularities and suspicious elements have emerged from the records examined so far,” said Ms. Sharada.
She also questioned claims made by the institutions that nearly 90% of their egg donors came from other States and donated their eggs voluntarily without receiving any remuneration or financial compensation. She said the claims raised several questions and warranted further investigation.
Health Department’s investigation
Commissioner of Health and Family Welfare, Sangeetha Satyanarayana, also attended the inquiry, during which Ms. Sharada sought details about the progress of the department’s investigation into the alleged illegal egg procurement practices. The discussions also covered shortcomings in the existing Assisted Reproductive Technology Act and its implementation, particularly the challenges in regulating and monitoring ART centres and egg banks.
Ms. Sharada said she would soon meet Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha and Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy to inform them of the findings and discuss corrective measures, including possible legislative amendments to strengthen regulation of the sector.
More ART centres likely to come under scanner
Ms. Sharada further said that the Commission has also received information indicating the possible involvement of several other ART centres and egg banks in the alleged racket. It plans to issue notices to their management and summon them for questioning as part of the ongoing inquiry.
“The Commission will not tolerate illegal practices that compromise women’s health, dignity and rights. We will continue the investigation in coordination with the concerned government departments to identify those responsible and ensure appropriate legal action,” she added.

Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
- Published
Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.
Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.
The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.
Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.
The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024.
Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".
The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.
The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.
In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean.
In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda".
Once in Rwanda, people will be able to integrate into society, which means they will have the right of residence, as well as access to education, healthcare, the labour market and the legal system.
Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the country is commmited to working with European partners to provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants".
He added that they would also work on "correcting the global imbalance in economic opportunities", which he called a "key driver of irregular migration".
Ahead of the announcement, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants.
The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.
"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".
With elections approaching in several EU nations, administrations have been under pressure to show they can control migration.
Concerns around security, struggling economies and disillusionment with governing parties have all had a major role in shaping attitudes towards people leaving their home countries.
Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.
"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."
The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution.
The agency added that unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, which the Dutch government has confirmed will not take place.
According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, there were almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first 10 months of 2026, which represents a 29% decrease compared to the previous year.
In October, about 18,100 crossings were detected, which is about 6% less than October 2025 but 22% more than in September "largely because of a sharp rise in arrivals on the Western African route to the Canary Islands".

How the East Potomac golf course became a D.C. landmark — and what could happen to it
Runners and cyclists still have access to D.C.'s East Potomac Park, despite the Trump administration's plans to close it over the weekend. But its golf course is conspicuously missing the flags that typically mark the holes — and at least some of the people who typically play them.
Federal Judge Ana Reyes issued a restraining order late Saturday to keep the beloved park open for two weeks, just hours before the National Park Service planned to cut off public access to most of it indefinitely.
But Sunday marked the last day of the government's lease with the National Links Trust, which had operated the golf course since 2020. And Reyes did not order the government to keep operating the golf course — though she has since signaled she may consider it.
"Whether and how Defendants do so is solely within their discretion, but Defendants cannot use the absence of golf operations as a reason to exclude the public from the Course," Reyes wrote in her 30-page order.
Reyes criticized the government's "pretextual" justification and "arbitrary" timeline for closing the park, which she said would "irreparably harm" the people who enjoy it on a daily basis — including the local preservationists and golfers who first sued to protect the course in February.
In comments on social media and to the press, President Trump slammed her decision and said his administration will appeal. The White House referred NPR to those comments.
"What she's done is she stopped it for 15 days," Trump told reporters when asked about the case on Monday. "You can't stop that."
The National Park Service and Interior Department did not respond to NPR's questions about the future of the course.
Trump has his sights set on redeveloping the golf course — which he has repeatedly decried as decrepit and dangerous — into a championship-level venue. Administration officials are due to present that vision to the federal Commission of Fine Arts on Thursday.
According to the government's 64-page submission, architect Tom Fazio's design would replace East Potomac's three courses of varying difficulty levels with one 18-hole layout stretching across almost the entire peninsula.
The plan is broadly unpopular in D.C., as it would eliminate the perimeter road beloved by runners and cyclists, and the grassy areas where people picnic and birdwatch. Critics worry the new course would be less accessible for beginners and less affordable for everyone. Prices currently range from $17 to $48 per round, and the Trump administration has not said what a round at the new course would cost, only that locals would be able to play at a discount.
Locals agree that East Potomac could use some improvements, including to its long-eroded seawall. But that's very different from overhauling the course entirely. Reyes pressed government lawyers at a Friday hearing on why the National Park Service chose the latter.
Officials pointed to Trump's social media directives, but also argued that the park needs to be closed for other reasons: to repair the seawall (for which it acknowledged Friday there is no plan yet) and because of the lack of a golf course operator (a situation Reyes described as "entirely self-inflicted"). And it says there are nearby recreational areas people can use instead — though critics say there is no substitute. Reyes seemed to agree.
"Plaintiffs' harms are tied to 'East Potomac's beauty, historic layout, and historic designs,'" Reyes wrote. "While there are other parks in Washington, D.C., there is no other East Potomac Park."
The East Potomac golf course is known for its history of accessibility
East Potomac is a man-made peninsula, originally dredged from the Potomac River to facilitate shipping channels. Congress designated the land a public park in 1897, declaring it should be "forever held and used as a park for the recreation and pleasure of the people." It houses many forms of recreation, including a tennis complex, a perimeter road and a 220-acre golf course.
The golf course at East Potomac is one of seven that the federal government built in D.C. between 1917 and 1948, according to a 2017 National Park Service historical report. It calls that "a testament to the rise in popularity of the sport of golf and the demand for public golf courses for those who could not [afford] private memberships to exclusive golf clubs in the early decades of the 20th century."
That number has since dwindled to three. East Potomac is the busiest, especially after a renewed interest in golf during the COVID-19 pandemic: It hosted some 125,000 rounds of golf in 2025 alone.
"In a city where politicians are constantly focused on what separates us, East Potomac is one of the few remaining spaces where no matter who you are, what you do, or the state of your game, everyone is welcome and everyone is treated the same," plaintiff Dave Roberts said in a statement when the lawsuit was first filed.
Its first 18 holes were designed by Walter Travis, one of the top amateur golfers in the U.S., who shaped dozens of courses during the "golden age of golf" (which ended around the onset of the Great Depression).
He modeled East Potomac after Scottish "links-style" courses, which are known for their coastal terrain and relative lack of trees — in this case offering clear views of the Potomac River and the Washington Monument. And, in a unique twist, Travis designed the course to be reversible, for the durability of the grounds and to the delight of those who played them.
"Travis captured a design style that characterized the era's greatest courses, including East Potomac: difficult for aggressive elite players, yet playable for unskilled beginners," plaintiffs wrote in their February complaint.
The first portion of the course opened to the public in July 1920. It cost 25 cents to play a round, including locker room privileges. The course was a huge hit, drawing 16,345 golfers in its first year. That number nearly quadrupled by 1921, according to the National Park Service.
The links grew to meet demand over the next decade, ultimately expanding into three courses (red, white and blue) plus one of the first miniature golf courses in the U.S., which features tiny replicas of the White House and U.S. Capitol and is now the country's oldest continually operating mini-golf course.
But despite its broad appeal, East Potomac initially allowed Black players access only during limited hours one day per week. A separate course, Langston, opened to serve Black residents in 1939 — on the site of a former city dump — but suffered from neglect and downright hazardous conditions.
One day in June 1941, three Black golfers showed up at East Potomac and demanded to play.
According to historical accounts, they had a "fair-skinned" friend purchase their tickets but were turned away. They returned with some powerful government allies, and park police ruled that the men should be allowed to play since they had tickets. The trio completed 18 holes, accompanied by police and amidst the "boos and chorus of insults" from white onlookers.
The next day, the interior secretary issued an order opening the course to all players, regardless of race.
Harassment and other forms of segregation persisted at the city's municipal courses for over a decade, but the golfers' 1941 protest is seen as a turning point in the fight for equal access to public spaces. The National Park Service says it "opened the door for the full integration of all national park facilities in 1945."
Judge Reyes has nodded to that part of the park's history throughout the case, including while grilling government lawyers at a mid-October hearing.
"We're not just talking about some putt-putt thing that went up by the beach you take your kids to," she said, adding that the course holds a rich history and "deep amount of meaning" to locals. "There was bravery in the people who first desegregated this golf course."
The course has only closed — temporarily — a few times in its history, including for a portion of World War II and for a few days after Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination, in 1968, when National Guard troops responding to riots set up camp at East Potomac.
What would change?
There have been changes at East Potomac over the decades, like the addition of a two-tiered driving range in the 1990s.
But, as the National Park Service said in its 2017 report, the city's courses continue their original intent "to allow golfers of all ages and skill levels to play at an [affordable] cost compared to private and even semi-private clubs in the area and remain extremely popular."
Plaintiffs note in their lawsuit that a weekend round at East Potomac's blue course costs $48, compared to $89 for a Sunday morning round at the Laurel Hill Golf Club, a municipal golf course in nearby Fairfax County, Va.
Critics worry a championship-style course would be even less affordable — especially one that Trump described over the weekend this way: "All over the World it will be acclaimed as being the Best Golf Course anywhere."
Trump said locals will get a 50% discount. But the administration has not said how much it will cost to play. The administration's proposal only points to "benchmark" championship courses in California, Texas and New York, where locals pay up to $90 per weekend round, even with a discount. The government admitted Friday that those were merely illustrations.
There's also the question of how beginner-friendly the redesigned course would be.
Reyes pointed out last week that under the administration's proposal, even from the shortest tee at every hole, the course adds up to 6,013 yards. She asked the government how that compares to recommended course length averages for different types of players, including seniors and young players, and did not get an answer.
The administration said repeatedly that its plan is not yet final, as it still needs to undergo various federal reviews that require input from experts and the public. Lawyers told Reyes that there is no contract between the government and Fazio, the architect — despite Trump's repeated social media posts saying work would begin on Nov. 15.
Even so, the government said it had to close the park that day in part because there was no one left to run the course.
The nonprofit National Links Trust had entered into a 50-year lease to operate the city's municipal golf courses in 2020. But the government terminated its East Potomac lease last December, accusing it of failing to make capital improvements. The trust continued to manage the course on an interim basis — and still manages the city's other courses — but announced last month that its role would end at East Potomac on Nov. 15.
Reyes said that timing was no coincidence.
"[The National Park Service] claims that it would be unable to safely manage the course itself. In other words, the Government's hands are tied," she wrote in her order. "But the Government tied the knot itself."
Reyes has been openly hesitant to take the administration at its word at this point in the increasingly inflammatory case. She ordered an inquiry into potential misconduct by government lawyers and officials after they cut down hundreds of trees on short notice in October and repeatedly contradicted the president's social media announcements in court.
At Friday's hearing, Reyes questioned why the National Park Service couldn't renew its lease with the operator, especially since it has already entrusted it to manage two other municipal golf courses for another 50 years. She mulled whether the government could theoretically step in to run the golf course, at least until it finds another party to do so.
Reyes appears to be weighing whether she has the legal authority to compel the Trump administration to do that. On Monday, she ordered both parties to submit briefings discussing "whether the Court may require the Government to operate East Potomac Golf Course in order to maintain the status quo."

Here is a thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama from director Nitesh Tiwari, with music by Hans Zimmer and AR Rahman, based on the ancient classical poem about Rama, the avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu. It has often been adapted for live-action and animated movies in the past, though surely not on this scale, the current three-hour blockbuster being only the first half. (There are no musical numbers though.) The idea of aristocrats submitting stoically and yet playfully to exile in the forest has something Shakespearean about it, and if you are suffering from Homer-withdrawal after Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, a story about the noble Prince Rama finally vowing to wage war on a distant city where his wife has been abducted might just fit the bill.
Ranbir Kapoor plays the mythical Rama, a noble warrior and statesman who has been brought into being in the city state of Ayodhya as a bodily representative of Vishnu, and from the first his sense of destiny is overwhelming. But what exactly is that destiny? In broad terms, his fate is to face off with Ravana (Naveen “Yash” Kumar), king of far-off Lanka, a figure whose former slave status once triggered in him such a cosmically intense prayer for justice that Lord Brahma offered him the superpower of athletic strength and indifference to pain.
In Ayodhya, Rama marries the sweetly devoted Sita (Sai Pallavi), he enjoys an intense bond of comradeship with his brother Lakshmana (Ravi Dubey), and is the apple of his father’s eye; this is King Dasharatha (Arun Govil) who, careworn by affairs of state, is about cede the throne to Rama. But Rama’s stepmother Kaikeyi (Lara Dutta) furiously reminds Dasharatha that he promised the crown to Bharata (Adinath Kothare), the son they had together. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana are banished to the forest.
Over in Lanka, a toxic stew of plotting against Ravana is being stirred by his slippery, smirking brother-in-law Vidyutjihva (played by Bollywood veteran Vivek Oberoi), whom Ravana ruthlessly slays in single combat; this man’s widow Shurpanakha (Rakul Preet Singh), who is Ravana’s sister, is banished to the same forest where Rama is humbly eking out his civilian existence. She falls in love with Rama, using her witchy wiles to trick and bamboozle the happily married man, and this is to lead to a cataclysmic confrontation between Rama and Ravana.
With its giant canvas and some truly beautiful sunset skyscapes, this very enjoyable film has a little of Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings and even Disney’s The Lion King (the latter surely influenced the animal-kingdom tableaux). The bizarre flying machine piloted by Ravana (who does not have the ability to fly as such) has something engagingly Gilliamesque about it. As so often with Indian cinema, this movie reminds you of the forthright, unselfconscious storytelling energy that popular Hollywood films had in the 1950s and 60s, the era of sword-and-sandal. It’s a rather amazing adventure.

Every year in Delhi, the arrival of the winter months also signals the beginning of what residents widely call “pollution season”. A thick toxic smog shrouds the city, home to 30 million people who have no choice but to breathe the poisonous air as they go about their daily lives, often while suffering from wheezy coughs, nausea and itchy eyes. While successive state governments have brought in measures intended to improve air quality, the situation has remained the same for more than a decade. Delhi is widely regarded as the world’s most polluted city. Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Pollution season usually begins around the same time as Diwali, the Hindu festival of light. Amidst the plummeting air quality, people still gather in the markets for festival shopping and at festivities outside. Diwali is also known to cause a surge in the pollution levels, due to the tens of millions of cars that hit the roads and the use of firecrackers for the celebration. In previous years, firecrackers were banned, but this year the state government has allowed “green” firecrackers”. However environmentalists argue that these are still highly polluting.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The causes of Delhi’s apocalyptic pollution are multi-faceted. In recent years, one of the biggest causes has been vehicle emissions, from the almost 10m cars, rickshaws, motorcycles and trucks on the city’s roads. It is also the season where farmers in the neighbouring states of Haryana and Punjab often burn their fields to ready them for the next crop. These fires are illegal but still occur. Factory emissions, dust from construction and rubbish burning also contribute to the toxic air quality levels.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
So far, the air quality index (AQI) has already soared above 650, more than 30 times the limit the World Health Organization (WHO) deems to be safe. Air pollution is linked to numerous serious diseases, particularly respiratory, and hospitals have already reported a surge in patients suffering from breathing difficulties.The pollution season is expected to last until January, when the weather warms up.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
Millions of Delhi’s residents are poor families or migrant workers, who have no choice but to go out to work in the toxic air, often suffering long term impacts on their health. Doctors and campaigners have described the pollution as a “health emergency”. According to a study last year, at least 15% of deaths in the capital are linked to air pollution. Pollution now kills more people in Delhi than obesity of diabetes.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
As in previous years, the state government has introduced various restrictions to try and bring air quality levels under control. Coal and firewood have been banned as fuel. Construction has also been halted and so have older diesel and petrol cars. Offices have been instructed to get people to work from home to limit traffic on the roads. Trucks can often be seen spraying water on the roads. However, it is widely acknowledged that, so far, these restrictions have had little impact on the pollution levels. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
The pollution has been a problem for so long in Delhi that it has become normalised and people carry on with their daily lives in the toxic smog.Residents rarely wear masks outside and the parks will still be full of families and children and people exercising outside.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
While rich and middle class families will buy air purifiers for their homes, they are unaffordable for most poorer families who often live in makeshift tents or informal homes. As a result, breathing clean air during pollution season has become a luxury privilege in Delhi.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The pollution is not restricted to Delhi alone. All across north India, in states such as Punjab and Haryana, the air is also toxic due to coal-powered plants, vehicles and farm fires. Cities such as Amritsar in Punjab, on the border with Pakistan, also suffer from extremely dangerous air quality levels during the winter months. Photograph: Narinder Nanu/AFP/Getty Images
Campaigners say more money needs to be invested into proper public transport and better vehicle emission regulation in Delhi to tackle the root causes of pollution. Every year, the number of cars on Delhi’s roads keeps rising, releasing more harmful pollutants, and yet few the percentage of electric vehicles remains very low.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Delhi has an extensive bus and metro network, but it is not sufficient to cope with the huge daily demand and still has poor connectivity in many areas. Most people still rely on polluting rickshaws, cars and motorcycles to get them to the bus stops or metro stations. Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
Delhi’s topography – a city built in a bowl-like valley, which has little breeze or rain in the winter months – means most of the emissions get trapped over the city as the cold weather hits and cloak the city in brown smog. Some call it Delhi’s “death shroud”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
In past years, the state and national government has been accused of manipulating the data to disguise how bad pollution levels are in the capital. Last year, it was found that water was being sprayed around the air quality monitors, allegedly to bring down the readings. Campaigners and opposition politicians have alleged that a lot of data from the air quality measuring stations has gone “missing”.
Environmental campaigners have argued that much more extreme measures are needed to bring pollution under control, similar to how Beijing successfully cleaned up its air in recent years. However, others have argued this would have an economic cost that India, as a developing country, can not afford.Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
One of the plans being prepared by the government this year is to experiment with “cloud-seeding”, to create rain which would clear the skies. But many residents and campaigners say that until the root causes are tackled, these plans are nothing more than a “gimmick”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images

William Saliba or Ezri Konsa? Mikel Arteta has tough Arsenal selection dilemma when French defender returns to full fitness
Ezri Konsa has starred for Arsenal at centre-back following his £55m move from Aston Villa this summer, but William Saliba has now returned to take back his position in the Arsenal team; the Gunners have important games against Man City, Real Madrid and Spurs after the break
Tuesday 10 November 2026 08:52, UK
Arsenal have a big set of fixtures coming up after the November international break. Big games require big team selections - and Mikel Arteta has a huge decision to make in his defence.
William Saliba is coming back, which is a major boost for the Premier League champions, but to say Arsenal have missed him in recent weeks has been an understatement. Ezri Konsa has stepped up.
