You can now see and edit what Google Gemini remembers about you
Editing the AI’s memory is one way you can shape its responses.
Besides the ability to connect and use other applications and services, a lot of AI assistants' utility comes from their capacity to shape their responses based on what they learn and remember about you. Google's Personal Intelligence feature allows Gemini to pull in context from Gmail, YouTube, Search and other Google apps, and the AI also builds out its memory based on your preferences and other personal facts that come up in chats. For example, if you share with Gemini that you're lactose intolerant, the bot will avoid recommending milk-based products.
Depending on what you share, Gemini's picture of you can be fairly intimate, which makes the ability to edit the AI's memory all the more important. If you're curious about what Gemini knows or you want to edit what the AI can draw from to personalize its responses, Google is rolling out a way to see and change Gemini's memory directly from the settings menu.
Gemini's two layers of memory
Google has two layers of settings for what you could call Gemini's memory, though the company only refers to one of them by that name. The first layer, the Keep Activity toggle, determines whether chats with Gemini are saved and associated with your Google Account. If you're 18 or older and you're logged into your personal account while using Gemini, the toggle is on by default. With Keep Activity enabled, whenever you sign in with your account you can pull up and re-engage past chats. If you disable it, chats won't be saved to your account, meaning they'll disappear after 72 hours and won't follow you across devices.
The second layer is what Google actually calls the AI's Memory. Using the content of past chats, Gemini is able to build out a profile of you that it can reference to personalize its responses. The AI isn't able to create any memories unless it can remember and access your inputs, so Keep Activity needs to be on for this to work. If it is, you may notice Gemini taking your preferences and personal information into account in its responses. That's the AI's memory at work.
How to view and edit Gemini's memory summary
If you're in the US, have a paid Google AI plan and memory is on, you can access Gemini's memory summary to see what it's compiled about you and edit this information to your liking. In the Gemini web app, click the Settings button (the gear icon) in the bottom left corner, click Personal Intelligence and then click Memory summary. Gemini will then generate a bulleted list of the major details it's gleaned about you, sorted into categories focused on things like your personal data, career information and various interests. It tends to know your pets' names, too.
You can stop there if you only care about what Gemini knows, or you can tweak the AI's memory by clicking on the Edit button (the pen icon) in the top-right corner of the Memory summary window. In edit mode, any line in the summary can be rewritten or deleted, just like a Google Doc. If you'd prefer to prompt Gemini to make additions or subtractions, you can alternatively enter a prompt via the text box at the bottom of the window. Once you're happy with your changes, you can click Save to commit them to Gemini's memory. Gemini also saves a memory history of these changes and when they were made. So, while you can easily alter your personal timeline as it pertains to Gemini's reality, any adjustments will be tracked.
How to turn off or limit Gemini's memory
If you'd prefer to turn off the memory system entirely rather than simply edit it, you can do so by clicking on the Memory toggle in the Personal Intelligence menu. Deselecting the toggle will stop Gemini from committing new facts to memory, but it doesn't delete old things it's learned. You can edit those details using the Memory summary, or delete chats completely from the Activity menu.
To delete chats, head to the Gemini web app, click Settings and then select Activity. From the Activity menu, you can scroll through interactions you've had with Gemini by date and delete whichever ones you'd like by clicking on the "X" next to them. Deleting them removes those chats from the context pool that Gemini uses to personalize its responses.
By combining all of these options, you can exert more control over what Google's AI knows and how it responds to your inputs, and ideally get more useful outputs in the process.

Despite advances in financial inclusion, a large section of India’s salaried and self-employed population continues to struggle to access formal credit. The challenge is particularly pronounced in smaller towns, where borrowers often lack conventional income documentation or established credit histories. Fintech startup Olyv is looking to bridge this gap by expanding beyond digital personal loans into a broader financial services ecosystem focused on credit access and financial health. Founded in 2016 by Rohit Garg, Amit Chandel, Vinay Singh and Jayant Upadhyay, the startup has raised $6 Mn (around ₹57 Cr) from Nippon Life India AIF Management Ltd and existing investors. The latest fundraise takes its total equity capital raised to around $50 Mn. Olyv has also raised $150 Mn in debt funding since inception. The latest investment is an extension of its $23 Mn Series B round in February, led by Nandan Nilekani-backed Fundamentum Partnership. In a conversation with Inc42, CEO and cofounder Garg said the fresh capital will primarily go towards investments in AI and data science to strengthen the company’s proprietary underwriting technology. These investments are aimed at improving risk assessment and personalising financial products, particularly for customers outside India’s major metropolitan markets. Olyv also wants to deepen its engagement with existing customers by introducing products beyond personal loans. In the near term, it plans to expand into health insurance and credit health management. The startup is also developing AI-powered financial advisory services to help customers understand their financial data, improve their credit scores and make better financial decisions. “The idea is that there should be a personalised companion which can help people build their credit scores and manage their data. AI advisory will help them look at their data deeply, advise them and guide them towards actions to create a much stronger credit profile,” Garg said. Olyv’s $1 Bn Ambition Olyv operates in a competitive digital lending market, where fintechs such as Navi, KreditBee and Fibe are vying for a larger share of India’s consumer credit market. However, Garg believes the market is expanding fast enough to accommodate multiple players, with digitisation and financial inclusion bringing more consumers into the formal financial system. “While the top 50-100 Mn consumers in India are adequately served by large institutions, the next 200-300 Mn is where I believe the next phase of growth over the next decade will come from, and I think Olyv will play a significant role in that,” he said. The startup claims that 70-75% of its customers come from Tier II, III and IV towns. These include micro-merchants running small neighbourhood businesses, freelancers and salaried employees working with smaller organisations. Olyv currently has nearly 2 Mn monthly active users and more than 50 Mn app downloads, with a presence across over 19,000 pin codes. It has disbursed approximately 80 Lakh loans, facilitating cumulative transactions worth more than ₹13,000 Cr. According to Garg, the company currently manages assets under management (AUM) of nearly ₹2,000 Cr. It is targeting 100 Mn users and AUM of more than $1 Bn (around ₹9,348 Cr) by FY29. While Garg declined to disclose the company’s absolute financials, he said revenue grew around 50% year-on-year (YoY) in FY26, while profit after tax (PAT) increased 80-90%. Olyv also claims to have recorded sequential PAT growth for 14 consecutive quarters. Inc42 Take: Can Olyv Become More Than A Lender? Olyv has built a sizable digital lending business by targeting consumers who often remain underserved by traditional financial institutions. Its reported profitability and loan disbursement numbers suggest that it has established a meaningful presence in this segment. However, expanding from lending into a diversified financial services business is a considerably bigger challenge. Offering health insurance, credit management and AI-led financial advisory services will require capabilities beyond underwriting and loan distribution. The immediate test will be whether Olyv can convert its existing customer base into users of these additional services. A large lending customer base offers a distribution advantage, but it does not automatically translate into demand for insurance or financial advisory products. The startup will also need to demonstrate that these new verticals can generate meaningful revenue without disproportionately increasing customer acquisition and operating costs. There is also the question of asset quality. As Olyv expands its lending business among customers with limited formal credit histories, maintaining underwriting discipline will be critical. Investments in AI and data science could strengthen its risk assessment capabilities, but the effectiveness of these systems will ultimately be reflected in loan performance. Olyv’s ambition to reach 100 Mn users and cross $1 Bn in AUM by FY29 is therefore not just a question of scaling its existing lending business. It will need to show that it can build commercially viable financial services around that lending base while maintaining profitability and asset quality.

Palmer Luckey says his SLAB seastead is ‘way cooler’ than a floating data center
It would act as a sovereign city state free from things like laws and governments.
Oculus founder and Oxytocin booster Palmer Luckey is touting a new project that combines some of his favorite things like wacky projects and libertarianism. SLAB is an informal plan for a floating "seastead" designed to last a thousand years that would act as a sovereign state to avoid pesky laws that "cripple" corporations, Luckey said.
An initial AI render depicts a massive artificial island built high above the sea with what looks like office buildings, apartments, refineries... and is that a data center at the top left?
"At a time when most of the seasteading community wanted to escape the US and smoke pot, this was the one project explicitly designed to make America stronger, a relief valve for ill-considered or outdated rules and regulations," Luckey wrote in a post that must be read to be believed.
You may have questions like "wtf is seasteading" and "isn't this just a floating AI data center?" That confusion is understandable, as it uses language and ideas around far-out moonshot concepts that may not be familiar to normal, non-tech-billionaires.
Selling Oculus to Facebook in 2014 gave me money for helicopter flight lessons and developing a seastead called SLAB with a 1,000 year design life.
The goal was to be cheaper than land and absent state/local laws that cripple critical American industries like metal processing,... pic.twitter.com/aJkd0eOgLF
— Palmer Luckey (@PalmerLuckey) November 18, 2026
The idea with seasteading is that if you build a floating structure far enough out in the ocean, you can create your own city-state and make whatever laws you want. The concept has been touted for years by several tech bros including Peter Thiel and Joe Lonsdale. However, the only real seastead you may have heard about was Sea Island that the piracy site Pirate Bay eyed at one point as a base of operations.
"The goal was to be cheaper than land and absent state/local laws that cripple critical American industries like metal processing, medical research/treatment, desalination, oil refining [and] chemical engineering," said Luckey. "[W]hile it still has a long way to go, there has been significant progress towards my goal of reviving manifest destiny and westward expansion."
That raises even more questions! Like, why is Luckey talking about manifest destiny? And what kind of medical research needs to be done at sea beyond the reach of laws? In any case, Luckey, who runs the defense contract firm Anduril and plans on breeding military dogs, said he wanted to get this SLAB info out now as he was being asked about it by reporters (who later identified themselves as Liz Hoffman and Reed Albergotti, both from Semafor).
Palmer said that the journalists "plan on calling SLAB my new floating AI datacenter project." However, he offered a riposte that may be the most cringe thing you'll read today: "It is way cooler than that, way older than that, and I hate looking like a hype-chasing consensus loser, so now you have to read this tweet."

Instagram is beginning to roll out a “content protection” feature that lets creators see and review copies of their videos posted to the platform.
Instagram is helping creators crack down on copycat videos
Meta will let creators decide to hide copies of their videos flagged by a new ‘content protection’ feature.
“For eligible creators who enroll, content protection is a tool that automatically looks out for visual matches of your original videos, alerts you when we find a match across Instagram and Facebook, and lets you decide what happens next,” Meta says in a blog post. Meta launched a similar tool for Facebook last year to help users “safeguard” their Reels and “maintain control” over their creative work.
When an Instagram creator is notified of a matched video, they can see how many views the match has and decide if they want to track the video, hide it from everyone on Instagram and Facebook, add a credit link, or release their claim on the match.
After a creator enrolls, every “original video” they post on Instagram is protected, and creators can retroactively protect older videos manually. Creators can also put accounts on an allow list that lets them use their videos.
In addition, Instagram will start flagging AI-generated videos that “match the spoken words” in a creator’s original video but have visuals replaced with AI. Initially, Instagram will test this with a “small group of creators” in “the coming weeks.” The platform says it’s exploring ways to limit the reach of content and profiles that “use AI tools to post this type of content repeatedly.”

An eight-year-old Haitian boy who was put into restraints and detained by immigration agents in San Diego on 4 November and transferred to a facility in Texas has been reunited with his family in California.
Representative Juan Vargas shared a photograph of the boy and his family in a social media post on Monda, writing: “11 days ago, an 8-year-old in San Diego was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in. He was separated from his loved ones and held in a facility in Texas. Today, he’s finally home.”
The Haitian Bridge Alliance, an immigration advocacy group, confirmed that the third-grader had been released from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody.
“An eight-year-old child belongs in a classroom, on a playground, and surrounded by love – not in immigration detention. We welcome his release, but his freedom should never have required a public outcry,” Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, said in a statement.
The third-grader at Fay elementary school was put in restraints and taken into custody by federal immigration officers at a check-in earlier in the month, according to video obtained by NBC News and an oversight letter Democratic lawmakers sent to the Departments of Homeland Security and Health and Human Services.
A spokesperson for the homeland security department said ICE took the child into custody “out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety”.
The uncle, the spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian, was unable to prove legal guardianship – and that officials were obliged by federal anti-trafficking laws to take the boy into care as an “unaccompanied alien child”.
The Haitian Bridge Alliance said the boy was in the care of his uncle and cousins after his father was deported last year.
“I’m so grateful that he’s home, but this should have never happened in the first place,” Vargas said in a second social media post, adding that he would be asking the Trump administration for answers. While he was detained, the child was “held in a facility in Texas, far away from his home in San Diego”, Vargas said.
Celebrating the boy’s return, Jozef of the Haitian Bridge Alliance told NBC News: “The aunt was literally crying, and she said: ‘I have not eaten since the Wednesday they took my baby.’ They haven’t been able to sleep because of that.” She added: “The cousins were there when they took him, and wondering: will they ever see him again? But today [Monday] they are able to see him again. They are able to hug him.”

Glastonbury Festival has revealed its 2027 lineup, headlined by Harry Styles, Billie Eilish, Sam Fender and Cher.
This will be Styles’ and Fender’s first time headlining the Pyramid Stage, while it marks a return for Eilish, who last led the fest in 2022. Cher, who has also never played Glasto, is presumably taking the festival’s Sunday afternoon Legends slot.
After taking a fallow year this summer to allow Worthy Farm’s land to recover, the U.K. festival is set to return June 23-27. As always, the lineup spans genres and generations, including Massive Attack, Sombr, Little Simz, Chase & Status, the XX, Lily Allen, Ezra Collective, Kraftwerk, Adéla, Angine de Poitrine, the Avalanches, Blood Orange, Dinosaur Jr., Ellie Goulding, FKA Twigs, Kacey Musgraves, Kng Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard, Leon Bridges, Lola Young, Nia Archives, Primal Scream, Robyn, Sienna Spiro, Skye Newman, Thundercat, Underscores, the Streets, the War on Drugs and more.
Styles released his fourth album, “Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally,” in March and is currently on his “Together, Together” world tour, recently wrapping a 30-date residency at New York City’s Madison Square Garden. He’s headed to Australia later this month for shows in Melbourne and Sydney, before resuming the tour in April in Arizona. His Glastonbury headlining slot will come after a string of shows in Chicago and before Berlin, where he’ll begin another European leg.
Eilish’s third record, “Hit Me Hard and Soft,” released in 2024, with her Glastonbury headline slot leading to speculation that new music must be on the way. She wrapped that album’s tour last year and has been focusing on acting as of late, filming her acting debut in Sarah Polley’s adaptation of Sylvia Plath’s “The Bell Jar.”
Fender broke records this year as his duet with Olivia Dean, “Rein Me In,” became the longest-running U.K. No. 1 hit ever. The North Shields-born singer-songwriter released his third album, “People Watching,” last year and just announced a massive stadium tour for 2027, with new music also coming next year.
Iconic singer Cher will make her Glasto debut in the Legends slot, which has been played by Rod Stewart, Shania Twain and Yusuf/Cat Stevens in recent years. One of the bestselling artists of all time with hits like “Believe” and “I Got You Babe,” Glastonbury will mark the 80-year-old’s first major performance since her “Here We Go Again” tour, which concluded in 2020.

Retirement may bring a little more time for family, hobbies, and things you had put off during your working years. Healthcare, however, can become a bigger part of your monthly budget as you grow older. If you are arranging medical cover, senior citizen health insurance deserves careful consideration. Age, existing health conditions, hospital preferences, and affordability all matter when you assess the available options.Retirement may bring a little more time for family, hobbies, and things you had put off during your working years. Healthcare, however, can become a bigger part of your monthly budget as you grow older. If you are arranging medical cover, senior citizen health insurance deserves careful consideration. Age, existing health conditions, hospital preferences, and affordability all matter when you assess the available options.
Why Does Health Insurance Become More Important as You Age?
A routine health check-up, a consultation, or an unexpected hospital visit can add to your healthcare expenses. As you get older, you may also need more frequent medical attention.
A health insurance policy can help manage eligible medical expenses, depending on its terms and conditions. You can compare different health insurance plans based on your age, medical history, and budget. Some policies are specifically intended for older individuals.
What Should You Look for in Senior Citizen Health Insurance?What Should You Look for in Senior Citizen Health Insurance?
A policy that works for someone in their 40s may not meet the requirements of someone in their 60s or 70s. When comparing senior citizen health insurance, pay attention to the following features:
- Pre-existing disease waiting period: Check how long you must wait for conditions you already have before related expenses become eligible, subject to policy terms.
- Co-payment: Some policies require you to pay a percentage of eligible medical expenses. Check how much you would need to contribute.
- Room rent limits: Find out whether the policy has restrictions on hospital room categories and related expenses.
- Day-care procedures: Check which treatments that do not require a full 24-hour hospital stay are included.
- Pre- and post-hospitalisation expenses: Review the applicable coverage period and expense limits.
- Network hospitals: Check whether hospitals near your home are part of the insurer’s network.
Which Health Insurance Features Deserve Extra Attention After 60?
Beyond the usual policy benefits, a few details become particularly relevant when you are choosing cover for seniors.
| Feature | What You Should Check | 
| Sum insured | Whether the amount is appropriate for your healthcare requirements | 
| Medical check-ups | Whether routine preventive check-ups are included and subject to what limits | 
| Home healthcare | Whether eligible treatment at home forms part of the policy | 
| Ambulance expenses | The applicable limits and conditions | 
| Renewability | The conditions for continuing the policy in subsequent years | 
Not every policy includes these benefits in the same way. Some may offer them as additional benefits, while others may have specific conditions or limits. Read the policy wording to understand what applies.
How Can You Manage the Cost of Health Insurance After Retirement?
Once you retire, you may rely on savings, pensions, or other fixed sources of income. This makes the premium an important consideration when selecting medical cover.
Here are a few things worth checking:
- Compare premiums across different sum insured options.
- Check whether the policy has a deductible or co-payment requirement.
- Review how premiums may change at renewal.
- Look at the renewal conditions before purchasing a new policy.
A lower premium may come with a different set of limits or cost-sharing requirements. Compare these details rather than looking at the premium alone.
Conclusion
Your healthcare needs deserve attention at every stage of life, and retirement is a good time to review your medical cover. If you already have a policy, check whether its benefits and sum insured still match your requirements. If you are buying one for the first time, take time to compare the available options, understand the waiting periods, and review the costs you may have to bear. The goal should be to choose senior citizen health insurance cover that fits your healthcare needs and financial circumstances.

A video showing people vandalising and fighting inside a restaurant is going viral on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows an incident in West Bengal, where RSS workers allegedly created a ruckus and vandalised the restaurant when asked to pay for their food. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows RSS workers vandalising a restaurant in West Bengal after being asked to pay for their food.
Fact: The video shows an incident at Durbin Bangla Restaurant in Dhaka, Bangladesh, where a group of people vandalised the premises following a dispute over seating arrangements. The restaurant authorities alleged that students of Government Titumir College were involved in the attack. The incident has no connection to RSS workers or West Bengal. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple Bangladeshi media reports (here, here, and here) featuring the same video. According to these reports, the incident took place at Durbin Bangla Restaurant in Mohakhali, Dhaka, Bangladesh, on 13 November 2026. The incident reportedly began with an argument over seating arrangements between a customer and restaurant staff. According to the restaurant owner, a young man took a seat that a family was already waiting for. When a staff member intervened, the young man left but later returned with others and assaulted an employee named Khalil outside the restaurant. The group then vandalised the restaurant, damaging furniture and other items. The incident caused panic among customers and left several people injured. Police visited the spot and said they were examining CCTV footage to identify those involved and take legal action. The restaurant authorities alleged that students of Government Titumir College were involved, an allegation that police said they were investigating (here, here, and here).
The restaurant is located in the Mohakhali area of Dhaka, Bangladesh. Photos of the restaurant available on Google Maps match the visuals in the viral video, confirming that the incident took place in Bangladesh and not West Bengal.
To sum up, the video of a ruckus at a restaurant in Bangladesh is being shared as RSS workers’ hooliganism at a restaurant in West Bengal.

Mountains of scientific evidence support both the negative and positive effects of our eating habits on our health. Research shows that a healthy diet can help those suffering from chronic health conditions like Type 2 diabetes, heart disease and high blood pressure.
This is where “food is medicine” comes in. Food is medicine, also known as “food as medicine” and “food prescriptions,” is a movement dedicated to providing healthy food – fruits, vegetables and sometimes healthy proteins – based on a clinician’s prescription in order to prevent, manage or treat specific clinical conditions.
Prescribing food to patients is intended to convey that food is just as important as medication for health and wellness.
As researchers whose work focuses on food access and health in rural communities, we have firsthand experience running food is medicine programs in our local area in northern Mississippi. This experience has shown us the benefits and limitations of these programs in our community.
Fighting food insecurity
Food is medicine programs can be delivered through curated food boxes, grocery vouchers and medically tailored meals. Most programs are collaborations between nonprofit organizations, health clinics and healthcare providers. The goal of food is medicine is to improve patient health, especially for those with chronic conditions, while reducing healthcare costs.
Increasingly, food is medicine programs have become lifelines for people with food insecurity. In 2024, more than 47 million Americans, including 7.3 million children, lived in food-insecure households – meaning they were at some point uncertain of having, or did not have, enough food for everyone in the household.
Internationally, the number of people experiencing hunger rises to roughly 673 million. Rural populations are more likely to be food insecure due to the loss of local grocery stores and distance from urban centers. Unlike a food bank, food is medicine programs provide only healthy foods, which are often curated by a dietitian, to optimize patient health.
Forward momentum
Though food is medicine isn’t formally connected to the Make American Healthy Again movement, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. has brought new energy and attention to the concept. In January 2026, the second Trump administration launched a campaign encouraging Americans to “Eat Real Food.”
But the food is medicine movement actually began more than 60 years ago. One of the early providers who prescribed food as medicine was civil rights activist and multiple Nobel Peace Prize winner Dr. Jack Geiger. In the 1960s, he co-founded community health centers in South Boston and the Mississippi Delta.
When government officials chastised him for prescribing food to patients in the Delta, Geiger responded, “The last time I looked at my textbooks, the most specific therapy for malnutrition was food.”
Since then, thousands of community organizations like Community Servings and Project Open Hand have provided healthy food to vulnerable community members.
In 2023, the president of the American Heart Association convened an advisory group of researchers and physicians to review current food is medicine research and suggest next steps for work in this area. This advisory has suggested that these programs could help prevent or manage chronic conditions, saving the U.S. healthcare system an estimated US$4.3 trillion annually.
Food is medicine has also started to gain international momentum. In 2025, the Rockefeller Foundation supported a meeting of international scholars, policy experts and practitioners that established the Food Is Medicine Global Alliance. This organization plans to help integrate, sustainably finance and routinely deliver food is medicine programs worldwide by 2030. So far, it has released several reports highlighting the current food is medicine environment and made resources available to providers looking to start their own programs.
Food is medicine in our local community
Food is medicine programs can use food from local farms or grocery stores, and the means of getting the food to patients varies. The four projects we have run to date have been relatively small and local.
One was a food box pickup program that supplemented fruits and vegetables for 55 households whose members demonstrated food insecurity. We followed the participants for two years and found statistically significant reductions in weight, waist circumference and triglyceride levels in the primary adult participants.
For two of our other programs, including one that is ongoing, we partnered with local farmers. One was a pilot test of a food box delivery program for housebound people. Both the recipients of the food and the farmers reported high satisfaction with the program’s delivery and felt the program strengthened community connections while also supporting local agricultural livelihoods.
What other researchers have found
One recent large-scale literature review identified 14 trials of food is medicine interventions and found that these approaches often positively influenced diet quality and food security.
Another review of food is medicine programs for people with diabetes found significant increases in fruit and vegetable intake and reductions in blood sugar levels. This data supports our own previous findings.
However, the effect of food is medicine programs on long-term health outcomes has been inconsistent, in part because many trials have been too small or not rigorous enough to determine causation. In some cases, the “dose” – that is, the amount of food provided – is limited by grant funding. Our food box pickup project supplemented only four to five meals each week, which may have been insufficient to significantly improve all health outcomes.
Moreover, it will be important for researchers to consider the logistics of making these programs work in various local food environments. Global factors like changing weather patterns and, more recently, delays in fuel and supplies from the Strait of Hormuz have increased prices of staple food products like cereals and vegetable oil and led to shortages of cooking oil in some countries.
Food is medicine can be appealing because it makes intuitive sense. But going forward, larger, high-quality studies are needed to adequately track clinical outcomes from the various types of food is medicine programming. If studies show food is medicine is beneficial, it could lead to a shift in how healthcare practitioners approach diet for patients with chronic illness. Access to healthy food would be considered as essential as medications for patients with chronic illness.
Meagen Rosenthal, University of Mississippi and Natalie Minton, University of Mississippi

At 2:20 p.m. Eastern time Nov. 17, the Federal Emergency Management Agency and Federal Communications Commission plan to conduct a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System, which was announced in September.
According to some posts on social media, however, the test will be followed by a catastrophic 90-day electric and/or Internet blackout, plunging the world into darkness and chaos.
The claim may have felt unusually plausible, given several large failures in digital and physical infrastructure in the days leading up to the test — a Microsoft Outlook outage Nov. 12, a nationwide aircraft ground stop Nov. 13 due to a failure in telecommunication infrastructure, and software outages at several major banks on Nov. 16.
Add to that the curious claim that a 2023 episode of "The Simpsons," the long-running animated TV show somewhat notorious for predicting the future, featured a plot centered around a global blackout that began on Nov. 17. It all seemed to line up.
Snopes readers contacted us ahead of the Nov. 17 emergency alert test, asking for a review of these rumors.
We reached out to FEMA, the FCC and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency for comment on the rumor, asking about the agencies' involvement in the EAS test and the nation's protections against attacks on Internet and electric infrastructure. None of them replied to us by the time of publication.
As with all predictions of cataclysmic events, though, we urge readers to take this one with a grain of salt. There is no evidence indicating that a 90-day blackout will follow the nationwide EAS test, for any of the countless reasons posed online — be it a grand plan from the government, a targeted cybersecurity attack or just because "The Simpsons" said so.
Because Snopes requires substantial evidence to rate a story, however, and we can neither predict nor travel into the future, we're leaving this claim unrated until Nov. 17 has come and gone.
The EAS test
FEMA, in coordination with the FCC, is required by law to conduct a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System at least once every three years, according to its website. The last nationwide test of the EAS, familiar to many Americans as the loud, warbling "beep beep beep" that comes on TV or radio before a severe weather warning or an Amber Alert, occurred Oct. 4, 2023.
In the 2023 test, FEMA and the FCC also sent test emergency alerts to cellphones. However, FEMA's webpage says it will not be testing cellphone alerts this time around. The agency also noted that it may reschedule the test if an actual emergency or severe weather happens Nov. 17. The backup test would be conducted Dec. 3.
No information about the test suggests that any sort of digital blackout will follow, for any reason. If the supposed blackout is supposed to be an act of sabotage by a foreign adversary, why would they have announced the attack beforehand? If the supposed blackout was planned by the United States government, meanwhile, why would it have neglected to warn everyone beforehand through official channels?
The 'Simpsons' episode
As for "The Simpsons" — Snopes has covered many claims implying that the sitcom predicted this or that future event.
The show's oracular reputation grew out of the few times where an absurd plot device ended up being a spot-on prediction, as perhaps most famously happened in a 2000 episode in which Lisa Simpson becomes president and inherits a budget crisis from Donald Trump. (Notably, Trump briefly considered running as the Reform Party's nominee in that year's presidential election.)
We chalk it up to the show's longevity — more than 850 episodes over 38 seasons — above anything else. "The Simpsons" routinely satirizes current real-world events, so given enough opportunities, it's unsurprising the writers occasionally come off as having the gift of prophecy.
In this case, the episode, titled "It's a Blunderful Life," was real, and did feature a plot based around a blackout starting on Nov. 17. Beyond that, the episode's plot bore no resemblance to the claim at hand.
The episode aired Nov. 19, 2023, as the sitcom's Thanksgiving special. It begins decades into the future, as the Simpson family sits down to eat Thanksgiving dinner and Lisa tells everyone to light a candle in remembrance. When asked why by her grandchild, Lisa recounts that a "great blackout" nearly destroyed Springfield. She opens a diary labeled "Apocalyptic Memories" to Nov. 17 (no year is given), and begins explaining as the camera cuts to a shot of the Simpson home "six days before Thanksgiving."
But, there's a problem for the fantasists here — Thanksgiving isn't on the same day each year. In 2023, when the episode aired, Thanksgiving fell on Nov. 23, conveniently, six days after Nov. 17. In 2026, however, Thanksgiving is on Nov. 26, meaning that if the year in the episode truly was 2026, Lisa should have opened the diary to Nov. 20 (i.e., six days before). Sorry to spoil anyone's doomsday prepping.
For more reading, we also previously explained a recent surge in government messaging around emergency preparedness, and a Department of Defense initiative that aims to keep military bases operational for at least 90 days without relying on civilian infrastructure.

The World Health Organisation warned on Friday (November 13, 2026) of surging respiratory illnesses in Gaza, with worse expected after heavy rains flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced Palestinians.
“The numbers already show the pressure. Acute respiratory infections are 33,000 cases higher than at the same time last year,” Dr. Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO representative in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, told reporters in Geneva from Jerusalem.
Poor living conditions and severe overcrowding are driving up infections as Gaza’s population is squeezed into an ever-smaller area, WHO said. The crunch has worsened as the Israeli military expands its control by advancing the “Yellow Line” — a demarcation established under October’s U.S.-brokered ceasefire.
“That means people are living in more crowded conditions, where of course the spread between humans of a virus is much more prone to spread,” Ms. Van De Weerdt explained.
The Israeli military told Reuters the Yellow Line aims to protect Israeli civilians and army troops from threats and that adjustments to its location follow the ceasefire agreement and international law, and are not intended to harm the civilian population.
“The IDF categorically rejects the claim that it operates to deliberately reduce the area available to the civilian population in the Gaza Strip.”
COGAT, the Israeli military agency that coordinates aid, said that more than 93,000 tents and over 8,600 trucks carrying tarpaulin sheets, blankets and winter clothing have entered Gaza since the Board of Peace, UN agencies and NGOs launched the winterisation plan. Equipment intended for the reconstruction of Gaza will be permitted to enter only after Hamas has been fully disarmed, it added.
Last week COGAT said that it had stepped up efforts to improve sanitary conditions before the heavy rain, in coordination with international organisations.
Respiratory infections currently make up 11% of all consultations, with the WHO expecting cold weather, flooding, overcrowded shelters and poor ventilation to push these numbers higher.
“It is shocking that just a few days of rain really showed us what the coming months will bring. And winter has not even fully set in. The worst really is yet to come,” Ms. Van De Weerdt said.
Nearly a million displaced people in Gaza live in flood-exposed areas, and 400,000 of them are in locations that are considered at extremely high risk, according to the WHO.
The agency said flooding heightened the risk of contaminated water, while standing water gave mosquitoes and pests more places to breed. Dampness encouraged mould and bacteria that are major drivers of respiratory infections, especially in young children, it said.
While the majority of medicines are getting into Gaza, the WHO faces difficulty getting laboratory supplies, which it says are vital for diagnosing patients before they can be treated.
“To prevent outbreaks, we really call to let laboratory equipment enter Gaza today, so that we can avoid a public health disaster on top of a disaster.“
COGAT said Israel has facilitated the entry of all medicines requested by international aid organisations and has not rejected any requests received, adding that X-ray machines, oxygen generators, batteries, generators, and other equipment have entered Gaza.

Egg brand Henfruit has raised $15 Mn (about ₹140 Cr) in a Series A round from Lok Capital, DSG Consumer Partners, and RPSG Capital Ventures. The round marks the company’s first external fundraise since Tarun Gupta founded it in 2014. Henfruit said it will use the capital to widen its online and offline distribution across India, expand production capacity, and scale its supply chain. The company says it processes over 4 Cr eggs a month, serves customers in 15 cities, and employs more than 300 people. It expects revenue to exceed ₹350 Cr in FY27. The brand sells through its website and platforms including Zepto, Swiggy Instamart, Blinkit, and Milkbasket. Its products are also available on BigBasket, Amazon India, and Flipkart. Henfruit uses traceability and testing to distinguish its products in India’s largely unorganised egg market. The company says it conducts daily quality tests through its own lab and independent third-party labs, and publishes the results on its website. The fundraise comes amid growing consumer interest in branded and quality-assured food products, with food safety and transparency gaining importance in the FMCG sector. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has also stepped up scrutiny of food brands over misleading advertisements, unsubstantiated product claims and labelling violations, issuing more than 150 notices to food companies in recent months. The increased regulatory focus has put greater emphasis on quality checks, traceability and transparency across the food value chain. Meanwhile, investor interest in India's consumer brands has also picked up, with startups in the food and snacking segments raising capital to expand manufacturing capabilities and strengthen distribution. Last month, healthy snacking startup Troovy raised ₹100 Cr ($10.5 Mn) in a Series B round led by Fireside Ventures to expand manufacturing capacity, invest in R&D and strengthen its quick commerce and offline distribution. Before that, D2C nutrition and dietary supplements startup Ace Blend raised $9.9 Mn to fund clinical trials, strengthen its supply chain, invest in R&D and develop new nutrition formats. Last year, Henfruit’s rival Eggoz raised $20 Mn in a Series C round led by Gaja Capital.

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week following media reports of two extramarital relationships, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who was also allegedly suspected of being a Chinese spy, and his public acknowledgement of being unfaithful to his wife. While the developments have drawn attention to the personal life of one of the world's richest executives, they have also brought the spotlight on the often staggering financial consequences of high-profile divorces. Following Huang's acknowledgement, reports have focused on how much his wife, Lori Mills, could receive if she decides to divorce the former Nvidia CEO, who currently ranks 16th on the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, with an estimated net worth of $130 billion. From Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' reported $38.3 billion settlement with MacKenzie Scott to media mogul Rupert Murdoch's estimated $1.7 billion divorce settlement with Anna Murdoch, several billionaire breakups have made headlines because of the fortunes involved. Here is a look at some of the world's most expensive divorces. In May 2021, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates and Melinda French Gates announced their separation after nearly 27 years of marriage. While the exact terms of their divorce settlement remain undisclosed, NDTV Profit reported that Melinda received more than $2 billion in shares. In 2024, Melinda announced that she would be leaving the Gates Foundation following an agreement that included $12.5 billion for her philanthropic work. Although this amount was not part of a publicly confirmed divorce settlement, reports have put the combined value of the financial arrangements at more than $14.5 billion. The couple said they had reached an agreement on dividing their marital assets. According to the divorce filing, Melinda did not seek spousal support. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos divorced MacKenzie Scott in July 2019 after 25 years of marriage. As part of the settlement, Scott received about 4% of Amazon's total outstanding shares, amounting to 19.7 million shares valued at approximately $38.3 billion at the time. Bezos retained a 12% stake in the company and control over the voting rights attached to the shares transferred to Scott. Scott later committed to donating at least half of her wealth to charitable causes through the Giving Pledge. Their divorce settlement was significant because it involved the transfer of a substantial stake in one of the world's largest companies, rather than being limited to a cash payment. French-American billionaire art dealer Alec Wildenstein married Jocelyn in 1978. The couple divorced in 1999 after 21 years of marriage. Jocelyn reportedly received an initial settlement of $2.5 billion, followed by annual payments of $100 million for 13 years. The combined reported settlement reached approximately $3.8 billion. Alec Wildenstein died in 2008. His divorce from Jocelyn attracted widespread attention because of the enormous fortune involved and the high-profile nature of the proceedings. Media mogul Rupert Murdoch divorced his journalist wife, Anna Murdoch, in 1999 after nearly three decades of marriage. The couple had three children together. Their settlement was widely reported to be worth $1.7 billion, with much of the amount reportedly associated with News Corporation shares. Although the exact financial terms were never publicly disclosed, the reported figure has frequently been questioned. The settlement was also structured to protect the media tycoon's control over his business empire. Billionaire investor Bill Gross, co-founder of Pacific Investment Management Company (PIMCO), one of the world's largest investment management firms at the time, married Sue Gross in 1985. The couple, who had a son together, were also known for their philanthropic activities through the William and Sue Gross Family Foundation. They separated in 2016, after more than three decades of marriage, when Sue filed for divorce in November that year. She reportedly received assets worth $1.3 billion. These included a $36 million property in Laguna Beach and half of the couple's art collection. From billion-dollar settlements involving company shares and investment assets to large financial awards made by courts, these divorces demonstrate how the end of high-profile marriages can have significant financial consequences. While the exact terms of several settlements remain private, the reported figures underline the scale of wealth at stake when some of the world's richest couples separate. Taking Korea's toughest exam from behind bars
- Published
Students intently focus on maths formulas written on a board before lowering their heads and taking notes as the teacher works through a sum.
The teacher's voice and the scratch of pens fill the room.
At first glance, this could be any classroom in South Korea.
But thick metal bars cover the windows and the students are wearing blue prison uniforms and rubber shoes emblazoned with the words "Korea Correctional Service".
This is Mandela Boys' School, an education facility for young prisoners inside the Seoul Southern Correctional Institution in Guro, south-west Seoul. In South Korea, young people who are sentenced to imprisonment by a criminal court must serve their time in prison.
"The boys here have committed serious offences and received criminal sentences," Jeong Yeo-gyeong, a correctional officer in the Korea Correctional Service's social reintegration division, told the BBC.
"As well as theft, there is a high proportion of serious offences, including violence, bodily injury, sexual violence and robbery."
But by opening educational institutes like Mandela, authorities are hoping to give these young offenders a chance to better their lives after they serve out their sentences.
Opened by the justice ministry in March 2023, it allows boys who were aged 17 and under when their sentences became final to prepare for school equivalency exams as well as the Suneung - the country's notoriously difficult university entrance examination - while still serving their sentences.
Held every November, the Suneung is an infamous eight-hour marathon of back-to-back exams.
Students attempt about 200 questions across various subjects, which include Korean, maths, English, social and natural sciences, among others.
The country itself comes to a standstill - construction work halts, planes are grounded and military training gets suspended to facilitate an optimal testing environment.
A total of 551,864 people have applied to take this year's Suneung on 19 November.
Around 30 prisoners are enrolled in the Suneung preparation class at Mandela Boys' School, and 11 of them have applied to take this year's exam.
Park Soo-young (not his real name), a 17-year-old inmate, has been at the Mandela Boys' Suneung preparation class for two months and hopes to study social welfare.
He tells the BBC that he had dreams of becoming a police officer before committing the crime that landed him behind bars.
He says he could not bring himself to look properly at his mother during his trial. When he turned towards her after his sentence was announced, she was crying.
"Seeing her like that, I broke down too. I wondered how I was going to live from then on, and how I could look after my mother, who was on her own. I think I kept crying for about a week while I was in the detention centre."
Looking back on his offence, he says he feels "very ashamed that I couldn't control that impulse". If he could meet his younger self, he would tell him: "Control that impulse. If you do, everything will be different."
"I'd grab myself by the collar and shake myself as I said it."
He hopes the Suneung and university will offer him a chance to start again.
"Once I'm out, I need to cut ties with the friends and people I used to know and start a new life. I think university is the only way to do that. Going to university would let me leave the area where I used to live, move somewhere else and start something new. That's why I began studying again."
But he describes beginning Suneung preparation as "a struggle every day".
"But the teachers don't let anything slip past. They keep helping us until we understand. If I don't understand something, I put my hand up and they come over and explain it.
Sometimes, if I've missed something, I keep working at it on my own. If I still can't get it, I ask the students next to me to explain," he said.
Park's day begins at 06:30 with a morning check by prison officers. He starts memorising English vocabulary and working through Korean reading passages early in the morning.
"I learn English words whenever I can, even before breakfast. From 07:00, I work through a Korean passage, something like literature or speech. We have to come down to the classroom at 08:00, so we have another check and then come down for lessons."
During breaks, students make calls to their families or leave the classroom for scheduled visits. In the evening, they return for supervised study. Once the day's activities are over, they must go back to their cells together.
Park says he studies until 22:00 before finishing for the day. If he wants to study longer hours, he needs permission from a prison officer.
But even if gets a good result this year, Park will not be allowed to leave prison and attend university straight away. He is only due to be released in 2028, but plans to use this exam as experience and continue studying next year.
"This time, I want to experience how the Suneung works and how competitive it is. Then, next year, I'll work hard from the start so I can get in the year after that."
Some former students from Mandela Boys' School have managed to get into university, according to the justice ministry.
Others have continued their studies after leaving prison, including by enrolling in residential exam preparation academies.
The inmates are taught by a team of seven prison officers, all of whom hold teaching certificates. Each is responsible for a subject.
Visiting instructors provide classes in the humanities, arts and sport, while university student volunteers help with learning. Professional psychological counselling is also available.
Park Min-yong, who applied to work here in 2023, teaches science. And alongside Suneung lessons, he works with the students' to change their habits and behaviour.
One thing he often tells them is that they need to "learn how to become adults".
He believes that while studying in itself does not necessarily turn inmates away from a life of crime, the experience of having worked hard at something: staying with a concept that makes little sense, revisiting a wrong answer and continuing even when grades do not improve straight away, is valuable in itself.
"Studying properly means pushing yourself to your limits, and that takes considerable stamina and patience," he says.
"Whether they chose to do it or not, the experience of persevering, enduring and not giving up easily may help them to some extent when they face the difficulties of life after release."
He says the material they encounter while preparing for the Suneung also gives them new things to think about.
Korean reading passages cover literature, society, science and philosophy. Students have to consider a character's perspective, examine the evidence behind an argument and understand unfamiliar concepts. They also encounter explanations that differ from their own and have to reconsider what they think.
"They gradually learn that it's not just about their own personal view - that these concepts and relationships have been developed through a shared understanding among many people," Park said.
There are difficult moments too.
Park says students sometimes cheat in classroom tests even while he is watching.
"They cheat as if it's nothing. They give each other answers, even when I'm watching them. Some repeat it after being told off. There may be an element of doing it deliberately, but often they haven't thought it through. They don't think about the impact their actions or words could have on others."
The boys also have a strong desire for recognition, he says.
"It's all the time. 'Look how much I've done. Look how much my grades have improved. I've done this much - haven't I done well?' They're always like that. They're hungry for it."
Not everyone agrees with this initiative though.
One criticism is that young people who have not committed crimes also face fierce competition for university places: so there is some anger that the state provides offenders with separate education and opportunities to prepare for this exam.
Father Jeong Min-ha, of the Archdiocese of Seoul's correctional ministry committee, worked with Seoul Southern Correctional Institution from September 2023 until last year.
He acknowledges these criticisms.
"Studying gives them a sense of achievement and time to look seriously at their own lives. That's why I think it matters. I think that is the most important part of rehabilitation."
Of course, there is no guarantee.
Park recalls a student who had done well at the school but later returned to prison.
"He was doing well when he left, but in the end he came back. So something went wrong. I'd hoped he would carry on with what he'd been doing here, but he couldn't. That's disappointing."
According to the justice ministry's 2026 corrections statistical yearbook, 35.5% of prisoners aged under 20 who were released in 2021 were imprisoned again within three years. That was about 1.7 times the overall rate of 21.2%, and the highest of any age group.
But Park hopes the students will continue learning after they leave prison. "We don't know what the outcome will be," he says.
"They say the way to clear a glass of dirty water is to keep pouring clean water into it, rather than trying to remove each bit of dirt. I hope they fill their minds with good things, learn to use their energy and intellect in the right way, and put that learning into practice at the right time and place."
Additional reporting by Hosu Lee.

Japan ranked 86th in the world in the 2026 edition of the largest global ranking of adult English proficiency, showing signs of a turnaround after years of decline.
The ranking, released Wednesday by Education First (EF), an international education organization, showed that Japan rose 10 places from the previous year, when it ranked 96th among 123 countries. The 2025 index marked an all-time low, extending a downward trend in Japan’s English proficiency, which fell continuously in recent years.
This year’s data was compiled from the test results of 2.3 million participants across 117 countries and regions.
In the 2026 index, Japan also moved from the lowest proficiency band “very low,” to the “low” band.
Despite the improvement in this year’s index, Japan continued to lag behind its peers in Asia and elsewhere in the world in English proficiency.
Compared to South Korea, for example, which reached 50th place in the index, Japan was significantly lower — ranking 36 places below its neighbor.
European countries dominated the top of this year’s rankings, with Sweden claiming the top spot followed by Austria and Denmark.
Japan also scored below the overall average in EF’s assessment, receiving 450 points — 35 points below the 485-point average.
In terms of specific areas of proficiency, Japanese learners performed better in reading than in speaking and writing.
EF also found regional differences in English proficiency, with learners in urban hubs such as Yokohama, Tokyo and Kyoto performing better than those in Hiroshima, Shizuoka and Kochi.
As in many other countries covered by the index, younger people in Japan showed particularly low levels of English language ability — with 18- to 20-year-olds recording the lowest scores of all age groups.
EF suggested that the decline in English proficiency among younger people, observed worldwide, was partly attributable to the COVID-19 pandemic.
The organization suggested that there is still a knock-on effect on this cohort who had to take online rather than in-person English classes between 2019 and 2022, which is being seen in Japan and across the world.
Masato Suzuki, business development manager for EF Japan, said “Raising the English proficiency of this (young) generation will create a bottom-up effect that elevates proficiency levels when they enter the workforce.”
In recommending ways to improve Japanese people’s English proficiency, Nana Gronning Ito, EF country manager, advised not relying solely on digital learning and instead communicating in real life.
“We believe the next step is very clear: it is to build on the foundation there already. We want people to experience the joy of expressing their feelings — even if they make mistakes along the way,” she said.

Hundreds of people have been arrested in heated demonstrations against Donald Trump in Manila, as authorities braced for more protests ahead of the US president’s arrival in the city for a leaders’ summit.
Organisers claim as many as 10,000 people will join protests against Trump in the Philippine capital on Tuesday, when he will attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit. The crowds are expected to try to walk to the summit site.
Authorities have arrested nearly 300 people in widespread protests in held in the days leading up to the summit, with large parts of the capital closed off and tight security in place.
Some burned effigies of Trump and faced off with police officers armed with batons and shields. Slogans on placards called the American leader the world’s “number one terrorist” in protests held on Monday.
Demonstrators angry at the cost-of-living and energy shock caused by the Iran war, and the new US-led Pax Silica initiative on AI and critical minerals, tried to reach the summit at the Philippine International Convention Center on Monday, but were blocked by police.
Pax Silica has sparked tensions in the Philippines over plans to build a tech hub outside Manila that critics say will affect water and energy supplies, and displace members of the Ayta Indigenous community.
Large sections of central Manila were closed to the public as part of the security cordon, and public holidays instituted for the Asean summit.
Trump will meet with the leaders of Australia, Japan and India on Tuesday night before heading to Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday. There he will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and hold trilateral talks with China’s president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.
The backlash against Trump follows the ouster of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, and allegations members of the US administration, including the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, knew about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump’s delegation was expected to include businessman Elon Musk.
Protest leader Renato Reyes blamed the arrests in Manila on the heavy handed response of the government on the president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr., calling Monday the largest single day of police arrests since Marcos came to office in 2022.
“It is really crazy that the Philippine government is rolling out the red carpet for someone who has been so flatly rejected by the American people,” Reyes said.
“Trump started a war that devastated the global economy and pushed oil prices in the Philippines to historic highs. It has caused untold suffering on the Filipino people.
“So yes, Trump will have to pay for his crimes and he will have to be answerable, not just to the American people, but to the people of the world.”
The Philippine national police said some officers were injured during confrontations with demonstrators opposed to the summit, including when objects were allegedly thrown at officers.
Pax Silica will include a technology hub planned at New Clark City in Tarlac, about 120km from Manila.
Intended to bolster western stocks of AI technology and reduce “excessive dependencies” on single source supply chains, including from China, Pax Silica will provide chips and critical minerals to 25 participating signatory governments.
Amnesty Philippines said demonstrations should not be forcibly or violently dispersed.
“Reports of arrests during the protests demand immediate scrutiny,” director Ritz Lee Santos III said.
“Authorities must explain the specific grounds for each arrest and any continued detention. Anyone detained solely for peacefully exercising their rights must be released immediately.”

YouTube will start boosting public view counts when you watch on a TV
It will estimate co-views based on a ‘privacy-safe statistical model.’
YouTube view counts are about to go up (again) thanks to a new metric. Google's video streaming platform may count more than one person when videos are viewed on a TV, according to an X post from YouTube Creator Insider. These extra "co-views" will apply to long form, Shorts, and Live videos, for TV views only.
YouTube thinks that is has been undercounting viewers in group-watching situations, thus not giving creators a true picture of a video's reach. The goal with the new metric, the platform wrote, is to "[align] with TV industry standards — including how traditional broadcast and streaming networks estimate the total number of people exposed to content."
How, you might wonder, will YouTube know who else is watching besides the account-holder? The platform emphasized that it won't use "devices, cameras, microphones or anything like that." Rather, views will be estimated using a "privacy-safe statistical mode" based on things like demographic patterns and viewing times, calibrated against real-life testing data. YouTube didn't share any other methodology details.
The new system will show higher public view counts and watch times for videos, giving creators more data to guide their channel strategy, brand pitches and more (the co-view parameter won't be retroactively applied). What it won't get them is more ad money. "Co-views don't impact ad revenue or YPP thresholds," YouTube Creator Insider wrote. "Creator earnings, AdSense payouts and YouTube Partner Program eligibility remain based on Qualified Views and Watch Hours."

The government has introduced a one-time settlement scheme offering 30 to 75% relief in environmental compensation imposed on industries, infrastructure projects, mining units and other groundwater users for extracting the resource without mandatory permissions, delayed renewal of permits or extracting it beyond the permitted limit.
The Ground Water Charges (Dispute Resolution) Scheme, 2026, notified by the Ministry of Jal Shakti on November 12, aims to encourage project proponents to regularise groundwater extraction, bring more users into the regulatory framework and facilitate settlement of disputes and pending litigation over environmental compensation.
The scheme will remain in force for one year from the date of its publication in the official gazette and will cover projects in 19 States and Union Territories where groundwater regulation is being carried out by the Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA).
According to the notification, the scheme has been conceived as a “voluntary, one-time strategic resolution and settlement mechanism” with the primary objective of achieving wider regulatory compliance.
The notification said substantial environmental compensation liabilities had discouraged several project proponents from voluntarily entering the regulatory framework, while a significant number of cases remained entangled in prolonged representations and litigation, delaying recovery of compensation.
The scheme provides relief in three categories of violations — existing projects extracting groundwater without a valid No Objection Certificate (NOC), projects applying late for renewal of NOCs and projects extracting groundwater beyond the quantity permitted under their NOCs.
The maximum relief of 75% will be available to projects that have extracted groundwater in excess of the permitted quantity, while those applying late for renewal of NOCs can get relief ranging from 40 to 70%. Projects operating without NOCs will be eligible for 30 to 60% relief.
The extent of relief will depend on the groundwater assessment category of the area and the quantity of groundwater extracted by a project.
The notification classifies assessment units into five categories — safe, semi-critical, critical, over-exploited and saline — and prescribes different rates of concessions based on groundwater consumption slabs of less than 200 kilolitres per day (KLD), 200 to less than 1,000 KLD, 1,000 to less than 5,000 KLD and 5,000 KLD or above.
For existing projects operating without NOCs, the relief will range from 60% in safe and saline assessment units to 30% in over-exploited areas for projects extracting 5,000 KLD or more.
In the case of delayed NOC renewals, the relief will range from 70% in safe and saline areas to 40% in over-exploited areas for projects extracting 5,000 KLD or more.
For projects extracting groundwater beyond the permitted quantity, the relief will range from 75% to 45%, depending on the assessment category and consumption level.
The scheme will cover both fresh and renewal applications. Projects whose applications were rejected earlier for any reason and those pending with the CGWA, where environmental compensation is applicable, will also be eligible. It will extend to all types of projects, including infrastructure, industrial, mining and others, across all five groundwater assessment categories, subject to fulfilment of the basic eligibility criteria under the existing guidelines.
Project proponents will have to register on the BhuNeer app portal to avail the benefits. The payable amount will be communicated through the portal and the registered email address of the applicant, and the entire amount will have to be deposited in a single transaction.
Applicants will have 60 days from the communication of the charges to make the payment. Failure to deposit the amount within the prescribed period will render them ineligible for the relief, and no representation will be entertained in this regard.
Project proponents with pending cases before courts, tribunals or other competent authorities will have to furnish an irrevocable undertaking on non-judicial stamp paper agreeing to withdraw or get the proceedings disposed of in accordance with law after acceptance of the settlement.
A provisional settlement order will be issued after receipt of payment, while a final settlement order will follow only after satisfactory documentary proof of withdrawal or disposal of the pending proceedings is furnished within the prescribed period.
The benefits, however, will not be available in cases where environmental compensation has already been finally adjudicated by a court or tribunal.
This includes compensation imposed by the National Green Tribunal in matters presently under challenge before the Supreme Court.
The notification makes it clear that the scheme is a “last and final opportunity” for project proponents to regularise groundwater abstraction and avail relief in environmental compensation.
It also clarifies that the scheme neither condones past violations nor creates any vested right to similar relief in future. After its expiry, environmental compensation will be applicable under the existing guidelines without any relaxation or rebate.
Any subsequent non-compliance by projects after availing the benefits will attract strict enforcement action, including full environmental compensation, applicable penalties and sealing of borewells.
The CGWA will constitute a Scheme Implementation Committee under the chairmanship of its Member Secretary to oversee implementation, maintain the portal and act as an appellate forum for grievance redressal.
The scheme seeks to balance the government’s Ease of Doing Business initiative with the mandate of sustainable development of groundwater and inter-generational equity, the notification said.

What the U.S. might learn from Canada's privatized air traffic control
Grounding of U.S. flights days ago has sparked calls to follow Canada's lead
It's not often that commentators from the U.S. political right will look to Canada as a model for how their country should run a particular function.
Yet the grounding of thousands of flights due to a router issue days ago has sparked some renewed calls for the U.S. to privatize its air traffic control system, much like its neighbour to the north did 30 years ago.
A recent editorial in the conservative magazine National Review called on the U.S. to privatize air traffic control and heaped praise on Canada's approach for its lead in technological advancement and the speed at which its able to upgrade its system.
And Canadian aviation experts agree that the American air traffic control system, sorely in need of upgrading, could certainly learn from Canada's own privatized structure.
"We can feel very smug and superior. We've been doing it right for 30 years, and the Americans have finally recognized that. At least some of them," said Anthony Perl, a political science professor and transportation policy specialist at Simon Fraser University.
Nav Canada takes off
Back in the '80s and early '90s, Canada's government-run air traffic control system was outdated, and in need of millions of dollars of investment to update its infrastructure, says John Gradek, a faculty lecturer in supply networks and aviation management at McGill University.
Facing a potentially enormous bill, the government decided to transition its air traffic services to a privatized model, he said.
Nav Canada, a non-profit company, began managing air traffic in 1996. It was a move, according to the Nav Canada website, that made Canada the first country in the world to privatize its civil air navigation system.
That means, instead of being controlled by the government and collecting money through taxes that have to go through Parliament and different ministries, Nav Canada charts its own course. For revenue, it charges user fees, sending bills to airlines using their services.
"It's kind of like your cell phone, if you don't have an unlimited plan, they send bills out based on the volume of use, and the rates are correlated to what it actually costs to run the system, to deliver those services," Perl said.
Perl pointed out that regulation is an essential ingredient in this formula. He said Transport Canada is still a key player in making sure Nav Canada doesn't cut corners "because you have to have strong regulation."
Nav Canada uses business modelling to forecast the costs of what it takes to actually run the system and keep it in a state of good repair, he said.
'Control their own destiny'
Gradek added that this also means that at any point in time Nav Canada knows the state of its finances, its operating expenses and where they are in terms of funding for programs.
"So they control their own destiny in terms of 'We're not going to overspend. We're going to spend money where we think we get the biggest bang for the buck.'"
As an example of Nav Canada's quick ability to modernize, Gradek points to paper-based flight data strips that it replaced with electronic strips that are accessible through touchscreens. Nav Canada made this upgrade in 1998, two years after it began running air traffic control.
Meanwhile, the U.S. has yet to replace that system.
The reason for this is simple, says Gradek.
"Money, money, money, money," he said.
Funding for the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration, the agency overseeing air traffic, is "a political football," he said.
Getting operating funds from U.S. Congress for capital expenditures to improve the system and get projects running quickly and efficiently is a challenge, Gradek said.
In Canada, it's up to Nav Canada to determine the priorities for investment to improve the productivity and efficiency of the system, he said.
Travellers pay
Still, the user-fee structure of Canada's air traffic control system means Canadians are seemingly paying more for flights since the costs of air traffic control in the U.S. are covered by the government.
But Perl said that just means Canadians are actually paying for the costs of the infrastructure instead of underfunding it.
Travellers wait at LaGuardia Airport in New York on Friday after the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide. (Ryan Murphy/The Associated Press)
Aidan Hollis, an economics professor and academic director of the research program in competition and regulation at the University of Calgary, said air traffic control is funded either by taxes or the flying traveller.
"It makes sense to pay for it on the basis of users, rather than someone who's never flown in their life having to pay taxes to support a system, which they don't use."
In 2017, during Donald Trump's first term, the U.S. president urged Congress to approve a privatization plan that he said would increase safety and reduce wait times for passengers.
That plan, however, got stalled. Some U.S. politicians and organizations have expressed doubts about the efficiency of a privatized air traffic control system.
The non-partisan Congressional Research Service issued a report in 2017 that concluded there does not appear to be "conclusive evidence" that a privatized model "is either superior or inferior to others ... including FAA, with respect to productivity, cost-effectiveness, service quality, and safety and security."
Meanwhile, the U.S.-based National Business Aviation Association (NBAA) says privatization in Canada has resulted in funding instability, technological disruptions, flight delays and safety concerns. It cited a 2023 International Civil Aviation Organization report giving Canada a C grade score on oversight and safety.
In an email to CBC News, Maryam Amini, a spokeswoman for Nav Canada, said those claims being made about Canada's system are not supported by facts.
She said the ICAO audit being cited was not an audit of Nav Canada but instead assessed Canada's safety oversight system, which is the responsibility of Transport Canada.
"Canada's air navigation system is among the safest in the world," she said.

Salah scores twice as Egypt and Nigeria win Afcon 2027 qualifiers
- Published
Tolu Arokodare was the hero as Nigeria boosted their hopes of reaching the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) with a 3-1 home win over tournament co-hosts Tanzania.
With the East Africans already assured of a spot at the finals, the Super Eagles are battling for the one qualification spot available in Group L and have little margin for error after losing 3-0 in Guinea-Bissau in September.
Alhassan Yusuf kept his composure to slot Nigeria into a second-minute lead in Uyo from Ademola Lookman's pass, but the visitors equalised through Alphonce Msanga just after the half-hour mark.
Arokodare climbed off the bench at half-time and cleverly flicked home Wilfred Ndidi's low ball to restore the lead for the West Africans in the 52nd minute.
And the Ajax striker, who is on a season-long loan from Wolves, gave the Super Eagles breathing space eight minutes later when he controlled Moses Usor's cross from the left and smashed in from 12 yards out.
With three games played in the group, Eric Chelle's side are now one point behind leaders Guinea-Bissau, who drew 1-1 with Madagascar on Thursday.
