Elsewhere, Mohamed Salah scored twice late on against Malawi as Egypt cruised to a 5-0 victory in Ali Maher's first match in charge.
Achraf Hakimi netted two stunning goals and Yassine Bounou saved a penalty to help Morocco continue their unbeaten start with a 5-1 win over Niger.
Meanwhile, Tunisia are in danger of missing out on the finals for the first time since 1992 after suffering a 2-0 defeat at home against Libya, and Kenya scored a last-minute equaliser to end South Africa's perfect start.
The third round of qualifying culminates with three games on Saturday, while the fourth round of fixtures are split across Monday and Tuesday.
Salah and Hakimi shine
Egypt reached the semi-finals of Afcon 2025 and the last 16 of this year's Fifa World Cup under Hossam Hassan but parted company with the 60-year-old earlier this month.
The Pharaohs had taken four points from their opening two games in Group B, with Salah substituted after an hour in their 0-0 draw with Angola before missing the win in South Sudan.
The former Liverpool forward returned as captain against Malawi, and Egypt cruised into a 3-0 lead at the break through goals from Nasser Maher, Omar Marmoush and Mohamed Hany.
Salah got on the scoresheet when he stooped to head in a cross from the left and rounded off proceedings by dinking in a penalty after Hamza Abdelkarim was tripped in the box.
Victory in Maher's first game at the helm puts Egypt three points clear of Angola, who take on South Sudan on Saturday.
In Group A, Morocco had also looked like they would ease to three points against Niger in Casablanca after Yassir Zabiri's early effort and a brilliant long-range strike from right-back Hakimi put them 2-0 up after 27 minutes.
But Mohamed Abdourahmane headed in to halve the deficit and Niger had a chance to level from the spot on the stroke of half-time after a handball by Noussair Mazraoui.
However, Atlas Lions goalkeeper Bounou moved to his left to keep out Youssouf Oumarou's penalty, and Hakimi made it 3-1 in first-half stoppage time with a dipping free-kick from distance.
Youssef En-Nesyri steered in the fourth in the 77th minute from a Hakimi pass and Ayoub Oufkir completed the scoring from close range in the final minute.
Earlier in Group A on Friday Gabon beat Lesotho to move on to six points thanks to two second-half goals from Denis Bouanga.
The LA FC forward smashed the right-hand upright with a penalty but broke the deadlock with a header a minute later and then scored from 12 yards when the Panthers were awarded a second spot kick.
Tunisia downed as McCarthy frustrates Bafana
Tunisia have appeared at a record 17 consecutive Afcons but are winless and bottom of Group H - another section with just one qualifying place on offer - after defeat by their North African neighbours Libya.
The Carthage Eagles could complain about refereeing decisions going against them in Sfax, with Ali Maaloul penalised for a shirt pull on Muad Eisay just before half-time and Ali Youssef converting the resulting spot-kick.
Tunisia had a goal ruled out following a marginal offside call in the second half and three minutes later a low shot from Hamdou El Houni made it 2-0 to the Mediterranean Knights.
Libya, who last played at an Afcon in 2012, climb to second in the table and go level on points with Uganda.
South Africa are a point clear of Guinea at the top of Group D after a 2-2 draw against Benni McCarthy's Kenya in Johannesburg.
Amos Wanjala's own goal gifted the hosts an early lead before Michael Olunga levelled from the penalty spot just before half-time.
Relebohile Mofokeng restored Bafana Bafana's advantage with 13 minutes remaining, but Kenya claimed a point when Ryan Ogam's low shot from 20 yards crept inside the left-hand upright in the 90th minute.
Elsewhere, Burkina Faso joined Benin on seven points at the top of Group F thanks to Elohim Kabore's 94th-minute winner against Mauritania in Ouagadougou.
Ethiopia upset Mozambique
Mali extended their winning start to go top of Group K after Mamadou Camara completed a 3-2 comeback win at home against Rwanda, who had led twice in Bamako.
Rwanda had won their first two fixtures and are three points ahead of Cape Verde, who registered their first points with a 4-2 victory over Liberia in Praia.
Ethiopia registered their first win to upset Mozambique in Maputo, with Kenean Markneh scoring the only goal in the 87th minute after Mambas keeper Ernan spilled a low shot from Carlos Damtew.
The East Africans move on to three points but remain bottom of Group J, behind Sudan on head-to-head record, while Mozambique are on four points and three behind leaders Senegal.
Zambia moved level on four points with Group I leaders Algeria after a 1-1 draw at home to Burundi. The North Africans have the chance to open up a three-point gap when they host Togo on Saturday.
In Group G, Comoros were held to a goalless draw by Congo-Brazzaville in Moroni. Cameroon lead the section on seven points, with Comoros on four, Namibia on three and the Congolese bottom on two points.

Opetaia pulls out of Wilder bout due to hand injury
Nov 18 : Former cruiserweight champion Jai Opetaia has been forced to withdraw from next month's heavyweight debut against Deontay Wilder due to a hand injury, the Australian boxer announced in an Instagram post on Wednesday.
Opetaia, who is 31-0 as a professional, vacated the WBA cruiserweight title earlier this month to take on the American former heavyweight champion on the undercard of Tyson Fury's showdown with Anthony Joshua on December 11.
The 31-year-old apologised to Wilder and his team for pulling out of the bout.
"Fighter to fighter I know the feeling and it's frustrating... I've always prided myself of fighting anyone, anyplace," Opetaia posted.
His co-promoter Mick Francis told Sky Sports that Opetaia had suffered the injury during his September bout with Noel Mikaelian, and later aggravated it during training.
"His focus now is on making a full recovery and continuing his quest to become the undisputed cruiserweight champion of the world," Francis added.

Encounter breaks out between terrorists, security forces in J&K's Kulgam
“Encounter started with terrorists and Joint party of JKP and SF in Kulgam,” Kashmir Police said in a post on X.
An encounter broke out between between security forces and terrorists on Wednesday in Jammu and Kashmir's Kulgam district.
“Encounter started with terrorists and Joint party of JKP and SF in Kulgam,” Kashmir Police said in a post on X.
This comes after Umar Nisar Dar, an associate of Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) militant commander Mohammed Lateef Bhat, was killed in an encounter in Kulgam on Monday.
Hunt for Bhat is still underway. The two are suspected of carrying out the attack on the CRPF post at Akhran on November 11.
Police officials, requesting anonymity, identified Dar, a former bread-maker, as the LeT commander’s associate. Dar had joined The Resistance Front, an offshoot of the Pakistan-based LeT, barely a week before the November 11 Akhran attack, which left three CRPF personnel injured, officials said.
During the searches on early Wednesday morning, contact with the terrorists was established, leading to a renewed firefight that is ongoing, news agency PTI reported.
CCTV footage shows Dar, Bhat
Surveillance footage from November 10 and 11 purportedly captured the duo conducting reconnaissance at multiple locations on November 10, police officials familiar with the investigation said on Tuesday.
CCTV footage also captured their movements as they fled following an attack on a CRPF post that left three soldiers injured, police sources said.
During the reconnaissance, the two visited several locations, including Mir Bazar, Akhran, Hablish and Kilam, to identify potential targets and plan attacks on security forces.
Dar's encounter
Dar and Bhat were intercepted by security forces at Laroo on Monday. During the ensuing encounter, Dar was killed, while a search operation to track down Bhat continued.
Officials said the operation began after local police received intelligence inputs that two people suspected of involvement in the November 11 attack were moving near the Laru bypass. On noticing the movement of security forces, the two suspects fled to two nearby schools located near an apple orchard, where students were present.
Nearby Army units and the CRPF joined the operation, and an initial cordon was established. The immediate priority was to evacuate the children from the two schools to prevent civilian casualties. The process took around 90 minutes, officials said. Security forces launched the operation after the area had been cleared of civilians.
Bhat is believed to have escaped the initial cordon and may have sustained bullet injuries. Security forces have intensified efforts to trace him, cordoning off several areas around the orchard, officials said.
Drones and sniffer dogs have been deployed as part of the extensive search operation, and additional forces have also been deployed to strengthen the cordon, they said.
The officials said the search operation has been extended to dozens of villages surrounding the site of Monday’s encounter, with security forces maintaining heightened surveillance and carrying out door-to-door searches at identified locations.
During the investigation, agencies established that Umar had been providing shelter and assistance to LeT commander Bhat for the past five to six months.

Triumph or flop? The Rugby League World Cup that split opinion
- Published
Has the 2026 Rugby League World Cup been a success or not?
It depends on who you listen to - and perhaps where in the world you are.
The men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments provided plenty of stories - from Kalyn Ponga's return from a broken arm in 23 days, to Jodie Cunningham's mangled ear,, external to the England wheelchair team's golden ladder, to the men's group format that caused widespread bafflement.
But was the World Cup a triumph? The northern and southern hemisphere perspectives provide contrasting answers.
For the fourth tournament running, Australia won the men's and women's titles, with New Zealand unable to deliver a twist in either final.
Tonga and Samoa brought vibrancy and passion - performing to a level that underlined why they are being elevated to Tier One status. The large Polynesian population in the USA - which will co-host the 2030 men's and women's World Cups - is likely to be key in spreading the rugby league word further around the world.
England's Wheelchair World Cup win, in a thunderous final against their old foes France, offset some of the disappointment felt when Brian McDermott's men and Stuart Barrow's women went home early.
And unlike when the game was emerging from post-pandemic constraints in 2022, the tournament has also worked financially by posting a profit.
"This whole tournament's been incredible," said Australia men's captain Isaah Yeo.
"Not just the fans here for New Zealand and Australia, but just everyone. I thought it was all outstanding.
"I think it's to date the most competitive and the best World Cup there's been. I think that's only going to continue to grow."
That sentiment has been endorsed repeatedly by Australian television broadcaster Channel Seven, which paid a reported A$12m (£6.1m) for exclusive domestic free-to-air coverage of the men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments.
Not everyone has been able to feel that positivity, though.
The decision to cut the men's tournament from 16 teams to 10 reduced the overall number of matches - and deprived teams such as Jamaica and Greece of a chance to build on the feelgood factor they provided as debutants in 2022.
That decision was made after Australia stepped in to stage the tournament, postponed for a year when scheduled hosts France pulled out for financial reasons.
For those who did get to the party this time, it has not always been an even contest. The disparity between the haves and have-nots has been significant.
While the Jillaroos and Kangaroos players will each receive equal payments of $40,000 (£20,500) for competing, Wales will reportedly spread a total of $15,000 (£7,689) across their women's and wheelchair teams., external
Viewer access to the World Cup has varied too. While Australia had free-to-air live television coverage, fans in the UK only got it for the wheelchair final, shown on BBC iPlayer. For all other games, they needed a Premier Sports subscription, which was also the only way to watch the tournament in North America.
With many matches staged at times when British and American viewers were likely to be in bed, it feels as if a chance to spread the game's gospel has been missed.
Festival feel or competitive balance? Or neither?
Many of the players at this World Cup were Australia-based, as they play club rugby in either the NRL's men's competition or its Women's Premiership.
That helped the International Rugby League - the world governing body - to keep costs down, after it spent a vast sum transporting players from the southern hemisphere to England four years ago.
Paring back the men's competition also helped on the costs front, though another supposed benefit - cutting out the lopsided group-stage scorelines of four years ago - has not been evident.
France and the Cook Islands both conceded more than 180 points in the group stage, while scoring a combined 58.
Former England international Ryan Hall told BBC Radio 5 Live earlier this month that the men's World Cup had suffered for being slimmed down - with Scotland, Ireland, Italy and Wales also missing out.
"I don't think it is a World Cup," Hall said. "The essence of any World Cup in any sport is that it's a festival of the sport.
"Compare it to the football World Cup. Curacao were one of the 48 teams in the World Cup.
"I'm not saying rugby league could get 48 teams in the World Cup because that's not achievable, but [they could] certainly [have] more than 10.
"It's meant to be a festival and showcasing everyone of all levels of different countries who's eligible to play."
A format that contained no quarter-finals came in for widespread criticism from pundits, external before a ball was kicked.
The men's tournament featured one group of four and another of six. But two teams went through from both groups, and not everyone in the six-team pool played each other.
In the words of Castleford Tigers head coach Paul Rowley, the former England hooker: "It's trying to make a square with five sides." England captain George Williams, during the build-up, called the format "weird".
And England turned out to be the major losers. The draw left them with no margin for error as an underprepared and jet-lagged squad faced a dangerous Tonga side first up, and lost 30-12.
And ultimately, McDermott's side paid the price. Of the 26 teams across the three World Cups, only one side won two out of three group games and still failed to make the semi-finals: England's men.

A growing audience?
An October and November tournament brings a different vibe depending on where you are. The last World Cup, in the UK, was staged as the temperatures dropped. This time around, it was held with co-hosts Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea heading towards summer.
Fans have gone to games in T-shirts and shorts instead of thick winter garments - and tellingly, average footfall increased.
That is despite the fact that the capacity 52,000 crowd in Brisbane for finals night was lower than the 67,000 at Old Trafford four years ago.
In 2022, the men's group stage - spanning 24 games - was watched by an average crowd of 9,811, itself down on the 14,345 figure from 2013, when England and Wales played hosts.
This time around, the average crowd rose to 21,360. It probably helped that there were fewer group games. It certainly helped that every Australia match was well attended, and that there was strong backing for New Zealand, Samoa, Tonga and Papua New Guinea, who played twice in their capital Port Moresby.
Lessons have also clearly been learned from 2022's heavily criticised ticket pricing structure.
Instead of adults paying more than £20 to attend matches, it has been a more friendly A$19, which equates to £9.74 per ticket.
But while attendances at this year's tournament are up, there is still work to be done around the women's game.
The sight of more empty seats than supporters in grounds for a number of double-headers is hardly a good look for the organisers or broadcasters.
Jillaroos coach Jess Skinner notably raised the issue after her team defeated Samoa 40-0 in their Pool A opener at the home of Parramatta Eels on 16 October.
That match had followed Samoa's men thrashing France 78-4 - but in a stadium with a capacity of 30,000, many of the recorded 13,174 crowd had dispersed before the women's game got under way, with the stands appearing barely 20% full.
"Let's get around women in sport, right? All women in sport, particularly at this Rugby League World Cup," Skinner said. "We've got a lot of talented women across all the teams and the message would be to stay and support that.
"Something really cool's happening in this generation of sport, with our ladies, and you're going to miss history-making moments at this World Cup, no doubt."
Sadly for Skinner and her peerless team, it was a pattern that was repeated in Sunday's final, with the stands in Brisbane's Suncorp Stadium only filling as kick-off time for the men's game approached.
Northern hemisphere indifference?
Four years ago, the Rugby League World Cup was shown free-to-air in the UK by the BBC, with record-breaking viewing figures.
Almost 30 million people tuned in to watch the five-week extravaganza.
This time, the action has largely been behind a paywall. Premier Sports has shown all the World Cup matches live. The BBC showed the wheelchair final live, plus online highlights of selected games from all three tournaments.
In addition, it provided live radio coverage of all men's matches and some women's games, plus live text commentaries on selected games.
Rights were awarded by the International Rugby League - and not the Rugby Football League. Last month, IRL chair Troy Grant told the iPaper that it made the decision to go with Premier because the BBC did not offer enough money - though no other free-to-air broadcaster made a suitable offer either.
Former England international Jon Wilkin highlighted the issue during a BBC Radio 5 Live discussion at the start of this month, saying: "The World Cup should have been on the BBC.
"There is no doubt in my mind as a public service broadcaster, this had so many reasons to be a slam dunk home run to be free to air on the BBC. It had to be."
In response, a BBC spokesperson said: "We must make difficult choices to deliver the savings required while continuing to serve audiences as effectively as possible."
And therein lies a problem for the sport in the northern hemisphere, where more backing, more financial support and more coverage is needed to reverse the fortunes of the Super League and international teams largely bound to that competition.
The financial gulf to southern hemisphere's elite competitions was laid bare, when the NRL struck a record A$5.3bn (£2.78bn) television deal over seven years in July.
Super League's TV deal with Sky Sports, which expired at the end of 2026, was worth around £21.5m per year.
Even with the pending announcement of a deal to bring NRL investment into Super League, that particular playing field is a long way from being levelled.
And it means that when the next World Cup comes around, Australia can expect to be favourites to win the men's and women's tournaments again.

The 3pm football blackout: outdated or still relevant in 2026?
- Published
After 60 years, is time finally running out on the 3pm blackout in football?
With pretty much every available television slot now exhausted, next year the Premier League and the EFL are set to hold serious discussions about its future.
There are concerns, especially within non-league football, that removing the blackout could have detrimental effects on attendances and finances.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham agrees, urging caution and suggesting the health of the football pyramid should come first.
But many Premier League fans feel they are short-changed, locked out of many of their team's fixtures just because they live in this country.
Go anywhere else in the world, and every single match is available live.
With streaming so prevalent, to some the blackout feels archaic.
Yet it is a complex situation, and many feel the depth of English football's pyramid is like nowhere else.
BBC Sport looks at the history of the blackout, why it is unique to British football and the arguments for and against keeping it.
How Match of the Day ushered in the blackout
It is the start of the 1964-65 season and the BBC launches a programme called Match of the Day.
Highlights of one match would be broadcast on BBC Two, a channel which at the time was only available in London.
Yet some clubs were concerned. Would fans still turn up to games?
Burnley chairman Bob Lord was the first owner to refuse to allow the cameras into Turf Moor. At the end of the season, several other clubs tried to block the renewal of the deal.
A compromise was reached and the BBC agreed not to reveal the televised Saturday match until all games had ended.
Shortly afterwards came the blackout for live matches.
Fast forward 20 years to 1987. With dwindling attendances across the European domestic leagues, partly influenced by crowd trouble, Uefa took up England's idea.
Article 48 was added to the Uefa Statutes.
Each country could designate a two-and-a-half-hour "transmission-free period", as long as at least 50% of matches in the top two leagues were taking place.
This was "designed to ensure that spectators are not deterred from attending local football matches of any kind and/or participating in matches at amateur and/or youth level".
Why does no other country have the blackout?
Today, the situation has gone full circle. The only leagues that apply Article 48 are England, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
The reason for this is simpler than you might imagine.
No other major country qualifies for the blackout - because no other major country has a kick-off time that runs from the top flight and through the divisions.
It is a tradition that is unique to football in the United Kingdom.
Let's take Germany, often held up as an example of a country with excellent attendances despite not having a blackout.
This misses a key point. The Bundesliga has its own kick-off slot, 3:30pm on a Saturday, and no other division plays at the same time. The 2. Bundesliga, for instance, has a standard Saturday kick-off time of 1:30pm.
Could you imagine English football replicating this?
The other top leagues are the same.
In Spain, it is rare for either of the top two divisions to have games that kick off simultaneously. Each match has its own slot, and is broadcast live.
In Italy, Serie A plays on a Sunday afternoon, and Serie B on a Saturday.
In France, Ligue 1 has Saturday night as its main time slot, Ligue 2 plays largely on a Friday night, and Ligue 3 on a Saturday lunchtime.
So there is no blackout, because the football calendar works in a completely different way.
Why the blackout is now under threat
The next television rights cycle presents a unique opportunity.
The deals for the Premier League, EFL and Scottish Premiership are all up for renewal in 2029-30.
There is the chance for all the top stakeholders to come together and agree to end the blackout.
Last year, Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said there were no plans to remove the blackout.
But this summer there was a clear shift in emphasis, with Masters admitting there would be talks with the EFL ahead of the renewal of TV rights.
Scottish football has gone first, with broadcasters invited to bid to show all matches live - and is open to those shown on a Saturday afternoon.
It will be another year before we discover what the Premier League and the EFL - which seriously considered ending the blackout three years ago - are prepared to offer to broadcasters.
So, why would the leagues need to offer up the Saturday 3pm slot to broadcasters? After all, the latest domestic Premier League deal was worth a record £6.7bn - an increase of 4%.
However, to achieve that figure, the Premier League had to make an additional 70 games available. In real terms, it means each live Premier League game is worth less than it was before.
Now every single game not shown at 3pm on a Saturday - and there are only 110 left - is on TV.
Could the Premier League need to offer more matches for the rights to keep their overall value?
If so there are two options: try to find more TV slots, or show games at 3pm on a Saturday.
Could the Women's Super League benefit too? It looked into playing a 3pm on a Saturday but could not find a way around the blackout.
Most of the competition's games are shown live already, with a greater concern being stadium availability and consistency of kick-off times.
'Football doesn't begin and end with the Premier League'
There is a danger that the issue of the 3pm blackout is viewed only through the lens of Premier League and EFL television rights.
But it goes much deeper than that.
Tom Greatrex, the chair of the Football Supporters' Association, says there are attendances in non-league football that some top flights in Europe "would look at jealously".
"We have one of the strongest football pyramids in the world, with excellent matchday attendances deep into the non-league game," Greatrex said.
"The prime minister is right to point out the value of the blackout to clubs further down the pyramid, and to urge caution over the impact rushed change could have on the overall health of the game."
BBC Sport understands that senior executives at the National League, which has a long-term global streaming deal with DAZN, are steadfastly against the blackout ending.
It has serious reservations, shared by the vast majority of its 72 clubs, that attendances would be impacted.
Included in this is transient attendance from season ticket holders of league clubs, who attend non-league football when their team is away from home, boosting receipts considerably.
The fear is this could be lost if all league games are streamed at 3pm.
Nicky Bloom, the chair of Northern Premier League side FC United of Manchester, worries that the issue is only viewed through the lens of top-flight football.
"Football doesn't begin and end with the Premier League," Bloom told BBC Sport.
"Every Saturday, thousands of people turn out to support their local clubs.
"For many of those clubs, the income from people coming through the turnstiles, buying a pint or something to eat is what keeps them alive.
"The 3pm blackout isn't about nostalgia. It's about protecting something that matters."
Bloom added that clubs in non-league football are huge community assets, and losing them would have an impact "well beyond 90 minutes on a Saturday".
Streaming could still be an opportunity for some clubs
Some clubs are more open-minded about what ending the blackout could mean for non-league football.
Others have changed the way they operate to get around it.
North West Counties League Premier Division side FC Isle of Man have stopped playing at 3:00pm on a Saturday so they can stream all their games live.
Brian Shotton, a director at eighth-tier Ashington FC, told BBC Sport that he would not be automatically against removing the blackout.
"I would still have concerns, because every person through the gate makes a difference," Shotton said.
"I don't think we should just assume it would damage non-league football, but equally you need to know what it could mean for clubs like ours."
Ashington, which have attendances of about 400, see gates rise by up to 25% when Newcastle are not at home - but they already see the impact of illegal streaming of the Magpies' games.
For the official broadcasters like Sky Sports, these supporters are seen as lost revenue.
There is an argument that the blackout drives piracy. Just how many of those particular fans would pay for a legal subscription is open to debate.
Added to that, there are now many weekends when when fewer than 50% of matches in the top two divisions are played at 3pm on a Saturday anyway.
For instance, on 28 November there are just two in the Premier League, and seven in the Championship.
Other non-league clubs, like Dorking Wanders and Hashtag United, have spoken of the opportunities ending the blackout could bring, such as more income streams and fewer inconvenient kick-off times.
But this, for now, seems to be a minority view. The concerns for the health of the entire pyramid, on attendances and finances, are real.
Once the blackout is gone, it is unlikely to come back.

What happens when the technology designed to keep our digital identities safe is challenged by a new generation of technology? For cybersecurity professionals, preparing for that future has already begun.
Think about how often you use your digital identity. You might log into a government portal, verify your details online or access a service using a digital ID. It takes just a few seconds, and most of us overlook the technology working behind the scenes to keep our information safe.
But what if the security systems we trust today are not strong enough tomorrow?
This is a question that is gaining importance as quantum computing moves closer to practical use. While the technology promises major advances in science, healthcare and computing, it could also challenge some of the encryption methods that protect our digital lives.
For Dr Swati Kumari, Senior Lecturer at Deakin University GIFT City Campus, these questions are already shaping her research agenda.
Recently awarded funding through the Australia-India Cyber and Critical Technology Partnership (AICCTP) programme, Dr Kumari is leading a research project on Quantum-Safe Digital Public Infrastructure. The project looks at two major digital identity ecosystems, India's Aadhaar and Australia's MyID.
The aim is to understand how advances in quantum computing could affect the security systems that protect them.
Also to identify possible weaknesses, explore newer forms of encryption and develop practical ways to make digital identity systems safe.
"Digital identity systems protect highly sensitive information and provide access to essential services for millions of people," says Dr Kumari. "Many of the cryptographic mechanisms we rely on today were designed long before quantum computing became a realistic possibility. Preparing now is a necessity."
Why should students pay attention?
Quantum computing may sound like something out of a science fiction film, but its implications are real.
Much of the technology that protects our banking transactions, digital signatures, cloud services and online identities relies on encryption methods developed for conventional computers. Powerful quantum computers could eventually create new risks for individuals, businesses and governments.
Another reason why cybersecurity continues to be one of the world's fastest evolving and sought-after professions.
"What excites me most about cybersecurity is that it never stands still," says Dr Kumari.
"The challenges evolve alongside emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, quantum technologies and the Internet of Things. You're constantly learning, innovating and solving problems that have real-world impact."
Right skills for the cybersecurity leaders of tomorrow
Technical knowledge remains at the heart of cybersecurity, but the skills required are becoming much broader.
Dr Kumari believes that students need a strong grounding in networking, programming, cryptography, operating systems and secure software development. They should also understand emerging areas such as AI, cloud computing, privacy, governance and digital identity.
But technical skills alone are not enough.
Cybersecurity professionals increasingly work with people from different backgrounds, organisations and countries. They need to communicate clearly, work in teams and adapt cross-culturally.
Her own research project provides an example. By bringing together researchers from India and Australia, it addresses a shared challenge that requires expertise, collaboration and an understanding of different technological environments.
"Cybersecurity challenges are global challenges. The ability to work across teams, industries and borders will be as valuable as technical expertise," she says.
Breadth and depth of learning
For students at Deakin’s GIFT City Campus, research such as this offers a glimpse into the challenges shaping the cybersecurity industry.
The subject is not limited to understanding how cyber threats work. It is also about exploring how systems can be protected, tested and made more resilient.
While learning students engage with areas such as digital identity, threat modelling, cryptography, secure systems design and cyber resilience. These concepts help them understand how security works in practice. This becomes important as these systems serve millions of people and handle sensitive information.
They can also explore some of the emerging areas that are creating new opportunities across the industry, including:
· Artificial Intelligence Security
· Cloud Security
· Post-Quantum Cryptography
· Digital Identity and Trust Technologies
· Privacy and Data Protection
· IoT and Critical Infrastructure Security
· Threat Intelligence and Cyber Resilience
These subjects aren’t limited to academic research. They are increasingly relevant to modern organisations that need to protect their data, infrastructure and customers in a sensitive digital world.
They are active areas of innovation and industry demand today offering significant professional opportunities.
A future built on curiosity
Her advice to aspiring cybersecurity professionals is simple: build strong foundations, stay curious and never stop learning.
"Cybersecurity isn't just about mastering tools," she says. "It's about learning how to think critically, anticipate emerging risks and create solutions that make technology safer and more trustworthy."
As the world prepares for the quantum era, the mindset to receive it is more important.
At Deakin University GIFT City Campus, students are preparing for the future of cybersecurity. Through globally relevant research and industry-connected learning, they are gaining the skills to help shape it.

It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI. That is, of course, by design. The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot. The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app.
The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data. Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history. That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road.
As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history. The history setting will continue to support an adjustable limit, but you will no longer have to change it to stop Google from training on your Gemini usage. Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation. You’ll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training. It’s under Activity in the Gemini settings. You can also access the menu from your Google account under Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity.
Importantly, this only applies to future interactions with Gemini. If you have previously fed any data into Google’s AI, that’s already part of the training data. That can include your inputs, Gemini’s responses, uploaded files, tool calls, your location, and data from connected apps. Google says it may retain this data for up to three years to improve its models. The company has previously noted it attempts to filter personal information out of the Gemini activity history, but that isn’t a guarantee.

Body of Melbourne Cup horse found dumped in Sydney skip
- Published
The body of a top Australian racehorse has been found dumped in a skip bin, hours after its trainer revealed the horse had died from colic.
In a video shared online, only two weeks after So You Are raced in the Melbourne Cup, the deceased racehorse appeared to be lying in a large metal bin surrounded by other household rubbish in Sydney.
Trainer Bjorn Baker - who shared news of the horse's death from colic on Monday - has said he was "deeply distressed" by the video, and called for a "full explanation".
Racing NSW, the state's industry regulator, said a preliminary investigation had found the horse was later properly buried, but called the way its body was handled "completely unacceptable".
"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said in an statement shared online.
"He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death."
So You Are had a successful run during spring, winning four times at respected races including the Rosehill, Randwick and the Bendigo Cup.
The five-year-old recently finished eight in the Melbourne Cup, which was won by Point of Law, a horse previously owned by King Charles III.
The racehorse had received urgent treatment after a severe bout of colic, but was "unfortunately unable to be saved" and was euthanised under anaesthesia, Racing NSW said.
"So You Are was then transported for burial, and was being held temporarily, awaiting burial, when these images were recorded," it said.
Burial at a licensed landfill is typically recommended for animals that die from euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process, according to the racing body.
"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner," it added.
In a statement, REC Equine Specialists - the hospital where the horse died - said a contractor had been hired to dispose of the So You Are's body.
"We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that."
"We have spoken with So You Are's owners and trainer to apologise personally."
The company added that it had stopped using the contractor, and was reviewing its processes to make sure they known exactly how horses are handled after leaving their hospital.
"No owner should have to go through what So You Are's connections have experienced this week. We will make sure it does not happen again."
Jowett's video appeared to be filmed at a public rubbish drop-off and land facility called Lucas Heights, in Sutherland Shire, south of Sydney.
The waste management company that runs the landfill site said So You Are's body had been moved to a skip bin in a permitted area, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported.

Mumbai, Nov 18: The rupee appreciated 24 paise to 93.27 against the US dollar in early trade on Wednesday, supported by declining crude prices and surging foreign portfolio inflows into Indian equities.
Forex traders said the appreciation in the rupee was primarily fuelled by a steep overnight drop in Brent crude oil prices, which eases India's import bill and inflation concerns.
Moreover, robust foreign institutional inflows -- exceeding USD 8 billion into Indian equities so far this month -- and a broad rally in domestic stock benchmarks enthused investors.
At the interbank forex market, the domestic unit opened at 93.47 against the greenback and gained ground to touch 93.27, registering a rise of 24 paise over its previous close.
On Tuesday, the rupee gained 43 paise to close at its seven-month high of 93.51 against the US dollar.
"The rupee's gains have been mainly on account of falling oil and FPIs inflows which have taken share market also up and the gains may continue till 92.80 a strong support for the dollar," Anil Kumar Bhansali, Head of Treasury and Executive Director, Finrex Treasury Advisors LLP, said.
Meanwhile, the dollar index, which gauges the greenback's strength against a basket of six currencies, was at 103.60, higher by 0.12 per cent.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, was trading 0.46 per cent lower at USD 92.71 per barrel in futures trade.
According to Anindya Banerjee, Head of Commodity and Currency Research, Kotak NEO, exceptional foreign inflows and lower crude are overwhelming the strength of the global dollar.
"Until the dollar trend changes, I would respect the prevailing direction across commodities rather than try to anticipate a bottom prematurely," he said.
On the domestic equity market front, Sensex declined 75.10 points to 82,482.30 in early trade; Nifty fell 26.95 points to 25,355.65.
Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) bought equities worth Rs 4,195.38 crore on Tuesday, according to exchange data.

Noel Clarke is set to face trial next November over allegations of six sexual offenses.
The actor and director was present at Southwark Crown Court in London, U.K. on Wednesday morning for a pre-trial preparation hearing.
Dressed in a neat suit with glasses, Clarke was accompanied by his legal team. A smattering of press and fans were also in attendance.
Last month the actor pleaded not guilty to two charges of sexual assault, three charges of voyeurism and one charge of exposure at Westminster Magistrates Court.
The charges relate to five women and are alleged to have taken place between 2007 and 2016. Under British law, the complainants are entitled to lifelong anonymity.
At the hearing on Wednesday, lawyers for both Clarke and the Crown Prosecution Service agreed the tentative timeline for his trial next year, which will be heard before a High Court judge.
Clarke will have until March 5 to submit an application to dismiss the charges. If he does, the CPS will have an opportunity to respond and both sides will make their case at a hearing in April. A trial date has tentatively been set for Nov. 8.
The actor is currently on bail subject to conditions.
In a statement in September, CPS prosecutor Bethan David said: “Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court and that it is in the public interest to do so. We have worked closely with the Metropolitan Police as they have carried out their investigation into the allegations.”
“The Crown Prosecution Service reminds everyone that proceedings are now active, and the defendant has the right to a fair trial. It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information online which could in any way prejudice these proceedings.”
Clarke is known for playing Mickey Smith in “Doctor Who” from 2005 to 2010. He also wrote, directed and starred in a trio of teen crime dramas in the mid 2000s, “Kidulthood,” “Adulthood” and “Brotherhood,” before going on to co-created critically acclaimed Sky series “Bulletproof” with Ashley Walters.

Srinagar, Nov 18: The State Investigation Agency (SIA) Kashmir has scored a major courtroom victory after the NIA Court Srinagar rejected the bail application of an accused in a narco-terror conspiracy case.
The Court passed the order on November 17, 2026, after hearing detailed arguments from both sides.
The accused, Basharat Ali Poswal, son of Muhammad Siddiq Poswal, resident of Tad, Karnah in Kupwara district, presently residing at Bemina, Srinagar, is facing prosecution in FIR No. 19/2022 of Police Station CI-SIA Kashmir.
He has been booked under stringent provisions of law of NDPS Act - Sections 8-A, 27-B and 29, UAPA - Sections 13, 18, 39 and 40 and IPC -Sections 120-B, 121, 121-A and 201.
The case alleges a serious nexus between narcotics trafficking, unlawful activities and conspiracy against the State, including activities aimed at waging war against the nation.
When the bail plea was filed, the Court directed the prosecution to file objections. SIA Kashmir filed comprehensive, well-reasoned objections opposing bail.
The matter was argued over several hearings. The prosecution highlighted the gravity of the allegations, the nature of the offences and the strict statutory bars on bail under the UAPA and NDPS Act.
Charges against all accused persons were already framed by order dated July 15, 2026. The case is now listed for recording of prosecution evidence.
With the rejection of bail, the trial will proceed without the accused being released from custody.

“SIA Kashmir remains firmly resolved to dismantle the narco-terror ecosystem and to prosecute effectively everyone involved in activities that threaten the peace, security and integrity of the nation,” the statement said.
The agency reiterated its commitment to comprehensive investigations on merits, strong prosecution and safeguarding the interests of justice in cases involving serious offences.

In another major cybersecurity incident, malicious code injected into websites through digital experience platform (DXP) Optimizely exposed visitors to potential theft of cryptocurrency, payment card details and browser data. The attack affected 178 organisations, including Zoom, BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax and Ledger, after attackers compromised customer projects on Optimizely Web and used the platform's content delivery network (CDN) to distribute malware. The injected JavaScript also had capabilities to deliver two iOS exploit kits, Coruna and DarkSword, potentially exposing visitors using vulnerable Apple devices to further attacks. The attack was detected on November 16 by cybersecurity firm Report URI, which found 188 compromised JavaScript snippets linked to 178 organisations across 20 sectors, including banking, technology, retail, media, healthcare and telecommunications. The findings emerged from an analysis of 1,611 distinct Optimizely snippets. The malware could replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses with those controlled by attackers, capture payment card details, steal browser cookies and take screenshots of visitors' webpages. The attackers had received around $7,040 in cryptocurrency by November 16. Report URI revised this figure to approximately $7,151 in an update published on November 17. In response to an Inc42 query, Optimizely said it identified the incident on November 16, 2026, after an unauthorised party exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely Experimentation to inject malicious JavaScript into some customer projects. The company said it had contained the incident and fully remediated the vulnerability. As part of its response, Optimizely blocked access to the vulnerable path, deployed a fix and removed the injected code from affected projects. It also ended active sessions, revoked tokens and reset access for affected user accounts. "We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered through Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation. We have notified and are supporting all affected customers," the company said. The Mechanics Of The Optimizely Attack Optimizely Web allows businesses to experiment with different versions of their websites, personalise visitor experiences and analyse how users interact with their pages. To use the platform, customers integrate a JavaScript snippet hosted on Optimizely's CDN into their websites. The snippet also includes an optional field called Project JavaScript, which allows customers to add custom code that runs on their webpages. According to Report URI, attackers exploited access to customer projects to inject malicious JavaScript into these fields. As a result, visitors did not need to click suspicious links or visit unfamiliar websites to encounter the malware. Their browsers automatically loaded the compromised code when they accessed affected websites. Three variations of the injected code were traced. The first loaded a malicious script directly from an external domain, while the second concealed the domain using Base64 encoding. The third contained the entire malicious payload and could execute it through a function called eval if access to the external domain was blocked. The compromised code was also found in Zoom's Optimizely snippet, which instructed visitors' browsers to load another JavaScript file from the malicious domain. However, how the attackers gained access to multiple customer projects remains unclear. Possible explanations include a compromise of Optimizely's systems or the use of stolen credentials that allowed attackers to access customer accounts. What Could The Malware Do? The injected JavaScript, identified as track.js, was capable of carrying out multiple forms of malicious activity. Depending on the visitor's device and activity on a webpage, it could target financial information, collect browsing data or attempt to exploit Apple devices. Replacing cryptocurrency wallet addresses: One of the malware's key capabilities was to interfere with cryptocurrency transactions. For instance, a visitor could copy a wallet address displayed on a website, only for the malware to replace it with an address controlled by the attackers before the user pasted it into their wallet. The script could scan webpages for cryptocurrency wallet addresses and substitute them with the attackers' addresses. It supported several cryptocurrencies and networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, Tron, Toncoin, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash and Dogecoin. Stealing payment card details: The malware could also function as a payment card skimmer, capturing information entered by visitors into website forms. It monitored form submissions and outgoing network requests to identify payment card details, including card numbers, expiry dates and CVVs. The captured information could then be transmitted to an external server controlled by the attackers. However, the malware had a limitation. It could not access card details entered into hosted payment iframes operated by providers such as Stripe and Adyen. Details entered directly into a website's own payment fields were potentially exposed. Stealing cookies and screenshots: The malware could also collect information associated with visitors' browsing sessions. When it detected cryptocurrency addresses alongside wallet-related or payment-related terms, it could transmit information such as the webpage URL, non-HttpOnly cookies, original wallet addresses and a screenshot of the webpage to the attackers' server. Delivering iOS exploit kits: The malware could also target visitors using Apple devices, particularly iPhones and iPads, by delivering two iOS exploit kits called Coruna and DarkSword. These exploit kits are designed to exploit vulnerabilities in Apple's operating system. The script first checked the iOS version running on a visitor's device before attempting to load the relevant exploit chain. The exploit kits were delivered through hidden iframes and external domains controlled by the attackers. Devices running iOS 18.7.3 and later, as well as iOS 26.3 and later, were patched against the relevant vulnerabilities, based on comments found in the exploit kit. Edited by Akshit Pushkarna

Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.
The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.
Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.
It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.
The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.
The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.
The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecuties individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.
The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.
The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.
Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.
Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians”.
In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”
In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”
He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.
Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.
In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically.”
It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.
The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of the Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.
The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.
Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.
On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater US willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.

The meme appeared to have used outdated census estimates for the population of Texas, which increased by nearly 2.5 million people between 2020 and 2025. Even still, Snopes could not replicate the meme's alleged findings.
After Democrats in Texas flipped control of the state House of Representatives and won the governorship during the 2026 midterm elections, a meme circulated suggesting there may have been election fraud in the historically Republican stronghold.
According to the meme, the number of registered voters exceeded the number of voting-age citizens in counties across the state. Several social media posts relayed the image, which showed a map of Texas' 254 counties, including on Instagram and Facebook. Some posts on X also shared the meme, including one that said "97 counties are over the adult-citizen count" (archived):
The meme claimed the counties in red had more registered voters than adult citizens, and the ones in yellow had at least 10% more registered voters than adult citizens. The image gave numbers for only six counties as evidence of its claim — Collin, Denton, Fort Bend, Montgomery, Parker and Williamson — saying that in each of them, the number of registered voters exceeded the number of adult citizens.
The meme cited as its sources the Texas secretary of state's November voter registration figures and Census 2020-24 adult citizen estimates.
We could find no evidence for the meme's claim. Using the most recent U.S. Census' adult citizen estimates (2024) in these counties and comparing them with the Texas secretary of state's numbers on voter registration per county, we could not replicate the image's alleged findings. For this reason, we rate the claim false.
The meme carried a watermark for the X account @_Patriot1776Q_. We reached out to the account asking for more information about the numbers and we will update this report should we receive a response.
It should be noted that Texas' population was the fastest-growing in the country between 2024 and 2026, and our calculations do not account for this growth due to the fact that the U.S. Census' most recent estimate for adult citizens is for 2024. (This also means that comparing the number of registered voters in 2026 to an older, smaller population estimate, as the meme claims to do, would be a flawed comparison.)
An attempt to replicate the meme's calculations
In January, the Redistricting and Voting Rights Data Office of the U.S. Census published its estimates for citizens of voting age by race and ethnicity for 2024. Snopes uploaded that data into a spreadsheet organized by state and county, with the six counties the meme mentioned highlighted them in yellow.
Next, we pulled data about registered voters and actual voters in each county in Texas. (To reflect population changes, we included July 2025 U.S. Census data and calculated the estimated number of adults, citizens and noncitizens combined, per county.)
We compiled the data for the six counties used in the meme and six more among those marked yellow — that is, counties where there were supposedly at least 10% more registered voters than adult citizens. Our calculations did not demonstrate the map's claim.
In an attempt to replicate the meme's numbers, we used the 2024 estimated number of adult citizens against the 2026 number of registered voters. For these numbers to be accurate and definitive, we would need to have 2026 actual numbers of adult citizens in these counties, as opposed to estimates.
For example, the meme said there were 34,319 more registered voters in 2026 in Montgomery County than there were registered adults based on 2020-2024 estimates. We found there were in fact 20,076 fewer adult citizens (based on the 2024 estimate) than there were registered adults in 2026.
The meme also said Parker County counted 111% registered voters relative to the number of estimated number of adult citizens. Our calculation found 108%. Once again, this number did not reflect the updated number of adult citizens in the county in 2026; Parker County is reportedly one of the fastest-growing counties in the nation.
Texas also places voters "in suspense" before removing them from the voter rolls when election officials believe a registered voter may have moved. This means that the number of registered voters reported for a county includes people who may no longer live in that county. Parker County, for example, had just under 9,000 voters in suspense in November, according to the state.
It also should be noted that voter turnout across Texas was roughly 50% in the 2026 midterms, and no county had more votes than adult citizens.
For further reading, Snopes also debunked the claim that Texas "found" 20 million votes to flip it to a Democratic majority.

Waymo self-driving taxis are no longer driving on highways after the California Department of Motor Vehicles banned its vehicles from state freeway operations. The ban, which the DMV says began on November 11, comes after the department determined that Waymo’s freeway driving poses “an imminent hazard to public safety.”
In response, Waymo says it has stopped highway driving in all of its markets. The company may continue testing its vehicles on non-California highways with safety operators behind the wheels.
The ban follows two recent concerning incidents, California DMV spokesperson Jonathan Groveman wrote in a statement. In one, three Waymos entered an active highway construction closure on Route 101 on the San Francisco Peninsula. The other was captured in a viral video showing a Waymo vehicle interfering with California Highway Patrol cars on a San Francisco highway as they tried to enforce a “traffic break” as workers cleared debris from the crash.
Groveman said the California ban will remain in place until Waymo has proved that it has “taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies" that led to the incidents. It’s unclear how long that process will take.
In a written statement to WIRED, Waymo spokesperson Dana Gallagher said the company is “working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations." Waymo vehicles will continue to operate on surface streets in the 15 metros where it offers taxi service, including portions of Los Angeles, San Diego, and the San Francisco Bay Area.
This is the second time Waymo has publicly restricted its freeway operations after beginning to transport passengers on them last year. In June, the company recalled its software after federal regulators found that its system failed to recognize highway construction zones. Regulators with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) cited several incidents in April and May in which Waymo cars drove past ramp closure signs and into active lane closures. The events did not lead to collisions or injuries.
The NHTSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Last week, the agency said it was examining whether another Waymo recall software fix had actually solved its robotaxis’ safety issues. This recall, which occurred last December, was tied to incidents in which Waymo cars repeatedly drove by stopped school buses with their lights on and/or stop arms extended.
Self-driving cars have struggled with construction zones for at least a decade. The zones can look and be arranged differently based on what sort of construction is being done, and where. While humans can easily understand bollards, placards, and blinking arrows, the lack of hard-and-fast rules has proven difficult to reliably program into driving software. The issue is especially hazardous at high freeway speeds, where workers exist alongside fast-moving car traffic.

Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company’s vision for its new “frontier ecosystem,” announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as “the new OS for work.”
The announcement is a striking inversion of how we’ve traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent’s work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications.
The rollout marks a major step toward the Copilot redesign the company first announced in September. Parts of that vision are now becoming “generally available,” as Nadella puts it, with autonomous agents and new governance tools arriving alongside them.
All about agents
Copilot Autopilot (not to be confused with Windows Autopilot) is a “persistent, proactive agent for personal productivity” according to Microsoft. In a nutshell, Autopilot is a cloud-based autonomous AI agent that users can delegate responsibilities to, not just single tasks. Autopilot can be authorized to work across services like email and calendars and complete tasks assigned to it as part of its role. Autopilot will use usage-based billing via Copilot Credits, but final pricing has not been announced ahead of general availability.
Also announced as generally available at the keynote speech was Microsoft IQ, an intelligence platform that houses Work IQ, a context layer that helps agents understand a company’s communications, relationships, and ongoing work. Nadella described Work IQ as perhaps a company’s most valuable database: “It has a deep understanding of the people, their relationships to other people, your emails, your meetings, chats, projects that make up all the fabric of work.” Whether companies want autonomous agents to have access to internal documents and messaging data will have to be determined by their own internal IT review.

A gauze of dust covers everything in the Pakistani desert city of Quetta, rendering just about everything the same shade of bleached, parched beige — an in-between color for an in-between place, where many residents await change with no clear timeline. In the city quarter of Hazara Town, named for over half a million residents from the ethnic Hazara community, displaced refugees from Afghanistan live in indefinite limbo: violently imperiled in their current sanctuary, but not yet granted asylum anywhere else. It’s a despairing holding pattern through which everyday life, with its more modest domestic challenges and occasional joys, nonetheless continues: Khadim Dai‘s patiently observed, intensely moving documentary “Hazara Town” sharply chronicles that simultaneous stasis and progress.
The first feature-length film by the Afghan-born, Los Angeles-based Dai is a family affair, centered on the director’s own stranded relatives: his sister-in-law, Sedeqa; his two young nieces, Machid and Mitra; and their doting grandparents. All are stranded in Quetta since fleeing Afghanistan, while Dai’s brother Hussain has forged ahead, laying the groundwork for a new life in Canada. Following him is no simple matter, however. The asylum application process is slow and selective, and whole chapters of family life pass by as they wait to be reunited: Preteen Mitra, in particular, doesn’t remember much of her father’s presence at home, and communication by phone and video only partially bridges the gap.
Returning to Pakistan several years after his own departure, Dai embeds himself in the household, his camera capturing both the intimate daily routines of a splintered family — in particular, the growth of two girls around their father’s absence — and wider currents of fear and sorrow in the Hazara community, where people increasingly find themselves as unsafe from ethnic and religious persecution as they were in the homeland they fled. Targeted killings are disturbingly commonplace, the rising death toll sporadically flashing on the screen with no further commentary.
Dai’s camera records no violence, but instead spends much time in the local cemetery where the dead are buried with little ceremony — their portraits displayed for a time as a memorial before they, too, vanish. Deft, detailed sound design balances the lonely reverberations of the desert wind against the industrious tap-tap-tapping of local stonemasons at work on various grave markers: At least some in this stymied community have much to do. But the cemetery isn’t presented only as a place of grief: It’s also a gathering spot for people otherwise granted little social space, and in some of the film’s most poignant tableaux, children chatter and play amidst these humble resting places.
Home, though, remains the most secure of spaces in an otherwise stateless existence: With its modest interior courtyard and few windows to the outside world, Dai’s family’s residence feels significantly turned inward. Though Machid and Mitra both go to school, classroom freedoms are curbed as Pakistan hands over responsibility for refugee education to the Taliban; it’s within cramped domestic walls that the girls assert their evolving personalities and interests, rapidly maturing before our eyes.
Machid, a studious bookworm with a love of Judy Blume, dreams of richer education opportunities in the United States, while the rest of the family pins their hopes on Canada — sold to them via effortfully cheerful video missives from Hussain, marveling at differences in culture and weather. Good news does arrive from North America, but not for everyone, and so the family is further fragmented. Dai films each individual flight from the back window of the departing taxi, splashed with a bucket of water for good luck, the drips distorting one last look at those left behind in the rearview.
Also an accomplished cinematographer, Dai shoots these individually unremarkable episodes of daily survival — and occasional celebration — with a grace and sensitivity that cumulatively builds to something more than just diaristic in effect: “Hazara Town” is a quietly emphatic statement of presence for lives all too easily disappeared, or dismissed as statistics. And while it provides no tidy resolution to this collective narrative, there’s at least a temporary, heart-filling interlude of reunion, before life pulls in a multitude of directions: For the refugee family, there’s as much anguish in movement as in stillness, but a shred of hope too.

War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason
Environmentalists have long puzzled over a wide network of water projects lacking any obvious justification. Then their areas were targeted in airstrikes.
Environmentalists have long been mystified by the significant proliferation of dams and water transfer projects like pipelines and tunnels across Iran, especially in regions that had no apparent need for them.
Some analysts think they now know the answer after U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on concealed Iranian missile sites this year targeted many of the same areas. These analysts have concluded that the water projects may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup.
Given the secrecy surrounding Iran’s missile program, any connection between it and Iran’s ambitious, decades-old initiative to develop water infrastructure remains speculative. But some experts find the evidence highly suggestive.
Nima Shokri, an expert on water security, and his team at the Hamburg University of Technology, in Germany, had for years tracked an unusually high number of dams across Iran — at least 533 of them, among the most of any country in the region.
“It was always puzzling to me,” he said. “Why were they building so many dams?”
In the spring, Dr. Shokri was perusing news about the war in his home country when he came across a map plotting airstrikes that had targeted suspected military sites. The pattern — a semicircle of dots from north to south — nearly matched that of his own map marking the locations of dams.
His old question, he said, was superseded by a new one: “Why does it seem that wherever we have dams, there is a missile strike close by?”

After finding recent versions of Apple’s iPads and HomePods much easier to disassemble for battery replacements or other repairs, iFixit assumed it would be the same story for Apple’s new HomeView hub that looks like a seven-inch tablet stuck to a smart speaker. The reality was much different and by the time they got the HomeView apart iFixit’s skilled techs had “ripped a connector, snapped a speaker in two, and put more force on the poor logic board than any of us were comfortable with.”
iFixit’s Apple HomeView teardown reveals a device that will be difficult to repair
Apple’s inroads on designing repairable devices seems to have been abandoned with the HomeView.
The tablet section of the HomeView proved to be the bigger challenge to disassemble as a result of some questionable decisions with Apple’s design. The glue used to secure the display in place “held on harder than on any Apple product we’ve opened recently,” iFixit says. And while Apple’s decision to turn the HomeView’s entire aluminum chassis into a heat sink was clever, the thermal bond between a heat shield and the device’s logic board made separating the two a “remarkably risky operation.” While these design decisions possibly streamlined assembly at a factory, the extensive use of glue makes servicing the HomeView incredibly difficult.
In an accompanying teardown video iFixit also reveals how much smaller the speaker drivers are in the wall-mounted version of the HomeView versus the tabletop option. Although both versions are priced at $299, the wall version costs a little more when you factor in the required mount that’s not included, leaving iFixit feeling that you’re getting less performance while spending more money.

A widespread outage at iPhone maker Apple has brought many of its services to a standstill for thousands of users globally. According to DownDetector, users began to experience issues with some of Apple’s services at 9:51 PM IST on November 17. As per the outage tracking website, many of the big tech giant’s online services were reporting issues, including Apple Pay, iCloud, App Store, Apple Business Manager, Apple Music and Apple Support. Confirming the development, Apple’s systems update page noted that iCloud Mail, ‘Apple Care on Device’, and Apple School Manager were facing outages. Many users online also reported being signed out of services and unable to sign back in. Others reported being unable to activate new iPhones. Apple has not publicly commented on the development so far. However, the company told Bloomberg the outages were caused by an internal update and not a cyberattack. “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” the statement reportedly read. This follows a string of major outages at big tech giants. On November 12, Microsoft Outlook and Teams went offline worldwide for more than 30 hours after several of Microsoft's servers became unexpectedly unavailable, placing additional pressure on the remaining infrastructure. Prior to this in April, AI giant OpenAI also faced a partial outage which has impacted operations of its chatbot, ChatGPT, and agentic coding platform Codex and API platform. In March too, the Sam Altman-led company was also hit by an outage that left ChatGPT unavailable for thousands of users. The outages have renewed concerns over enterprise dependence on a handful of providers, with experts flagging the need for stronger business continuity plans and multi-vendor redundancy. Given the recent surge in AI-driven cyberattacks, social media users continue to speculate the reason behind the outages. So far, none of the outages in the past week have been attributed to cyberattacks, but rather to technical problems.
