The US Navy fired expired munitions during its war with Iran after changing their ammunition condition codes, the service's top civilian official told lawmakers Tuesday, comparing the practice to reviving stale bread with water and a microwave.
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao made the disclosure during his Senate confirmation hearing Tuesday, as lawmakers questioned the Pentagon's heavy expenditure of costly precision weapons during Operation Epic Fury.
"A lot of the munitions we used in Epic Fury, we were able to recode those," Cao said. "They were Code Echo, Code Foxtrot, which means they're expired."
According to a Defense Logistics Agency manual, codes Echo and Foxtrot represent materiel currently unserviceable but that could otherwise undergo limited restoration or repair.
Cao, a retired Navy captain and former explosive ordnance disposal officer, compared the practice to stretching food supplies.
"I came from a poor family," he said. "Things like bread, doesn't expire. You just rub some water on it and microwave for 15 seconds, and it's good to go."
Cao did not identify which particular munitions were recoded or how many were fired. Many of the precision weapons the US used in the Iran war cost millions of dollars each, potentially making the ability to restore and use older stock useful in a pinch.
The disclosure came while responding to Sen. Deb Fischer, a Nebraska Republican, who asked whether the Navy was striking the right balance between expensive precision weapons and cheaper weapons that could be produced in mass numbers.
Cao said the Navy had increased Tomahawk cruise missile production from roughly 125 annually during his military career to more than 60 a month now.
Cao's remarks come after months of worry surrounding whether the Pentagon has adequate quantities of costly missiles and other munitions on hand.
A Pentagon Inspector General report released in September cited findings from the Office of the Under Secretary for Acquisition and Sustainment that the munitions expenditures throughout the war with Iran had resulted in "strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply."

Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.
Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screwup grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.
Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.
The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.
“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”
So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.
1. Start With a Presumption of Innocence–or Negligence
The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.
As the head of internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One's default position should be that it isn't a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”
Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”
2. Look at Status Updates From Organizations That Might Be Involved
In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services, for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.
In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.
On top of these, there are also scenarios where one or more large services are down, and false (typically accidental or anecdotal) reports of additional outages create further confusion and opacity.
It can all feel overwhelming, even impossible, to attempt to parse these situations yourself—but there is a concrete place to start. If you think a website or service from a major tech company may be down, look for acknowledgment of the situation on their verified social media accounts or in the “newsroom” press release section of their websites. And keep in mind that you can find these pages and social media accounts through search engines, so you definitely don’t need to be familiar with every company’s communications strategy. Use this same approach for government agencies and other institutions.
Another concrete and vital source of information that you can find through search engines is what’s often known as “status dashboard” pages. Large digital platforms specifically offer these informational pages to provide transparency into whether different components of their service are functioning normally or dealing with issues. In a major incident, companies often thread incremental updates about system restoration on the status dashboard. AWS, Google Cloud Platform, and Microsoft Azure all offer these landing pages, and there are similar ones for other services like Meta business products, Google Workspace, telecom companies, AI companies, and so on.
3. Check Trusted Sources of Network Data
When a cascading tech failure causes outages across many services at once, and the point of failure isn’t clear, sources of network data that monitor the internet at a broad scale can also help determine the underlying issue. Amanda Meng, a research scientist at Georgia Tech who helps run its Internet Outage Detection and Analysis service, or IODA, points to not only IODA’s own data—and its social media accounts on BlueSky and Mastodon—but also tools like Cloudflare Radar and Watch the Net. Infoblox’s Madory also posts his own findings about network outages on his social media accounts.
When IODA sees evidence of a network disruption, “we’ll look at the timing of it, the start, the end, the network affected, anything we can find out about it, and then try and connect it with what we see from reporting,” Meng says. That scope, location, and timing of an outage can help determine a suspected cause, whether it’s a single network that might be the victim of a buggy update, a region cut off by damage to a fiber optic cable or, in rarer instances, a cyberattack or even a government purposefully cutting off internet access to its citizens to stifle protests.
Even with those network clues, however, Meng advises returning to step two: Once an affected service is identified, its actual owners are often the best source to monitor for updates. “Usually the operators have the most information about what's actually going on,” she says.
4. Look for Claims of Responsibility
Most often, mea culpa updates from companies or government agencies confirm an outage is caused by a tech mishap. In the rarer cases when that downtime results from an actual cyberattack or hacker breach, however, the hackers responsible often claim responsibility in some form.
Ransomware gangs, perhaps the most common source of serious malicious internet disruption, publicize their breaches on dark web pages that list their targets for the purposes of extortion, sometimes with a countdown timer designed to pressure victims to pay before they leak stolen information. In other cases, like the NotPetya or WannaCry worms—two of the worst cyberattacks in history—the hackers’ self-perpetuating code left behind ransom messages on machines that quickly spread on social media as the attacks unfolded. Ideological “hacktivist” groups—or state-sponsored hackers working for military or intelligence agencies but posing as hacktivists—also often take credit for their cyberattacks on platforms like X, Telegram, or their own websites. These messages then quickly spread to social media and through news reports.
Even these statements, however, should be taken as just another significant data point: Hacker groups exaggerate, misdirect, or lie when it serves their purposes. And some significant mass hacking incidents—such as the Mirai attack on the internet infrastructure company Dyn in 2016 that took down thousands of websites—have been accompanied by no public message at all from the hackers responsible.
In cases where neither the perpetrator of a hacking incident nor its target has confirmed the attack, confirmation can sometimes come first from a government agency—such as the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency—or even from threat intelligence researchers at private cybersecurity firms. Government and industry investigators sometimes post their findings to their websites or share them with media, but it often takes days, weeks, or even months to come to confirmed conclusions. Hence, step five.
5. Sit Tight and Reserve Judgment
If all these other measures of determining the cause of an outage don’t offer a clear understanding of the situation, the best approach may be patience. “It's going to get a little conclusive at some point,” Madory says. “Sometimes you just have to just sit and wait.”
Aside from the time it takes for companies to admit to their screwups—or hackers to claim a win—the length of an outage can also sometimes offer a clue to its cause. A faulty update, power outage, or cascading bug can often be resolved quickly. Determined hackers who have maximized their damage, who shift tactics to outsmart defenders, or who may still be in a network they’ve breached can cause far longer and more severe outages. “A rollback takes minutes or hours,” Tomé says, referring to reverting to older code as a fix for a faulty update that introduces a bug. “Ransomware takes days or sometimes even weeks.”
In other words, as with all breaking news, when facts are in short supply, it’s better to maintain skepticism about early rumors or conspiracy theories and wait for more concrete evidence.
In the information vacuum that precedes that evidence, it can be easy to see connections between events that may just be coincidences. What are the odds, you may ask, that five major IT outages occurred on a sequential Thursday, Friday, Monday, and Tuesday?
For Doug Madory, who tracks those network outages every day of the week, that string of failures may just be a sign of the increasing complexity of technology—and how fundamentally our civilization has come to depend on it. “For better or worse, modern society is completely mediated through internet-based services. They have outages from time to time. And that’s a reality I don't think we’ll ever completely eliminate,” Madory says.
“If you're immersed in that world of looking at outages for years on end, then they don't really surprise you,” he adds. “You just try to understand what's different about each one. And maybe what we can learn from it.”

Wales' Nations League campaign boosts Bellamy's belief
- Published
Craig Bellamy kept coming back to one word. Belief.
His Wales side had just lost a fifth game out of six to finish bottom of their Nations League group. Bellamy would have been forgiven for feeling a little bruised.
But there are ways of losing and ways of finishing bottom.
Wales were fearless against Portugal, exhilarating in attack and proving they can compete at the highest level of this competition, even as they were beaten 3-2 in Cardiff.
And while they were already consigned to the foot of the Group A4 table, Wales' previous performances meant they at least had the back-up of a relegation play-off in March to preserve their top-flight status.
"Belief's the biggest one," Bellamy said when he was asked what he and his team had taken from this campaign.
"Not just this game, but in general. We are beyond close to this level. We can more than compete at this level.
"We demand and want to expect to be. Getting into League A is big for us, but also staying in A is going to allow us to develop.
"You can only develop and improve by playing the best teams, and I felt we've taken another shift."
Wales have certainly fared better than they did when they were last in the top tier of the Nations League, when they finished with one point from six games and were relegated.
Victory against World Cup quarter-finalists Norway last month was their first at this level and, had they been more clinical in Oslo on Saturday, they might have got a second win of the campaign.
Ultimately, Wales' inability to take their chances, – combined with sloppy defensive mistakes – meant their results did not match their performances.
And the reality is that they were up against stellar opposition, whose vastly superior resources showed with their greater ruthlessness at both ends of the pitch.
"If there's anything you would have learned from these games, then you see killers. That's why they're at the top," Bellamy added.
"I know people look at results. I'm fully aware of the business. This is all I know. But I think when you look at reality as well, and you look at our performances during this group, I couldn't ask for more.
"I feel we're closer than probably maybe the players thought they were. It's fine margins.
"But I feel the biggest word out of this now has been belief, really, for me."
Relegation play-off awaits in March
Wales had the best record of the four teams who finished bottom of their top-flight groups, meaning they have a second chance to avoid relegation in the form of a two-leg play-off in March.
At Friday's draw in Switzerland, Bellamy's side will discover whether they will face Slovenia, Hungary, Republic of Ireland or Bosnia-Herzegovina, who beat them in a World Cup play-off earlier this year.
Those teams all finished second in their League B groups and, as the League A team, Wales will have home advantage in the second leg.
"Going into the next one, we have to be in this group," said Bellamy. "If we want to develop as a football nation and keep going forward, we have to be playing against the best teams. It's only going to improve you.
"I know we can go back to League B... It's about playing the best teams. That's how we're going to get better.
"I honestly believe it. I won't be here for the next Nations League. I won't be the manager then. So I'm doing it for the next one, but I'm also doing it for the players.
"We've got to. That's how we're going to be the best version of us and keep improving."

Prince and Princess of Wales arrive in India ahead of meeting with Modi
- Published
The Prince and Princess of Wales have arrived in India for a three-day visit that will include a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
The visit is the first time William and Catherine have been on an official overseas trip together in four years.
Her cancer treatment has limited the amount of international travel she has undertaken but she will be with her husband for several engagements this week.
Most are related to the Earthshot Prize, founded by Prince William, which awards five £1m prizes for the best solutions to the biggest climate challenges.
"The princess is enormously proud of what the prince has achieved with Earthshot and is really looking forward to being alongside him for what is one of the most important moments in his year," said a spokesperson for the royals.
"She's seen it develop into something truly remarkable and is excited to experience first-hand just how far it has come."
The meeting with Modi was a late addition to the royal schedule after the Indian prime minister confirmed he would be back from a scheduled trip to the Philippines in time to see the royals.
They will fly from Mumbai to Delhi for the meeting on Wednesday.
"For the Prince, it represents another significant engagement as he continues to take on a growing role on the international stage," a Kensington Palace spokesperson said.
"We've seen him increasingly support the UK's diplomatic relationships through his overseas engagements, and this meeting will provide an opportunity to build on those connections at the highest level."
The couple last met Modi on their official visit to India in 2016.
Arriving in Mumbai earlier on Monday Prince William posted a message about the trip on social media: "India has made an extraordinary contribution to Earthshot over the past six years and is home to more Earthshot finalists and winners than any other country."
The royals will carry out a number of engagements in Mumbai related to the environment, cricket, young families and the Bollywood film industry.
At an Earthshot Prize Awards ceremony, five innovations will be announced as winners of the million-pound prizes.
Nominees range from projects to increase the number of electric rickshaws in India to a scheme able to detect wildfires faster than Nasa.
The event will be hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.
Take That will perform and guests will include actor Rami Malek and Australian conservationist and TV presenter Robert Irwin, who joined Prince William when he was a surprise guest on The Graham Norton show last month.
"There is a lot of environmental potential here in Mumbai," said Irwin. "There is also a huge amount of young people who have a passion for environmentalism and I think Earthshot is mobilising that here in India."

Srinagar- Security forces on Wednesday shot dead Lashkar-e-Taiba commander Lateef Bhat, who was wanted for the attack on a CRPF post on November 11, in an encounter in Kulgam district of South Kashmir, officials said.
Bhat had taken shelter inside a mosque in Zangalpora village in the Devsar area of South Kashmir and refused to heed repeated appeals by senior officers of the Army and police to surrender, they said.
“Bhat has been killed, and his body, along with a weapon, was recovered from the encounter site,” an official said.
CRPF Director General G P Singh lauded the security forces for the operation. “Congratulations guys. Some dishes are best served cold, even in cold weather,” Singh posted on X.
In a post on X, Kashmir Zone Police said, “The body of one neutralised terrorist, along with a weapon, have been recovered from the encounter site. The killed Terrorist neutralised during the joint operation is identified as Mohd Lateef Bhat R/o Khrewan, Kulgam.Further details are awaited”.
According to officials, Bhat and his associate, Umar Nisar Dar, were involved in the November 11 attack on CRPF personnel in Kulgam that left three paramilitary personnel injured.
While Dar was killed in a gunfight in the Laru bypass area of the district on Monday, Bhat had managed to give security forces the slip.
Acting on specific intelligence inputs early Wednesday, the Army, along with a team of elite Special Operations Group of Jammu and Kashmir Police, launched a cordon-and-search operation in Zangalpora, located about nine km from Monday’s encounter site.
Once the cordon was tightened around the mosque where Bhat was hiding, security forces exercised “maximum restraint” owing to the sanctity of the religious place and made prolonged efforts to persuade him to lay down arms, Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP), Kulgam, Anayat Ali Chowdhary told reporters.
“We tried very hard and appealed to Lateef to surrender. Both I and the Commanding Officer (CO) of the Army had a very long conversation with him via a video call on a phone sent inside,” Chowdhary said, adding that officers told him he was still young and urged him to surrender, but he refused.
Videos of the security forces’ appeals to Bhat also surfaced on social media.
When Bhat refused to relent and opened fire on the security personnel, a gunfight ensued, the SSP said. The forces retaliated, resulting in his death.

On Monday, the Supreme Court announced it would not hear an appeal of a lower court decision that blocked the government from canceling the grants of a handful of researchers whose funding had been revoked during the Trump administration’s purge of DEI-related work. While the decision applies to only seven researchers in California, the lower court had ruled that the government’s actions violated the First Amendment and so may have broad implications.
The Supreme Court provided no discussion of its rejection, and no justices filed a dissent regarding the decision.
The suit was initially filed by a large group of researchers at the University of California, Berkeley and UC San Francisco, contesting grants originally issued by many federal agencies, from the National Institutes of Health to the Department of Transportation. At issue were grants that had been terminated because the agencies decided they violated a Trump executive order blocking the use of DEI. This occurred despite the fact that the government hadn’t bothered to define DEI, and targeted grants were often identified by little more than a keyword search.
In the wake of a Supreme Court decision that held that most grant termination cases had to be heard by a different court, the case was narrowed considerably to just seven UC researchers and a handful of agencies: The Environmental Protection Agency, the National Science Foundation, and the National Endowment for the Humanities.

For three months, Suraj Kumar’s job was to feed discarded clothes into shredding machines in Panipat, an industrial city in the north Indian state of Haryana. Clothes discarded in the US, Canada and Europe arrive in the city to be torn back into fibres and spun into yarn, feeding a textile recycling industry that supplies markets across the world.
Suraj, 19, had travelled from West Bengal state to work in Panipat’s factories, following his cousins and friends who had already found jobs there. He hoped to earn enough to send money home to his parents. But in late August, an electrical short circuit in the machine propelled him into the shredding mechanism. The accident crushed both arms.
“I wish I had died rather than lost both my arms,” Suraj says. An only child, he had hoped his job in Panipat would support his parents. Instead, he fears he has become a financial burden on them. The work he had taken up to help his family has left him dependent on others, with no certainty about what his future will look like.
By some estimates, Panipat processes more than 1m tons of used clothing from across the world every year, making it one of the world’s largest textile recycling hubs. In the city’s 20,000 factories, employing about 300,000 people, discarded clothes are shredded into yarn and made into finished products, including home furnishings for brands such as H&M Home, Ikea, Primark, Tesco and Walmart.
But the fast-fashion industry, built on buying more and more clothes and wearing them less, carries a devastating cost for workers tackling its waste. Ramesh Chaudhary, an environmental activist who has worked in Panipat’s labour department, has been tracking reports of injuries and amputations across the city for the past five years. He estimates that at least one worker a day loses a limb, rising to as many as five on some days.
“Every day, we come across cases of workers injured inside factories, sometimes losing a hand or a leg, and sometimes even dying,” Chaudhary says. He gathers his information through a network of labour contractors who supply workers to factories across Panipat. But not all news of injuries reaches him, he says, suggesting the scale of the problem could be greater.
Between 17 and 24 August this year, the Guardian monitored reports from 11 private hospitals and two government hospitals in Panipat. In that period, six cases of textile workers with severe limb injuries were reported: two had lost an arm, another man lost both, one lost a hand, one lost a leg and the sixth their fingers.
Such injuries are common in Panipat’s factories, says Chaudhary, because machinery often lacks the necessary safety mechanisms. If a worker gets caught in a spinning machine, he says, cutting the power may not stop it immediately. By the time the machine comes to a halt, a worker may already have catastrophic injuries.
During numerous visits to spinning units and factories, the Guardian did not see anyone wearing any kind of safety gear. None of the workers interviewed reported having safety training.
India’s 1948 Factories Act places a duty on factory owners to protect workers’ health and safety. It requires serious workplace accidents to be reported to the authorities. But the effectiveness of safety oversight remains a concern, says Sandeep Sachdeva, co-founder of the Safe in India Foundation, which works to reduce industrial injuries.
“Factories are often audited by buyers, especially where quality and critical components are involved, and inspected by government industrial safety and health departments. Buyer audits tend to focus more on commercial requirements and product quality than on workplace safety or working conditions,” he says.
“Government inspections are selected through a central software system, but inspectors are now required to inform factories before visiting. Their role is now that of a facilitator-cum-inspector – a shift that undermines the effectiveness of inspections, particularly in factories with unsafe working conditions.”
For workers, losing a limb means losing their livelihood. Ramashankar Singh, who is in his fifties, from Chapra in Bihar, spent 18 years in Panipat’s factories before an accident last year led to him having a leg amputated.
It happened when a hot ball bearing fell on his foot. Ramashankar’s injury was first just wrapped in discarded cloth, before the factory owner sent him to a pharmacy.
The wound worsened as the infection spread. When Ramashankar approached his employer again, the owner agreed to arrange treatment and admitted him to a private hospital. By then, the infection had progressed so far that doctors had to amputate his leg above the knee.
“The factory owner said he would give me another job, possibly as a cook or a security guard at the factory,” Ramashankar says. “But that never happened.” The owner also said he would help him secure a government disability pension, but he has received no pension since the accident and relies on a prosthetic leg provided by a charitable organisation.
After so much of his life spent in a factory, Ramashankar says: “I have almost forgotten how to live without work. Much of my day now passes lying on my bed, staring at the ceiling fan.”
He also struggles with guilt that he has become a burden on his family.
India’s textile industry is the country’s second-largest source of employment after agriculture, directly employing more than 45 million people. An estimated 92% of its workforce is informally employed. In Panipat, more than 90% of workers are employed informally, says Ina Bahuguna, programme manager at the Estonia-based Reverse Resources, which monitors the city’s textile waste.
“Formal employment contracts and the social security benefits that accompany them, including pensions, are largely limited to workers in management, clerical roles and some specialised jobs, such as tailoring,” says Bahuguna.
Most workers on the factory floor lack these protections, leaving those who suffer serious injuries particularly vulnerable. Without formal employment or adequate social security coverage, they are left without employer-backed compensation, rehabilitation support or a source of income.
The Guardian asked several factory owners why they hired workers on a contractual or piece-rate basis rather than in permanent positions, and most cited the workers’ seasonal migration, saying some did not return to Panipat after travelling home.
For workers who sustain life-changing injuries, getting employers to pay for medical treatment can be a struggle. Indrapal Singh, who lost his arm in 2017, had worked in Panipat for 15 years, two and a half of those at the factory where he was injured. His hand was caught in a Chinese-made carding machine, which tore away the skin. He was given a painkilling injection but, as the infection worsened, his arm had to be amputated. The factory owner refused to pay his hospital bills.
Indrapal spent six years fighting his case through the courts, but says he received no compensation. The police told him that he had signed documents withdrawing his complaint, something Indrapal, who says he cannot read or write, disputes.
“I lost my arm, fought for six years, and in the end, all I got was a government pension of 5,700 rupees [£45]. The factory owner has faced no consequences, and the factory continues to operate as before,” he says.
Chaudhary says: “Workers have very little bargaining power when they are up against factory owners who are not only financially powerful but sometimes politically influential too. For many workers, taking them on in a legal fight is simply not an option.”
Arvind Kumar, the officer in charge at one of Panipat’s 12 police stations, says three workplace injury cases have been registered at his station so far this year. One involved the death of a worker. “Fewer than 1% of workplace injury cases reach the police and are formally registered,” he says.
Most cases, the officer says, are settled outside the formal legal system. Workers may receive a one-time payment towards medical bills, but then are generally left to manage the long-term consequences of their injuries on their own. The police rarely get involved.
For now, Suraj Kumar’’s family are grateful that the factory owner covered his hospital bills. They are not sure whether to register a police complaint.
“He [the owner] is like God to us. He is paying for our boy’s treatment,” says his mother, Sita.
Suraj struggles to imagine what comes next. “I thought that if I worked hard for two years, I could buy myself a motorcycle. I had so many things I wanted to do with my life. I never thought I would have to start by figuring out how to live without my arms.”

A humanoid robotics company backed and advised by President Donald Trump’s son, Eric Trump, has reportedly missed payroll and may be on the brink of collapse after a funding shortfall. The Silicon Valley startup, Foundation Future Industries, claims it is developing and testing robots for military roles on battlefields from Ukraine to Gaza.
Foundation failed to pay employees for the payroll period ending on October 30, anonymous sources told CNBC. The startup’s staff is especially angry because Foundation’s co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak, supposedly borrowed $4.6 million in company funds to buy a luxury home overlooking San Francisco Bay about a year ago.
This comes as Pathak and Foundation’s leadership are still looking to raise funding to support a $3 billion valuation, based on their promise to develop a humanoid robot ready for combat duty and capable of wielding various weapons.
The company has demonstrated a humanoid robot named the Phantom MK-1 and is touting an upcoming robot called the Phantom MK-2. Foundation has touted its humanoid robots for roles in warehouses and other workplaces—but has courted media coverage by claiming it is developing humanoid robots for battlefield use.
Now CNBC’s reporting based on “people with direct knowledge of the matter” indicates that insiders worry the startup could soon collapse without additional funding.
Foundation’s business claims
Eric Trump holds an equity stake in Foundation and was announced as its chief strategy advisor in March 2026, according to the Financial Times. Investment funds linked to both Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. are involved with multiple military technology companies that have received Pentagon loans and contracts worth more than $3.2 billion as of July 2026, according to The Washington Post.

The European Film Academy will honor multi-award-winning Belgian directorial duo Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne with a Lifetime Achievement Award at its 39th European Film Awards in January 2027.
Among the most internationally acclaimed filmmakers to emerge from Belgium and Europe, the brothers have left an indelible mark on European cinema history over the past four decades with their films exploring what it means to live in a society shaped by inequality, migration, and economic pressure.
Born in Seraing, in the industrial region of Liège in Wallonia, the landscape and social realities of the region have been an important part of their cinema, providing both the setting and the social environment for many of their films.
Jean-Pierre Dardenne studied Dramatic Arts at the Institut des Arts de Diffusion in Brussels, where he was taught by the French playwright and director Armand Gatti.
Watch on Deadline
Through Gatti, the brothers became involved in filmmaking and started documenting the lives and experiences of people in their local community.
Beginning their careers in the late 1970s, the Dardennes established themselves as documentary filmmakers through their production company Dérives, before moving onto fiction.
The brothers made their first fiction feature film Falsch in 1987, adapted from a play by René Kalisky about the last surviving member of a Jewish family murdered during the Holocaust.
They founded their production company Les Films du Fleuve in 1987. Its early production including The Promise (1996) gave a taste of the distinctive cinematic approach steeped in social issues and authenticity.
Set in the industrial world of Liège, it followed Igor, a teenage mechanic’s apprentice whose father is involved in the exploitation of undocumented workers.
Three years later, they would break out internationally with Rosetta, which won the brothers their first Cannes Palme d’Or.
Starring now late actress Émilie Dequenne, the film revolved around a young woman struggling to find work and escape poverty.
Dardennes have continued their relationship with Cannes and its main competition throughout their career.
They won their second Palme d’Or in 2005 with The Child, starring Jérémie Renier as a young father who makes a devastating decision concerning his newborn son. In 2008, they won Best Screenplay for Lorna’s Silence, while The Kid With A Bike clinched the Grand Prix in 2011.
In 2019, the Dardennes received the Cannes Best Director Award for Young Ahmed, while Tori and Lokita, a drama about two young migrants from Africa who have arrived in Belgium alone, received the the festival’s 75th Anniversary Prize in 2022.
They were back at the festival in 2025 with Young Mothers, which received the Best Screenplay Award and the Ecumenical Jury Prize.
They also have a long relationship with European Film Academy. In 1997, Gigi, Monica… et Bianca won the European Film Award for Best Documentary, The Kid With A Bike received European Screenwriter Award, and Marion Cotillard clinched the European Film Award for Best Actress for her performance in their 2015 film Two Days, One Night.
“Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne have received some of the highest honours in European and international cinema,” the European Film Academy said in a statement announcing the honor. “Their work has been celebrated not only for its artistic achievement, but for its sustained engagement with questions of social inequality, migration, work, family and human dignity.”
The brothers will receive their Lifetime Achievement Award at the European Awards Ceremony on January 17, 2027.

Tracking China’s War of Words Against Japan
Beijing is running a concerted campaign to paint Japan as an aggressor and resurgent military threat, according to a Times analysis.
When China’s leader, Xi Jinping, met with President Trump at the White House earlier this fall, the two leaders toasted to friendly relations.
But in private, Mr. Xi offered Mr. Trump a stark warning about Japan, a U.S. ally, according to two officials briefed on the talks, who requested anonymity to discuss private conversations. Mr. Xi told Mr. Trump that Japan’s recent military buildup threatened to destabilize Asia, the officials said, and that Mr. Trump should be cautious about working with Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, describing her as a “militarist.”
The warning from Mr. Xi was part of a broader effort by China to isolate and undermine Japan after Ms. Takaichi said last year that Japan could be forced to defend Taiwan in case of a Chinese invasion. China considers Taiwan, a self-governed democracy that lies just 69 miles from Japan’s westernmost island, part of its territory.
Since the comments, Mr. Xi has overseen a campaign involving propaganda and diplomacy to target Japan, according to interviews with officials and scholars, and an analysis by The New York Times of Chinese Foreign Ministry briefings and state media. It is all part of a push, analysts say, to persuade the world that Japan is a resurgent aggressor.
The Times found that:
- China has deployed words and images to portray Japan as a World War II-era enemy, using phrases like “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism,” and videos that compare Japan to a “rampaging gray rhino.”
- Chinese officials have repeatedly sought to belittle Ms. Takaichi, Japan’s first female prime minister, omitting her title in official briefings, breaking with longstanding practice. State media has depicted Ms. Takaichi in short skirts and a nurse’s uniform in cartoons, and described her as “Abe’s girl,” referring to Shinzo Abe, the former Japanese prime minister and Ms. Takaichi’s mentor.
- In private conversations with Western scholars, Chinese academics have recently pushed the narrative that Japan is the “Israel of East Asia,” poised to lead the United States into conflict and destabilize the region.
- Russia has helped amplify China’s talking points, branding Japan as a threat. Moscow has echoed Beijing in describing Japan as an “enemy state” that is not to be trusted, invoking a World War II-era designation used against former Axis powers.
Mr. Xi and Ms. Takaichi will cross paths this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit meeting in Shenzhen, China. The encounter is expected to be frosty; Mr. Xi might try to use the summit as an opportunity to alienate Ms. Takaichi from Japan’s allies, experts say.

Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

The Union government’s health expenditure more than tripled to ₹4.14 lakh crore in 2023-24, from ₹1.30 lakh crore in 2013-14, according to the latest National Health Accounts (NHA) estimates released by the Health Ministry.
The estimates also showed the share of out-of-pocket spending by households dropped by 21.5 percentage points over the same period, highlighting a significant transformation in the country’s healthcare financing.
As a share of total health expenditure, out-of-pocket spending fell from 64.2% in 2013-14 to 42.7% in 2023-24.
“The simultaneous increase in public healthcare financing and decline in the proportion of spending borne directly by households reflect India’s progress towards a more accessible, affordable, and financially protective healthcare system,” the Ministry said in a statement. It said out-of-pocket expenditure declined from 43.4% in 2022-23 to 42.7% in 2023-24.
“The sustained downward trend reflects the expanding role of government-supported healthcare services and financial protection mechanisms. Initiatives aimed at improving access to free and affordable treatment, medicines, diagnostics and hospital services are supporting efforts to reduce dependence on direct household spending,” it said.
Private insurance growth
The government’s share in total health expenditure increased by 14.9 percentage points over the decade, the estimates showed, while per capita government health expenditure rose from ₹1,042 in 2013-14 to ₹2,959 in 2023-24, an increase of nearly three times. Social security expenditure on health rose from 6% of total health expenditure in 2013-14 to 11% in 2023-24.
This includes government-financed health insurance schemes such as Ayushman Bharat-Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana, State insurance schemes, social health insurance, and medical expenditure for government employees. Private health insurance expenditure grew even faster, with its share rising from 3.4% to 10.2% over the decade.
Focus on primary healthcare
The government’s expenditure on primary healthcare stood at about ₹1.53 lakh crore in 2023-24, underscoring the increased focus on primary and community-level healthcare, the Ministry said.
Initiatives such as Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, free drugs and diagnostics, the Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme, the Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana and AMRIT pharmacies had contributed to efforts to improve access to affordable healthcare, it said.
The Ayushman Bharat-PMJAY had also strengthened financial protection by providing cashless hospitalisation benefits to eligible beneficiaries, it added.
The NHA Estimates for India 2023-24 are the 11th round of estimates prepared by the NHA3 Technical Secretariat, which operates within the National Health Systems Resource Centre of the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. They are prepared using the internationally recognised System of Health Accounts 2011 framework.

FAA suspends installation of router that led to a ground stop of flights across the US
The router malfunctioned and flooded other routers with data, prompting the FAA to order the ground stop.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has suspended the installation of a router model made by Hewlett-Packard Enterprise-owned Juniper Networks, which was part of its modernization efforts. As The New York Times reports, the agency believes the router played a major role in the issue that caused it to order a ground stop for all flights in the US on November 13. In addition to suspending new installations, it has also disabled more than 60 routers that had already been installed.
If you'll recall, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the ground stop on old hardware the first time he spoke about the event. But Duffy revealed a day later that the issue was connected to the modernization of America's aviation facilities.
He said a contractor from tech company L3Harris was working on switching telecommunication lines from old copper wires to fiber and on installing the new router at an FAA site in El Dorado, Arkansas. That router started flooding other routers in the air traffic control system with data. Another router in Amarillo, Texas had also gone haywire, and the FAA responded by disabling both of them.
The agency said the router was tested for a year before installations started. "Sixty-eight times it worked well," he sad at a news conference. "This one router started to broadcast into our network, and it started to overload the network." In aviation, routers are used to transmit data, including radar feeds, flight plans and weather information.
Despite knowing that it was the router that caused the issue, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said they still don't know what triggered it. The Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee's Democratic members are urging the agency to find out why it had malfunctioned. They also asked the FAA to report to Congress on how it's going to prevent the same thing from happening in the future.
Duffy said he was told by national security agencies that the issue wasn't caused by a cyberattack, but he still asked the FBI to be part of the team analyzing the router from Arkansas. The Transport Secretary has also renewed his calls for Congress to approve an additional $50 billion in funding to modernize America's air traffic control system. "I would just tell you, the longer we stay on an old rickety network, the less safe it becomes," he said. "We do have to get this work done. Otherwise, staying on the old system for longer is going to mean more risk as opposed to fixing the system, and you're going to reduce the risk."

There is no evidence Trump plans to revive the legislation. Even if he was, it would be impossible to use that specific act to bar Muslims from holding public office. It would also likely be unconstitutional.
In November, a claim spread that President Donald Trump was planning to "revive" immigration and nationality legislation from 1952 in order to bar Muslims from holding public office in the United States.
For example, one Facebook user wrote (archived):
BREAKING: President Trump is reportedly pushing to ban Muslims from holding public office!
Reports suggest that President Trump wants to revive the 1952 McCarran-Walter Act to bar Muslims from holding public office.
(David J Harris Jr., accessed via Facebook)
The rumor also circulated on X and TikTok, starting at the end of October, while Snopes readers searched our site seeking more information.
Snopes investigated part of this claim in 2018. At that time, social media users falsely claimed the McCarran-Walter Act of 1952, which is named in the posts above, barred people of Muslim faith from holding public office.
This remains false in 2026, as the 1952 act is unchanged.
There is also no evidence the Trump administration is seeking to use the act, which upheld controversial immigration quotas, to bar Muslims from holding public office, as of this writing. His administration has invoked the act before, according to reputable news reports, but never to bar people from public office.
Trump has also previously talked about a "Muslim ban" on social media, though this also refers to immigration policy rather than blocking anyone from public office. As of this writing, he has not explicitly mentioned the McCarran-Walter Act on Truth Social — his social media app where he regularly discusses his policy ideas — according to Trump's Truth, which archives his posts on the platform.
Using the legislation in this way would not only be impossible, given what it actually governed, but also potentially unconstitutional due to the Constitution's Article Six, Clause Three, which bars "religious tests" from ever being used to determine whether a person can hold public office.
We contacted the White House Press Office for comment on the claim that Trump is planning to use the 1952 act, or any other legislative powers, to ban people of the Muslim faith from running for office. We await a reply to our inquiries.
Snopes wrote about the McCarran-Walter Act in 2018. Rather than barring people from public office, the legislation focused on denying people entry into the U.S. if they were deemed a threat to the government:
The McCarran-Walter Act of 1952 allowed the U.S. to deny citizenship to persons belonging to organizations deemed to be a threat to the government. While that singular aspect of the law remains on the books, not one aspect of that law or its successors is concerned with the suitability of any person to hold public office, and therefore the claim that this act bars Muslims from holding office is false.
The Constitution's Article Six, Clause Three, reads (emphasis ours):
The Senators and Representatives before mentioned, and the Members of the several State Legislatures, and all executive and judicial Officers, both of the United States and of the several States, shall be bound by Oath or Affirmation, to support this Constitution; but no religious Test shall ever be required as a Qualification to any Office or public Trust under the United States.
FactCheck.org, a fellow fact-checking organization, also reported on fake claims about the scope of the McCarran-Walter Act in 2018.
The outlet says that social media posts claiming the act could be used to bar people of the Muslim faith from public office first circulated after Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib, both Muslim women, were elected to the House in Minnesota and Michigan, respectively, that year.
For further reading, Snopes frequently investigates rumors about immigration and Islam.

Haryana CM launches 'Namo Morni Mission' to promote organic, natural farming
Chief Minister Nayab Singh Saini launched the Namo Morni Mission and announced farmer-focused facilities. The initiative seeks to develop Morni as an organic farming block by 2029.
Haryana Chief Minister Nayab Singh Saini on Tuesday launched the 'Namo Morni Mission', saying the initiative aims to transform Morni in Panchkula district into an ideal block for organic and natural farming by 2029.
Saini also announced several significant initiatives for local farmers, including a dedicated helpline, 01733-297010, to address all their concerns.
A joint office of the Departments of Agriculture, Horticulture, and Soil and Water Conservation will also be set up in Morni, and experts will train farmers and make organic fertilisers, seeds, and bio-inputs available to them, he said.
The Chief Minister was addressing a gathering after inaugurating a two-day state-level 'natural-organic farming farmers' fair' at the Government Polytechnic College, Morni. He also launched the 'Mati Vandan Pakhwada' and unveiled its poster.
Saini said under 'Mati Vandan Pakhwada', 15 special programmes will be organised across Haryana, bringing together farmers, doctors, youth, traders, eminent citizens, and agricultural scientists.
The objective is to transform this government initiative into a mass movement through active public participation, he added.
A state-level programme will be organised on December 5, on the occasion of World Soil Day, where agricultural scientists from various states, including Sikkim, will share their experiences and successful models.
Announcing the 'Namo Morni Mission', the Chief Minister said that the initiative aims to transform Morni into an ideal block for organic and natural farming by 2029, on the lines of Sikkim.
Under the mission, efforts will be made to provide facilities to farmers, keeping their landholdings in view, while four modern laboratories dedicated to soil testing, bio-analysis, nutritional assessment, and pesticide residue testing will be established, he said.
“These facilities will also strengthen the implementation of the Soil Health Card Scheme,” he added.
Keeping in view the hilly and difficult terrain of Morni, the government has also decided to provide a 75 per cent subsidy on small agricultural implements to facilitate farming activities and provide relief to local farmers.
Saini further announced that Morni would have its own agricultural produce, own brand, and own local marketplace.
Haryana State Cooperative Supply and Marketing Federation Limited (HAFED) will serve as the nodal agency for the procurement of organic and naturally grown products, which will be marketed under the brand name 'Morni Organic Fresh'.
An app will also be developed to facilitate online sales, while the Haryana State Agricultural Marketing Board will establish a dedicated organic mandi in Morni itself, he said. He also announced that the entire Morni block would be developed as an 'organic block'.
“Over the next three years, approximately 5,600 acres of land will be brought under this initiative, including 3,360 acres for agriculture and 2,240 acres for horticulture,” Saini said.
The Chief Minister said that under the National Mission on Natural Farming, community resource persons in Morni block, currently receiving an honorarium of Rs 5,000 per month, will get an additional Rs 5,000 per month, taking their total monthly honorarium to Rs 10,000.
Highlighting another initiative, Saini said that local farmers, in collaboration with the Haryana unit of the International Potato Centre, are producing potato seedlings using the 'apical root cutting' technique.
"A 70 per cent subsidy is being provided for the construction of polyhouses for this purpose, while farmers contribute the remaining 30 per cent,” he said.
“So far, 15 polyhouses have been established in Morni, producing approximately 15 to 20 lakh potato seedlings annually. These seedlings are being supplied not only to farmers across Haryana but also to other states, significantly enhancing the income of farmers in Morni,” the CM added.
Pointing out that the natural farming scheme was launched in 2022, Saini said approximately 2 lakh farmers have registered nearly 3 lakh acres of land under the scheme, while around 24,000 farmers have adopted natural farming practices on more than 44,000 acres.
The target is to bring 1.5 lakh acres of land under actual natural and organic cultivation by 2030-31, he added.

New Delhi- The Supreme Court on Wednesday issued notice on a plea filed by the Supreme Court Bar Association seeking contempt action against a lawyer who made unsavoury remarks against Chief Justice of India Surya Kant.
A three-judge bench of Justices Dipankar Datta, Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana sought response from the lawyer.
“Having perused the papers before us, which include the consent of the AG under Section 15(1)(b) of the Contempt Act, we are prima facie satisfied that the motion of SCBA for initiation of pleading against the sole respondent referred in the petition requires to be taken forward. We issue notice returnable January 20, 2027,” the bench said.
The Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) president and senior advocate Pradeep Rai, appearing for the SCBA, submitted that this kind of conduct is totally unacceptable.
In an unusual turn of events on Monday, a lawyer was escorted out of a courtroom of the apex court after he made unsubstantiated and unsavoury remarks against the CJI.
After a bench comprising the CJI and Justices Bagchi and Mohana assembled in the afternoon on Monday, the lawyer sought an urgent hearing on his submissions regarding alleged corruption in the judiciary.
He alleged that he had not received any response from the CJI’s office to his communication on the issue sent on November 2.
The lawyer urged the top court to accord a hearing straightaway.
“You cannot mention anything like this,” Justice Mohana observed.
When the lawyer persisted, the CJI said, “We will see, you just wait.”
However, the lawyer allegedly proceeded to make unsavoury remarks against the CJI.
“No, I will not wait. You cannot sit in that chair. You do not deserve. You do not have the integrity for that,” the lawyer had said.
After that, the virtual proceedings of the court were stopped for some time.
Later, according to sources, the lawyer was escorted out of the courtroom by the security personnel present there.

Nabeel Rajab, prominent Bahraini human rights activist, dies at 62
Nabeel Rajab, a prominent democracy activist who advocated for the rights of Bahrain’s Shiite majority and spent years in prison for challenging the country’s monarchy, has died
Nabeel Rajab, a prominent democracy activist from Bahrain who helped lead the island nation’s 2011 Arab Spring protests and spent years in prison for challenging its monarchy, died on Tuesday. He was 62.
His family found him unresponsive at their home in Turkey on Tuesday morning, friends and activists said. The Bahrain Center for Human Rights, which Rajab once led as president, confirmed his death in a post on X.
“We extend our sincere condolences and heartfelt sympathy to his esteemed family. We pray that God may encompass him with his vast mercy and reward him abundantly for his efforts and contributions,” the group wrote.
Ebrahim Sharif, an activist and close friend of the family, said Rajab's wife and daughter took him to a hospital in Istanbul, where he was pronounced dead. He said after speaking with Rajab's brother that the family believes Rajab likely died of a heart attack.
Rajab for decades was one of Bahrain's leading human rights activists. He frequently posted on social media about Bahrain's treatment of dissidents, and was an unusually visible figure in a country where voicing criticism can carry enormous risk.
In 2002, Rajab helped establish the Bahrain Center for Human Rights, which became a platform for him and his colleagues to call for democratic reforms in the island nation, where a Sunni monarchy rules over a predominantly Shiite Muslim population.
He rose to international prominence in 2011 as the Arab Spring uprisings swept the region and demonstrations erupted in Bahrain.
As one of the movement’s best-known voices, he joined thousands of demonstrators occupying Manama’s Pearl Roundabout and kept protesting even after a violent crackdown by security forces. He and the protesters described their demands as fair elections, constitutional democracy and an end to preferential treatment for Bahrain’s Sunni minority.
Bahrain ultimately put down the uprising with the help of troops from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
Though Bahrain’s constitution guarantees freedom of speech, Rajab was prosecuted under laws criminalizing remarks that insult foreign countries or government agencies or spread false rumors during wartime.
He was imprisoned on multiple occasions in the years that followed. The detentions drew international criticism from the United Nations, human rights groups and some of Bahrain’s closest allies, including the United States, which bases its Navy’s 5th Fleet in the island kingdom.
He was released to home detention in June 2020 during the coronavirus pandemic while serving a five-year sentence over tweets criticizing the Saudi-led war in Yemen and alleging prison abuse.
“Nabeel really stood out for standing up for the most vulnerable even when he knew the cost would be extremely heavy,” said Sayed Ahmed AlWadaei of the London-based Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy.
Rajab left Bahrain with his family early in the Iran war, as authorities cracked down on Shiite-led protests. Rajab accused the government of torturing an imprisoned activist and feared he would be arrested if he returned, he told The Associated Press at the time.
The International Federation for Human Rights, where Rajab served as deputy secretary-general from 2010 to 2020, called him an inspiration.
“The world has lost a truly exceptional human rights defender. He paid for his commitment to a more just world with many years in prison and constant harassment by the Bahraini authorities. This must have taken a toll on his health,” said Alexis Deswaef, the group's president.

The Kashmiri wazwan, an array of dishes adding up to 4,500-5,500 calories partaken during festivals and weddings, is one of the key cultural factors contributing to a spike in cases of diabetes in Kashmir, experts said.
Kashmir’s social life is organised around large, meat-centred feasts, most visibly the wazwan served at weddings or on Eid. Diabetes Simplified for Kashmir, a book released on World Diabetes Day (November 14), said the multi-course meal can run to over 30 mutton and chicken preparations, with the calorie intake “several times the average daily requirement”.
“Such exposure accumulates rather than occurs in isolation, and repeated post-prandial glucose and lipid excursions of this magnitude plausibly contribute to the region’s rising dysglycaemia burden,” the book, co-authored by endocrinologists Mohammad Hayat Bhat and Shahnawaz Mir, and cardiologist Nasir Shams, stated.
J&K has witnessed a spike in the incidence of diabetes in the past three years. The Union Territory screened more than 2.15 million people for diabetes; 48,623 individuals have been diagnosed to have diabetes, according to data from the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. In 2025-2026, 2.84 million people were screened and 85,948 were found to have diabetes. “In the past three years, J&K added 2.18 lakh new patients to its diabetes burden,” the Ministry’s data suggested.
Apart from more universally seen factors, including poor physical activity and consumption of tobacco, the book identifies Kashmir’s unique lifestyle among the contributing factors.
“Kashmir’s daily plate remains rice-centric with rice typically supplying the bulk of meal volume and carbohydrate load. Large portions of rice translate directly into high postprandial glycaemic load,” it said.
“Type 2 diabetes prevalence in Kashmir has risen sharply within a single generation. A survey in 1999 found known diabetes in just 1.89% of adults, with 4.25% undiagnosed. Recent Indian Council of Medical Research-INDIA data show 7.8% prevalence,” the authors said, attributing the rising incidence of Type 2 diabetes to lifestyle in Kashmir.
The book noted that such a rapid shift cannot reflect genetic change. “It points instead to a compressed nutrition and lifestyle transition, as subsistence agriculture and labour-intensive living have been replaced by urbanisation and declining physical activity, while traditional dietary patterns — rice-centric meals, salt tea, preserved winter foods, and elaborate festive feasting — persist largely unchanged,” the experts said.
They also attributed the rise in cases of diabetes to Kashmir’s winters. “The glycaemic and fat load of the traditional meat and generous portion sizes do not act in isolation. Their convergence with a pronounced winter sedentary period appears to produce a compounding rather than merely additive metabolic burden across the Kashmiri annual cycle, in which periods of highest intake coincide with the lowest levels of expenditure,” they added.
Seasonal confinement and winter lifestyle patterns in the Kashmir Valley’s prolonged winter, which are marked by heavy snowfall and sub-zero temperatures for several months, compress daily life to indoor spaces, warmed by the hammam, a built-in masonry hearth, and the kangri, a portable wicker-encased firepot carried beneath the pheran, a long woollen robe.
“Large meals could be risky or other sudden triggers for heart attacks. Overeating should be considered as a heart attack trigger, much in the same way that extreme physical activities and severe anger episodes can provoke an attack,” the doctors warned.

Despite being a new Grand Theft Auto game, the sixth main entry in the franchise comes with its fair share of cameos you might not have expected. From celebrity radio appearances to returning GTA characters, there are plenty of GTA 6 cameos from major celebrities, streamers, and singers, and there are even more surprises to uncover.
All GTA 6 Cameos Confirmed So Far
Before we jump to theories and speculations, there are confirmed characters in GTA 6 we know will return from the previous games. Here is a list of all the GTA 6 cameos and surprise appearances we have spotted so far:
Valentina
Valentina is a returning character from GTA Online who appears in GTA 6. She originally appeared in the 2025 Money Fronts update, where players briefly encounter her during the introduction to Mr. Faber. She works as a coordinator for wealthy clients and mentions that she is only visiting San Andreas for 24 hours.
Valentina appears at the airport location of Vice City in GTA 6. She hires Jason and Lucia as bodyguards for a wealthy client, Andres de Leon, at an event connected to Megamundo, a Spanish-language television network. Lucia calls her “Val” when they meet, while Andres greets her as “Tina”, revealing her name.
Tony Prince (Gay Tony)
Fans believe Tony Prince appears briefly in the GTA 6 preload promotional trailer. The character originally appeared in GTA 4: The Ballad of Gay Tony as a nightclub owner and later returned in GTA Online’s After Hours update.
With one GTA Online character already confirmed, we can expect Tony Prince to also make an appearance. It will be interesting to see the Liberty City legend stumble upon the neon-soaked locations of GTA 6.
Phil Cassidy
Speaking of returning legends, we also spotted Phil Cassidy, the character who owns Phil’s Ammu-Nation. However, we know that the GTA HD and 3D universes do not share characters. This means the original Phil Cassidy might not be the one helping you stock up on weapons in GTA 6.
Still, it could work like Nurse Joy in Pokemon, with different versions of the same character appearing across the franchise. If that’s the case, one of the Phils could return as an arms dealer in GTA 6.
CJ and Big Smoke

N3on
In GTA 6, a character resembling the streamer N3on is featured doing a viral “trunk challenge”. He is seen lounging and live-streaming from the trunk of a moving car while wearing shades and mimicking his real-life appearance and mannerisms.

Russia and Ukraine Trade Strikes Against Key Bridges
The attacks, far from the front lines, forced the only bridge between Russia and the occupied Crimean Peninsula to close. Traffic on two bridges in Kyiv was also stopped.
The only bridge linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula was temporarily closed on Tuesday morning after suffering damage from a series of Ukrainian attacks, according to Russian officials.
Overnight, two of the main bridges over the Dnipro River in Kyiv, Ukraine’s capital, were also temporarily closed after Russian strikes on the structures late on Monday, Ukrainian officials said.
The dual strikes on important bridges hundreds of miles from the front lines were part of a long-running battle in Russia’s war against Ukraine, involving logistics, symbols and survival. Bridges are some of the hardest structures to bring down using long-range weapons and such structures have repeatedly defied quick destruction.
The extent of the damage to the Ukrainian and Russian bridges was not immediately clear as engineering teams on both sides were dispatched to assess the aftermath of the attacks.
The Kerch Strait Bridge between Russia and Crimea, a 12-mile span that holds both military and political significance for the Kremlin, suffered structural damage, according to Russia’s Investigative Committee, the country’s equivalent of the F.B.I.
The Russian Transport Ministry said in a statement that road and rail traffic on the bridge had been suspended while inspections were conducted.
“Motorists are advised not to travel toward the Crimean Bridge and to monitor the operational situation in official sources,” the ministry said.
Russia illegally annexed Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, and Kyiv has repeatedly attacked the Kerch Strait Bridge since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Ukrainian forces have tried, unsuccessfully, to take the bridge down in unconventional sabotage operations and by direct bombardments.
In October 2022, a truck bombing collapsed sections of the bridge and ignited a passing fuel train. Ukrainian forces followed up with a naval drone strike in July 2023 that damaged the road deck. In June 2025, Ukraine carried out an underwater demolition operation in which operatives detonated more than a metric ton of explosives against the bridge’s submerged support pillars.
Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said on Tuesday that the capital’s Northern and Southern bridges were closed to traffic after the Russian missile attack Monday night.
“We will provide updates as soon as new information becomes available. Municipal services are working on the ground,” Mr. Klitschko said in a statement. “We are doing everything possible to restore traffic as quickly as possible.”
Marc Santora has been reporting from Ukraine since the beginning of the war with Russia. He was previously based in London as an international news editor focused on breaking news events and earlier the bureau chief for East and Central Europe, based in Warsaw. He has also reported extensively from Iraq and Africa.

Japan sends up jets after alleged Russian incursion of its airspace
- Published
Japan says it launched fighter jets and "strongly" protested after two suspected Russian aircraft violated its airspace early on Tuesday.
South Korea also says it deployed fighter jets, while Taiwan says it "responded" to Russian military aircraft detected in their respective air defence identification zones.
These are unofficial buffer areas beyond territorial airspace where governments identify approaching aircraft for security purposes. Moscow has yet to comment.
The alleged incursions are a reminder of Russia's military power ahead of the Apec economic summit in China this week, which Vladimir Putin will attend alongside US President Donald Trump.
Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the flight paths of the Russian aircraft, off the south-western Okinoshima island, were a "serious infringement of Japan's sovereignty" and "completely unacceptable".
The last such incursion was in 2024, when a Russian military patrol plane entered Japanese airspace off Rebun island, Hokkaido.
Taiwan says its military "responded accordingly" after two Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone, also on Tuesday.
South Korea says it sent up jets after an unspecified number of Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone over the Sea of Japan. The aircraft departed without violating South Korean airspace, authorities said.
It is unclear if the three neighbours were responding to the same or different aircraft.
The East China Sea contains self-declared, overlapping air defence identification zones between China, Taiwan, Japan and South Korea.
Foreign military aircraft are expected, but not legally required, to notify governments before entering such air defence identification zones.
Tensions are flaring between Japan and Russia, which are locked in a decades-old territorial dispute over a cluster of islands in the Pacific Ocean.
For months, Moscow has been ratcheting up the pressure on Tokyo.
In August, Putin paid his first visit to one of these islands, prompting sharp rebuke from Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. In October, Russia detained a Japanese journalist on spying allegations.

The Madras High Court has barred Eternal-owned quick commerce platform Blinkit from using the likeness of Chennai Super Kings (CSK) superfan Saravanan Hari without his written consent. The interim order came in a suit in which Saravanan has sought ₹1.1 Cr in damages, alleging that a Blinkit newspaper advertisement used his likeness and gave readers the impression that he endorsed the platform. Justice P B Balaji observed that the Constitution protects the rights of every individual and that personality rights can extend to people who have built a distinct public identity. “This is an interesting case, where a diehard fan of the Chennai Super Kings (CSK) has filed the present suit, seeking to protect his individual personality rights,” the court observed. Inc42 has reached out to Blinkit for comment. This story will be updated on receiving a response. What Sparked The Dispute? The dispute stems from a full-page Blinkit ad published in the Chennai edition of The Sunday Times of India on March 23, 2025. The ad promoted a match-ticket voucher offer with the slogan “The men in yellow always deliver”. In the bottom-right corner was a cartoon of a yellow-painted cricket fan with curly hair, a moustache, and “THALA 7” on his torso, giving a double thumbs-up. According to the plaint, Saravanan developed his match-day look around 2013. It includes yellow face and body paint, lettering across his torso, red lipstick, a curly wig, a thick moustache, dark eyebrows, and his signature double thumbs-up pose. Saravanan said he has travelled with CSK and attended matches in India and overseas. He cited television appearances, newspaper coverage, brand collaborations, and public engagements, along with his association with CSK, recognition from CSK veteran MS Dhoni, and an appearance in the Tamil film GOAT, as evidence that his look had become recognisable. Saravanan alleged that the advertisement created a false impression that he endorsed Blinkit. According to him, friends, fans and acquaintances contacted him to ask whether he had formally associated with the company. Some customers dissatisfied with Blinkit's services even expected him to resolve their complaints, he alleged. What The Court Ordered Blink Commerce, which operates Blinkit, said in its reply to Saravanan’s legal notice that the characters in the ad were fictional and bore no connection to him. It also said it would refrain from using the character in future ads as a gesture of goodwill. Justice Balaji found a prima facie resemblance between the cartoon and Saravanan, pointing to TV and newspaper coverage showing the same pose. The court said the ad could lead readers to believe that Saravanan had appeared in it or consented to the use of his likeness. It granted an interim injunction against Blink Commerce, finding that Saravanan had made out a preliminary case for protection against commercial use of his persona. Bennett, Coleman & Company Limited, the publisher of The Times of India, denied liability, saying its role was limited to providing ad space and that the advertiser supplied the material. The court said the publisher’s liability would be examined at trial. The court directed Blink Commerce and the publisher to preserve materials relating to the ad, including artwork, samples, design records, emails, and correspondence with designers and external vendors. It deferred consideration of Saravanan’s separate request to preserve and produce the defendants’ books of accounts until they appear and file their replies. Besides damages, Saravanan has sought a declaration recognising his distinctive persona as his property and protection against unauthorised commercial use by unknown parties. The matter is listed for December 14.
