We found no evidence of Trump sharing the above post on any of his social media accounts. As such, we've rated the screenshot fake.
Searches for variations of the quote on Google, DuckDuckGo (archived) and Bing uncovered no reporting from reliable media outlets connecting it to the president, which would have been the case if it were authentic. We searched for various phrases within the purported post, including "New intelligence and global developments," "Stock up on at least 90 DAYS of food" and "This is about being prepared, not panicking," none of which returned any relevant results.
Likewise, searches of Roll Call's archive of Trump's posts on X and Truth Social and Trump's Truth, a website dedicated to archiving his Truth Social posts, did not return any results for posts resembling the screenshot.
As of this writing, we were unable to determine who originally shared the fake post.
For further reading, Snopes has frequently debunked many fake quotes attributed to Trump.

When the Indian team returned to India after the South Africa tour of 2010 to prepare for the preliminary rounds of the 2011 Cricket World Cup, skipper Mahendra Singh Dhoni, along with the entire support staff, implemented a change in physical preparedness through various protocols. These included strict diet control, fitness logs with minimum scores for each week and each session, no newspapers, proper team bonding, etc.
He saw this as an indicative sacrifice of what would be needed to win the prestigious tournament, especially with the World Cup being held in India after 28 years and it being Sachin Tendulkar’s last appearance in the marquee tournament. Whatever needed to be done to win, the entire team was aligned in its thought process.
Sachin and the other senior players, along with the newcomers, took it upon themselves to excel in their respective departments, with Gary, Paddy, Eric, Nitin, Amit, Mane kaka, DJ and me providing support behind the scenes. Representing the team’s collective approach through an upgrade in diet, fitness, recovery and other protocols was the right way to go. Like all great leaders, MSD listened to good advice from his trusted coach and senior players, while also engaging the youngsters in implementing the process.
An intuitive understanding of the human element is paramount to any successful programme, sporting or corporate. Decision-making that incorporates both this understanding and the critical data points crucial to success can create a system for elite and sustainable high performance.
What makes a team great? The answer usually points to talent, chemistry or some imperceptible spark that you either have or don’t. Research often suggests otherwise. Peak performance isn’t luck or magic. It is created by two ingredients working together: the measurable science of what actually drives results, and the immeasurable art of leadership and teamwork that brings those drivers to life. Teams that master only one of the two plateau at various stages; those that master both power ahead.
The science
According to the research findings, four key health drivers explain most of the gap between low- and high-performing teams: trust, communication, innovative thinking and decision-making. Together, they account for 69 to 76 per cent of the difference. Teams strong in trust are 5.1 times more likely to produce results. Strong communicators are 2.8 times more efficient. Teams with strong innovative thinking are 2.7 times more innovative in their outcomes, while strong decision-making adds another 2.8 times.
For innovative thinking and effective decision-making to exist, teams need the other two drivers — trust and communication — as well as an environment that offers a healthy dose of clarity, collaboration and psychological safety.
The science extends to the system around the team. Teams that endorse a real ‘operating system’ — shared storytelling, one-on-one conversations, intentional reflection and detailed, ego-less handovers — score 10 to 23 points higher on impact measures than teams without one.
The art
Scientific diagnosis is often the easy part. The harder part is the art: the coaching conversation; the moment a leader tells an uncomfortable personal story to rebuild trust, something no scorecard could measure.
Data tells a team where to focus. Craft is how it actually happens. Sport has understood this instinctively, long before consultants developed a framework for it.
The Indian cricket team’s 2011 World Cup win is a good example. At one point in the tournament, with the team needing to win almost every remaining match to surge ahead, MSD told the team something simple: take one game at a time, without any pressure, and keep the entire process and protocols grounded and simple. We did win the remaining matches with flying colours. The semifinal against Pakistan and the final went on to become part of one of the greatest campaigns in Indian cricket history. That’s a system with brutal clarity on what had to happen, wedded to an Indian team culture that turned pressure into a robust bond instead of panic.
Science directs. Art erects. This is where science and art came together to make the team different and bring home the World Cup after 28 years. The best teams consider this a reiterative cycle: analyse honestly, prioritise the few systems that matter most in a given context, practise and coach the exclusive behaviours that follow, and then reflect and sustain the change through meaningful retrospectives and interactions.
Neither science nor art can work in isolation. They must function as a holistic entity. Data tells you where to target. But leadership, through honest conversations, team rituals and the willingness to change yourself before asking your team to change, can provide the impetus for the team to surge ahead.

Andhra Pradesh Home Minister Vangalapudi Anitha has said that 13 National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) teams, 11 State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) teams and fire service units have been kept ready for emergency relief operations arising out of Cyclone Akvan.
Ms. Anitha, who reviewed the preparedness with officials on Wednesday (November 18, 2026), directed the State machinery to remain on high alert for the next 48 hours. She asked officials to take all possible measures to prevent loss of life and property. She said heavy to very heavy rainfall was expected in the coastal districts for the next two days, starting November 19.
Ms. Anitha advised the public to remain vigilant and urged people living in coastal areas to avoid stepping out unless absolutely necessary. She asked people living in low-lying areas to move to relief centres as and when instructed by the authorities.
Meanwhile, Energy Minister Gottipati Ravikumar reviewed preparedness for Cyclone Akvan with officials of the Energy Department and asked them to remain on high alert across the region from Nellore to Visakhapatnam.
The Minister said the government had already written to the Telangana government requesting additional personnel to take up restoration works. Since the cyclone is likely to cause considerable damage to infrastructure, the Minister asked the officials to stock sufficient equipment and materials as a precautionary measure.
Mr. Ravikumar asked officials to set up a dedicated toll-free number for each district and ensure continuous monitoring. He asked them to keep the public informed if power supply was shut off or if any disruptions occurred as part of precautionary measures.
Agriculture Minister K. Atchannaidu reviewed the preparedness of the administration with the District Collectors of Srikakulam, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema and Parvathipuram Manyam. The Minister advised fishermen against venturing into the sea and urged residents in river catchment areas to remain cautious.
Since heavy rain in Odisha could cause flooding in the neighbouring districts, he directed Irrigation Department officials to remain alert. He said people living in flood-prone areas must be relocated to safer places.
He asked for a 24-hour control room to be set up to provide immediate assistance to people in cyclone-affected areas.
People can call the toll-free numbers 112, 1070 or 18004250101 in an emergency. Power outages, fallen trees, waterlogging and other problems can be reported on WhatsApp at 95523 00009.

The next industrial revolution — or a potential existential threat to humanity —is coming to the public markets.
In a year of blockbuster deals, Anthropic's initial public offering is poised to be the largest by money raised ever.
Later on Wednesday, Anthropic will take orders for the IPO, opening ownership to institutional and some retail investors. Before the end of trading Thursday, anyone will have a shot to buy one of the biggest names in tech.
The IPO comes at a turbulent time for AI: a data-center pushback helped fuel the Democrats' blue wave, the Jensen Huang-Nvidia scandal is raising national security concerns, and the market's AI sell-off continues.
So is Anthropic a chance to get in on a historic technological transformation — or an expensive bet on an increasingly uncertain future?
Amid this backdrop, we asked five investors whether they would buy shares in the IPO. They were split on the prospect, citing both how the company could be at the forefront of a true global transformation and the financial and existential risks the company holds.
Phil Blancato, chief market strategist at Osaic
Would you buy? Yes.
Anthropic's IPO is a must-buy event "if you believe AI will transform how we work and live," Blancato, who leads market strategy for Osaic, a wealth management network that oversees $810 billion in client assets, said.
The firm points to a massive potential market: It estimates that the entire earnings of work by knowledge workers globally exceeded $40 trillion in 2025. Anthropic also cited IDC's estimate that AI will have a $22.5 trillion economic impact by 2031.
While those figures don't directly translate to potential revenue, they illustrate the scale of opportunity and "extreme change" as AI takes on more work, he said.
"Even if Anthropic captures only a small fraction of that value, there's still room for the business to grow well beyond where it is today," Blancato said.
That doesn't mean there's no risk to a bet this big. Computing and infrastructure costs in the most recent quarter rose higher than revenue, and Anthropic does need to commit to data centers "years in advance," while customers can "cut back their usage much sooner," Blancato said. That, plus the possibility that customers may find low-cost alternatives in the future, is a real risk that could "limit future earnings," he said.
Christian Giadolor, investment analyst at Chicory Wealth
Would you buy? No.
One of the first risks Anthropic disclosed in its S-1 filing is that it might not be able to secure sufficient computing power.
The IPO and its $131 billion in cash could help it skip the queue, says Giadolor, who previously worked in macro and sustainable investing at Bridgewater Associates. But with compute costs "skyrocketing," he questioned whether the economics are "sustainable," especially as Americans increasingly push back against data centers.
In the first half of the year, nearly 50% of Anthropic's revenue came from cloud service providers, putting them at significant risk of a slowdown in data-center construction or demand from the hyperscalers. This may be why the company is signaling that it could build its own data center infrastructure, Giadolor said, but thought doing so would expose it to the risks of asset-heavy ownership of physical infrastructure.
Then there are the risks posed by potential future regulations. Anthropic has warned that "its models could pose an existential risk to humanity," Giadolor said. They could also carry a more boring risk: there's very little insurance available for AI models to protect them if they do something wrong.
"If Rogue AI and this 'existential' threat emerges, it could place Anthropic in unprecedented legal jeopardy," Giadolor said.
Dhruv Maniktala, chief investment officer at True North Advisors and Western Alternative Strategies
Would you buy? Maybe.
Maniktala's multi-family office, which manages $5.9 billion, previously acquired Anthropic shares at "much cheaper" valuations in the private market. The current valuations are too high for him to issue a blanket buy suggestion.
It's not that Anthropic isn't a great firm in the midst of rolling out solutions for different verticals of the economy, he told Business Insider, but there's an "unreasonable amount of growth built in."
In order to fund its projected data center buildout, the company will need $3.5 trillion in annual revenue, Maniktala estimated, the equivalent of spending $1,750 a month on AI per employee in the US, even including hairdressers and fast-food workers.
But whether the valuation is $500 billion or $2 trillion matters less than the fact that it's "impossible to predict" what happens next, Maniktala said, given the scale of possibilities presented by Anthropic's IPO. If you have the money sitting around to make a small allocation to the company, it could make sense to buy and take a chance on the "big unknown," he said.
Stephanie Link, chief investment strategist at Hightower Advisors
Would you buy? Yes
Link, who leads investment strategy for $350 billion wealth management firm Hightower, would invest in the company but keep the allocation small given the expected volatility, similar to the advice she gave to potential SpaceX investors earlier this year.
Instead of the $2 trillion valuation that was floated earlier this year, $1.13 to $1.3 trillion offers a much more palatable entry point for investors, she said. As of Tuesday evening, there were reports that the company may be pricing closer to $1.5 or $1.6 trillion. She also likes that the IPO is six times oversubscribed.
Add to that the company's "amazing" revenue growth — revenue grew 1,206% year-over-year, and third-quarter revenue was up 47% sequentially — and it makes sense to buy. That's not to say there aren't concerns Link is watching for.
"I'm mildly concerned about the top five customers accounting for 21% of revenue, but I expect that to decline in the coming years as Anthropic signs up more customers," she said.
Kristin Hull, founder and chief investment officer at Nia Impact Capital
Would you buy? No
Nia Impact Capital's Kristin Hull is "sitting on the sidelines" for this IPO.
There are financial reasons to be wary, according to Hull. These include the company's debt load, its complicated relationships with partners who are also competitors, its long-term lease commitments, an untested business model, and uncertainty about future AI margins as usage increases.
"On the business model alone, and given the growing range of competitors, I would wait to see a clearer path toward both independence and profitability," Hull said. But the long-time impact investor said that there are also many "negative externalities" beyond the pure finances that also aren't being priced in.
There's a pushback brewing: whether it's "future intellectual property litigation risk," the concern over mass surveillance and privacy currently manifesting against Flock cameras, or over their massive environmental costs. Earlier this month, more than 50 localities voted to limit or ban data center construction through ballot measures, according to Ballotpedia. All of this could create major financial challenges for Anthropic.
"The recent November election also brought up important questions about who bears the environmental costs: Anthropic and its investors, or the communities hosting the infrastructure?" Hull said.

The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.
WHO today has more than 300 staff working hard in Iraq to support the health system and to bring badly needed medical assistance to people across the country. During the current conflict, WHO has successfully sent teams to help with an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease in northern Iraq and to assess the health needs of people who have left their homes. WHO is ready to do much more work across the whole country in support of the health system.
In the weeks and months to come, Iraq's health system will almost inevitably come under unprecedented pressure. Health is a crucial part of the economic and social system.

Calgary high school says too many students are getting food delivered
St. Francis asks parents to ask kids to stop ordering food during class time
A Calgary high school sent parents a memo this week asking them to rein in their children’s increasing use of food delivery apps like Uber Eats and DoorDash during school hours.
In the letter, St. Francis High School administrators said while the deliveries may be convenient, they can also be disruptive to classrooms, and pose security risks to have students interacting with individuals they don’t know on school grounds.
“As the safety and security of everyone at St. Francis is our priority, we ask that you please have a conversation with your child and ask them to not use any food delivery services during the instructional time of the day," the letter said.
Lee Martin, who represents Calgary Catholic teachers for the Alberta Teachers’ Association, told CBC News it's become more of an issue in recent years. He heard from one teacher just this week who said a driver tried to deliver food right to a classroom window.
“I think that as public educators we want our children fed,” said Martin. “However, this seems to be a bit out of control.”
A food drop-off cart outside an elementary school in Calgary's southeast. (Submitted by Lee Martin)
And it’s not only at high schools.
At one elementary school, he said upwards of 30 parents were either dropping off food or sending deliveries there daily, so the school set up a table in the foyer where students can go search for their bag at lunchtime.
A spokesperson for the Calgary Catholic School District said to their knowledge, St. Francis is the only school in its board addressing the matter.
In a statement, the Calgary Board of Education said it doesn’t have a specific policy on food deliveries, and it’s up to principals at individual schools to set guidelines if it is an issue.
“Students are discouraged from ordering deliveries into the building, though we are aware they may meet the driver in other locations on school property,” the statement said.
Students say it’s common, not necessarily an issue
Outside St. Francis, delivery driver Ali Nuru dropped off food for a student Tuesday. He says he’ll typically end up doing a couple of school deliveries a week.
“Most of the time I bring from McDonald's,” he said.
Delivery driver Ali Nuru says he typically delivers a couple of times a week to high schools, with McDonald's the No. 1 meal of choice. (Colleen Underwood/CBC)
Students said it’s fairly routine to see classmates meeting drivers in the parking lot to pick up their orders.
“A lot of times — I'm kind of snitching — but they'll be like, ‘Oh, can I go to the bathroom?' and then they just go meet the driver around the school, like the front of the school and then bring the food in with them,” said Grade 11 student Rebira Assefa.
However, she said it hasn’t been a big deal in her classrooms, with most students unbothered by it.
The bathroom excuse can be an issue though, said Grade 11 student Bradley White, since only so many students are allowed out of a class at a time.
“Like if someone's out for too long, then the teacher will be like, ‘OK, no one's allowed to use the bathroom for the rest of class because this person ruined it for everyone,’” said White.
Plus, he said it can be a distraction when someone orders an “excessive” amount of food for themselves and their friends, and brings it into class.
Cracking down on it, though, could be tricky.
“I don't really know how they would enforce a policy where you're not allowed to order something, because kids are going to do it anyways. They'll end up rebelling because you put another policy in,” said Grade 12 student Alysa Utigard.

Lawrence Bishnoi gang calls Goldy Dhillon 'publicity hungry'
NEW DELHI: Gangster Goldy Dhillon had a narrow escape in Germany during an attack by the Lawrence Bishnoi gang's Canada handler, Manna Brampton, and his Madrid counterpart, Mandeep Spain, in Jan this year, the duo said in a statement on social media Tuesday.A day after Dhillon's post threatening actor Amitabh Bachchan, the duo hit out at Dhillon for killing an LGBTQ+ influencer, Mad Sandhu, in Amritsar and called him "publicity hungry" for targeting Bachchan.Claiming Dhillon used to wash utensils at a restaurant in Germany for a living, they said he lacked the wherewithal to target Bachchan or even his domestic staff.Calling Dhillon's claims of seeking revenge for the 1984 anti-Sikh riots a desperate bid for attention, Brampton and Spain said he was no-thing more than a petty thief and a "chitta" (heroin) peddler from Punjab with FIRs against him for drug-dealing and stealing cable wires.On the attack, the gang said despite constantly boasting about weapons, Dhillon had nothing but a knife to defend himself. Ukraine's refinery strikes on Russia are pushing the world's second-biggest energy exporter to buy vast volumes of petrol from overseas and instruct officials to prioritize lower-quality fuel.
The crisis has been months in the making, as Kyiv wages a long-range strike campaign pummeling Russian energy facilities, claiming this week to have knocked out about 55% of total refinery capacity so far.
A new readout from a Russian government meeting on Tuesday signals how deep the Kremlin's fuel woes are growing.
Alexander Novak, a deputy prime minister and Russia's senior official overseeing energy, was cited telling his subordinates to prioritize expanding petrol imports and "securing additional volumes of out-of-class fuel."
The latter means that Moscow is now focusing on making lower-grade fuel available. It's traditionally held to a K5 rating, a quality standard its gas stations have maintained for 10 years.
Fuel below this rating was typically reserved for exports outside Russia's Eurasian trade bloc, as well as for niche uses such as the military, state reserves, or oilfields.
Meanwhile, local officials and media in at least six Russian regions announced gasoline rationing at some pump stations earlier this month, typically capping customers at 30 liters of petrol, or about 7.93 gallons, a day.
Reuters reported in August that similar restrictions had rolled out in Moscow areas among some chains, depending on the station type, with long queues forming outside some pumps near the capital.
Russia remains a net fuel exporter, shipping millions of tons of crude oil and other products like diesel abroad.
But with its refineries under siege, it's struggled to turn enough of that crude into refined petrol for gas stations at home.
International organizations that track fuel shipments say Moscow has surged imports for those products over the last few months, mostly from Morocco, India, and Turkey.
While Russia's monthly fuel imports roughly maxed out at 5,000 metric tons of petrol products and additives from 2023 to 2025, it brought in over 416,000 metric tons of such goods by sea this August, according to the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
The Helsinki-based non-profit said Russia further imported another 234,000 metric tons of seaborne oil products in September.
London-based shipping analytics firm Vortexa separately put Russia's August fuel imports at about 470,000 metric tons.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military intelligence agency, GUR, said on Tuesday that Kyiv's attacks had forced Russia to import about 989,000 metric tons of fuel and high-octane additives by sea from July 18 to October 23.
Russia has also been importing fuel by rail, from countries like Belarus or Kazakhstan, though these aren't tracked as closely.
Reuters reported in July that Russia had imported about 453,000 metric tons in the first six months of 2026 over land, or about a 20-fold increase year-on-year.
Historic import levels
The most recent time Russia shipped in fuel on those levels was in 2014, when it imported 1.6 million metric tons of motor gasoline amid a domestic supply squeeze.
Moscow had arranged a deal with Belarus to trade Russian crude oil for refined petrol it had previously sold to Minsk. The arrangement brought in another 808,000 metric tons in 2015.
But those imports took place over entire years, while GUR's estimate of nearly 1 million metric tons in imports covers just four months.
Novak, the senior Russian energy official, said in October that Russia was importing about 10% of its gasoline, though he did not provide any specific trade figures.
"We'll be importing at least until the end of the year," Novak told state media, adding that Russia also had to top up reserves depleted during the summer when gas ran short.
Novak's office and the Russian energy ministry did not immediately respond to comment requests sent outside regular business hours by Business Insider.

Preparations underway for PM Balendra Shah's India visit: Nepal foreign ministry sources
Nepal’s foreign ministry is preparing for PM Balendra Shah’s proposed India visit, to cover connectivity, infrastructure, trade and tourism.
A wide range of issues, including rail, road, and air connectivity, infrastructure development, cooperation, and trade and tourism, will feature during Prime Minister Balendra Shah's proposed official visit to India, Nepal Ministry of Foreign Affairs sources said on Tuesday.
Shah, who took office on March 27, has not yet undertaken an official bilateral foreign visit. He travelled to the United States in September to attend the United Nations General Assembly.
Spokesperson at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs Lok Bahadur Chetri said the ministry is engaged in necessary preparations for Shah's forthcoming visit. According to Foreign Ministry sources, Shah will visit Delhi on November 22. However, an official announcement is awaited.
Deep Dive
Shah had received an invitation from Prime Minister Narendra Modi to visit India when the government led by the Rastriya Swatantra Party leader was formed in March, around six months after the youth-led Gen Z protest toppled the KP Sharma Oli government in September last year.
Shah's first visit to India may last two or three days, the sources said.
Connectivity is one of the major priority areas that would get attention during bilateral talks, which may include expanding air, road, and railway connectivity, as well as power transmission lines and optical fibre, the sources said.
Construction of border infrastructure such as integrated check posts and petroleum pipelines is another important area for cooperation that would come up during the high-level discussions, the ministry sources said.
Nepal would also seek grant assistance and concessional loans from India to build infrastructure and reconstruct road sections and bridges damaged by the Bhotekoshi flood in August.
Also read: Nepal in talks with China to reopen Tatopani border point
Dozens of bridges were damaged during the devastating flood that killed at least 1,500 people and left over 5,000 missing.
Tourism promotion, agricultural development, and border security are other important areas that may come up during bilateral discussions. Nepal will also seek new air routes from India to help fully operationalise its two airports, Pokhara International Airport and Gautam Buddha International Airport in Bhairahawa.
The weekly train service connecting Janakpurdham in Nepal and Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh, India, covering around 600 km distance, will be inaugurated during Prime Minister Shah's visit, Foreign Ministry sources said.
Prime Minister Shah, 35, will be accompanied by at least four ministers, which may include the foreign minister, minister for finance, minister for infrastructure, minister for tourism and civil aviation and minister for energy and water resources.
A small number of businessmen and industrialists will also join Shah's entourage to hold discussions with the private sector in India and explore business and investment opportunities.
It has been a longstanding practice for newly elected Nepali prime ministers to make India their first official bilateral foreign destination, although the convention is not an absolute rule. Former prime minister KP Sharma Oli broke with the practice in 2024 by visiting China first.

A proposal by the Trump administration to cap the amount of time foreign students and scholars can spend in the country has been struck down in court.
In a Monday ruling, Boston federal Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV wrote that the rule “is arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, and otherwise not in accordance with law.”
Saylor previously blocked the rule temporarily on the day before the policy was set to take effect. Monday’s ruling is a final decision on the case, though an appeal from the government on the initial ruling is still pending. Universities and research advocates worried that the four-year cap on visas could deter international students from pursuing graduate studies in the U.S., because such degrees often take longer than four years.

కాంగ్రెస్ నాయకురాలు సోనియా గాంధీ రాసిన ఆత్మకథ ‘బిలాంగింగ్: ఎ జర్నీ ఆఫ్ లవ్’ 10 నవంబర్ 2026న విడుదలైంది. ఇటలీలో ఆమె బాల్యం నుండి 1965లో కేంబ్రిడ్జ్లో రాజీవ్ గాంధీని కలవడం, ఆ తర్వాత భారతదేశానికి వచ్చి ఇక్కడి సంస్కృతికి అలవాటు పడటం వంటి అనేక విషయాలను ఈ పుస్తకం వివరిస్తుంది. మొదటి వారంలోనే ఈ పుస్తకం 2 లక్షల కాపీలకు పైగా అమ్ముడయ్యాయని పబ్లిషర్ హార్పర్ కాలిన్స్ సంస్థ పేర్కొంది.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, ఈ పుస్తకాలను కాంగ్రెస్ కార్యకర్తలు కిలోల చొప్పున ముంబైలోని ఫోర్ట్ మార్కెట్లో దుకాణదారులకు అమ్మారని, అయితే వీటిని కొనడానికి ఎవరూ ముందుకు రావడం లేదని, అందువలన వీటిని స్క్రా ప్లో(తుక్కు) అమ్ముతున్నట్లు ఒక దుకాణదారుడు చెప్తున్నట్లుగా ఉన్న వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ఒకటి సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: సోనియా గాంధీ ఆత్మకథను ఎవరూ కొనని కారణంగా ఈ పుస్తకాలను ముంబైలో తుక్కాగా అమ్ముతున్నామంటూ దుకాణదారుడు చెప్తున్న వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ ప్రచారంలో ఎలాంటి నిజం లేదు. ఇది ఆర్టిఫిషియల్ ఇంటెలిజెన్స్(AI) టెక్నాలజీతో సృష్టించిన ఫేక్ వీడియో. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ వీడియోను పరిశీలించగా ఇందులో పుస్తకం పైన ఉన్న అక్షరాలు అసహజంగా ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. అలాగే, దుకాణదారుడి చేతి వేళ్లు కూడా ఒకదానితో ఒకటి కలిసిపోయినట్లుగా ఉన్నాయి. ఇంకా పాదచారుల కదలికలు కూడా అస్పష్టంగా ఉన్నట్లు చూడవచ్చు. సాధారణంగా AI తో రూపొందించిన వీడియోలలో ఇటువంటి పొరపాట్లు కనిపిస్తాయి.
దీని ఆధారంగా, ఈ వీడియోను AI డిటెక్షన్ టూల్స్తో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) పరీక్షించగా, ఇది AI తో రూపొందించిన వీడియో అని నిర్ధారించబడింది.
అలాగే, ఈ వీడియోను ఫేస్బుక్లో అప్లోడ్ చేసిన పోస్ట్ (ఆర్కైవ్) కింద “AI Content” అనే లేబుల్ ఉండటాన్ని చూడవచ్చు. దీన్ని బట్టి, వైరల్ వీడియో నిజమైన ఘటన కాదని, ఇది AI ద్వారా రూపొందించిన వీడియో అని నిర్ధారించవచ్చు.
చివరిగా, సోనియా గాంధీ పుస్తకాలను తుక్కుగా అమ్ముతున్నారంటూ షేర్ అవుతున్న ఈ వీడియో AIతో సృష్టించబడింది.

Six months after an Ebola outbreak was declared in Congo, the disease remains out of control and efforts to contain it are faltering.
More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, and nearly half of those infected have died, according to Government data. It is the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.
Basic containment measures, including contact tracing and isolation, remain inadequate, raising doubts about authorities' ability to halt the outbreak. Experts say there is little chance of bringing it under control within the next year.
By the time the outbreak was announced in mid-May, 43 deaths had already been recorded, suggesting the virus had circulated undetected for an extended period. It has since spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces, moving at a pace aid groups have likened to wildfire.
New hotspots continue to emerge, stretching an already strained health care system.
Questions over funding and management
Community transmission remains high. According to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, 80% of new cases are being detected outside health surveillance, meaning most infections have not been tracked by authorities.
One-third of deaths occur at home or elsewhere in the community, where burials and other procedures are often conducted without specialist supervision, increasing the risk of transmission.
Health workers have repeatedly gone on strike over pay that is months overdue, sometimes leaving patients with confirmed infections without treatment.
Aid groups have also questioned how the response is being managed. Last month, the Africa CDC raised concerns about more than $700 million in Ebola aid that remains unaccounted for.
“A troubling disconnect between the considerable resources mobilised for the response and what is actually reaching patients, frontline workers, and communities continues,” said the humanitarian organisation Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF.
Children face high death rates
Children are particularly vulnerable to Ebola, especially those with preexisting conditions such as malnutrition, experts say.
Most children affected by the disease have not received specialised care, contributing to high death rates.
According to UNICEF, children accounted for 35% of deaths recorded through November 4. Children under 5 accounted for 21% of all deaths, and nearly 72% of infected children in that age group have died.
Conflict and attacks hamper response
Health workers face difficult conditions as Ebola prevention and containment measures clash with social and cultural practices.
Since the outbreak began, health workers have been attacked, some fatally, adding to the dangers of working in an already volatile region. Health facilities have also come under attack.
The outbreak has been concentrated in eastern Congo, particularly Ituri and North Kivu, where communities face both the epidemic and armed conflict.
Fighting between Government forces and hundreds of rebel groups, including the Rwanda-backed M23, had already helped create one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises. The Allied Democratic Forces, an Islamic State-affiliated rebel group, also attacks civilians.
The virus's rapid spread has raised fears of wider transmission across Africa. Nigeria, Kenya and Uganda have confirmed cases, making this the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak on record.

Monica was not prepared for a caesarean section. She had done everything right and had been assured of a vaginal delivery. Then two weeks before the expected date of delivery, she had to be rushed to the emergency for a caesarean. Monica felt that she had completely lost control of the situation. She found herself alone in an intensive care ward away from her baby, who was in the neonatal ICU and described her birth experience as being extremely traumatic. She is now unable to bond with her baby and keeps questioning herself. Am I such a terrible mother? Will I be like this lifelong?
Priya became pregnant after multiple IVF procedures but did not disclose the pregnancy to anyone till the third trimester, as she didn’t want to jinx it. After a healthy baby girl was born, Priya continued to be anxious and could not trust anyone else to take care of the baby. She would be hypervigilant, and even the smallest change in the infant’s spit-up or breathing would make her panic.

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

Meta has tightened Instagram’s recommendation filters in India to show less sexually suggestive and violent content. The changes apply to posts from accounts users don’t follow that Instagram recommends across Explore, Reels, and Feed. In a blog post, Meta said it strengthened Instagram’s default safeguards in India over the past year based on user feedback. Separately, the company has upgraded its detection systems globally with AI models that check posts against Instagram’s recommendation guidelines before surfacing them, without relying on users to report or hide them. Meta said users in India now report recommended content about half as often as they did a year ago. The company did not disclose the absolute number of reports or how much content it had filtered out. Instagram users can further limit sensitive content in Search, Reels, Explore, Feed recommendations, and suggested accounts through Sensitive Content Control. They can also use Political Content Control to see less political content from accounts they don’t follow, or select ‘Not Interested’ from a post or reel’s menu to shape future recommendations. Meta Faces Regulatory Scrutiny The recommendation update comes amid regulatory scrutiny of Meta over the alleged circulation and promotion of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on Instagram. A BBC investigation alleged that paid Instagram ads directed users to Telegram channels offering CSAM. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) summoned Meta executives following the allegations, and the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) opened an inquiry. In September, Meta agreed to report child safety cases directly to Indian authorities through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, operated by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C). Later, the company said it had taken action against 5.3 Mn pieces of child sexual exploitation content across Facebook and Instagram in India in the first half of 2026. Meta said it identified and acted on more than 98% of that content before users reported it. Meanwhile, the Centre is also exploring withdrawing safe harbour protection under Section 79 of the IT Act for social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, and X. The protection limits platforms’ liability for user-generated content.

British government ministers were told not to engage formally with Vantara, the controversial mega-zoo run by the Indian billionaire Anant Ambani, after lobbying efforts by the private animal sanctuary in the run-up to a UK-chaired meeting on the trade in endangered species, according to documents.
This week, the UK heads a 32-country committee meeting in Geneva of Cites, the United Nations body that regulates trade in endangered species. The meeting will examine how India has responded to compliance concerns about imports of endangered animals.
Documents obtained by the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay under the UK’s Freedom of Information Act reveal Vantara’s efforts to lobby British officials and ministers before the meeting.
Ambani, 31, is the heir to the oil and gas fortune of one of India’s richest men, Mukesh Ambani. He set up a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near his family’s oil-refining facilities in Gujarat, where more than 150,000 animals have reportedly been amassed since 2022. Vantara boasts high welfare standards for animals in its care, including facilities such as an elephant hydrotherapy pool, where more than 260 elephants can also receive oil therapies and Ayurvedic massage.
But conservation groups have repeatedly questioned how such a vast number of species, many of which are endangered, were gathered so quickly. Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing.
A subsequent Cites fact-finding mission looking into the zoo raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn.
Its November 2025 report said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”
In May, officials from the UK’s Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) met a representative from Vantara and the US lobbyist firm Checkmate Government Relations, founded by Ches McDowell, a hunting friend of Donald Trump Jr.
Before the meeting, internal briefing documents said Checkmate was “seeking to persuade the UK to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara and of Checkmate’s argument that responsibility for verifying legality sits primarily with exporting or re-exporting parties rather than with India as importer”.
During the meeting, the Vantara representative invited UK officials to visit the zoo – an invitation that was subsequently declined to ensure the impartiality of the UK’s Cites chair role.
After the meeting, a representative from another lobbying firm, Atlas Strategy, working on behalf of Vantara, approached the then secretary of state, Emma Reynolds, and then nature minister, Mary Creagh, also raising the prospect of a visit to the zoo.
When a department official asked for advice, a note was issued recommending that ministers did not engage formally with Vantara.
The government documents also reveal concerns about an application by Vantara to import falcons and falcon hybrids, after an unnamed organisation made a £50,000 “donation” to a breeder in the UK, whose identity was also not disclosed. British Cites officials classified the transaction as commercial, according to the documents. The falcons were not exported to India.
A spokesperson for Vantara said it had not imported falcons from the UK, nor had the zoo hired or paid a lobbying firm. It is understood that Checkmate and Altas Strategy were working pro bono for Vantara and not required to register with the Office of the Registrar of Consultant Lobbyists.
After recent scrutiny, Vantara has sought to “reset” its activities by voluntarily suspending animal imports for a year and hiring John Scanlon, a former Cites chief, to oversee its operations. In an interview with the Sunday Times this year, Ambani said he only brought animals to Vantara legally to ensure their welfare, mentioning a group of hippos he had saved from a hunting lodge in South Africa and jackass penguins saved from a shopping centre in Qatar.
“I think since I was a baby I have been taking care of animals. It’s always been a passion,” he said.
Vantara was used to host Ambani’s lavish pre-wedding celebrations in 2024, which were attended by celebrity guests and politicians. In September, Newcastle University awarded the oil heir a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship”, sparking a backlash from conservationists.
A Defra spokesperson said: “The UK has strict rules in place to protect endangered species and ensuring international wildlife trade is legal and sustainable, with every application assessed individually against internationally agreed and domestic requirements.”

Pesticides sold by European chemical companies were named in more than 1,600 poisoning reports in Brazil last year, an investigation has found.
About a third of the cases involved chemicals banned from use on farms in the EU because of the risks they pose to people and the environment. But European companies are not banned from manufacturing these chemicals, as long as they export them overseas to countries where they are legally allowed to be used.
Analysis of Brazilian health ministry data by Unearthed and Public Eye in a report published on Tuesday found that of 2,857 poisoning reports that named an identifiable agricultural product, 1,605 named brands sold by European pesticide companies.
Farm workers in Brazil have described their flesh rotting, skin burning, difficulty breathing and vomiting after using the chemicals at work, according to the report. A small number have died accidentally or killed themselves by drinking the pesticides.
Under Brazilian law, reports must be submitted by healthcare professionals to Brazil’s national disease notification system in all suspected pesticide poisoning cases. These reports can be marked “confirmed” poisoning or “exposure” only by the doctor or nurse who saw the patient.
Clinicians sometimes record cases as exposure when they lack the training or support to confirm a diagnosis, but are presented with a patient who says they have been exposed to pesticides or present symptoms of pesticide poisoning. Laboratory confirmation is rare, so recording a diagnosis of “confirmed” poisoning usually depends on clinical judgment.
Experts say clinicians can be reluctant to confirm cases because of a lack of training or support. A brand being named in a poisoning report is not proof that it caused poisoning or death.
“The insufficient training of healthcare professionals to recognise and manage these cases is a major limiting factor,” said Vanda Garibotti, a public health biologist at the State Centre for Health Surveillance in Rio Grande do Sul, southern Brazil.
High staff turnover and a lack of institutional support meant poisoning cases were rarely confirmed through laboratory tests and often relied on clinical judgment, Garibotti added.
In more than 6,700 medical reports involving agricultural pesticides last year, 2,857 named an identifiable product. Of those, 1,420 were classified as confirmed poisonings. A further 1,108 were classified as exposures; for the remainder the classification was unknown or other diagnoses.
Some of the products are made in Britain. Reglone is the most frequently cited UK-made weedkiller. It contains diquat, a chemical that was banned in the UK in 2020 after experts concluded it posed a high risk to people living near fields where it was sprayed. Diquat is also found in other pesticides.
Despite the usage ban, Reglone is still manufactured by the Swiss-headquartered pesticides company Syngenta at its factory in Huddersfield for export to countries with more permissive regulations, including Brazil.
Nelson Castoldi died last year after accidentally ingesting Reglone on his family farm in Rio Grande do Sul. To save money, his family had bought the weedkiller in bulk, decanting a single litre into an empty cola bottle to avoid hauling a heavy 20-litre canister into the fields.
Working under the scorching sun, Castoldi mistook the black chemical for a soft drink and took a sip. Though he spat it out immediately, the chemical caused his kidneys to fail before attacking his lungs. He died two days later.
“We fell apart,” Ivan Castoldi said of his father’s death. “Four months after our father passed away, our mother also passed away. She cried day and night. She became depressive and had a stroke. She was left alone.
“That poison, Reglone, should be banned in Brazil,” he added. “Not because of what happened to us, but because of its toxicity.”
The Brazilian health ministry recorded 75 cases involving diquat last year, compared with 36 over the five years from 2018 to 2022.
The investigation found Reglone was specifically named in 44 reports, including four deaths. Of those cases, 26 were classified as confirmed poisonings and the rest were classified as exposure, unknown, or adverse reaction.
Dormex, a pesticide manufactured in Germany by Alzchem and distributed in Brazil by the German chemical company BASF, is another product workers said injured them or made them ill.
Sidnei Souza de Oliveira, 49, suffered a severe injury after a jug of Dormex spilled on his leg while he was filling a sprayer. The handle broke as he was transferring the chemical into the tank. At first, his leg turned red, and he continued spraying.
He carried on working for four days before going to hospital. “After 15 days, my leg was black. Chunks of flesh were falling off,” Oliveira said. A doctor said the injury was serious and had to remove dead tissue to stop it spreading towards the bone.
Oliveira said the protective trousers supplied by his employer were thin and allowed the chemical to seep through. He said he had been afraid of losing his job if he stayed away from work for too long.
Dormex contains cyanamide, which was banned from use in the EU in 2008 because of concerns about its effects on human health, particularly among farm workers spraying the chemical. Analysis shows the Brazilian health ministry database recorded 17 confirmed poisonings involving Dormex last year.
Finale, a BASF product identified in the investigation, contains glufosinate, which was banned in the EU in 2018. Roundup – a glyphosate-based weedkiller manufactured by the German chemical company Bayer – was frequently cited in Brazilian poisoning reports, including 12 deaths.
Across all the poisoning reports identified by the investigation as involving products sold by European companies, there were 32 reported deaths. Of these cases, 31 were classified as confirmed poisonings, and 26 were recorded as suicides.
Syngenta products were cited 425 times in the poisoning reports, and BASF 179 times. The company figures are not mutually exclusive: some poisoning reports named products sold by more than one manufacturer.
Nina Schrank, a senior campaigner at Greenpeace UK, said the findings were a “deadly double standard”.
“If a pesticide is too dangerous to use in Britain, it should be too dangerous to export. Ministers must stop allowing Britain to be part of a production line for toxic chemicals that are putting lives at risk overseas.”
The EU’s pesticide approval system requires chemicals to meet strict standards for human and animal health and the environment. Diquat has been banned on EU and UK farms since 2019 and 2020 respectively, after experts concluded it posed a high risk to workers, people living nearby and birds. Cyanamide was withdrawn after an assessment found exposure among agricultural operators could exceed safe levels. Glufosinate, meanwhile, is classified in the EU as toxic to reproduction, meaning it can harm fertility or the development of unborn children.
Suicide prevention is also a factor. A 2020 study found national bans on highly hazardous pesticides could be a cost-effective intervention for reducing the number of people who kill themselves in countries with a high burden of suicides attributable to pesticides.
A Syngenta spokesperson said almost half the Brazilian cases attributed to the company were not classified as confirmed poisonings, adding: “Public Eye and Unearthed are aware of this but have explicitly chosen to disregard the dataset’s final classification.” The company accused the investigation of disregarding the dataset’s final classifications and identified “numerous other inconsistencies” that it said raised “serious concerns” that the evidence was “being selectively interpreted to support a predetermined conclusion”.
“There are real people behind these statistics. Every genuine case of poisoning matters, and every family affected deserves our concern,” the spokesperson added.
Syngenta said Brazil had its own “robust regulatory system” and that products banned in Europe could still be independently assessed and legally registered in the country, citing differences in crops, growing conditions and pest pressures. It said it trained 95,000 people in Brazil in the safe use of its products in 2025, including through free online courses.
Bayer said its products were safe when used according to label instructions, citing what it described as rigorous testing and assessments by global health authorities. The company said it took pesticide poisoning seriously but questioned the reliability of the data, arguing that products and circumstances of exposure had not been independently verified, some chemicals may have been incorrectly identified and symptoms such as headaches and skin irritation could have other causes.
It said “Roundup” was “widely used as a generic term” that could refer to weedkillers made by other manufacturers or counterfeit products.
The company said it provided training on the safe handling and use of pesticides, including protective equipment, and that its programmes reached more than 4 million people globally in 2025. It also argued that a pesticide being banned in the EU did not necessarily mean it was unsafe, saying other countries had robust regulatory systems that took account of local agricultural conditions.
It added: “While the data presented helps to provide information on broad trends of exposure, the data has limitations and warrants caution when drawing conclusions, particularly when looking at individual cases.”
BASF said it was deeply concerned by reports of poisoning that might be linked to its products, adding that it took all such incidents seriously.
A spokesperson said publicly available information suggested some incidents might have involved the intentional ingestion of crop protection products, describing such acts as “deliberate misuse” of products intended exclusively for agricultural use.
BASF said it had global and local procedures to assess and investigate incidents potentially involving its products, and worked with authorities and experts where appropriate to understand cases and identify ways to prevent similar incidents. It said it invested in education and training to promote the safe handling and use of its products, with initiatives in Brazil reaching more than 14,475 participants in 2025.
The company said it was confident in the safety of its products when used in accordance with label instructions and applicable regulatory standards.
It added that Brazilian law required crop protection products to be handled and applied only by authorised and properly trained individuals, and said it took its responsibility for ensuring their safe use seriously.

Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders
"If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30."
That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago.
From the outside looking in, his career was flying.
By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage.
But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat.
Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over.
After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport.
It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems.
The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027.
But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence.
BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science.
REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues.
Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake.
"Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says.
"In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely."
Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check".
Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs has her periods "switched off".
For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue.
The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad".
But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes.
"We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says.
"It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented."
Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men.
Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability.
So why is REDs so common?
One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'.
For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics.
And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started.
"I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says.
"I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went."
Initially, the strategy can work.
When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement.
It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results.
But eventually, the luck runs out.
Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries.
Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries.
"I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport.
"You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well."
Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue".
"In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.
"I think there's a stigma attached in there, or it's not looked at as the obvious answer to some of your problems, it's found later down the line. Men also don't like to talk about under-fuelling because it's just seen as 'you probably should feel better and you should be on top of that'."
It is those attitudes among male athletes that prompted Keay to conduct an experiment in 2019.
Assessing 50 male competitive cyclists, Keay found in her initial screenings that nearly half had poor bone health and 25% were suffering from REDs.
The cyclists were then split into two groups and across a six-month period, one half continued their training and fuelling habits as before while the others were tutored by Keay and offered nutrition and training advice.
"The group that I left to their own devices unfortunately went on the default and they lost even more bone mineral density, similar to an astronaut in space… And they performed OK, but relative to their functional threshold power, they didn't get the race results that you would have expected.
"For the group I took under my wing, there was an improvement in their bone health and really good race results.
"So, I had evidence that REDs definitely does exist quite extensively in my group of the male cyclists and you're going to underperform if you don't fuel sufficiently. The good news is that REDs is reversible. But if you don't take action, it's a decline."
As the syndrome and its symptoms are still not commonly known, it is often difficult to know where to find help.
After former GB runner Pippa Woolven's struggles with the condition, she set up a website called Project REDs which offers information and practical resources for athletes, coaches, parents and healthcare professionals.
Keay also helps people competing at all levels to recover from REDs. Most of her patients are women, but she is starting to see more men reach out for help who, she says, are often in "bad shape".
"I think the men are maybe more reluctant than the women, or maybe they don't realise they've got it. Sometimes they might use a different word for it, they say burnout," Keay says.
"I don't mind that though because there is definitely a psychological aspect to REDs. Why are you doing this? Why are you not eating the carbohydrates?"
Sometimes, it's hard to answer those questions because the under-fuelling is unintentional, either from not understanding or underestimating energy requirements or failing to match an increase in the intensity or duration of exercise with higher calorie or carbohydrate intake.
For others, former British cycling champion Brian Smith among them, the answer comes from intention.
Competing in the road race for Great Britain at the 1996 Olympics should have been the highlight of his career but, behind the scenes of the success, Smith was suffering with an eating disorder and serious mental health condition called bulimia – something he believes he developed from his sport's obsession with weight.
"I always felt like I was overweight. Everybody was under pressure regarding weight, but nobody really spoke about it," he says.
"I'm just under six foot and I've got large glutes and thigh muscles. As a road cyclist, I used to race at 68kg and for my height and build, that's quite skinny. I even got down to about 66kg and when I got down to that, I felt underpowered, I felt bad."
Smith, now 59, only discovered he had been suffering from REDs during his career when he started running eight years ago and developed three severe stress fractures, including one in his femur.
Such has been the toll on his body that Smith says he would now never encourage anyone to pursue a career as a professional cyclist.
"It really is not healthy," he says. "If you want to go to the highest levels of the sport, you will suffer later on in life. You're destroying your body.
"Sporting teams don't care - all they're worried about is performance. So they will nurture a rider, they will feed a rider, they'll get a rider to be a certain weight. They don't care about what happens to them later in life.
"I'm suffering now and I've so many regrets. I just wish I'd known more about this."
While Smith believes his sport has a long way to go in changing attitudes, British Cycling says a lot of progress has been made through education that starts at academy level and annual physical and psychological screenings.
"One of the big things we've done in the past 10 years is try and turn this into a performance-related conversation," Dr Nigel Jones, British Cycling chief medical officer, tells BBC Sport.
"Now, we couch the conversation with an athlete around 'if you under-fuel, you will not be able to perform at your best', whereas previously, conversations in power-to-weight ratio sports might have been 'you need to be lighter'.
"I think it would be naive to say REDs is never going to be an issue. But I would like to believe that its prevalence will reduce with the work that we're doing," he adds.
British Cycling is not alone in this approach, with World Climbing taking things a step further two years ago with the introduction of mandatory health checks on athletes.
Using a combination of pre-season questionnaires and 'random and targeted' screenings at competitions - similar to the way doping tests are enforced – climbers at World Championship or World Cup-level competitions are monitored for any indicators of low energy availability or REDs and could be prevented from competing if they are not deemed to be healthy.
The policy was drawn up by expert Professor Naama Constantini, who says she is "proud" of the move by World Climbing and believes other federations should follow suit.
"We are trying to educate and prevent. I'm not a policeman and we're not looking for cheaters. I'm a medical doctor and we want to make sure our athletes are healthy," she says.
"Prevention is the best medicine you can give. We want athletes and coaches to understand that it's not about weight. It's about strength, it's about performance and fuelling the body and you pay a price if you lose weight in an unhealthy way."
With more awareness and education, it is hoped the tide can be turned on REDs.
But many still suffer in ignorance, as well as silence. That is what motivates Jake Smith to keep sharing his recovery on social media, with hundreds of men and women messaging him for advice and support.
Smith has managed to reverse his condition and is now racing better than ever, recently completing the Berlin marathon in a personal-best time of two hours, nine minutes and 24 seconds.
The big goal is the 2028 Olympics, but he is adamant that the priority is making sure he stands on every start line as healthy as possible.
"I'd never want to see an athlete go through the years I've had. I'm 10-15 kilos heavier than I've ever been and the biggest thing I can say is I've never been so happy. You need a healthy body to do everything else.
"I'm heavier, I'm faster, I'm happier."

An eight-year-old boy diagnosed with Type II achalasia – a rare disorder that affects the ability to swallow food and liquids – has undergone a Perora-l Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM) procedure at Rela Hospital.
Achalasia affects the nerves controlling the muscles of the oesophagus, causing the lower oesophageal sphincter – a muscular valve connecting the food pipe to the stomach – to remain abnormally tight. This prevents food and liquids from passing normally into the stomach. The condition is estimated to affect 0.1 to 0.18 children per 100,000 annually.
The child had progressively worsening difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids. Following the procedure, he was able to resume consuming clear liquids and subsequently, a soft diet, within 24 hours.
POEM involves passing an endoscope through the mouth and creating a small tunnel within the oesophageal wall to reach and divide the muscle fibres causing the obstruction. Unlike conventional surgery, the procedure does not require external incisions or stitches.
S.N.K. Chenduran, senior consultant and endoscopic surgeon, Department of Medical Gastroenterology, performed the procedure, which took about 50 minutes. He said performing POEM in children required particular precision because of the smaller dimensions of the oesophagus and the delicate tissues.
Dinesh Jothimani, director, Hepatology and Medical Gastroenterology, said persistent swallowing difficulties, regurgitation, vomiting, and unexplained weight loss in children warranted medical evaluation.
