US has lost measles elimination status, global health authorities say
The U.S. has lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, a public health triumph secured a quarter century ago.
Researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations on the country's status told KFF Health News that the Pan American Health Organization reached the conclusion this week: Measles has reestablished regular transmission in the country.
PAHO had planned a public announcement on Nov. 17.
In public health parlance, measles elimination depends on a country's sporadic outbreaks ending within a year. That's no longer happening in the United States.
"It's a very sad moment," said Anne Schuchat, an epidemiologist and a former deputy director at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention who was not involved in PAHO's decision.
"Measles causes so much unnecessary suffering, everything from a high fever and missed work and school to long-term complications like progressive degenerative nerve disease and death," Schuchat said.
Measles outbreaks are entirely preventable: Two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine prevent about 97% of infections, so when almost everyone in a community is fully vaccinated, the virus can't spread.
In the past two years, over 830 people have been hospitalized with measles in the U.S. More than 8,000 people have been sickened in outbreaks that have cost roughly $125 million in medical care, public health response, and productivity losses, Johns Hopkins University researchers estimate.
States have reported 13 measles-associated deaths, including a 7-month-old in New York and infants in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin in recent months. Babies typically aren't vaccinated before they're a year old.
PAHO, an international group that oversees health in the Americas and works with the World Health Organization, based its assessment on two analyses: one by the CDC and another by an independent group of measles experts.
Researchers anticipated this conclusion after an outbreak in Utah surpassed the one-year mark in June.
A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, Emily Hilliard, attributed the resurgence of measles to vaccination gaps that opened years before this administration. Indeed, rates of childhood vaccination have steadily declined since the COVID pandemic started.
But many scientists also blame the Trump administration for spreading vaccine misinformation and stifling a swift, strong response to outbreaks.
For example, the administration cut millions of dollars from children's immunization programs run by state health departments and terminated funds for research on vaccine hesitancy.
After Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. sacked CDC director Susan Monarez in August 2025, she told Congress she was fired because she would not preapprove changes to vaccine recommendations "without reviewing the evidence."
Monarez added that "we already have seen the largest measles outbreak in more than 30 years" and that, "if vaccine protections are weakened, preventable diseases will return."
Spokespeople for HHS and the White House defended the administration, and Kennedy, who led a prominent anti-vaccine organization before he took the helm at HHS. "The President and the Secretary have repeatedly encouraged measles vaccination, coordinated with states, and facilitated the deployment of vaccine doses across the country," White House spokesperson Allison Schuster wrote in an email.
Past administrations sounded alarms
For more than three decades, the federal government treated measles as a preventable tragedy, with sizable outbreaks triggering national efforts to boost vaccination and stop the virus from spreading.
That's no longer the case, said Patsy Stinchfield, executive director of the Measles Collaborative, a new initiative that educates the public about vaccines and assists health workers responding to outbreaks.
Stinchfield was a pediatric nurse at a children's hospital in Minnesota during the nation's last surge of measles before elimination, from 1989 to 1991. She recalled an entire ward devoted to children with measles and the enormous effort required to prevent the virus from spreading to kids with cancer and weakened immune systems.
Two children at the hospital died of measles. "That changed my career forever," she said.
Back then, she said, the federal government "saw the urgency." Officials held press conferences, spoke on the news about vaccines, issued clinical guidelines, and published reports in the CDC's flagship journal — the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, or MMWR — that drove policies.
When data suggested that some children weren't mounting a strong response to a single dose of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine, a CDC advisory committee recommended two doses of the shot.
When CDC analyses found that many children with measles hadn't been vaccinated due to cost, the government launched the Vaccines for Children program to make immunizations available free of charge to underinsured families.
Cases plummeted. By 2000, the CDC and PAHO determined that measles was no longer a national threat — measles transmission had been eliminated.
"Elimination" allows for occasional outbreaks, because measles is not eradicated worldwide and a small fraction of people, such as young infants, can't be protected by vaccines.
People infected abroad sparked occasional outbreaks after U.S. elimination, but — until now — those fizzled out because of herd immunity, when 95% of people within a community are immunized. In those situations, outbreaks peter out and vulnerable people are protected.
It would be 14 years before another significant outbreak in the U.S. Then in 2015, the virus took off among unvaccinated children at Disney parks in California, giving rise to outbreaks elsewhere. Congress saw some 125 cases as an emergency and summoned the CDC's Schuchat to testify on the situation.
"Vaccination wasn't a partisan issue," she recalled. "This was about problem-solving: What can we do about this?"
National television aired a video of then-U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy talking with Sesame Street's Elmo about vaccination. HHS officials worked with vaccine experts on strategies to boost public confidence in vaccines. California and Vermont tightened vaccine requirements.
In 2019, House and Senate committees met again about measles, as a large outbreak took hold in Orthodox Jewish communities in New York and New Jersey took hold. Congress asked HHS leaders how the administration planned to curb the rise of vaccine misinformation online.
"Internet fraudsters who claim that vaccines are not safe are preying on the unfounded fears and daily struggles of parents, and they are creating a public health hazard that is entirely preventable," Lamar Alexander, then a Republican senator from Tennessee, said at the time.
Alex Azar, health secretary during the first Trump administration, and then-CDC Director Robert Redfield held a press conference stressing the "importance of on-time vaccination."
And during the 2014, 2015, and 2019 outbreaks, the CDC's MMWR published detailed articles within weeks of data collection. Timing matters since the reports guide emergency response. "The MMWR is the voice of the CDC," Schuchat said, "alerting the nation, the media, clinicians, and public health experts to events that require action."
'The dog didn't bark'
Just after President Donald Trump took office in 2025, a measles outbreak exploded in West Texas. Within seven months, it surpassed the size of any in the U.S. since 1992, spread to Mexico and at least three other states, sickened more than 4,500 people in the two countries, and killed at least 16.
Instead of broadcasting clear, repeated messages on the importance of measles vaccines, Kennedy falsely claimed on Fox News that they lead to "deaths every year."
Congress didn't call a hearing, and HHS didn't send funds until after the emergency in West Texas had subsided. Besides an annual measles update, the MMWR didn't publish a single report on the outbreaks that year.
"A lot of this is the dog didn't bark," said Dorit Reiss, a vaccine policy researcher at the University of California Law San Francisco. "Something that normally happens isn't happening."
Political appointees have delayed or blocked several MMWR articles, according to multiple CDC officials whom KFF Health News agreed not to identify because they feared retaliation for speaking with the press. "There's a deliberate effort to downplay vaccine-preventable diseases by the administration," one official said.
"Measles reports from West Texas and New Mexico were intentionally shelved," another scientist at the agency said. In April, The Washington Post reported that Jay Bhattacharya, who temporarily led the CDC this year and remains head of the National Institutes of Health, had blocked the publication of a study in the MMWR finding that COVID vaccines halved the likelihood of emergency department visits.
"The suggestion that HHS is deliberately suppressing information about measles or other vaccine-preventable diseases is false," Hilliard, the HHS spokesperson, said in an email to KFF Health News.
Hilliard said Kennedy and the CDC have provided approximately $100 million in additional funding to respond to outbreaks. The timing of MMWR reports, she added, varies due to factors such as data analysis and scientific review.
More than a year after data was collected from Texas, a few reports came out in the CDC's journal. One study on 60 people hospitalized for measles in West Texas revealed that two required intubation and mechanical ventilation and that a baby born to a mother with measles experienced dangerous brain swelling due to the virus.
The MMWR still hasn't published detailed reports on massive outbreaks in South Carolina, Utah, and Pennsylvania. The CDC's national measles update hasn't appeared in the MMWR this year either. Instead, the journal has featured less urgent articles on scientific techniques that may help characterize future outbreaks.
CDC scientists told KFF Health News that they continue to analyze data but no longer expect to publish their findings in the MMWR because the process has become slow, opaque, and unpredictable. An urgent CDC report on the risks of measles to pregnant women was withheld, The Washington Post reported recently.
"We have two CDCs now," an official at the agency said. "One is staffed by CDC scientists and civil servants who are committed to public health, and the other is political appointees who go in and change the website."
The CDC's measles dashboard counts four fewer measles deaths than state health departments have reported this year. Kennedy has disputed some deaths and made unsubstantiated claims that Pennsylvania health officials misrepresented data.
Kennedy personally instructed the CDC to alter language on a webpage that said vaccines do not cause autism, he told The New York Times last year.
The page now suggests a potential link between the two and no longer lists a slew of peer-reviewed studies that rigorously searched for an association and found none. These have been replaced with speculation about a correlation and unsubstantiated accusations that the scientific establishment has buried a potential link in order "to prevent vaccine hesitancy."
The Trump administration has muddied the message on vaccines in other ways, Reiss said. Trump incorrectly said in August that the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine could be "quite lethal," and he repeated the debunked idea that vaccines may cause autism.
Stephen Miller, now Trump's White House chief of staff, has falsely said doctors "pump your kids full of shots days after birth with no understanding of the long-term consequences." Recommended vaccines and the vaccine schedule have been thoroughly studied.
Kennedy has made such claims for two decades, including as health secretary. "Having top leadership disseminating rumors, disinformation and flat-out falsehoods has been unforgivable," Schuchat said.
When pressed by journalists and Congress, Kennedy and Trump have recommended measles vaccines. But they haven't repeated the message clearly and unprompted on social media or on the podcasts and videos that Kennedy regularly appears in.
Kennedy also replaced vaccine experts on a panel advising the CDC with fringe researchers holding anti-vaccine views. And under his leadership, the CDC has laid off or forced out many vaccine specialists, including all of those in a group that partners with community organizations and pharmacies, the Immunization Services Division partnership branch.
At the same time, Kennedy has devoted resources to searching for potential harms from vaccines, including through an attempted clinical trial considered unnecessary and unethical by medical societies and the WHO.
To regain measles elimination status, the current U.S. outbreaks must end — then, future outbreaks must stop spreading within a year, said Paul Rota, a microbiologist and former CDC official. With outbreaks expanding in several states, he said, that moment isn't on the horizon.
"Bigger fires create more embers, and any one of those embers can seed another fire," he said.

If you feel like the digital world is ending, you're not alone.
A string of high-profile technology outages over the past week has disrupted the lives of many Americans trying to travel, transfer money, or make purchases, and caused speculation that something bigger and more nefarious could be going on.
There has been no indication from government officials or the companies affected that cyberattacks or AI were responsible. And despite the uncanny timing, there are no signs the incidents were connected.
"At this point, there is no indication that these incidents are the result of a cyberattack, foreign interference, or some coordinated effort," Sen. Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence committee, said in a statement Tuesday, adding that the evidence suggested the outages were due to "legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity."
Warner said AI was allowing vulnerabilities to be identified faster and creating pressure to fix them immediately, "putting tremendous strain on systems that weren't built to handle that pace of change."
"These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call," he said. "It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences."
Here are the major outages reported and what we know about each one.
Microsoft
Microsoft experienced a major outage last week that impacted its 365 tool suite, affecting products such as Outlook, Teams, and Copilot.
By late Friday morning, the company said services were stabilizing.
Microsoft said the cause of the outage was "technical" and "not related to cyber or AI / agents."
Federal Aviation Administration
The Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday, citing issues with its air traffic control systems.
Flights were grounded for over four hours, leading to thousands of delays and cancellations on Friday and Saturday.
Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin blamed the outage on aging air traffic control infrastructure.
Mullin said they did not believe the outage was related to cybersecurity or an AI attack.
JPMorgan Chase
JPMorgan Chase said Monday said it experienced service issues related to a "software bug in on-premise hardware systems."
Customers had reported issues accessing account information and delayed transactions. Customers of other banks also reported issues, including Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and US Bank, with the latter saying customers attempting to use Chase's Zelle may have been affected.
"There is no evidence this is cyber-related," Chase said.
United Airlines
United Airlines on Monday said it fixed a "technology issue" after a system outage caused delays to departing flights.
The airline said flights in progress and United Express flights weren't affected. United had 945 delayed flights on Monday, according to the flight tracking site FlightAware.
"There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue," United said.
Charles Schwab
Charles Schwab experienced issues with its website on Tuesday. Some users were unable to access the site, which temporarily displayed a message that said its server "encountered an internal error or misconfiguration and was unable to complete your request."
The spokesperson for the brokerage firm said a "brief webpage loading issue has been resolved."
Apple
Apple said an "internal update" caused outages to some of its services after users online said they were having issues accessing Apple Pay and iCloud.
"Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning," Apple said in a statement. "We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible."
Apple said the incident was not a cyberattack.

Tata Sons had sought guidance from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in a letter dated October 6 regarding the listing requirement for upper layer non-banking financial companies (NBFCs).
According to a report by Moneycontrol, it was to this letter that the RBI clarified that the company must comply with regulations applicable to upper-layer NBFCs, including the stock exchange listing requirement.
The central bank's communication, issued late on Nov 16, followed a letter sent by the Tata Group holding company on Oct 6 seeking guidance on its regulatory obligations.
As per the report, Tata Sons wanted clarity on when the listing requirement would apply and the steps necessary to ensure compliance.
The company reportedly informed the RBI that it intended to follow all applicable regulations and was prepared to initiate the required process.
In its response, the RBI advised Tata Sons to comply with existing guidelines governing upper-layer NBFCs, including mandatory listing provisions.
As per the sources cited in the report, the clarification strengthened the expectation that Tata Sons would have to pursue a stock exchange listing.
However, the precise still deadline remains uncertain.
As per the report, a banker associated with the company said establishing the applicable timeline was among the objectives of the October correspondence.
The RBI first classified Tata Sons as an upper-layer NBFC in September 2022, following the introduction of scale-based regulations in 2021.
Under the framework, companies placed in this category are generally required to list their shares within three years of classification.
Tata Sons remained on the regulator's upper-layer NBFC list in September 2023.
The RBI again included the company in its Jan 16, 2025, list while acknowledging its application to surrender its NBFC registration.
At that time, the regulator clarified that the classification would remain subject to the outcome of the deregistration request, which was under examination.
The latest communication has renewed attention on Tata Sons' regulatory obligations.
The central question now concerns the listing deadline and how the existing rules apply to the company's circumstances.

Around 86% of the spending on measures against tuberculosis (TB) in 2025 came from domestic sources, the recently released Global Tuberculosis Report 2026 by the World Health Organisation (WHO) said, even as the reduction in international donor funding to combat the infectious disease remains a cause of concern.
TB cases remain one of the leading causes of death from a single infectious agent, with a quarter of all cases concentrated in India in 2025. The report notes that $22 billion is needed annually for TB prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care to achieve the global targets agreed on at the 2023 United Nations high-level TB meeting by 2027.
In absolute terms, Brazil, China, India, the Russian Federation, and South Africa accounted for $3.7 billion (65%) of the total of $5.63 billion provided from domestic sources in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).
The report notes that international donor funding fell by 14%, from $1.1 billion in 2024 to $0.94 billion in 2025, having been relatively stable at about $1.1–1.3 billion per year between 2015 and 2024.
Financing for TB research and innovation, at $1.2 billion in 2023, also continued to fall far short of the global target of $5 billion per year. Progress to date has been constrained by the overall level of investment, said the report.
“TB mostly affects adults in their most productive years. However, all age groups are at risk. Over 80% of cases and deaths are in low- and middle-income countries. In 2025, the largest number of new TB cases occurred in the WHO South-East Asia Region (35%),’’ said the report.
South-East Asia Region
The WHO on Friday (November 13, 2026) called on countries in the South-East Asia Region to accelerate action to end TB. The latest TB estimates show the region accounts for 3.6 million people who developed TB in 2025 — 34% of the global total — and 4,00,000 TB-related deaths, or 35% of the global total. "These numbers are a stark reminder that TB remains one of the Region’s most pressing public health and development challenges,” said Nilesh Buddha, officer-in-charge, WHO South-East Asia Region.
A release issued by the regional office added that in 2025, $1.03 billion was available for TB prevention and care in the region, with 91% from domestic sources. Yet this represented only around 16% of global TB funding, despite the region accounting for 34% of global cases. "Closing this gap in resources is critical to sustaining progress," the WHO said.
“Ending TB is not simply a health sector responsibility. It requires leadership across government, sustained investment, strong health systems and communities at the centre of the response. We have tools to prevent, diagnose and treat TB. What is needed now is the commitment to ensure they reach everyone who needs them, without delay or financial hardship,” said Dr. Buddha, adding that ending TB by 2030 will depend on countries turning political commitments into measurable action, with greater urgency and scale.
Far from target
Meanwhile, the Global TB Report said that across the world, about 50% of people treated for TB and their households face total costs (direct medical expenditures, non-medical expenditures, and indirect costs such as income losses) that are catastrophic (more than 20% of total household income). This is far from the target of the WHO End TB Strategy of zero.
In 2025, globally there were an estimated 0.96 million new TB cases that were attributable to undernutrition, 0.92 million to diabetes, 0.73 million to alcohol use disorders, 0.69 million to smoking, and 0.55 million to HIV infection.

Owono did not deserve 12-match ban - Pique
- Published
FC Andorra owner Gerard Pique says goalkeeper Jesus Owono did not deserve the 12-match suspension he received following his challenge which resulted in the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
Owono, 25, was sent off after colliding with De Miguel late on in the second-tier match between Andorra and Tenerife on 2 November.
De Miguel died the following day, aged 30, and a disciplinary committee from the Spanish football federation confirmed Owono's ban last week.
In a video posted on social media, Pique said players past and present, plus coaches and other goalkeepers, felt the incident was "an accident".
The former Spain and Barcelona defender added: "I truly believe that imposing the maximum sanction on Jesus for this action puts him in a situation he does not deserve, because he is not to blame for all of this having happened."
- Tenerife striker De Miguel dies after on-field collision 
  - Published3 November
- Goalkeeper involved in fatal collision gets 12-game ban 
  - Published3 days ago
The 12-match suspension was the maximum punishment Owono, 25, could have received, as the disciplinary committee could only consider the offence on the pitch and not "the tragic outcome of the incident".
Following the decision, Tenerife manager Alvaro Cervera said he accepted the regulations do not specifically account for what happened, but acknowledged the ban "might feel light".
Pique also highlighted a recent on-field incident in Spain, when Albacete winger Jose Corpas accidentally kicked Sabadell midfielder Quadri Liameed in the head during a Spanish second division match.
Nigerian Liameed was knocked unconscious but was later discharged from hospital following medical checks, while Spaniard Corpas was shown a straight red card and handed a three-match ban.
"Fortunately Quadri is fine, the consequences in this case were not fatal, and the committee decided to sanction Corpas with three matches," Pique said.
"With all this, my reflection is: what is being sanctioned, the action or the consequences?"
Owono has withdrawn from Equatorial Guinea's squad for Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against Zimbabwe this month, and Pique said it was unlikely he would return to action as soon as his suspension is served.
He added: "Jesus is going to need far more than 12 matches before he is available and able to compete.
"No sanction is going to bring [De Miguel] back to us."

Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act, 2026 earlier this year. The new Act represents a significant shift from the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019. The 2026 amendment removes the principle of self-identification and demands a medical board’s recommendation; a selection from prescribed categories; and certification by a District Magistrate. It fundamentally changes legal recognition for transgender persons from self-identification to medical assessment. While the 2026 Act does increase protection, it changes the philosophical foundation of transgender rights — from recognition based substantially on autonomy and self-identification towards recognition mediated by medical and administrative authorities.
The definition of “transgender” as introduced in the Amendment Act is in contradiction to established international evidence and guidelines laid down in the World Health Organization ICD-11 and the World Professional Association for Transgender Health Standards of Care Version 8.

Quad leaders unveil initiatives to boost Indo-Pacific trade, connectivity; oppose coercion
PM Modi joined US President Donald Trump, Australian PM Anthony Albanese and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi for the Quad Leaders Summit in Manila.
The leaders of the four Quad nations met in Manila on Tuesday for the first time in more than two years, reiterating their commitment to a free and open Indo-Pacific and unveiling new initiatives meant to bolster maritime surveillance, trade and connectivity across the region.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi joined US President Donald Trump, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi for the Quad Leaders Summit, which – without naming China – opposed unilateral actions to alter the status quo by force or coercion and expressed concern over economic coercion, including arbitrary export restrictions.
ALSO READ: 'He's a very tough man and a great leader’: Trump praises Modi during Quad Summit meet
Deep Dive
This was Trump’s first Quad Summit and came ahead of his participation in a meeting of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum to be hosted by China's President Xi Jinping, who has objected to the Quad as an effort to encircle Beijing, and a trilateral meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US on Thursday.
“For India, the Quad is a constructive and trusted partnership. From maritime security to trusted supply chains, new technologies and disaster response, our endeavour is to ensure that the Quad delivers trusted solutions to the entire Indo-Pacific,” Modi said in his opening remarks at the meeting.
Modi announced Mumbai will host the inaugural Quad Business Leaders Forum in early 2027, while Trump said the grouping will conduct its first military exercise with maritime patrol aircraft to “protect peace through strength”.
“As four major market economies, we have a shared responsibility to create greater trade opportunities and build stronger supply chains. To turn our strategic cooperation into commercial partnerships, India has announced the Quad Business Leaders Forum,” Modi said.
The forum will gather business leaders, government officials and policy experts to foster greater business ties across private sectors, including the promotion of commercial deals and partnerships, a joint press release said.
“If Australia's mining experience, Japan's recycling technology, America's expertise and India's manufacturing base come together, they could provide new strength to supply chains,” Modi added.
The Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration, which takes forward the Quad’s earlier maritime domain awareness initiative, is meant to enhance information-sharing and maritime awareness. The P-8 and P-3 maritime patrol aircraft of the four countries will join “a maritime exercise for the first time in a Quad context, making our seas safer”, the release said.
This exercise will be conducted on the sidelines of Exercise Sea Dragon in Guam in March 2027 to address shared challenges such as illegal fishing and trafficking, foreign secretary Vikram Misri said.
The four leaders also announced an expansion of the Quad Partnership for Cable Connectivity and Resilience, currently focused on the safety of telecommunications cables. “This will now expand to undersea energy cables as well,” Misri said, referring to Australia’s contribution focused on electricity cables to strengthen regional energy security.
The four countries also welcomed upcoming undersea cable projects in the Indian Ocean intended to strengthen regional connectivity.
The Quad acknowledged a “rapid increase in the number and scale of cyber incidents” in the region and announced enhanced cybersecurity cooperation between the four countries to “achieve an open and secure cyberspace”.
The Quad nations said in the joint press release that the grouping is a “force for good and a partnership of action, committed to peace, stability, and prosperity”, while strongly opposing “any destabilising or unilateral actions that seek to change the status quo, including by force or coercion, which escalate tensions and undermine regional peace and stability”.
This was an apparent reference to China's assertive actions in the South China Sea, where it is engaged in territorial disputes with several Asean states.
The Quad expressed “grave concerns about economic coercion, including through arbitrary export restrictions” – again, an apparent reference to China's restrictions on the export of crucial commodities such as rare earths and fertilisers.
The Quad nations said they are securing critical supply chains, protecting freedom of navigation and overflight, driving growth through future technologies, including investments in trusted Artificial Intelligence (AI), and responding to disasters with life-saving assistance. “We commit to work together to ensure open, safe, and resilient maritime transit corridors in the Indo-Pacific,” the press release added.
Modi noted that the Quad's maritime domain awareness partnership has already created a real-time data sharing mechanism that is used to address illegal fishing and illicit activities in the Indo-Pacific, and said the grouping should aim to promote peace and prosperity, economic and technological resilience, and delivery of public goods.
“Safeguarding maritime security begins with ensuring the safety of the seafarers who keep it moving,” Modi said. “Therefore, we must work together to establish a robust international framework for the safety of seafarers. In this regard, India has proposed the Quad Sea Lanes Safety Initiative.”
Democracies should play a leading role in developing emerging technologies and setting standards for them to ensure they become “instruments of freedom and development”, he added.
This was the seventh Quad Summit and the first to be held outside the member countries. However, Manila has a special connection with Quad – it was in the Philippines capital that officials of the grouping first met in 2007, and activities of the grouping were subsequently revived after a hiatus at a meeting held in the city in 2017.
The Quad reiterated it will work with regional partners to tackle shared challenges and drive opportunities to deliver benefits to the Indo-Pacific, and emphasised the importance of the AI Accelerator, announced at a recent Quad foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta to coordinate and fund efforts to support trusted AI access, deployment and technical assistance.
The four countries also unequivocally condemned all forms of terrorism and violent extremism, including cross-border terrorism, and said they are committed to strengthening Quad’s ongoing cooperation on counter-terrorism.
While India struggled to convene a Quad Leaders’ Summit last year mainly because of uncertainty over Trump’s travel plans amid widespread bilateral differences over trade issues, the US President said the grouping’s members are the “four corners of a free, open, stable and prosperous Indo-Pacific”, and his “phone…and the Oval Office is always open to you”.
Trump added, “We have outstanding relationships and coordinate closely on matters of regional security, economic security and diplomacy, and we talk quite often. The three countries that we deal with, we talk a lot when they have a problem, when they have difficulty, when they want to tell me something.”
The Quad states have also made several important critical mineral deals to secure supply chains and “ensure that none of our nations is vulnerable to coercion by any single foreign supplier”, Trump said. He said initiatives by the Quad states on rare earths and other issues “over the next 12 months…will very much surprise people”.
Takaichi said the Quad will work with regional partners to shape a free and open Indo-Pacific by strengthening the resilience of countries and promoting their freedom to decide for themselves in a wide range of areas, including maritime security, economic security, energy and emerging technologies. Albanese said the Quad has a critical role in achieving the common objective of a peaceful, secure, stable and prosperous Indo-Pacific, which in turn will make the world a safer and more secure place.
However, former US deputy secretary of state Kurt Campbell said the Quad had lost ambition under Trump, and credited secretary of state Marco Rubio with the reconvening of the grouping. “Part of what [Rubio] is thinking is that this is probably the best possible signal if you're going to go into a trilateral meeting,” Campbell said, referring to Thursday's US-China-Russia talks.
The short time allotted for Tuesday's meeting meant it was unlikely to extend beyond pleasantries, Ryan Hass of the Brookings Institution told AFP. “It's a way of inoculating Trump against criticism of caving to authoritarians when he meets with [Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin] in Shenzhen,” Hass said.

Iran war dents Middle East sports as events are canceled. F1 bucks the trend
The season-ending Formula 1 races in the Middle East are going ahead despite the war in Iran and retaliatory attacks across the region that have canceled or postponed other large sports events
Two season-ending Formula 1 races in the Middle East are going ahead despite the war in Iran and retaliatory attacks across the region that have canceled or postponed other large sports events. This includes two Formula 1 races earlier this year in Saudi Arabia and Bahrain.
The conflict has upended the region's image as a safe haven where governments and sponsors have kicked in billions to lure mega-sports events. This comes as Europe and North America appear wary of such lavish spending.
“The situation could change but the geography will not change,” Sebastian Sons, who follows sports in the Middle East with the German research institute CARPO, told The Associated Press. “The Middle East and the Gulf region are always a volatile and fragile region.”
Going ahead is an endorsement for doing business in the region, but has also prompted concerns about safety from some teams and staff. Mohammed Ben Sulayem, the president of auto racing's world governing body FIA, has said “we are fully prepared” to pull off the two races: Qatar on Nov. 29 and Abu Dhabi on Dec. 6.
Ben Sulayem is from the United Arab Emirates.
A MotoGP race was held in Qatar on Nov. 8 on the track where F1 races. MotoGP is operated by Liberty Media, which also runs F1.
“Holding the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi signals that those two are stable and able to host large-scale sporting events. It is important they are seen to be open for business,” Kristian Ulrichsen, a political scientist at Rice University's Baker Institute, told The AP.
“Predictability in long-term decision-making and policy planning,” Ulrichsen added, “made the region so attractive as a host of mega-events at a time when many cities and countries around the world are rethinking the cost of doing so.”
Qatar’s reputation is on the line. It held the 2022 World Cup and is a co-favorite — with India — to land the 2036 Olympics. It’s also host next year to the basketball World Cup (Aug. 27-Sept. 12) and has the 2030 Asian Games.
It took a hit last week when the United States pulled its team from the boys’ under-17 World Cup being played in Qatar.
Saudi Arabia and its Persian Gulf neighbors have spent big to hold major sports events but were cutting back on mega-sports funding before the war began nine months ago.
“For Saudi, the war has accelerated the need to find economies, to maybe reassess what was feasible and what wasn’t,” Ulrichsen said. He said landing the “big prize,” two years ago — the 2034 World Cup — probably honed Saudi's focus.
“Qatar and the UAE will probably have to at some point do the same,” he added.
Major events called off, postponed or relocated include the two Formula 1 races earlier in the season, and the WTA season-ending tennis finals and soccer’s monthlong Asian Cup — both originally scheduled for Saudi Arabia. The 2027 Dakar Rally was also moved from Saudi Arabia to Portugal and Morocco.
The region has been using sports to promote “soft power” to enhance its brand. But Saudi Arabia now faces hard power with Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels having struck Saudi Arabia’s main international airport in Riyadh. Riyadh’s business district has also recently been targeted.
The war has also affected the large Gulf air carriers and changed travel patterns in the region.
“One of the things Iran did during the war was to deliberately attack the connective tissue between Gulf states and the world,” Sascha Bruchmann, an analyst at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told The AP. “This includes ports, airports, hotels and data centers — signaling that Iran can attack important issues beyond hydrocarbons and challenge the Gulf states’ ambitions to diversify.”
Sons, the researcher at the German think tank, estimated that Saudi Arabia invested more than $6 billion in international sports between 2021 and 2023. Sons said the country hosted more than 100 international sports events between 2019 and 2024.
A visible failure was the bankruptcy of LIV Golf, which reports say was funded by approximately $5 billion from Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund. Saudi Arabia also canceled the 2029 Asian Winter Games, planned for the Trojena ski village in the south of the desert kingdom.
The event has been moved to Almaty, Kazakhstan, which lost to Beijing in a close vote for the 2022 Winter Olympics.
Ulrichsen said Saudi Arabia was backing off what seemed like a “scattergun approach,” backing LIV Golf, planning an unlikely Winter Asian Games, bankrolling soccer star Cristiano Ronaldo, and buying the Premier League team Newcastle. All are varied approaches to “soft power.”
Ronaldo is reported to earn more than $200 million annually with Saudi club Al-Nassr.
Qatar's sovereign wealth fund controls French club Paris Saint-Germain, and Manchester City is controlled by an Abu Dhabi investment group. Ulrichsen argued sports teams are a more effective investment than World Cups or Olympics “because people care more about the teams they support than an event that happens for three or four weeks.”
“When Ronaldo would post on Instagram about the amazing lifestyle he was enjoying in Riyadh, that would reach upward of a half a billion people,” Ulrichsen added. “You simply can't buy that kind of reach with a conventional PR campaign.”

The AI start-ups fixing India's broken roads and messy land records
- Published
In 2020, Sanjay Mandava flew down from Chicago to Chennai in southern India to resolve a personal land dispute.
Over the next few months, he was running around between government offices to access a dozen records that would conclusively prove that the property belonged to his family.
Just a sale deed dating back to when his parents bought the land was not enough. Authorities asked him to produce a string of other documents.
Frustrated by the experience, he built Landeed - an AI-led digital platform that enables users to aggregate fragmented, multi-source land-records, verify titles and conduct legal checks at the click of a few buttons, across 24 states in India.
He's solving a problem that is uniquely Indian.
"In the US or UK, when you purchase a property, the government verifies ownership. In India by contrast, we follow presumptive titling - the buyer is responsible for establishing ownership. A sale deed merely records the transaction - multiple other documents may be needed to prove title," Mandava told the BBC.
These include building certificates, property tax receipts and land survey maps among others.
The system is rife for misuse - property disputes account for a bulk of civil litigation cases in the country where some 80% of household wealth is held in real estate.
Landeed has mapped large swathes of India using geo-spatial technology and data from state land revenue departments, registration offices, survey records and municipal databases.
Using this, it has linked registered properties to their official land identification and survey numbers and ownership records.
An additional AI-layer can read these titles, extract information and spot inconsistencies within minutes - a process that takes lawyers and brokers several days.
With the largest repository of title data in the country, consisting of 1.8 billion documents, the app is now used by millions of individual and enterprise customers while doing real estate transactions.
The app is among a burgeoning list of Indian start-ups trying to address some of India's most complex challenges in sectors ranging from legal-tech to healthcare, infrastructure, education and agriculture using AI.
Unlike the US and China which have a global dominance in building frontier language models like ChatGPT, India's AI revolution is happening downstream in data centre infrastructure and consumer applications rather than in research.
Start-ups are solving issues for everything from pothole detection to tribal language translation to assisting overworked public-health professionals with medical tasks - often working with highly fragmented, multilingual datasets in extremely cost sensitive industries.
Bengaluru-based YouTube teacher Gaurav Sen's AI app detects potholes using a dash-cam, satellite-based navigation and an AI vision model to analyse images.
It then identifies civic officials responsible for fixing them and sends them this data. He got viral attention recently given how widespread the menace of potholes is across India's urban sprawls.
On last count, there are at least half a dozen other similar offerings that map and report road damage to authorities across the country.
"A municipal corporation can take the app and use it on public buses and taxis, to access real-time, updated data on road conditions," Sen told the BBC.
In Mumbai on India's western coast, Fractal Analytics - among the few Indian listed AI companies - has deployed its AI tool "Vaidya" in hospitals run by the local civic authority.
The app allows citizens to receive AI-generated, simplified summaries of their lab reports in multiple languages, identify nearby healthcare facilities based on their needs and gives doctors AI-guided pre-consultation support such as medical history and medication details of patients.
It also provides hospital administrators with a public health dashboard based on aggregated, anonymous insights from lab reports accessed through its tie-up with municipal hospitals, giving them crucial visibility into emerging infections or other disease trends.
This boom has led to a surge in funding for AI start-ups - up 265% year-on-year according to Inc42, external, a start-up information platform. They raised over $1bn in the first nine months of this year amid a relatively muted fundraising environment for the broader ecosystem.
Yet, these companies face an uphill task in commercialising their ideas and taking them beyond pilot.
"The cost of building in India is sometimes much higher than what Indian customers are willing to pay," Fractal's co-founder Srikanth Velamakanni told the BBC at his sprawling office overlooking Mumbai's film city.
"The computing power needed to run an AI model is the same whether it is built in India or the US - but American customers have a far bigger paying capacity than those here."
Indian AI founders are also being forced to build around scarcity, with availability of high quality chips at the right scale and price, a major impediment for many.
"I believe I am building one of the most impactful things for this country," says Mandava.
"But I am starved for GPUs [chips that perform millions of calculations and help train AI models]. I have a hellish time trying to acquire them," he says.
The country has promised its start-ups 38,000 GPUs through its government-led AI mission, external, but demand for this compute power is far greater than supply.
Cumbersome regulation and bureaucracy are other major challenges.
Without these fundamental issues being addressed, there's a risk that Indian AI companies will build shallow solutions that a next generation of founders will immediately make redundant, say experts.
"Someone like a Google will probably laugh if I tell them of my pilot. To make it sustainable and hard to replicate, it will have to be much more sophisticated," says Sen, displaying a self-awareness of where his product currently stands.
From a lack of experienced talent to the struggle to turn successful pilots into recurring government contracts to heavy dependence on expensive foreign technology, Indian founders are powering through many odds.
"We can still do it. We don't want protection, but propel us, give us the weapons to compete against the best," Mandava says, when asked what he wants from policymakers.
"To quote Jay-Z - I can't help the poor if I'm one of them," he adds.

Pakistan's solar revolution seems unstoppable - but there's a problem
- Published
Jewellery, glimmering silverware, sofas and an air-conditioning unit. Three months after his wedding, Faisal Shahzad's home in rural Punjab is bursting with gifts from his bride's family, as part of the dowry.
But the most prized possession is tucked under the bed: a 340W solar panel.
"In the summer we ran it from 08:00 in the morning until the evening," he says, adding they didn't need to use grid power at all during the day. "We ran our air cooler on it all day."
Pakistan has seen a boom in imported solar panels, which glisten from the rooftops of homes and hospitals; from farmers' fields to industrial complexes.
From 2018 to 2025, the share of electricity generated from solar energy in the country rose from 1% to 28%, according to Pakistan-based think tank Renewables First, with some seven million households now owning panels.
People used to gift motorbikes or other household items at weddings, Shahzad says. "Now they give a solar panel and an air cooler. It has almost become a must."
Alongside the solar panel he still uses the national grid to meet his energy needs, particularly as he lives in a house with his family and brothers' families, who often use multiple appliances simultaneously. But in a country where the average wage is just under 40,000 Pakistani rupees (£110; $145) per month, bills are becoming unaffordable, rising to 15,000-18,000 rupees.
This year, COP31 is pushing the world to move away from fossil-powered vehicles, boilers and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment. And while Pakistan has become a poster child for solarisation, the national grid system is experiencing knock-on eﬀects.
The power grid death spiral
The big pivot to solar wasn't driven by government policy but by individual Pakistani households. Most people we spoke to said they installed panels to escape soaring electricity prices from an often unreliable national grid.
Electricity tariffs have more than doubled in a few years, says Muhammad Hassan Dajana, industry liaison at Renewables First, while the cost of Chinese solar panels has "decreased by 93%".
"People have just found another way to be able to survive," says Energy Minister Awais Ahmad Leghari. "It's a very healthy thing. We have adapted to the situation. The people have reacted and responded in a very economically viable and efficient manner."
While the solar boom brings clear benefits, particularly for a country that imports huge amounts of fuel, there are worries too.
Pakistan needs to avoid the so-called utility death spiral.
When people buy less energy from the national grid, fewer customers are left to cover the fixed costs of maintaining it. That can force prices up - which in turn encourages even more people to switch to solar.
Over time, this can lead to a two-tier system in which those who can't afford to buy panels face ever-rising bills, while the national grid becomes an increasing burden on the state.
"You'll have a white elephant in the form of a state-owned enterprise that requires a lot of public funding to just stay afloat," says Dajana.
Pakistan's government says the costs are already being felt.
"In just the past two years, the exodus from the grid has cost the rest of the consumers more than $500 million [£378m] a year," says Leghari. "That's a very big burden."
The government doesn't want to pull people away from solar, he explains, but wants the grid to be more competitive to be able to offer better energy prices.
Private power producers, which feed into the grid, have been heavily criticised inside Pakistan for locking the country into costly, inflexible contracts. Producers themselves point to broader structural problems like poor grid maintenance as contributing to higher bills. Leghari says the government has renegotiated most of the contracts and is now focused on making the grid more efficient with better storage, less waste and more innovation.
Leghari wants the country to run on "up to 90% clean power" by the end of 2036 - including renewables and nuclear - with dependence on imported energy reducing from 26% to 4%.
The solar power boom in Pakistan and the Philippines
Cheap solar panels, mainly imported from China, are transforming lives and slashing electricity bills across Asia.
Solar-powered business
But as the government tries to improve the grid, solar is still expanding with widespread adoption in industry.
Kohinoor Textiles Mills in Islamabad, which is powered by a sea of huge blue solar panels, is one example. Utilities manager Sabawoon Khan describes them as his "baby", pointing at construction work levelling the ground for more panels.
When the sun shines, the mills' hundreds of machines are powered entirely by solar energy, Khan says. The heavy-furnace-oil engines they once relied on sit mothballed in a warehouse.
But there are limits. When it's too cloudy or polluted, and during the night, the company takes more energy from the national grid. In the coming weeks, like other firms, it will start using industrial batteries which can store excess solar energy.
"We needed to reduce our energy costs and this was one way to do it," says Taufique Sayeed Saigol, the mills' CEO, who adds the plan is not to disconnect from the grid altogether.
"The state unfortunately doesn't have the resources so we can't really say that we blame everything on the state. We do some of the things ourselves."
Critics accuse the government of moving the goalposts on solar power. Previously, households could feed excess electricity into the grid and earn credits, which were then used to offset the cost of grid power when the sun wasn't shining. That policy changed earlier this year.
"Initially their policy was very helpful," says Arif Ehsan Malik, president of Faisalabad's chamber of commerce. "But then the policy changed. Now they have started purchasing at a lower rate and selling back at a higher rate."
Malik says that makes a big difference for small and medium businesses. Leghari counters that the costs of the initial model didn't add up; the electricity the solar producers put into the system was much cheaper than the electricity they ended up taking out of it.
"Those profits were coming at the cost of the rest of the consumers of the grid. Had we not changed those regulations, the rest of the consumers would have been burdened by at least 150 to 200 billion rupees a year, say, two years from now."
Despite admitting that the first wave of solar adoption was a "surprise" to the government, Leghari says he has no fear that solar could outrun their plans, saying it has been incorporated into their 10-year forecasts and the numbers leaving the grid have slowed.
Pakistan has big ambitions for solar; there are plans to open solar battery factories around the country and encourage more electric vehicles.
But it's also at a crossroads.
"There are two paths ahead," Dajana says. One is a future where solar and the grid work in parallel, demonstrating how a gradual energy transition can succeed. The other is where Pakistan becomes a cautionary tale, burdened with a costly, declining grid.
Shahzad's solar ambitions for his home in rural Punjab certainly have not slowed.
"We plan to get another 10-15 panels and install them on the roof, then connect a full system with batteries and back up.
"The plan is to be fully self-sufficient."

The spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is threatening modern medicine despite progress in combating drug-resistant bacteria, senior World Health Organization officials said Monday, November 16, 2026.
WHO officials said countries had expanded efforts to tackle AMR, but warned that progress in prevention, diagnosis and the appropriate use of antibiotics remained too slow to meet global targets.
Bacteria have long evolved resistance to medicines designed to kill them.
The widespread use of antibiotics in human health, animal husbandry and food production has accelerated the problem, making AMR one of the leading causes of infectious-disease deaths worldwide.
"Antimicrobial resistance is widespread and threatening the future of modern medicine," said Jean-Pierre Nyemazi, interim head of antimicrobial resistance at the WHO. "Unlike COVID-19, which was very visible, drug-resistant infections have been taking people's lives for years without us noticing it and raising the alarm as we should," said Nyemazi.
In 2021 alone, AMR was directly responsible for more than one million deaths and linked to some 4.7 million others, said the agency.
A WHO investigation in 183 countries into the progress of the fight against antimicrobial resistance this year revealed that nearly nine countries in 10 had a national action plan against the phenomenon. In 2017, the figure was only around four in 10.
But only 42 countries -- less than one in five -- said they had a plan that was financed, implemented and monitored, said Pravasha Prakash, an AMR technical officer with the global health agency.
"Countries are moving forward in every step but progress still needs to be speeded up to reach the 2030 targets," she added.
Poor access to diagnostics
One of the main weaknesses remains access to diagnostics. Only 36% of countries had a national reference laboratory capable of testing for resistance in all bacteria and fungi monitored by the WHO -- well short of the 80% target set for 2030.
"Without testing, clinicians must treat without knowing the cause of infection or which antibiotic will work," said Sylvia Bertagnolo, head of surveillance for AMR at the WHO.
The latest global surveillance data show that in 2023, one in every six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections flagged to the WHO was resistant to antibiotics used to treat it.
As a result, the WHO has announced the release of two new tools designed to help countries strengthen their diagnostic capacities.
The first defines the tests that should be available at every level of the healthcare system, from primary care centres to referral hospitals. The second compiles 73 laboratory procedures, from sample collection to the identification of pathogens and antibiotic susceptibility testing.
The WHO has estimated that AMR could cause some 39 million deaths between now and 2050.
There needed to be improved use of existing antibiotics, at a time when the development of new treatments is failing to keep pace with the rise of resistance, it said.
Infection prevention, vaccination, improved access to water and sanitation, and the appropriate use of antimicrobials are the main levers to combat the issue, it added.

CRPF attack to LeT commander's killing: Seven days, two encounters in Kulgam
NEW DELHI: Security forces on Wednesday eliminated top Lashkar-e-Taiba commander Lateef Bhat in an encounter in Jammu and Kashmir's Kulgam district, avenging the attack on CRPF personnel. The terror strike, which left three security personnel injured, took place seven days ago.Bhat, described by security forces as the last active local terrorist in the Valley, was trapped inside a mosque after an extensive search operation involving CCTV footage and repeated intelligence inputs. He refused to surrender despite repeated appeals by security forces and was eventually neutralised.Union home minister Amit Shah hailed the operation, praising the "coordinated efforts" of the forces.Shah wrote on X, "With the coordinated efforts of JKP, Indian Army, CRPF and intelligence agencies, Lashkar's last known active local terrorist in the valley, Lateef Bhat, was neutralised in an operation in Kulgam in the early morning hours today. One of his terrorist associates, Umar Nisar, was also neutralised in Kulgam, the day before. The entire operation was marked by a very high level of synergy."Bhat's alleged associate, Umar Nisar Dar, had been killed two days earlier.Also Read| Trapped in Kulgam mosque, LeT commander Lateef Bhat refuses to surrender
November 11: Attack on CRPF post leaves three personnel injured
Two armed men opened fire on a CRPF post in Akhran village in Kulgam district, injuring three personnel, one of them critically. Officials initially received reports that the attackers had arrived on a motorcycle.
However, subsequent ground verification established that the two men had approached the checkpost on foot from a nearby forested area.According to officials, one attacker opened fire while the other provided cover. Both fled towards Naupur through the tree line. "The area has dense vegetation resembling a small forest, which the terrorists used as cover before and after the attack," an official told news agency PTI.
Security forces launched a cordon-and-search operation, increased deployments and began examining CCTV footage from the surrounding areas.
November 10-15: CCTV footage helps investigators trace movements
Investigators examining footage from November 10 and 11 identified Bhat and Dar at multiple locations, including Mir Bazar, Akhran, Hablish and Kilam. According to police, the two had conducted reconnaissance at these locations to identify potential targets and plan attacks against security forces.The footage also documented their movements while fleeing after the November 11 attack on the CRPF naka at Akhran, police said.“During the analysis of CCTV footage from November 10 and 11, security agencies found both Umar Nisar Dar and Lateef Bhat captured on multiple CCTV cameras installed at the identified locations,” officials said.“The footage documented their movements while conducting reconnaissance and subsequently fleeing after the Akhran attack.”
Investigators also found that Dar had allegedly been providing shelter and logistical assistance to Bhat for five to six months. His family had lodged a missing-person report at Kulgam police station after he disappeared. Investigators subsequently established that Dar had joined The Resistance Front (TRF), an offshoot of LeT, after the November 11 attack, officials said.Also Read| 'Some dishes best served cold': LeT commander Lateef Bhat killed in Kulgam encounter
November 16: Umar Nisar Dar killed, Bhat escapes
Following intelligence inputs about the movement of two suspected terrorists near Laru bypass, the Army and the Special Operations Group of Jammu and Kashmir Police launched a cordon-and-search operation.The suspects fled towards two nearby schools situated close to an apple orchard, where students were present. Officials said security forces prioritised evacuating the children before beginning the operation.The evacuation took around 90 minutes, according to officials quoted by PTI. Dar was subsequently killed in the encounter, while Bhat managed to escape.Officials said Bhat was believed to have sustained bullet injuries. Security forces continued searches across the surrounding area to trace him.
November 17: Search operation widened
Security forces extended the search to dozens of villages around the encounter site, with drones and sniffer dogs deployed to locate Bhat. Officials said additional forces were positioned to strengthen the cordon, while teams searched suspected hideouts and carried out door-to-door searches at identified locations.The police also reiterated their findings about the alleged reconnaissance conducted by Bhat and Dar before the attack on the CRPF post. The prolonged security restrictions, however, drew criticism from political leaders in Kashmir, who said ordinary residents were facing hardship.
November 18: Bhat trapped in Kulgam, refuses to surrender
Acting on specific intelligence inputs, security forces launched another cordon-and-search operation in Zangalpora village in the Devsar area of south Kashmir.Officials said contact with Bhat was re-established early Wednesday morning, leading to a renewed encounter. The operation began before morning prayers, with security forces offering him an opportunity to surrender after trapping him inside the cordon.Videos of security personnel appealing to him to surrender circulated on social media. However, officials said Bhat refused.
According to Kulgam Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Anayat Ali Chowdhary, the encounter escalated when the terrorist opened fire at around 2:45 pm."An encounter was initiated based on credible intelligence gathered through proper planning and a coordinated effort by the Jammu and Kashmir Police alongside other security forces, successfully cordoning off the area where a local terrorist named Lateef is trapped," Chowdhary said.
He added, "Throughout this operation, security forces have maintained maximum restraint to protect the mosque situated within the cordon, strictly following standard operating procedures while handling the situation over time with patience and careful planning."The SSP said security forces attempted to persuade Bhat to surrender through a lengthy video call involving him, the SSP and the chief executive officer of the 9 Rashtriya Rifles."Despite these appeals, the terrorist refused to surrender and instead entered a mosque, prompting repeated public announcements urging him to come out," Chowdhary said. Police sources subsequently confirmed that Bhat had been killed. They said he was trapped inside the mosque during the operation and that no damage was caused to the structure.Reacting to the operation, Director General of the CRPF GP Singh posted on X, "Congratulations, guys. Some dishes are best served cold, even in cold weather."

Two days after Diwali was celebrated across India, on November 10, Tuesday, the nation woke up to grim newspaper headlines and reports highlighting the sharp deterioration of air quality across major cities. According to reports, 93 Indian cities appeared among the world’s 100 most polluted locations, several parts of Delhi reportedly witnessed a staggering Air Quality Index (AQI) of 3,000+, and six cities recorded an AQI above 1,000 at 9 pm on Diwali night.
Newspaper reports suggested that despite bans and restrictions, the bursting of firecrackers remained untethered across states, resulting in not only a severe surge in air pollution, but major fire accidents, noise pollution, and several people, stray animals and birds suffering burn injuries.
The front page of the Delhi edition of The Times of India on Tuesday led with a report headlined ‘Delhi pollution on Diwali rockets to worst in 5 yrs’.
“Delhi saw its most polluted Diwali day in five years, with AQI touching 376 at 4pm Nov 8, the worst since 2021. The city, however, narrowly escaped its worst post-Diwali pollution day in five years, with Monday’s AQI touching 370 at 11am before improving to 344 by 4pm, better than 2025’s post-Diwali air quality,” the report read, while highlighting that “several monitoring stations failed to report crucial AQI data”.
The front page also carried reports on the death of 10-year-old Rishi Garg in Delhi’s Narela after suffering a deep injury on his chest while bursting a firecracker; the hourly PM2.5 concentration at Jahangirpuri surging to 4,985 µg/m³ on Diwali night, which is 83 times the daily national ambient air quality standard; and X “locking” the account of TOI photojournalist Anindya Chattopadhyay after he posted visuals of smog in Delhi, citing violation of its rules.
The Mumbai edition of the paper on Tuesday reported “a record number of firecracker accidents” across the city on Diwali, with the headline ‘390 fires caused by crackers across Mum region on Diwali’. The report highlighted that the local train services on the Western line were disrupted due to a fire damaging signalling cables between Virar and Nalasopara. It noted that over 60 people suffered burns across Mumbai Metropolitan Region and over 30 stray animals and birds sustained burn injuries due to crackers, among various other major accidents and mishaps across MMR.
Similarly, the Kolkata edition led with a story on firecracker-related noise complaints. With the headline, ‘This Diwali, city seeks max number of noise complaints’, the report highlighted the widespread bursting of banned high-decibel firecrackers across the city, well beyond the permissible hours, making Sunday night one of the noisiest in recent years. Kolkata’s air quality deteriorated sharply over the same period, with readings lying between the “very poor” and “severe” categories from Sunday night to the intervening morning, and PM2.5 rising from 74 to 409 in Ballygunge and 115 to 444 in Salt Lake within a span of 2 hours, the report highlighted.
The front page Delhi edition of The Indian Express on Tuesday carried the lead story on pollution with the headline ‘Delhi wakes up to toxic post-Diwali air, 8 stations in ‘severe’ zone’. It reported that the capital had recorded its “worst” Diwali-day air quality in the last five years. Pollution levels rose sharply after sunset and remained elevated into the following morning, with PM2.5 concentrations touching nearly 5,000 µg/m³ at some monitoring stations. India’s 24-hour national ambient air quality standards prescribe a safe limit of 60 µg/m³ for PM2.5 and 100 µg/m³ for PM10.
The lead story of the Hindustan Times carried the headline, ‘Delhi pollution monitors went dark as AQI surged on Diwali’. According to the report, 43 of Delhi’s 59 air quality monitoring stations went “blank” on Diwali night just as PM2.5 readings surged towards 1,000 µg/m³. The data gaps reportedly affected the calculation of the capital’s daily AQI, raising questions about the reliability of pollution monitoring during peak pollution hours.
The front page also featured reports on Punjab recording nearly 200 stubble burning incidents on November 9, Monday; the sale of firecrackers continuing in Delhi despite a Supreme Court ban; and the rampant bursting of firecrackers leading to an increase in ambient noise levels across most monitoring stations in Delhi.
The Telegraph featured a collage showing the contrast of visibility of Delhi’s India Gate before and after Diwali, with photographs taken on October 30 and November 9 respectively. With the lead headline reading ‘Diwali cocktail of cacophony’, the front page reports covered the aftermath in both Delhi and Kolkata, highlighting data gaps in Delhi’s pollution monitoring during peak pollution hours and administrative inaction in Kolkata.
“Slackness in the seizure of banned fireworks. Stalls selling crackers at almost every neighbourhood. Lackadaisical police response to noise complaints. Political endorsement at the highest level in the name of religion. Several factors made this Diwali the most deafening in years, according to environmentalists, former pollution control board members, Opposition politicians and ordinary Calcuttans,” the report read.
The Telegraph reported that this Diwali celebration was Delhi’s most polluted Diwali in five years. It noted that, over 18 hours, from 10 pm on Sunday to 4 am on Monday, 59 air quality stations in the national capital should have recorded 1062 hourly readings; however, around 24% are missing from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data.
On Kolkata’s exceeding noise pollution levels, the report stated that “even a minister and an MLA from the BJP complained of the “unbearable” noise…However, asked about the rampant violation of noise pollution norms, chief minister Suvendu Adhikari politicised the issue, saying it was the “communists” and those unnerved by the “stupendous rise of Sanatan” that were complaining.”

On Page 6, it further reported that air pollution levels in Delhi had spiked to 200 times the World Health Organization’s recommended limits during Diwali.
Hospitals Report Burn Patients; Doctors Raise Concerns
“I am honestly surprised that we are still alive. I do not think this kind of air is suitable for human survival,” Dr Vijay Hadda, professor, department of pulmonary medicine and sleep disorders at AIIMS, told ANI on Monday.
He said that the green crackers reduced emissions by only 30 per cent, but as far as the particulate matter was concerned, 70 per cent of the emissions remained the same as conventional firecrackers. He raised concerns over people breathing this ‘poisonous’ smoke and said, “You should understand that you are simply inhaling poison and exhaling it.”
#WATCH | Delhi: On air pollution, Dr Vijay Hadda, Professor, Department of Pulmonary Medicine & Sleep Disorders, AIIMS, says, “These green crackers reduce emissions by only 30%. As far as the gases and particulate matter are concerned, 70% of the emissions remain the same as those from conventional firecrackers. The AQI, which used to be in three digits, has now reached four digits. If you compare Delhi’s air quality with that of other cities, you will find that there is almost a 50% difference. Obviously, life is not going to be easy for the people living here. You keep inhaling this poisonous smoke, breathing it in continuously. Every minute, you breathe at least 20 times, taking in at least half a litre of air with each breath. I am honestly surprised that we are still alive. I do not think this kind of air is suitable for human survival. I am absolutely certain that as time passes, we will begin to see its effects. Many of my colleagues who are otherwise completely healthy have been calling me and saying, “I am unable to get rid of this irritation. It feels as though something is stuck in my throat.” We saw patients during our last OPD session, and they have returned again today. This happens every year, but somehow, we all forget. The general public forgets, and even policies remain somewhat in a grey area, making it difficult to understand how they should be interpreted. Overall, the situation is not good at all. You should understand that you are simply inhaling poison and exhaling it…”
— ANI (@ANI) November 9, 2026
In the aftermath of Diwali, doctors in Delhi began reporting an alarming number of juvenile patients, including newborns, arriving with breathing difficulties, even as hospitals are witnessing a significant rise in respiratory illnesses. According to reports, 397 patients with Diwali-related injuries were treated at four major hospitals in Delhi. The cases included burns, firecracker injuries and eye trauma.
AIIMS reported 42 burn injury cases by 11 am on November 9. Of these, 37 were caused by firecrackers. Eleven patients sustained major injuries, while 31 had minor injuries. Eight were admitted, including one in critical condition. Moreover, 18 of the 42 patients were under 18, including six below the age of 10. An eight-year-old child at AIIMS was in critical condition after sustaining burns over 45 per cent of their body surface area. Safdarjung Hospital recorded 135 burn injury cases. Of these, 129 were attributed to firecrackers and six to traditional diyas. Seven patients sustained major burns requiring hospital admission. The hospital also treated 35 children with firecracker-related injuries in its outpatient department.
Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital treated 41 patients with burn injuries from 9 am on Saturday. 18 of these injuries were reportedly caused by firecrackers, with two patients requiring admission. Eight patients were hospitalised overall, while approximately 10–12 of those treated were children. Guru Tegh Bahadur Hospital reported 172 patients with firecracker burns and other Diwali-related injuries within 24 hours. Among them were 25 children and 56 women. Thirty-four patients also suffered eye injuries.
The toll was not limited to burn injuries. The Dr Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences at AIIMS received nearly 110 patients with eye injuries on Sunday and during the early hours of Monday, most of them with firecracker-related ocular injuries. 18 patients suffered corneal perforations or lacerations and underwent surgical intervention.
In Pali, Rajasthan, sparks from firecrackers being burst on a road reportedly reached a firecracker shop near Swarn Mandir in Falna town, gutting three shops and killing two people. One person sustained burn injuries and three others were initially reported missing.
