Shortly after singer-songwriter Dolly Parton's death on Aug. 25, a claim circulated widely that she once performed a one-of-a-kind duet with Queen lead singer Freddie Mercury.
According to the rumor, the legendary musicians sang one of the British band's most popular songs, "Bohemian Rhapsody," as part of a charity concert at London's Royal Albert Hall.
One popular YouTube video (archived) featuring the claim, titled, "Dolly Parton Faced Freddie Mercury's Unexpected Musical Challenge — The Result Was Unbelievable," said the concert took place on March 15, 1986.
Iterations of the rumor spread elsewhere on YouTube (archived) and on Facebook (archived), where a different video said the concert was held in 1978. Snopes readers searched the site wondering if the collaboration between the musical icons ever really happened.
In short, the duo never performed "Bohemian Rhapsody" together at London's Royal Albert Hall, nor anywhere else. The videos listed above featuring the fictitious story all contain content that was generated with artificial intelligence tools. Therefore, we've rated the claim false.
No evidence of joint performance
Searches of Google, DuckDuckGo, Bing and Yahoo produce no evidence of Mercury and Parton ever performing the Queen song together on stage anywhere, let alone at the Royal Albert Hall in 1978 or 1986. If the two legendary and widely popularly musicians did sing together at such a historic venue, there would be an authentic recording or photos documenting at least part of the show, or some mention of it by credible news or music media outlets, not just random social media posts.
Similarly, searching for "Dolly Parton" and "Freddie Mercury" on Getty Images and PA Images — the photo repository of the Press Association, the news agency for the U.K. and Ireland — uncovers no authentic photographs of them together.
In addition, none of the social media posts listed above include any such authentic recording or pictures. One Facebook post (archived) purportedly shows a video from the concert, but the lyrics Parton sings are gibberish and there are numerous inconsistencies in the visuals, such as the lighting, clothing and instruments, all of which is consistent with AI generation.
More evidence of AI-generated content
The YouTube video with more than 2.5 million views is both the most popular and the oldest example of the claim we found. That post includes a content label in its description acknowledging the footage is "Made with AI." Google, which owns YouTube, says this label "indicates that a video contains content that has been meaningfully altered or synthetically generated" with generative AI tools.
The fake images of Parton in that video, as well as in other posts sharing the claim, do not match what she looked like in 1978 or in 1986. The AI-generated images of her and Mercury together are seemingly based on what she looked like in the last couple of decades of her life. Those fabricated images also show the pair performing in several different settings, despite the story framing the "charity concert" as a one-time event.
Further proof claim is false
London's Royal Albert Hall did host a performance on the March 15, 1986, date. Rather than a charity concert, however, the venue hosted a youth marching band competition. Similarly, none of the events listed in 1978 feature Dolly Parton, Freddie Mercury or his band, Queen.
It was also not possible to find any evidence that Mercury or Parton ever performed songs at the Royal Albert Hall. Mercury did appear onstage at the venue for Fashion Aid, which was part of the Live Aid benefit concert movement, in November 1985. However, that was as a performer in a staged "wedding ceremony," rather than as a musician. While Parton did not play at the Royal Albert Hall, her music was performed there as a tribute to her in September 2026, after she died.
Parton never released a cover of "Bohemian Rhapsody," however she did cover another pair of Queen songs, "We Are The Champions/We Will Rock You," for her 2023 "Rockstar" album.
For further reading, we put together a collection of our fact checks about Parton following her death.

Wider access to diabetes technology needs policy support, experts say
Continuous glucose monitors and automated insulin delivery systems drastically improve glycaemic control and cut hospitalisations, yet steep out-of-pocket costs and socioeconomic disparities leave a massive adoption gap
Technology can improve monitoring and support treatment decisions |Image used for representational purpose only
| Photo Credit: Wikimedia commons
Diabetes management is moving beyond periodic finger-prick tests and clinic visits, with technologies such as continuous glucose monitors (CGMs), insulin pumps and mobile applications providing more detailed information on glucose levels and helping patients make day-to-day decisions about their care.
CGMs use a sensor placed on the arm or abdomen to measure glucose levels at regular intervals, offering a picture of fluctuations through the day and night. Insulin pumps deliver insulin continuously, while automated insulin delivery systems combine CGM readings with algorithms to adjust insulin delivery. Mobile applications can bring together information on glucose levels, food intake, physical activity and medication.

The Best Smart Bed Doesn’t Sleep on the Job
While they may not be able to levitate or act like a Jetsons-style robot personal assistant (yet), smart beds these days come pretty close to accomplishing both. Like adjustable mattresses, smart beds offer modifiable firmness and the ability to raise and lower the head and foot. These days, though, smart beds offer so much more, integrating features like dual-climate control, sleep tracking, and massage therapies.
The best smart bed is, by far, the Bryte Balance Pro Smart Mattress, and if you’re looking for the most luxurious, it’s the Tempur-Pedic Tempur-ActiveBreeze. Let me break it down for you below.
For more old-school mattresses, check out our guides to the Best Mattresses, the Best Organic Mattresses, and the Best Mattresses for Back Pain.
Updated November 2026: I’ve updated product information and the FAQ section. Discontinued products were removed, and I updated specs, prices, and links.
What Am I Testing Next?
I’m currently testing the Eight Sleep Pod 6.
Honorable Mention
Personal Comfort’s Rejuvenate is a solid adjustable mattress for side sleepers. It doesn’t offer any additional features or sleep-tracking capabilities, so it doesn’t truly qualify as a smart bed in my book.
Nevertheless, the Rejuvenate is a side-sleeper-friendly option because of its deep memory foam layers that contour to the body. If you want to sink in while still relying on the 45 firmness levels to ensure you're getting the support you need, this is it. Former WIRED reviewer Julia Forbes found a medium-firm 30 to be ideal for a healthy spine alignment when side sleeping.
What About Personal Comfort’s Adjustable Base?
An adjustable base is available as an add-on and helpful if you opt for one of Personal Comfort’s specialty bed sizes, such as the Queen Flex-Head or King Flex-Head. It’s the only way to move the head and foot of the Rejuvenate, as well as implement adjustable lumbar support, pillow tilt, and massage features.
Julia tested the Power Flex 4. It provides a firmer feel right around the midsection, and its lumbar adjustment setting really amps up back support. She did find the massage features to be uncomfortable, though, describing them as “increasingly aggressive vibrations, akin to tectonic plates.”
FYI, Personal Comfort often runs a bundle promotion.
FAQs
Should I Use a Sleep Tracker With a Smart Bed?
Some smart beds offer contactless sleep tracking, which eliminates the need for an additional wearable. That said, they do carry some limitations. They’re generally not as accurate as contact-based trackers and can overestimate sleep stages and miscalculate duration. They often can’t track the same breadth of physiological measurements as smartwatches and smart rings do. And they can misattribute data from a partner or pet sharing the bed. But they’re convenient, especially if you dislike wearing trackers to bed.
Personally, I still sleep with my Apple Watch Series 12 and/or Oura Ring 5 to bed to compare. But, if I forget to wear either, my smart bed is auto-tracking my slumber in the background.
Do I Need an Adjustable Base to Go With My Smart Bed?
You are very likely going to want an adjustable base to go with your smart bed in order to enjoy everything your smart bed has to offer. This is especially true if you are purchasing one with the expectation of being able to move the top and bottom of the bed into different angles, like “TV watching” and “zero gravity” settings.
What’s the Difference Between an Adjustable Bed and a Smart Bed?
Generally speaking, adjustable beds and smart beds are similar in that they both can raise or lower different sections of your mattress, with a remote control or companion app. Smart beds take it up a notch by incorporating additional features, such as sleep tracking, temperature control, and automated adjustments.
Can a Smart Bed Work for All Sleeping Positions?
Smart beds often come in adjustable firmness levels, and therefore can work for all sleeping positions. However, just like with any other mattress, the fabric technology is a huge deciding factor when it comes to comfort.
For example, the Bryte Balance Pro is a much better choice for stomach sleepers or if you have a heavier body type. Coil support simply does not compare to even the firmest of inflated air chambers, which are usually what make smart beds' firmness levels “adjustable.” On the other hand, the Rejuvenate has a softer feel right off the bat because of its memory foam layers, making it ideal for side sleepers who need pressure relief.
Do I Need Wi-Fi Connectivity for My Smart Bed to Work?
Yes—if the power goes out, your smart bed will likely go offline. Smart beds are factored into smart home technology, meaning they rely on Wi-Fi for full functionality, especially to track sleep data and maintain the firmness level you've chosen.
What Does WIRED Do With the Mattresses After Testing Them?
These smart beds were provided for free as media samples, and we either return them to the company or donate without personal benefit when testing is done. Most of these beds went to nurses, students, families in need, or those with medical conditions that were affecting their sleep.

The Indian adaptation of Universal Television’s medical drama “House,” starring Nawazuddin Siddiqui as a brilliant but difficult diagnostician, will premiere Dec. 11 on JioHotstar under the title “Dr. Hassan.”
Dia Mirza co-stars in the show, directed by Rohan Sippy, with a cast that also includes Faisal Rashid, Rehmat Rattan, Jayson Thaam and Smaran Sanu. JioHotstar commissioned the series and Banijay Asia produced it, under a license for the format from NBCUniversal Formats, a Universal Studio Group company.
Siddiqui’s character is an unconventional doctor with a knack for solving baffling cases and an eccentric streak to match. When a medical mystery has stumped everyone else, Hassan is the one people call on, though his quirks make him as hard to predict as the illnesses he treats. JioHotstar is positioning the show as more than a standard hospital drama, mixing puzzling cases with humor and friction between its characters.
Siddiqui recalled time spent as a child around the clinics and dispensaries of his hometown. “There were always such interesting people and situations unfolding there. Some of those memories came back to me when I read ‘Dr. Hassan.’ What I enjoyed about playing him was finding the balance between his exceptional intelligence and his very particular way of looking at the world,” he said.
Vinay Chhawal and Ketan Pedgaonkar adapted and wrote the series, with dialogue by Virat Basoya. Deepak Dhar, Rishi Negi, Rajesh Chadha, Mrinalini Jain and Shyam Rathi are producers, and Vibhas Singh Gautam is executive producer for Banijay Asia.
“Great characters travel, but they truly come alive when they are rooted in the world of the audience watching them. ‘House’ gave the world one of television’s most unforgettable characters, and with ‘Dr. Hassan,’ we wanted to reimagine that spirit through an Indian lens, with its own humor and humanity,” said Alok Jain, head of Hindi and English entertainment business (streaming, TV and studios) at JioStar.
“Dr. Hassan” is the third international version of “House,” after adaptations in Russia and Turkey. It is also the latest show NBCUniversal Formats and Banijay Asia have co-produced in India, following “Mistry,” the local take on “Monk,” and “Million Dollar Listing India,” which has had two seasons.
Dhar, founder and CEO of Banijay Asia and Endemol Shine India, said the company had approached the Indian version with care, given the show’s global fan base. “At its heart is a truly singular character: sharp, flawed, often difficult, and impossible to ignore. Bringing him to life needed a creative team and cast that could balance gripping medical mysteries with wit and emotional depth, and Nawazuddin is an actor who brings real depth to everything he does,” Dhar said.
Created by David Shore, the original “House” starred Hugh Laurie and ran for eight seasons on Fox between 2004 and 2012. Heel and Toe Films, Shore Z Productions, Bad Hat Harry Productions and Universal Television produced the series, which picked up five Primetime Emmys, two Golden Globes, a Peabody and nine People’s Choice Awards. Katie Jacobs, Shore, Paul Attanasio, Bryan Singer and Dan Sackheim were executive producers.
Linfield Ng, VP of format sales and production at NBCUniversal Formats, said the company was pleased to be working with Banijay Asia and JioHotstar once again. “With an exceptional cast and creative team, we’re excited to see this latest adaptation offer a fresh perspective on a globally loved series,” Ng said.
The India titles form part of a wider push across Asia for NBCUniversal Formats, which had 39 seasons on air in 17 territories in 2025.

Jeff Bezos says Big Tech has become America's new favorite villain.
Speaking with Semafor's Liz Hoffman at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World conference, the Amazon founder said on Tuesday that politicians have a habit of picking villains rather than addressing the root causes of economic problems.
"That is the age-old political technique, which is pick a villain," Bezos said. "And pick a villain is a good political technique, but it's a terrible technique for solving problems."
Bezos said public perceptions of powerful industries have shifted over time, from lawyers to Wall Street to landlords, and now it's Big Tech's turn.
"From time to time, landlords are the villains. And now, Big Tech is the villain. Tech is the villain," Bezos said. "That is the picture that is being painted. It's not correct. It's not a true picture."
"I think most people in tech just want to stay heads down doing the work. I don't think there's a lot of villainy here," Bezos added.
Bezos's comments come as Big Tech faces growing public scrutiny over its expanding footprint in everyday life, from data centers that can drive up local utility costs to AI surveillance tools such as Flock's network of license-plate-reading cameras. Concerns about privacy, energy costs, and the impact of AI on jobs have fueled resistance to the industry's growing influence.
Those concerns have intersected with a broader affordability backlash. Higher household costs, including war-related pressure on fuel and some consumer prices, and persistently high housing costs weighed on voters in the 2026 midterm elections.
In ABC News' election polling, 89% of voters said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in their vote. Affordability concerns have become a defining political issue, helping Democrats flip key seats and win majorities in both chambers of Congress in the latest election.
Economic anxiety cut across party lines. Some Democrats who won, including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas, made data-center development and AI's potential effects on workers part of their campaigns.

Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy assured the Public Health Foundation of India (PHFI) of the State government’s full support for establishing its Institute of Public Health Sciences (IPHS) Deemed-to-be University in Hyderabad, setting June 2, 2028, as the deadline for completing the proposed campus and promising assistance with land, funds, permissions and other requirements.
Speaking at the foundation-laying ceremony and unveiling of the campus master plan on Saturday, Mr. Reddy said the government was committed to developing the institution into a world-class university that would contribute to public health education, research and healthcare in India and internationally.
He further added that the proposed university was not merely another educational institution but a project of global significance. Expressing confidence in its potential, he said he hoped that in the coming years, people would discuss the PHFI university alongside established institutions such as Harvard and Oxford.
The Chief Minister recalled how institutions such as the Indian School of Business (ISB) had contributed to Hyderabad’s emergence as an educational and knowledge hub. He said individuals who had established successful institutions had helped create a distinct identity for the city and that the PHFI university would add to this legacy.
PHFI Chairman Rajat Gupta said the university aspired to achieve excellence through world-class faculty, students, international collaborations and infrastructure.
PHFI IPHS Chancellor Dr. K. Srinath Reddy said PHFI aspired to become the world’s leading public health institution with the establishment of the university in Hyderabad. Dr. Reddy said the foundation’s work involved advancing multidisciplinary education and research through multi-sectoral implementation and multi-stakeholder engagement. The objective was to improve life expectancy, strengthen health systems, align policies across sectors with population health goals and encourage active community engagement.
Pro-Chancellor Sanjay Zodpey said the university was being conceived as a long-term institution that would serve generations of students, researchers, public health professionals and communities. He said the public health challenges of the 21st century required professionals with interdisciplinary perspectives, evidence-based knowledge and a commitment to equity and social impact.
Vice-Chancellor M. Vishnu Vardhana Rao outlined the university’s academic journey and expansion plans. The Indian Institute of Public Health Hyderabad was established in 2008 under the aegis of PHFI, with the objective of advancing public health through education, research and community engagement. The institution received recognition as a deemed-to-be university from the University Grants Commission in 2025, with Hyderabad as its main campus and Bengaluru as another campus, he said.
With the proposed campus and modern infrastructure, the institution plans to expand its academic offerings to at least six postgraduate programmes, two undergraduate programmes, PhD programmes and institute-level Master of Public Health programmes. It aims to build an academic community of approximately 2,500 students and research scholars over the next five years.
Dr. Rao said the university’s research priorities would include infectious diseases and pandemic preparedness, non-communicable diseases, maternal and child health, One Health, mental health and disability. Digital health, artificial intelligence and data science would serve as cross-cutting areas across its research activities, he added.

Austria Looks to Strip Citizenship of Ex-Minister Who Moved to Russia
The onetime foreign minister, Karin Kneissl, has lauded her new home for its “genuine freedom” and used it as a perch to attack her old one.
The Austrian authorities have taken initial steps to revoke the citizenship of a former foreign minister who moved to Russia — a country she has lauded for its “genuine freedom” — and who has repeatedly denigrated Austria while echoing Kremlin-friendly talking points.
Karin Kneissl made international headlines when she danced with President Vladimir Putin of Russia at her wedding in 2018, when she was her nation’s top diplomat.
Since then, she has angered many of her compatriots with regular barbs against her country of birth and its citizens.
That the Austrian state would even consider the extraordinary step of revoking her citizenship reflects a national weariness about the former foreign minister. It follows a prolonged national debate over whether Ms. Kneissl retained the right to remain Austrian after — both physically and by all appearances ideologically — turning her back on her homeland.
Ms. Kneissl, who served as foreign minister from 2017 to 2019, made her very public move to Russia in 2023, a year after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. She was hired to run a think tank in St. Petersburg.
Over the years, Ms. Kneissl, 61, seems to have taken pleasure in denigrating Austrians in interviews with Russian-friendly media. Earlier this year, for example, she repeated her claim that Hitler, who was born in Austria, was typically Austrian. She also said that her countrymen had acted like hyenas toward her.
Such comments served to bolster a push to strip her of her citizenship. The initiative has been led by the liberal party NEOS, which is run by the current foreign minister, Beate Meinl-Reisinger.
“Why does Kneissl continue to appear prominently as Austria’s former foreign minister when she so obviously despises and hates our country?” Yannick Shetty, a NEOS member of the Austrian Parliament, asked in January in response to Ms. Kneissl’s remarks.
On Monday, officials in Vienna confirmed that an inquiry into the former minister had been launched. They said they were looking at whether she had obtained a second citizenship and whether her conduct significantly harmed “the interests or reputation of the Republic.”
It remains unclear if the inquiry will actually lead to the revocation of her citizenship and, if so, how long it might take.
Ms. Kneissl was proposed for the post of foreign minister in 2017 by the far-right Freedom Party of Austria, though she was never a member of that party.
After leaving Austria in 2020, she went to France and Lebanon before moving to a little village southeast of Moscow in the heartland of Russia.
On Monday, Ms. Kneissl said she knew that steps were being taken to revoke her citizenship. In comments reported by the Russian state news agency Tass, she said that if Austria moved forward with the plan, she would end up stateless and need to apply for travel documents from the United Nations.

South Africa head coach Erasmus banned for six matches
- Published
South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus has been banned for six matches by World Rugby over comments he made about match officials in his side's Nations Championship defeat by France last week.
Speaking at a news conference conference in Dublin on Monday before the Springboks' match with Ireland, Erasmus questioned what he perceived as double standards in officiating to the point where he asked: "is that not match-fixing?".
The two-time Rugby World Cup-winning coach was referencing the implementation of new rules surrounding hip-drop and knee-drop tackles, and felt the laws were not being applied correctly.
It comes after Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast became the first player to be cited for a hip-drop tackle in Ireland's win over Fiji on Saturday, which was not penalised in-play by referee Angus Gardner and television match official [TMO] Mike Adamson.
World Rugby said an independent panel determined that Erasmus' comments "suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match".
In response, South Africa Rugby said it has requested a full misconduct hearing and an opportunity for Erasmus to "contextualise his comments and assure the panel that it was not his intention to allege that any match official had acted with ulterior motives".
It is the third time Erasmus has been sanctioned by World Rugby over his comments about match officials.
When he was South Africa's director of rugby, he was suspended for two months by World Rugby after he posted an hour-long video criticising the refereeing in the Springboks' opening Test defeat by the British and Irish Lions in 2021.
World Rugby found the video contained "multiple abusive and insulting comments and attacks on the officials".
In 2022, he received a two-match ban for a series of tweets criticising officials in a defeat by France.
Erasmus' latest ban has been imposed under World Rugby's match official abuse sanction process, which was introduced by the governing body in July.
If the suspension is upheld, Erasmus will miss Saturday's game with Ireland in Dublin (16:40 GMT), next week's finals weekend fixture at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium and the start of his side's Rugby Championship campaign next summer.
- 'Is that not match-fixing?' - Erasmus questions officiating 
  - Published22 hours ago
- Nations Championship final round - who needs what? 
  - Published1 day ago
- Prendergast cited and could miss South Africa game 
  - Published1 day ago
Erasmus said that 17 hip-drop or knee-drop tackles had been missed in South Africa's 21-19 defeat in France by match officials. Andrea Piardi was the referee for the Stade de France fixture, while Matteo Liperini was the TMO.
Erasmus added that if TMOs were not intervening for reviews to limit the number of interruptions during a match then it was "manipulation", before he added that his comments were "not an accusation".
"I'm saying if he didn't see it, it must be a technology problem. If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing?" Erasmus added.
"If the TMO didn't see it, maybe then technology must be better. If he saw it and he ignored it, what does that boil down to? Manipulation of the game or the result or injured players getting injured.
"So all I'm asking, don't take TMOs out and discourage them to get involved. Then the wrong team will win and players will get injured. That's all I'm saying."
'Unacceptable attack on credibility and competence of match officials'
In a statement on Tuesday, World Rugby said an independent panel determined that Erasmus' comments had met "the threshold for serious misconduct".
World Rugby confirmed the ban will stop Erasmus having any match day involvement for six matches, which includes coaching, direct or indirect contact with the team management or players on match days, entering the stadium, coaches' box, playing enclosure or technical area.
"The panel determined that the comments suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match, and when the conduct is considered as a whole a reasonable person would conclude that the conduct constituted an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the match officials," its statement said.
"In respect to the sanction, the panel determined that the conduct clearly amounts to disrespecting the authority of the match officials by impugning their integrity.
"Therefore, the panel reviewed a number of elements of the commentary including the timing and reach of the statements, combined with the allegations of bias or bad faith, and found that the comments attracted a six-match automatic suspension."
World Rugby added that "respect is fundamental to rugby, and match officials are central to the sport".
"Protecting their wellbeing and integrity, and their right to perform without abuse or intimidation, is a responsibility World Rugby and unions take seriously," their statement added.
"Coaches, players, unions and everyone in the game must uphold these standards.
"Robust, respectful debate is natural, but teams have access to well-established and supported channels and protocols for raising officiating matters before and after matches. Challenging a decision is not the same as questioning an official's integrity or making comments that expose them to personal abuse."
In the same news conference, which lasted more than half an hour at the Springboks' team hotel, Erasmus also questioned what he felt were double standards in terms of sanctions.
The outcome of the citing has yet to be released, but he predicted that Prendergast will be available to play against South Africa due to a "technicality", and also questioned the decision not to ban Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong for an alleged groin grab while playing for Leinster ahead of the November Tests.
Last year, South Africa prop Jan-Hendrik Wessels was handed a nine-match ban for a similar offence and missed November's matches for the Springboks.
Analysis
This is the third time in five years Erasmus has been banned for comments about referees, all of them coming after a Springboks loss.
In 2018, he picked South African rugby up off the floor and has won two World Cups to establish himself as one of the greatest coaches of all time.
To his rugby public - the people who really matter in Erasmus' eyes - he will forever be a hero in his homeland.
But outside South Africa his propensity to harangue officials after a rare defeat will tarnish his reputation in the eyes of many.

Recently, social media has been inundated with videos apparently depicting "rogue" or "freak" waves — unpredictable waves greater than twice the size of surrounding waves, according to NOAA — crashing over massive container ships. In November, a YouTube video (archived) of a massive wave rushing atop the containers and whiting out the wheelhouse's window of one such ship was viewed 32 million times in the first week since its upload.
While the video was most popular on YouTube, it was also shared to other social media sites such as X (archived) and Reddit (archived).
Although many people in comment sections reacted to the video as if it was real footage of a rogue wave striking a container ship, this video was actually generated by artificial intelligence tools. Therefore, we've rated the video fake.
To start, we did a reverse image search of frames from the video with Google Lens. We could not find a credible source for the video through the search. Based on the search, the YouTube video linked and embedded above is the earliest upload of the video.
The YouTube video was posted by the "UNIQUE SARANG" YouTube channel. Snopes reached out to the channel's creator by email to confirm it was the original source of the clip and will update this fact check if and when we receive a reply.
The channel's short videos appear to be mostly or entirely AI-generated videos of impossible or dramatic events.
For example, one video depicts a giant dragonfly far larger than any living species on Earth. When the dragonfly suddenly flies up and away from the camera, which is several feet away from the fisherman on the pier, the fisherman reacts as if the dragonfly just buzzed by his own ear. Such an inconsistency is evident of AI generation.
Another video shows the moon cracking into two pieces. That video has YouTube's "Made by AI" label.
On Nov. 9, two days after the upload of the widely viewed video of the wave crashing over the container ship, the channel posted three short videos depicting massive waves impacting ships. The first two were of a wave crashing into small craft, such as a sailboat, and in neither video is there any reaction from the people on the ship or from the people recording the footage. In the last of those three videos, the container ship seems remarkably unscathed despite the size of the wave. Similarly, there are no reactions from any people in that one, as well.
Evidence of AI generation within the video
Evidence within the contents of the container ship video viewed over 30 million times indicates that it was generated by AI.
The two most obvious pieces of evidence can be spotted by watching the mug in the foreground and looking at the containers closest to the camera. At about 16 seconds into the video, the mug falls over to its side and then immediately rights itself just before the wave actually hits. Additionally, throughout the video the two blue containers in the bottom right appear to be off the side of the ship, based on what we can see of the ship and the rest of the containers in the rest of the video.
A third giveaway to the video's AI origins is that the ship appears to be completely still, without any real interaction with the waves before the massive one. While it appears the ship could be riding up a significant wave at the very beginning of the video, there's no evidence of the ship impacting the water in any way when it appears like it should land back down after the wave. The water also appears to have a trough just before the massive wave hits, although the ship never seems to point down towards it.
Finally, the wave and it's interaction with the ship do not appear to be realistic at all based on what small amount of footage we have of real rogue waves caught on video.
Real and fake rogue wave footage
Massive, ship-wrecking "freak" waves have had a mystique to them for much of human history. They were once regarded as "marine folklore" from sailors to explain shipwrecks, but have been recognized by scientists as real in the past few decades.
One clip of a rogue wave caught on cameras for the Discovery show "Deadliest Catch," a reality show that follows fishermen off the Alaska coast, showed the vessel Aleutian Ballad rocking between its left and right on stormy seas. At 0:51, the rogue wave, which hits the boat from the side, crashes suddenly into the fishing vessel life a wall rather than falling upon it like a wave breaking near the shore.
A clip of a rogue wave hitting the crab-fishing boat Saga similarly shows the wave crashing into the boat like a suddenly appearing wall rather than a wave that breaks and falls on top of it.
Another clip of the Saga from "Deadliest Catch," this time with a different captain piloting the boat, shows two rogue waves rushing against and into the boat back-to-back. While the first wave crashes against the boat like the others, the second wave pours into it. Neither wave falls upon the boat from above like the wave does in the AI-generated video.
Similarly, yet another "Deadliest Catch" clip depicts a massive wave simply pouring over the boat's side.
The clip most similar to the AI-generated version of a rogue wave was not from "Deadliest Catch," but instead was a video of a New Zealand Navy ship in the Southern Ocean. That video has been promoted by the New Zealand Defence Force, which identified the ship as the HMNZS Otago and was uploaded in 2021, before generative AI video was of the quality it is now. While the wave that crashes into the ship does break just before colliding with the boat, the initial splash came from the warship landing upon the water after crossing the peak of the previous wave, which is something the AI-generated container ship did not do.
In all of the videos, a noticeable amount of water remained on the boat in the aftermath. In the real clips, objects on the boats were at minimum disturbed and dislodged, and in some cases the waves swept them entirely off the sides of the ships. The wave in the Navy ship video even disturbs the gun on the boat so that it points higher up after the wave.
However, in the AI-generated video, none of the containers appear so much as jostled slightly out of place after the wave crashes into them and the ship as a whole.
The video with over 32 million views is far from the only AI-generated video of a rogue wave hitting a container ship. One video from Instagram shows a massive wave failing to so much as nudge cargo containers, even though a few of them are already partially tipped over. A TikTok video of a cargo ship riding a giant wave like it's surfing is labeled by its creator as being made with AI.
For further reading, Snopes has previously fact-checked other AI-generated imagery involving the ocean, including this fake clip of an Amazon delivery robot driving itself off of a pier.

The Supreme Court declined an oral plea by the Directorate of Enforcement (ED) to immediately freeze an Allahabad High Court order granting interim bail to former Uttar Pradesh Minister and Samajwadi Party leader Mohammad Azam Khan in a money laundering case.
However, a Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant agreed to urgently list the ED appeal on November 19. The oral exchange happened during a mentioning made by Additional Solicitor General S.V. Raju, representing the ED, for early listing of the appeal.
Mr. Raju asked for a status quo in the meanwhile, but the apex court refused, with Justice Joymalya Bagchi remarking that “heavens will not fall, let him [Khan] be on interim bail”.
In its order granting interim bail on November 17, a Division Bench of the High Court found the arrest of Mr. Khan on October 31, at the very gates of jail as soon as he came out on bail in a PAN card case, both “motivated and malafide”.
This Bench concluded that the ED had not followed the necessary procedure of arrest. The politician had argued that his rights under Article 22(1) of the Constitution and Section 19 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), which lay down safeguards that must be followed during an arrest, were grossly violated by the ED’s actions.
Mr. Khan was arrested on October 31 shortly after he was released from Rampur District Jail in another case involving allegations related to dual PAN cards. He had secured bail in that case from the Allahabad High Court on October 29, and was physically released after furnishing bail bonds and sureties on October 31. However, the ED had arrested him again at the gate of the jail at around 7.10 p.m. He had been remanded to judicial custody by a trial judge on November 1.
On November 5, the Supreme Court had advised Mr. Khan to approach the High Court against his October 31 arrest, and requested the High Court, in turn, to give him priority hearing.
Senior advocate Kapil Sibal and advocate Nizam Pasha, for Mr. Khan, had submitted that their client was 78 years old, a ten-time Member of the Uttar Pradesh Legislative Assembly from Rampur, a former Cabinet Minister and Leader of Opposition in the State of Uttar Pradesh, and a former Member of the Rajya Sabha and of the 17th Lok Sabha.
They had contended that his arrest was actually intended to “keep an Opposition leader indefinitely in incarceration particularly on account of the approaching Assembly Elections in the State of Uttar Pradesh”.
Mr. Sibal had argued in the apex court that the ED has even accounted “goats and cows as proceeds of crime” under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act.
The senior counsel said Mr. Khan had been subjected to an “ever-greening” of cases by the law enforcement agencies ever since the government changed in the State of Uttar Pradesh.

From one of Ajax's future stars to quitting football for music
- Published
Elikia Mbinga dreamed of becoming a professional footballer and playing in sold-out arenas after captaining an Ajax side brimming with future stars.
But at 25, his life has taken an unexpected turn. Rather than showcasing his creativity on the pitch, Mbinga is making a name for himself through music.
He has become one of the most successful emerging afrobeat artists in the Netherlands, with more than 30 million Spotify streams.
It is a world away from Ajax's famed De Toekomst academy, where he trained alongside a host of Dutch talents who have since made their mark in the Premier League - from the Timber brothers to Ryan Gravenberch and Brian Brobbey.
It is clear the lessons Mbinga learned during his esteemed footballing education have helped shape his identity as an artist.
"As a footballer, I played in midfield and was a very creative player. That was my style on the pitch, and I try to bring that same creativity to my music," he tells BBC Sport.
"I want to experiment with songs, be as creative as possible and develop a sound of my own."
'You don't know they're going to become stars'
By the age of 17, Mbinga was living the dream of many aspiring footballers in the Netherlands.
After impressing at boyhood club PEC Zwolle, he earned a move to Ajax and began a new life in Amsterdam away from his mother and seven siblings.
During his four seasons at the club, he shared the dressing room with brothers Quinten and Jurrien Timber, now of Crystal Palace and Arsenal, who joined Ajax from Feyenoord around the same time Mbinga arrived from Zwolle.
"We had a feeling that we had joined this journey together," Mbinga recalls. "We stepped in together. Already then, you could see that Quinten and Jurrien were like machines. They were built like machines from a young age."
He remembers the technical elegance of Liverpool midfielder Gravenberch and the physical prowess of striker Brobbey, who went on to score 56 goals in 163 appearances for Ajax's first team before moving to Sunderland last September.
Mbinga also had the opportunity to test himself against some of Europe's biggest clubs, including Real Madrid, Manchester United and Manchester City.
At one point, he even captained the group and saw little to separate them in terms of ability. However, their careers would take very different paths.
"In terms of talent, there wasn't really a big difference at the time," he says.
"Then, maybe two or three years later, Ryan Gravenberch had already made his first-team debut for Ajax. So it's all about development, right? And the same goes for the other guys."
Looking back, Mbinga now deeply treasures those years and the opportunity to have played alongside such talented footballers.
"I played with some amazing, talented players, and at the time, you already knew that they were really talented, right? It's the highest level," he says.
"But you don't know that they're going to become Premier League stars in the upcoming years. So that's amazing to look back at."
Leaving the football dream for music
After struggling to break through, Mbinga returned to PEC Zwolle in 2021 at the age of 20, where the familiar, less pressurised surroundings prompted him to consider life beyond football and his ambition to build something of his own.
"I think it was also part of the personal growth. I really liked the music. I also liked looking up to the other artists at the time who were popping," Mbinga says.
"For me, it was also a dream to do something in music, create my own songs. But at that time, I was really talented with football, but I couldn't make music yet."
Mbinga made his professional debut for his local side in September 2021, coming off the bench against Ajax, of all teams, in the Eredivisie.
But the youngster would make just five further first-team appearances as Zwolle were relegated, before dropping down the Dutch football pyramid.
He ended up playing semi-professionally in the fourth tier to fund his music career.
"When I made my professional debut, everything went really well. I signed the contract and everything," he says.
"But the purpose of creating something for myself in terms of music, being very creative, was getting stronger."
Five years on, that gamble is paying off. He has almost 500,000 monthly Spotify listeners, while his 2024 track Mentality has surpassed 16 million streams.
Every now and again, making music offers Mbinga a thrill similar to that he once chased on the football pitch.
"For me, all the achievements in music are like I'm scoring a goal or I'm giving an assist or playing a good match," he laughs.
"And of course, if one of my songs really takes off, then it feels like I'm scoring the winning goal in a very important game - like a final!"
Touring the world and reconnecting with former team-mates
Although Mbinga remains content with his decision not to pursue a career in professional football, he remains closely connected to the sport that shaped his life.
Earlier this month, he travelled to the United Kingdom to promote his new album, First of a Kind, allowing him to reunite with former Ajax team-mates Jurrien and Quinten Timber.
Mbinga attended an Arsenal Champions League match at Emirates Stadium and a Premier League Crystal Palace game at Selhurst Park.
"I'm really focused on creating this world for the people, for the fans," says Mbinga. "Creating a world that can unite football and music - like a creative bridge."
Another footballer supporting his musical journey is Spain forward Ansu Fati, who plays for AS Monaco.
The pair met as teenagers at a youth tournament in Europe when Fati was at Barcelona and have remained close friends ever since.
In February, Mbinga released a song dedicated to the forward and the challenges he has faced since breaking through at Barcelona in 2019.
Fati was seen as one of the new generation of La Masia stars at Camp Nou, making 51 appearances for the first team in 2022-23.
But he was loaned to Brighton the following season and struggled for minutes on his return to the Catalan giants, eventually joining Monaco on loan last season in a deal that became permanent in the summer.
Mbinga wrote the track in 2024 but agreed with Fati to release it only when the "time was right".
"You know what's crazy? Seeing him again and seeing everything that he's gone through," he recalls. "We went out to eat, went out for dinner, and then he was playing my song in the car, singing it lyric for lyric.
"I was like, 'wow, this life is crazy, man'."

WASHINGTON — The Food and Drug Administration is proposing a new classification for a product that’s existed in a legal gray area for years, a win for proponents of dietary supplements, including members of the MAHA movement.
The proposed rule would classify N-acetyl-L-cysteine, known as NAC and already widely sold over the counter, as the agency’s first “Dietary Ingredient Not Excluded from the Dietary Supplement Definition” — in essence, not not a supplement.
The need for the legal backbending stems from the fact that the FDA previously approved NAC as a drug, and FDA regulations prohibit the agency from including approved drugs in the dietary supplement category. In 1963, the agency approved NAC to break up mucus in certain lung conditions, and in 1985 to treat acetaminophen overdose.
